诗经.b: China's oldest anthology of poetry: 305 songs from the Western Zhou to the Spring and Autumn period, gathered — tradition says — by Confucius. Folk songs, court odes and temple hymns, mostly in four-character lines, with the refrains and nature images that shaped all later Chinese verse.

虞世南.b: Statesman and one of the four great calligraphers of the early Tang, trusted counsellor of Emperor Taizong.

王绩.b: Early Tang recluse and wine lover who modelled himself on Tao Yuanming; his plain regulated verse pointed away from courtly ornament.

骆宾王.b: One of the "Four Paragons of the Early Tang". Wrote a famous poem about a goose at the age of seven; later composed the call to arms against Empress Wu, after which he vanished.

王勃.b: The most dazzling of the "Four Paragons of the Early Tang", a prodigy who wrote the *Preface to the Pavilion of Prince Teng*. He drowned at about 26 crossing the sea to visit his father.

杨炯.b: One of the "Four Paragons of the Early Tang", a child prodigy known for his vigorous frontier poems.

李峤.b: Early Tang chief minister and prolific poet of riddling object-poems, famous for his little poem on the wind.

宋之问.b: Court poet who, with Shen Quanqi, perfected the rules of regulated verse. Exiled to the far south, he wrote a famous quatrain on coming home.

陈子昂.b: Early Tang reformer who called poets back from court prettiness to the strength of the Han and Wei. His four lines on Youzhou Terrace are one of the loneliest cries in Chinese verse.

贺知章.b: Witty, wine-loving court official who called Li Bai "an immortal banished from heaven". Retired home at 85 after fifty years away and wrote about it.

张若虚.b: Known for only two surviving poems — one of them, *Spring River in the Flower Moon Night*, is called "the poem that overtops the whole Tang".

张九龄.b: Upright chief minister under Emperor Xuanzong, a southerner of great integrity whose dismissal marked the start of the court's decline. Patron of Wang Wei and Meng Haoran.

王之涣.b: High Tang poet of whom only six poems survive — but two of them, on Stork Tower and the Liangzhou frontier, are among the most famous ever written.

孟浩然.b: The great landscape poet of the High Tang who never held office, living as a recluse near Xiangyang. Friend of Li Bai and Wang Wei, whose name is always paired with his ("Wang–Meng").

王翰.b: Wealthy, flamboyant High Tang poet; one wine-soaked frontier quatrain made him immortal.

王湾.b: Early High Tang official; one couplet of his, on the sun born from the sea before night has ended, was hung by the chief minister in his hall as a model of poetry.

王昌龄.b: Called "the Lord of the Seven-character Quatrain". Master of frontier poems and of the laments of palace women; twice exiled, killed during the An Lushan rebellion.

李颀.b: High Tang poet of frontier ballads and of music, famed for his portraits of musicians and soldiers.

祖咏.b: Friend of Wang Wei. Asked to write a twelve-line exam poem, he stopped after four, saying "the meaning is complete" — and those four lines survive.

崔颢.b: His *Yellow Crane Tower* so impressed Li Bai that Li Bai declined to write about the place: "Cui Hao's poem is already above it."

王维.b: Poet, painter, musician and devout Buddhist — "in his poems there are paintings, in his paintings poems". Master of quiet landscape verse written at his Wangchuan estate. Called the "Poet Buddha".

李白.b: Also Li Po. The "Immortal of Poetry": a free spirit who wandered the empire with sword and wine jug, served briefly at Emperor Xuanzong's court, and wrote with dazzling spontaneity of the moon, mountains, friendship and wine. With Du Fu, the greatest of Chinese poets.

高适.b: Frontier poet who, unusually for a poet, rose to high military command. His verse is bold and generous-hearted.

常建.b: Minor official who withdrew to live as a recluse; remembered for one perfect temple poem.

刘长卿.b: Master of the five-character line ("the Great Wall of five-character verse"), twice exiled; his poems are spare, wintry and clear.

杜甫.b: The "Sage of Poetry". Lived through the An Lushan rebellion that shattered the Tang, and recorded it — war, famine, refugees, his own poverty — with unmatched compassion and craft. His poems are called "poetic history".

岑参.b: Spent years in the far western garrisons of Central Asia; the greatest painter in words of deserts, snowstorms and the frontier.

刘方平.b: High Tang recluse and painter who never sought office; a master of delicate quatrains on spring nights and lonely women.

钱起.b: Leader of the "Ten Talents of the Dali era"; legend says the famous last couplet of his examination poem was whispered to him by a ghost.

张继.b: Mid-Tang official known almost entirely for one quatrain, written at Maple Bridge near Suzhou — a poem that made a temple bell famous for 1,200 years.

张志和.b: Court scholar turned recluse who called himself "the Old Fisherman of the Misty Waves"; his fishing song is one of the earliest *ci* lyrics.

韩翃.b: One of the "Ten Talents of the Dali era"; his Cold Food Festival poem was a favourite of the emperor.

韦应物.b: Once a swaggering palace guard, he reformed and became a gentle, reclusive official-poet in the line of Tao Yuanming and Wang Wei.

卢纶.b: One of the "Ten Talents of the Dali era", known for his crisp frontier songs.

司空曙.b: One of the "Ten Talents of the Dali era"; master of understated poems of friendship and poverty.

李端.b: One of the "Ten Talents of the Dali era", remembered for a sly little poem about a zither player.

李益.b: Mid-Tang frontier poet whose quatrains were set to music and sung across the empire.

孟郊.b: Poor, bitter, austere poet and friend of Han Yu, who passed the examination only at 46. His poem for his mother is the most loved poem on a mother's love.

张籍.b: Mid-Tang poet and friend of Han Yu and Bai Juyi, champion of plain "new yuefu" ballads about ordinary lives.

王建.b: Mid-Tang poet of village life and the palace, writing in a plain ballad style alongside Zhang Ji.

韩愈.b: The great prose master and Confucian reformer of the mid Tang; as a poet, bold and unconventional. Exiled for protesting against the worship of a Buddha relic.

刘禹锡.b: Called the "Poet Hero". A reformer exiled for over twenty years who never lost his wit or defiance; he adapted southern folk songs into his "Bamboo Branch" lyrics.

白居易.b: Also Po Chü-i. Believed poems should be understood by everyone — he read drafts to an old woman and rewrote what she could not follow. Author of *The Song of Everlasting Sorrow* and *The Pipa Player*, and of satires on the people's suffering.

李绅.b: Mid-Tang chief minister, a friend of Bai Juyi and Yuan Zhen; his two short poems on farmers are learned by every Chinese schoolchild.

崔护.b: Mid-Tang official remembered for a single quatrain about a girl's face among peach blossoms.

柳宗元.b: Brilliant reformer exiled to the wild south for the rest of his life; great prose writer and a poet of solitary, crystalline landscapes.

元稹.b: Bai Juyi's closest friend and co-founder of the "new yuefu" movement; his elegies for his wife are among the most moving in Chinese.

贾岛.b: A former monk famous for agonising over single words — the story of him choosing between "push" and "knock" gave Chinese the word for careful revision, *tuiqiao*.

胡令能.b: A tinker and recluse of Henan whose few surviving poems are full of fresh country scenes.

张祜.b: Free-spirited mid-Tang poet who never held office; his palace poem was sung until listeners wept.

朱庆馀.b: Mid-Tang poet who sent a famous coded poem to his examiner Zhang Ji before the exams.

李贺.b: The "Ghost of Poetry": a sickly genius who rode out each day on a donkey, dropping lines into a brocade bag. Died at 26, leaving strange, dark, dazzling poems.

杜秋娘.b: A singing girl of Jinling who became a consort in the Tang palace; her song "The Gold-Threaded Robe" is a famous call to seize the day.

金昌绪.b: A poet of whom we know nothing except one perfect little poem.

许浑.b: Late Tang poet famous for his images of water and rain; "the mountain rain is coming and the wind fills the tower" is his.

杜牧.b: The "Little Du" (to Du Fu's "Old Du"). A brilliant, romantic late Tang poet of Yangzhou nights and southern landscapes, and a sharp critic of history.

温庭筠.b: Late Tang poet and pioneer of the *ci* lyric, leader of the "Huajian" school of richly ornamented love songs.

李商隐.b: The most mysterious of Chinese poets — his "Untitled" love poems are dense with allusion and longing, and still argued over a thousand years later.

陈陶.b: Late Tang poet and recluse whose one great frontier quatrain is among the saddest war poems in Chinese.

赵嘏.b: Late Tang poet much admired by Du Mu for his lines on autumn and rain.

曹松.b: Late Tang poet who passed the exams in his seventies; one line of his became a proverb against war.

罗隐.b: Failed the examinations ten times; a bitter, witty satirist of the late Tang.

聂夷中.b: Late Tang poet of humble birth who wrote with sympathy of the peasants' plight.

黄巢.b: A salt smuggler who failed the examinations and led the great rebellion that captured Chang'an and doomed the Tang.

韦庄.b: Late Tang poet who lived through the fall of the dynasty and became chief minister of Former Shu; a master of the early *ci*.

秦韬玉.b: Late Tang poet whose poem "The Poor Girl" gave Chinese the phrase "making wedding dresses for others".

高骈.b: Late Tang general and governor, also a refined poet.

王驾.b: Late Tang poet known for a few delicate quatrains on spring.

李璟.b: Second ruler of the Southern Tang kingdom and father of Li Yu; a gifted *ci* poet.

冯延巳.b: Chief minister of the Southern Tang and one of the great early *ci* poets, bridging the Huajian school and the Song masters.

李煜.b: Last ruler of the Southern Tang, captured by the Song in 975 and poisoned three years later. His lyrics of lost kingdom and endless sorrow made him the "Emperor of *Ci*".

林逋.b: Recluse who lived for twenty years on Solitary Hill by West Lake, never marrying — "plum blossoms were his wife and cranes his children".

范仲淹.b: Statesman, reformer and frontier commander of the Northern Song, whose motto was "to be first to worry about the world's worries, and last to enjoy its joys".

柳永.b: Northern Song *ci* poet of the pleasure quarters, who developed the long slow lyric; "wherever there is a well, people sing Liu Yong".

张先.b: Northern Song *ci* poet nicknamed "Zhang of the Three Shadows" for his lines on shadows.

晏殊.b: Child prodigy who became chief minister of the Northern Song; his polished, gently melancholy *ci* lyrics are models of the form.

宋祁.b: Northern Song historian and poet, called "the Red Apricot Minister" after one famous line.

欧阳修.b: The towering literary statesman of the Northern Song — historian, essayist, poet and mentor of Su Shi; "the Old Drunkard".

曾巩.b: One of the "Eight Great Prose Masters of the Tang and Song", a student of Ouyang Xiu.

王安石.b: Chief minister and radical reformer of the Northern Song, and a poet of exquisite, carefully chiselled quatrains.

王令.b: Precocious Northern Song poet admired by Wang Anshi; died at 27.

程颢.b: Neo-Confucian philosopher, one of the "Two Chengs" who shaped the thought of later China.

王观.b: Northern Song *ci* poet known for a witty farewell song.

苏轼.b: Also Su Dongpo. The universal genius of the Song — poet, essayist, painter, calligrapher, statesman, gourmet — repeatedly exiled for his outspokenness and serene through it all. His bold lyrics opened up the *ci* to every subject.

晏几道.b: Son of Yan Shu; a proud, unworldly poet of love and memory whose lyrics rival Li Yu's for melancholy.

黄庭坚.b: Su Shi's disciple and friend, founder of the Jiangxi school of poetry and a great calligrapher.

李之仪.b: Northern Song official and friend of Su Shi, remembered for one folk-song-like lyric of love by the Yangtze.

秦观.b: One of the "Four Scholars of Su's School", master of tender, melancholy love lyrics.

贺铸.b: Northern Song *ci* poet, an ugly, gallant man known as "He of the Plum Rain" for one line.

周邦彦.b: Director of the imperial music bureau, the great craftsman of the Song *ci*, renowned for exquisite music and diction.

李清照.b: The greatest woman poet in Chinese. Her early lyrics are bright and playful; after the Jurchen invasion and her husband's death, she wrote some of the most heartbroken poems in the language.

曾几.b: Southern Song poet and teacher of Lu You.

李重元.b: Northern Song poet whose four "Remembering the Prince" lyrics survive.

陈与义.b: Poet who fled south when the Jurchen took north China; his later poems are full of the loss.

岳飞.b: The Southern Song general who fought the Jurchen Jin to recover the north, and was put to death on false charges by Qin Hui. The supreme symbol of loyalty in Chinese culture.

陆游.b: The most prolific of all Chinese poets (nearly 10,000 surviving poems), a patriot who longed all his long life to see the north recovered. His one great love, Tang Wan, was taken from him by his mother.

唐琬.b: Lu You's cousin and first wife, forced to divorce him by his mother. Meeting him by chance in Shen Garden years later, she answered his poem with her own — and died soon after.

范成大.b: Southern Song statesman whose sixty "Seasonal Pastoral" poems are the fullest picture of Chinese farm life in verse.

杨万里.b: Southern Song poet of nature's small wonders — a dragonfly, a pond, a child chasing a butterfly — in a fresh, lively, humorous style.

朱熹.b: The greatest Neo-Confucian philosopher, whose commentaries on the classics were the basis of the civil exams for seven centuries; his short poems turn ideas into images.

张孝祥.b: Top graduate of his year who championed the war against the Jin; a bold lyricist in the manner of Su Shi.

辛弃疾.b: Born under Jurchen rule, he led a daring raid and fled south at 22 to serve the Song, but was given no army and spent decades in retirement. The greatest heroic *ci* poet, paired with Su Shi.

姜夔.b: Southern Song musician and poet who composed his own tunes; his lyrics are cool, crystalline and haunting.

叶绍翁.b: Southern Song poet of the "Jianghu" (rivers and lakes) school.

林升.b: Southern Song scholar known only for one stinging poem written on an inn wall.

赵师秀.b: One of the "Four Lings of Yongjia", poets of quiet, finely-wrought scenes.

翁卷.b: One of the "Four Lings of Yongjia", who wrote of village life.

卢梅坡.b: Southern Song poet known for two quatrains on plum blossom and snow.

吴文英.b: Southern Song *ci* poet of dense, jewelled imagery.

无门慧开.b: Chan (Zen) master, compiler of *The Gateless Gate*, the famous collection of koans.

杜耒.b: Southern Song poet remembered for one quatrain about a winter-night guest.

志南.b: A Buddhist monk of the Southern Song, known for one quatrain on spring.

雷震.b: Southern Song poet known for one evening village scene.

文天祥.b: Top graduate and last chief minister of the Song, who fought the Mongols to the end, and refused every offer to serve Kublai Khan through four years in prison before his execution.

蒋捷.b: Southern Song poet who refused to serve the Mongol Yuan after the fall of the Song.

元好问.b: The greatest poet of the Jurchen Jin dynasty, who lived through its fall to the Mongols.

白朴.b: One of the four great Yuan playwrights and a master of the *sanqu* song.

马致远.b: Yuan playwright and the "Champion of Autumn Thoughts" — his 28-character song is the most famous *sanqu* of all.

关汉卿.b: The greatest Yuan playwright, author of *The Injustice to Dou E*; also a master of the *sanqu*.

王实甫.b: Yuan playwright, author of *The Romance of the Western Chamber*, the most beloved love story of the Chinese stage.

张养浩.b: Upright Yuan official who died of exhaustion while bringing famine relief to Shaanxi; his songs meditate on history and the people's suffering.

王冕.b: A cowherd boy who taught himself to paint; became the most famous painter of ink plum blossom, refusing all office.

于谦.b: Ming minister of war who saved Beijing from the Mongols in 1449, and was later executed on false charges. His poem on limestone was his creed.

钱福.b: Top graduate of the Ming examinations, remembered for his "Song of Tomorrow".

唐寅.b: Tang Bohu, the legendary Suzhou painter and poet, barred from office by an examination scandal; lived as a carefree, impoverished artist among his peach blossoms.

王守仁.b: Wang Yangming, the great Ming philosopher of "the unity of knowledge and action", also a general and poet.

杨慎.b: Ming top graduate exiled to Yunnan for over thirty years for opposing the emperor; his lyric on the Yangtze opens *Romance of the Three Kingdoms*.

戚继光.b: The Ming general who drove the wokou pirates from China's coasts and later strengthened the Great Wall.

汤显祖.b: "China's Shakespeare" (they died in the same year), author of *The Peony Pavilion*.

纳兰性德.b: Manchu nobleman and imperial bodyguard to the Kangxi Emperor; his lyrics of love and loss, written before his death at 30, are the finest of the Qing.

郑燮.b: Zheng Banqiao, one of the "Eight Eccentrics of Yangzhou" — painter of bamboo and orchids, calligrapher, and a magistrate who cared for the poor.

曹雪芹.b: Author of *Dream of the Red Chamber*, the greatest Chinese novel, written in poverty after his family's fall.

袁枚.b: Qing poet and gourmet who retired young to his Sui Garden; championed poetry of "natural spirit" over imitation.

赵翼.b: Qing historian and poet who argued that every age has its own great talents.

黄景仁.b: Gifted, impoverished Qing poet who died at 34; his lines of melancholy and frustration are still widely quoted.

林则徐.b: The commissioner who destroyed the British opium at Humen in 1839, triggering the Opium War; exiled to Xinjiang.

龚自珍.b: Late Qing thinker and poet who called for reform; his 315 "Poems of the Year Jihai" were written on his journey home after resigning.

高鼎.b: Late Qing poet remembered for one bright spring poem about children flying kites.

谭嗣同.b: Reformer of the Hundred Days' Reform, who refused to flee when it was crushed — "change requires bloodshed; let it begin with me" — and was executed at 33.

秋瑾.b: Revolutionary, feminist and poet who called herself "the Woman Knight of Mirror Lake"; executed by the Qing at 31.

王国维.b: Scholar of genius — historian, philologist, and author of *Remarks on Lyrics in the Human World* — who drowned himself in Kunming Lake.

poems.s: day river reeds birds person
z: 关关雎鸠，在河之洲。
窈窕淑女，君子好逑。
参差荇菜，左右流之。
窈窕淑女，寤寐求之。
求之不得，寤寐思服。
悠哉悠哉，辗转反侧。
参差荇菜，左右采之。
窈窕淑女，琴瑟友之。
参差荇菜，左右芼之。
窈窕淑女，钟鼓乐之。
e: "Guan-guan!" the ospreys cry
On the islet in the stream.
A lovely, modest maiden —
A fine lord's bride, his dream.
The water-plants grow long and short;
She gathers left and right.
The lovely, modest maiden —
He seeks her day and night.
He seeks her and can't win her;
Waking, sleeping, she's in his mind.
Longing, longing, on and on,
He tosses, turns — no rest to find.
The water-plants grow long and short;
She picks them left and right.
The lovely, modest maiden —
With zither and lute he'll court her, as is right.
The water-plants grow long and short;
She sorts them left and right.
The lovely, modest maiden —
With bells and drums he'll bring her delight.
poems.n: The first poem of the *Book of Songs*, and so of all Chinese poetry — about three thousand years old. Ospreys, believed to mate for life, call to each other; a young man falls for a girl gathering water plants and dreams of winning her with music. Confucius said it showed "joy without excess, sorrow without harm". 窈窕淑女，君子好逑 is still the classic phrase for a perfect match.

poems.s: dawn autumn reeds river frost mist person
z: 蒹葭苍苍，白露为霜。
所谓伊人，在水一方。
溯洄从之，道阻且长。
溯游从之，宛在水中央。
蒹葭萋萋，白露未晞。
所谓伊人，在水之湄。
溯洄从之，道阻且跻。
溯游从之，宛在水中坻。
蒹葭采采，白露未已。
所谓伊人，在水之涘。
溯洄从之，道阻且右。
溯游从之，宛在水中沚。
e: The reeds are green, so green;
The white dew turns to frost.
The one that I am longing for
Is by the water, lost.
Upstream I go to find her —
The road is hard and long;
Downstream I go to find her —
She seems in midstream — gone.
The reeds are lush and thick;
The white dew is not dry.
The one that I am longing for
Is where the banks rise high.
Upstream I go to find her —
The road is steep to climb;
Downstream I go to find her —
She's on an isle, each time.
The reeds are bright and full;
The white dew's lingering still.
The one that I am longing for
Is at the water's sill.
Upstream I go to find her —
The road winds left and right;
Downstream I go to find her —
She's on a sandbar, out of sight.
poems.n: The most haunting love song of the *Book of Songs*: an autumn river, reeds white with frost, and a beloved — 伊人, "that person" — always glimpsed across the water or in the middle of the stream, never reached. It has been read as courtship, as the search for a worthy man, and as the pursuit of every unattainable ideal.

poems.s: spring peach cottage person
z: 桃之夭夭，灼灼其华。
之子于归，宜其室家。
桃之夭夭，有蕡其实。
之子于归，宜其家室。
桃之夭夭，其叶蓁蓁。
之子于归，宜其家人。
e: The peach tree, young and fair,
Its blossoms burning bright!
This girl is going to be wed —
She'll make her home a delight.
The peach tree, young and fair,
Its fruit is round and full!
This girl is going to be wed —
She'll make her household whole.
The peach tree, young and fair,
Its leaves grow thick and green!
This girl is going to be wed —
She'll bless her new kin within.
poems.n: A wedding song. The bride is a young peach tree — first its blazing blossoms (her beauty), then its fruit (children), then its thick leaves (a flourishing family). 桃之夭夭，灼灼其华 is still written on wedding cards, and 灼灼, "burning bright", is the classic word for peach blossom.

poems.s: winter snow willow person hills
z: 昔我往矣，杨柳依依。
今我来思，雨雪霏霏。
行道迟迟，载渴载饥。
我心伤悲，莫知我哀！
e: When I went away long ago,
The willows swayed so tenderly;
Now that I am coming home,
The snowflakes whirl and fly.
Slow, slow, I walk the road,
So thirsty, and so hungry, I.
My heart is full of sorrow —
No one knows my grief, or why.
poems.n: The last stanza of a soldier's song, describing his return from years of fighting the Xianyun nomads in the north. 昔我往矣，杨柳依依；今我来思，雨雪霏霏 — willows when he left, snow when he returns — is often called the most beautiful couplet in the *Book of Songs*: four images hold a whole lost youth.

poems.s: day fields cottage person
z: 硕鼠硕鼠，无食我黍！
三岁贯女，莫我肯顾。
逝将去女，适彼乐土。
乐土乐土，爰得我所。
硕鼠硕鼠，无食我麦！
三岁贯女，莫我肯德。
逝将去女，适彼乐国。
乐国乐国，爰得我直。
硕鼠硕鼠，无食我苗！
三岁贯女，莫我肯劳。
逝将去女，适彼乐郊。
乐郊乐郊，谁之永号？
e: Big rat, big rat,
Keep off my millet, I say!
Three years I've fed you,
And you've never looked my way.
I swear that I will leave you
For a happier land some day —
A happy land, a happy land,
Where I can find my way.
Big rat, big rat,
Keep off my wheat, I plead!
Three years I've fed you,
And you never paid me heed.
I swear that I will leave you
For a happier state indeed —
A happy state, a happy state,
Where I'll get what I need.
Big rat, big rat,
Keep off my sprouting grain!
Three years I've fed you,
And you've never eased my pain.
I swear that I will leave you
For a happier country plain —
A happy plain, a happy plain,
Where none will cry in vain.
poems.n: A peasants' protest from the state of Wei, around the 7th century BC: the "big rat" is the lord who devours their harvest. The dream of a "happy land" (乐土) where labour is rewarded is one of the oldest utopias in literature.

poems.s: day wall grass two
z: 静女其姝，俟我于城隅。
爱而不见，搔首踟蹰。
静女其娈，贻我彤管。
彤管有炜，说怿女美。
自牧归荑，洵美且异。
匪女之为美，美人之贻。
e: The gentle girl, so pretty,
Waits for me at the corner of the wall;
She hides — I cannot see her —
I scratch my head, and pace, and call.
The gentle girl, so lovely,
Gave me a crimson reed;
How brightly it is glowing —
I love its beauty, indeed.
From the pasture she brought me a shoot of grass,
Truly lovely, and so rare.
It's not that you're so lovely, little grass —
It's that you come from my lady fair.
poems.n: A lovers' tryst: the girl playfully hides; the young man frets; then he treasures her humble gifts — a red reed pipe, a sprout of grass from the pasture — because she gave them. 匪女之为美，美人之贻 — "it's not you that's beautiful, but the beauty who gave you" — is the whole logic of love in a line.

poems.s: day wall tower person
z: 青青子衿，悠悠我心。
纵我不往，子宁不嗣音？
青青子佩，悠悠我思。
纵我不往，子宁不来？
挑兮达兮，在城阙兮。
一日不见，如三月兮。
e: Blue, blue, your collar;
Long, long, my heart's desire.
Even if I don't come to you,
Can't you send word, or inquire?
Blue, blue, your girdle-jade;
Long, long, my longing grows.
Even if I don't come to you,
Why don't you come? Who knows?
I pace back and forth
Upon the city tower.
One day I do not see you
Feels like three months, every hour!
poems.n: A girl waits on the city wall for her lover, a student — the "blue collar" was a scholar's dress. 一日不见，如三月兮, "one day without seeing you is like three months", gave Chinese the idiom 一日三秋. Cao Cao borrowed the first couplet in his *Short Song*, turning it into a longing for men of talent.

poems.s: spring peach cottage two
z: 投我以木瓜，报之以琼琚。
匪报也，永以为好也！
投我以木桃，报之以琼瑶。
匪报也，永以为好也！
投我以木李，报之以琼九。
匪报也，永以为好也！
e: You threw a quince to me;
I gave you jade for your girdle in return.
Not as payment —
But so our love will forever burn!
You threw a peach to me;
I gave you a jade of fine repute.
Not as payment —
But so our love will forever take root!
You threw a plum to me;
I gave you a gem of black jade, bright.
Not as payment —
But so our love will last, day and night!
poems.n: A courtship game: a girl throws fruit to the young man she likes; he answers with jade — not to "repay" her, but to pledge lasting love. 投桃报李, "a plum in return for a peach", became the idiom for exchanging kindness.

poems.s: day flag rider horse pine
z: 击鼓其镗，踊跃用兵。
土国城漕，我独南行。
从孙子仲，平陈与宋。
不我以归，忧心有忡。
爰居爰处？
爰丧其马？
于以求之？
于林之下。
死生契阔，与子成说。
执子之手，与子偕老。
于嗟阔兮，不我活兮。
于嗟洵兮，不我信兮。
e: The war drums boom and boom;
We leap and train with spear and blade.
Some build walls at home or at Cao —
I alone march south, as I'm made.
Under Sun Zizhong we march
To make peace with Chen and Song.
He won't let me go back home;
My heart is grieved all along.
Where shall I stop? Where shall I stay?
Where has my horse gone astray?
Where shall I go to look for it?
Down in the woods, far away.
"In life or death, near or far," I said,
"With you this vow I'll keep:
I'll take your hand in mine, and we
Will grow old together, till we sleep."
Alas, we are so far apart —
I fear I'll never live to see you;
Alas, so long I've been away —
I cannot keep my word to you.
poems.n: A soldier's lament from the state of Wei: marching far to the south, he fears he will never return. 执子之手，与子偕老 — "I'll hold your hand and grow old with you" — originally a soldier's vow that he fears he cannot keep, is now the most popular wedding vow in China.

poems.s: day flag fort rider horse
z: 岂曰无衣？
与子同袍。
王于兴师，修我戈矛。
与子同仇！
岂曰无衣？
与子同泽。
王于兴师，修我矛戟。
与子偕作！
岂曰无衣？
与子同裳。
王于兴师，修我甲兵。
与子偕行！
e: Who says you have no clothes?
Share my cloak, my friend.
The king has raised an army;
Our axes and spears we'll mend —
Your foe is mine, to the end!
Who says you have no clothes?
Share my shirt, my brother.
The king has raised an army;
We'll sharpen our halberds, each for the other —
We'll rise up together!
Who says you have no clothes?
Share my coat of mail.
The king has raised an army;
We'll ready our armour and weapons for the trail —
We'll march together, and not fail!
poems.n: A war song of the state of Qin — the future conquerors of all China — full of comradeship: soldiers share their clothes and march against a common enemy. 同袍, "sharing a cloak", is still the word for comrades-in-arms.

poems.s: day fields wall person
z: 彼黍离离，彼稷之苗。
行迈靡靡，中心摇摇。
知我者，谓我心忧；
不知我者，谓我何求。
悠悠苍天，此何人哉？
彼黍离离，彼稷之穗。
行迈靡靡，中心如醉。
知我者，谓我心忧；
不知我者，谓我何求。
悠悠苍天，此何人哉？
彼黍离离，彼稷之实。
行迈靡靡，中心如噎。
知我者，谓我心忧；
不知我者，谓我何求。
悠悠苍天，此何人哉？
e: The millet grows in rows, row on row;
The sorghum's sprouting green.
I walk on slowly, slowly,
My heart shaken, as in a dream.
Those who know me say I'm grieving;
Those who don't, ask what I seek.
O distant, boundless blue sky —
Who has done this? Speak!
The millet grows in rows, row on row;
The sorghum is in ear.
I walk on slowly, slowly,
My heart as drunk with grief, I fear.
Those who know me say I'm grieving;
Those who don't, ask what I seek.
O distant, boundless blue sky —
Who has done this? Speak!
The millet grows in rows, row on row;
The sorghum's grain is grown.
I walk on slowly, slowly,
My heart is choked, like stone.
Those who know me say I'm grieving;
Those who don't, ask what I seek.
O distant, boundless blue sky —
Who has done this? Speak!
poems.n: Tradition says a Zhou official, passing the ruins of the old Western Zhou capital after it fell in 771 BC, found its palaces turned to millet fields and wrote this lament. 黍离之悲, "the grief of the millet rows", became the standard phrase for mourning a fallen dynasty or a lost homeland.

poems.s: spring flowers peach person
z: 劝君莫惜金缕衣，劝君惜取少年时。
花开堪折直须折，莫待无花空折枝。
e: Don't treasure, I beg you, your robe of golden thread;
Treasure your youth instead, while it is here.
When flowers are ripe for picking, pick them, then —
Don't wait to snap bare branches when the flowers disappear.
poems.n: Sung by Du Qiuniang, a singing girl of Jinling who became a consort in the Tang palace (the song is sometimes listed as anonymous). China's *carpe diem* — "gather ye rosebuds while ye may".

poems.s: dawn spring willow oriole cottage person
z: 打起黄莺儿，莫教枝上啼。
啼时惊妾梦，不得到辽西。
e: Go, shoo that oriole away!
Don't let it sing upon the bough —
Its singing woke me from my dream
Before I could reach Liaoxi, somehow.
poems.n: A young wife chases a singing oriole out of the tree — because it woke her just as, in her dream, she was about to reach her husband at the frontier in Liaoxi, in the far north-east. The whole story unfolds backwards, one line at a time.

poems.s: autumn day leaves pine
z: 垂緌饮清露，流响出疏桐。
居高声自远，非是藉秋风。
e: With tasselled mouth it sips the clear, pure dew;
Its flowing song pours from the wutong, sparse and tall.
Its voice goes far because it dwells up high —
And not because the autumn wind has carried it at all.
poems.n: The cicada's mouthparts look like the tassels of an official's cap, and it was believed to live on dew — so it is an upright official. A person of real worth is heard far and wide by his own merit, without needing powerful backing. One of the "three great cicada poems" of the Tang, with Luo Binwang's and Li Shangyin's.

poems.s: dusk autumn sun hills fields rider person
z: 东皋薄暮望，徙倚欲何依。
树树皆秋色，山山唯落晖。
牧人驱犊返，猎马带禽归。
相顾无相识，长歌怀采薇。
e: At dusk I gaze out from the eastern shore,
And wander — where's a place where I belong?
Each tree is tinged with autumn's colour now;
Each hill holds only sunset's glow, not long.
The herdsmen drive their calves back home;
The hunters' horses come with game in tow.
We look at each other; no one knows me here —
I sing of the fern-gatherers of long ago.
poems.n: One of the first true regulated poems of the Tang, plain and natural after the ornate court verse of the age before. The fern-gatherers were Boyi and Shuqi, princes who refused to serve the new Zhou dynasty and lived on wild ferns until they starved — models of the principled recluse.

poems.s: day summer lake birds willow
z: 鹅，鹅，鹅，曲项向天歌。
白毛浮绿水，红掌拨清波。
e: Goose, goose, goose!
It curves its neck and sings up to the sky.
White feathers float on water green;
Red feet paddle the clear waves by.
poems.n: Said to have been written by Luo Binwang at the age of seven, and the first poem many Chinese children learn: sound, shape and colour — white, green, red, clear — in eighteen characters.

poems.te: Ode to the Cicada, Written in Prison
poems.s: autumn wind leaves wall
z: 西陆蝉声唱，南冠客思深。
不堪玄鬓影，来对白头吟。
露重飞难进，风多响易沉。
无人信高洁，谁为表予心？
e: In autumn's western reach, the cicada sings;
The southern-capped prisoner's thoughts run deep.
How can I bear the shadow of those black-glossed wings
Come to sing "White Head" to me as I weep?
The dew is heavy — it can hardly fly ahead;
The wind is strong — its song is quickly drowned.
No one believes in its high purity — and who
Will speak my heart for me, and make it known around?
poems.n: Written in 678 when Luo Binwang was imprisoned on false charges after criticising Empress Wu. "Western land" (西陆) means autumn; a captive from Chu once wore his southern-style cap in prison, so "southern cap" means a prisoner. "White Head" is an old song of a rejected wife. The cicada, symbol of purity, is the poet himself.

poems.te: Seeing a Friend Off at the Yi River
poems.s: winter river wind two
z: 此地别燕丹，壮士发冲冠。
昔时人已没，今日水犹寒。
e: Here Jing Ke bade Prince Dan of Yan goodbye;
In fury the hero's hair stood up against his crown.
The men of those days are long gone, and lie
Long dead — yet still the water's cold, flowing down.
poems.n: In 227 BC the assassin Jing Ke set out from the Yi River to kill the king of Qin (later the First Emperor), singing "The wind is sighing, the Yi River is cold; the hero goes, and will not return." He failed and was killed. "The water is still cold": the heroic spirit endures.

poems.s: wind bamboo river leaves
z: 解落三秋叶，能开二月花。
过江千尺浪，入竹万竿斜。
e: It shakes down leaves when autumn's late,
And opens flowers when spring's begun.
Over the river, it raises thousand-foot waves;
Into the bamboo — it bends ten thousand, every one.
poems.n: A riddle-poem: the wind is never named, only shown through what it does. A favourite with Chinese children.

poems.s: winter snow fort flag rider wind
z: 烽火照西京，心中自不平。
牙璋辞凤阙，铁骑绕龙城。
雪暗凋旗画，风多杂鼓声。
宁为百夫长，胜作一书生。
e: The beacon fires light up the western capital's sky;
My heart cannot be calm; it burns inside.
With ivory tallies, generals leave the Phoenix Gate;
Iron cavalry encircle Dragon City wide.
Snow dims the painted banners till they fade;
The roaring wind is mingled with the drums.
I'd rather lead a hundred men in war
Than be a scholar poring over books, now war has come.
poems.n: The cry of a young scholar who wants action, not books, when the frontier is in danger. The ivory tally (牙璋) was half of a split token authorising a general to command. 宁为百夫长，胜作一书生 became the slogan of scholars turning soldier.

poems.te: Seeing Off Assistant Magistrate Du to His Post in Shu
poems.s: day wall mist river two rider
z: 城阙辅三秦，风烟望五津。
与君离别意，同是宦游人。
海内存知己，天涯若比邻。
无为在歧路，儿女共沾巾。
e: The walls of Chang'an guard the lands of Qin;
Through wind and mist I see the Five Fords far away.
The pain of parting we both feel within —
Both officials, far from home, we wander and we stray.
As long as somewhere in the world a true friend lives,
The world's end is as near as the house next door.
So here, where the roads divide, let's not, like girls and boys,
Wet our handkerchiefs with tears, and weep the more.
poems.n: Wang Bo's farewell to a friend posted to Sichuan (the "Five Fords" of the Min River). Instead of tears, comfort: 海内存知己，天涯若比邻 — "with a true friend anywhere in the world, the ends of the earth are like next door" — is one of the most quoted lines on friendship ever written.

poems.s: dusk tower river clouds rain mountains
z: 滕王高阁临江渚，佩玉鸣鸾罢歌舞。
画栋朝飞南浦云，珠帘暮卷西山雨。
闲云潭影日悠悠，物换星移几度秋。
阁中帝子今何在？槛外长江空自流。
e: Prince Teng's high pavilion overlooks the river's isle;
His jade and carriage bells are still; the songs have died away.
At dawn, the clouds of South Shore drift past the painted beams;
At dusk, pearl blinds roll up on Western Hills, all rain and grey.
Idle clouds and shadows in the pool — the long days slip on by;
Things change, the stars move on — how many autumns since that day?
The prince who feasted in this hall — where is he now?
Beyond the rail, the Long River flows on its lonely way.
poems.n: Composed in 675 at a banquet in the Pavilion of Prince Teng at Nanchang, as the closing poem of Wang Bo's famous *Preface*. Legend says the host intended his son-in-law to shine, but the twenty-five-year-old Wang Bo took up the brush and stunned everyone. The prince is gone; only the river remains. Wang Bo drowned the following year.

poems.s: autumn wind mountains leaves river
z: 长江悲已滞，万里念将归。
况属高风晚，山山黄叶飞。
e: By the Long River I grieve, so long held here;
Ten thousand li from home, I long to return.
And now the autumn wind blows high and late,
And yellow leaves fly over every hill in turn.
poems.n: Written in Sichuan, where Wang Bo had been sent away after offending the emperor with a playful essay. The yellow leaves whirling over every hill are homesickness made visible.

poems.s: spring river boat person hills
z: 岭外音书断，经冬复历春。
近乡情更怯，不敢问来人。
e: Beyond the Five Ridges, no word, no letter came;
Through winter, then through spring, I waited, all alone.
Now, nearing home, my heart grows timid, full of fear —
I dare not ask the travellers for news of home.
poems.n: Exiled to the far south (beyond the Five Ridges) in 705, Song Zhiwen secretly fled north. Crossing the Han River near home, he is afraid to ask about his family — what if the news is bad? 近乡情更怯, "the nearer home, the more timid the heart", describes every long-delayed homecoming.

poems.s: spring cottage willow person two
z: 少小离家老大回，乡音无改鬓毛衰。
儿童相见不相识，笑问客从何处来。
e: I left home young, and come back old;
My accent's the same, but my hair's grown thin.
The children see me, a stranger to them all —
"Where are you from, sir?" they ask, with a grin.
poems.n: He Zhizhang came home to Yuezhou (Zhejiang) in 744, aged eighty-five, after more than fifty years at court. The children's innocent question — asking a native where he comes from — holds all the gentle comedy and sadness of the poem.

poems.s: spring lake willow cottage person
z: 离别家乡岁月多，近来人事半消磨。
惟有门前镜湖水，春风不改旧时波。
e: I've been away from home so many, many years;
Of all the people I once knew, half have passed away.
Only Mirror Lake before my door, it appears,
In the spring wind still ripples as it did in the old days.
poems.n: The companion poem: people change and die, but the lake keeps its ripples. Nature's constancy deepens human transience.

poems.s: spring willow wind river
z: 碧玉妆成一树高，万条垂下绿丝绦。
不知细叶谁裁出，二月春风似剪刀。
e: A tree dressed up in green jade, standing tall,
Lets down ten thousand ribbons of green silk.
Who cut these slender leaves, so fine and small?
The spring wind of the second month — like scissors, cut them all.
poems.n: A child's favourite: the willow as a young woman dressed in green jade with silken ribbons, and the surprising last line — the spring wind is a tailor's scissors.

poems.te: Spring River in the Flower Moon Night
poems.s: night spring moon river sea tower boat flowers mist
z: 春江潮水连海平，海上明月共潮生。
滟滟随波千万里，何处春江无月明？
江流宛转遶芳甸，月照花林皆似霰。
空里流霜不觉飞，汀上白沙看不见。
江天一色无纤尘，皎皎空中孤月轮。
江畔何人初见月，江月何年初照人？
人生代代无穷已，江月年年秖相似。
不知江月待何人？
但见长江送流水。
白云一片去悠悠，青枫浦上不胜愁。
谁家今夜扁舟子，何处相思明月楼？
可怜楼上月裴回，应照离人妆镜台。
玉户帘中卷不去，捣衣砧上拂还来。
此时相望不相闻，愿逐月华流照君。
鸿雁长飞光不度，鱼龙潜跃水成文。
昨夜闲潭梦落花，可怜春半不还家。
江水流春去欲尽，江潭落月复西斜。
斜月沈沈藏海雾，碣石潇湘无限路。
不知乘月几人归，落月摇情满江树。
e: The spring river's tide flows level with the sea;
Upon the sea the bright moon rises with the tide.
It glitters on the waves ten thousand li or more —
Where on the spring river is the moonlight not spread wide?
The river winds and curls round fragrant meadowland;
On flowering woods the moonlight falls like sleet.
The flowing frost of light falls through the air unseen;
The white sand on the shoals has melted into it, complete.
River and sky are one colour, without a speck of dust;
Bright, bright in the empty air, the moon's lone wheel.
Who was the first by the river to see the moon?
And when did the river moon first shine on men?
Generation after generation, men live on without end;
The river moon looks the same, year after year, again.
I wonder whom the river moon has waited for so long —
I see the Long River speeding its waters on and on.
A single white cloud drifts slowly far away;
At Green Maple Shore, the sorrow is too much to bear.
Whose family is on a little boat tonight?
Where is the moonlit tower, where someone longs for him there?
How sadly the moon lingers above the tower,
Shining on the mirror-stand of the lonely one inside;
Within her jade door's curtain, it can't be rolled away;
On the fulling-stone, she brushes it off — it comes back to abide.
Now we gaze at it together, but cannot hear each other;
I wish I could follow the moonlight, to shine on you.
The wild geese fly far, but cannot carry the light;
The fish and dragons leap, and only ripples come through.
Last night by the quiet pool I dreamed of falling flowers;
Alas, spring is half gone, and still I'm not home.
The river carries spring away, now nearly gone;
Over the river pool, the moon sinks west alone.
The slanting moon sinks deep, hidden in the sea mist;
From Jieshi to Xiaoxiang, the roads are without end.
How many, I wonder, ride the moonlight home tonight?
The setting moon stirs feeling in the river trees that bend.
poems.n: Only two of Zhang Ruoxu's poems survive, and this one was nearly forgotten until the Ming; the modern scholar Wen Yiduo called it "the poem above all poems, the peak above all peaks". It follows a single spring night from moonrise to moonset, moving from the beauty of the river to questions about eternity — who first saw the moon? when did it first shine on man? — and to the longing of separated lovers, a husband on a boat and a wife in her tower, whom the same moon joins and divides. Geese and fish were the legendary carriers of letters; even they cannot bring word.

poems.s: dusk tower hills clouds person
z: 前不见古人，后不见来者。
念天地之悠悠，独怆然而涕下。
e: Before me, I cannot see the ancients gone;
Behind me, I cannot see those yet to be.
I think of heaven and earth, which go on and on,
And alone, in sorrow, my tears fall free.
poems.n: Youzhou Terrace (near Beijing) was said to be the Golden Terrace built by King Zhao of Yan in the 4th century BC to welcome men of talent. Chen Zi'ang, a frustrated adviser on a military campaign in 697, climbs it: the wise kings are gone, the future cannot be seen, and he stands alone in infinite time and space. One of the loneliest poems ever written.

poems.te: Gazing at the Moon, Longing for One Far Away
poems.s: night moon sea window person
z: 海上生明月，天涯共此时。
情人怨遥夜，竟夕起相思。
灭烛怜光满，披衣觉露滋。
不堪盈手赠，还寝梦佳期。
e: Over the sea the bright moon rises high;
At the ends of the earth, we share this hour.
Lovers resent the long, long night;
All night their longing grows in power.
I snuff the candle — the moonlight fills the room;
I throw a robe on, feeling the dew grow deep.
I cannot give you handfuls of its gleam,
So back to bed — to meet you in my sleep.
poems.n: 海上生明月，天涯共此时 — "the bright moon rises over the sea; at the ends of the earth we share this moment" — is the line every Chinese person thinks of at the Mid-Autumn Festival when loved ones are far away. Written by Zhang Jiuling around 737, after his dismissal as chief minister.

poems.s: spring flowers pine mountains
z: 兰叶春葳蕤，桂华秋皎洁。
欣欣此生意，自尔为佳节。
谁知林栖者，闻风坐相悦。
草木有本心，何求美人折？
e: In spring the orchid leaves grow lush and green;
In autumn cassia blossoms shine so pure and bright.
They flourish, full of life, serene,
Each in its own season, as is right.
Who'd think the hermits living in the woods
Would catch their fragrance on the wind and love them so?
But plants have their own nature — why should they
Seek to be picked by a beauty, just for show?
poems.n: The first of twelve poems written after Zhang Jiuling lost power in 737. Orchid and cassia are fragrant by their own nature, not to win admiration — like a person of virtue, who does not need to be "picked" by a ruler (the "beauty" of the old allegory). Integrity does not depend on recognition.

poems.s: night desert moon cup horse flag
z: 葡萄美酒夜光杯，欲饮琵琶马上催。
醉卧沙场君莫笑，古来征战几人回？
e: Fine wine of grapes in cups of jade that glow at night;
We go to drink — the pipas urge us on from horseback, too.
If I lie drunk upon the sands, don't laugh at the sight:
Since ancient times, of those who went to war, how few came through?
poems.n: Grape wine and "night-shining cups" of white jade were exotic luxuries from Central Asia, and the pipa was the instrument of the steppe. The soldiers drink before battle; the last couplet is both bravado and despair.

poems.s: dusk sun mountains river tower
z: 白日依山尽，黄河入海流。
欲穷千里目，更上一层楼。
e: The white sun leans on the hills and is gone;
The Yellow River flows on to the sea.
If you would see a thousand li beyond,
Climb one more storey higher — and you'll see.
poems.n: Stork Tower in Puzhou (Shanxi) overlooked the Yellow River. The vast first couplet — the sun vanishing behind mountains, the river rolling to a sea a thousand miles away — leads to the most quoted lines of encouragement in Chinese: to see further, climb higher (更上一层楼), now said of any effort to do better.

poems.s: day clouds mountains fort river desert
z: 黄河远上白云间，一片孤城万仞山。
羌笛何须怨杨柳，春风不度玉门关。
e: Far up, the Yellow River climbs into white cloud;
One lonely fort amid the mountains, ten thousand fathoms tall.
Why must the Qiang flute play "Willows" and mourn aloud?
The spring wind never crosses Jade Gate Pass at all.
poems.n: Liangzhou (Gansu) on the north-western frontier. "Breaking Willows" was the farewell tune — but beyond the Jade Gate there is no spring and there are no willows, so the soldiers' homesickness has nowhere to go. Legend says Wang Zhihuan, Wang Changling and Gao Shi once bet on whose poems the singing girls of a tavern would sing; the loveliest girl sang this one.

poems.s: dawn spring rain petals birds cottage window
z: 春眠不觉晓，处处闻啼鸟。
夜来风雨声，花落知多少。
e: In spring I sleep and miss the break of day;
Everywhere I hear the birds sing on.
Last night, the sound of wind and rain —
How many blossoms fell before the dawn?
poems.n: After *Quiet Night Thoughts*, perhaps the most famous poem in Chinese. Half awake on a spring morning, the poet hears birdsong and remembers the night's storm: a moment of pure contentment shadowed by the thought of fallen petals — beauty and its passing in twenty characters.

poems.s: autumn hills cottage fields chrysanthemum two jar
z: 故人具鸡黍，邀我至田家。
绿树村边合，青山郭外斜。
开轩面场圃，把酒话桑麻。
待到重阳日，还来就菊花。
e: My old friend made a meal of chicken and millet,
And invited me to his farm to dine.
Green trees encircle the village;
Blue hills slope beyond the town line.
We open the window on the threshing yard and garden,
And over wine we talk of mulberry and hemp.
When the Double Ninth comes round again,
I'll come back for the chrysanthemums — I won't be exempt!
poems.n: The great pastoral poem of the Tang. Everything is plain — chicken and millet, talk of crops — and that is the joy. The promise to return on the Double Ninth, when people drank chrysanthemum wine, is the warmest possible thank-you.

poems.s: dusk moon river boat mist hills
z: 移舟泊烟渚，日暮客愁新。
野旷天低树，江清月近人。
e: I steer my boat to moor by a misty isle;
As the sun sets, a traveller's grief comes new.
The plain is vast — the sky stoops below the trees;
The river's clear — the moon comes close to me, too.
poems.n: Mooring at dusk on the Xin'an River in Zhejiang. The last two lines are among the most admired in Chinese: on the open plain the sky seems lower than the trees; in the clear river, the moon's reflection floats right beside the boat — the only companion the lonely traveller has.

poems.te: Gazing at Dongting Lake: To Chancellor Zhang
poems.s: autumn lake wall fisher boat mist
z: 八月湖水平，涵虚混太清。
气蒸云梦泽，波撼岳阳城。
欲济无舟楫，端居耻圣明。
坐观垂钓者，徒有羡鱼情。
e: In the eighth month, the lake brims level with its shore;
It holds the void, and merges with the sky.
Its vapours steam over the Yunmeng Marsh;
Its waves shake Yueyang's walls on high.
I'd cross, but have no boat or oar;
To sit idle in this age of sages would be shame.
I sit and watch the men who fish,
And only envy the fish they claim.
poems.n: A poem asking Zhang Jiuling, the chief minister, for an official post — but it is the first half that made it famous: the colossal lake in autumn flood, steaming over the marshes and shaking the city walls. The second half pleads, gracefully: "I'd cross over (into office) but have no boat; watching others fish, I can only envy their catch."

poems.s: winter mountains river person two
z: 人事有代谢，往来成古今。
江山留胜迹，我辈复登临。
水落鱼梁浅，天寒梦泽深。
羊公碑尚在，读罢泪沾襟。
e: Human affairs succeed each other, waxing and waning;
Comings and goings make up past and present.
The rivers and hills keep their famous sites,
And now we, in our turn, come climbing here.
The water has fallen — Fish Weir isle lies shallow;
The air is cold — the Yunmeng marsh lies deep.
Lord Yang's stone tablet still stands;
Reading it, we wet our robes and weep.
poems.n: Mount Xian near Xiangyang held a memorial stone to Yang Hu, a beloved 3rd-century governor who loved to climb it, and once said sadly that all the worthies who had climbed it were forgotten. People wept on reading his tablet, so it was called the "Tablet of Falling Tears". Meng Haoran, a native of Xiangyang, adds his own tears and his own reflection on time.

poems.te: Thinking of Xin the Elder in the South Pavilion on a Summer Day
poems.s: night summer moon lotus bamboo pavilion
z: 山光忽西落，池月渐东上。
散发乘夕凉，开轩卧闲敞。
荷风送香气，竹露滴清响。
欲取鸣琴弹，恨无知音赏。
感此怀故人，中宵劳梦想。
e: The mountain light drops suddenly into the west;
The pond-moon slowly rises in the east.
I loosen my hair to enjoy the evening cool,
And open the window, lying at ease, at least.
The lotus wind wafts its fragrance by;
Dew drips from bamboos with a crystal sound.
I'd like to take my zither down and play —
But there's no one who understands it around.
Moved by this, I think of my old friend,
And all night long, in dreams, I seek him out.
poems.n: A summer night so quiet that dew dripping from bamboo leaves is audible. The music he would play needs a 知音 — "one who knows the tone", the word for a true friend, from the story of Boya, who broke his zither when the only man who understood his music died.

poems.te: Returning to the Southern Hills at Year's End
poems.s: night winter moon pine window cottage
z: 北阙休上书，南山归敝庐。
不才明主弃，多病故人疏。
白发催年老，青阳逼岁除。
永怀愁不寐，松月夜窗虚。
e: No more petitions to the northern palace gate;
I'm going home to my poor hut in the southern hills.
Lacking talent, I'm cast off by our wise ruler;
Often sick, I'm left by old friends, as old age fills.
White hairs hurry my years toward age;
The green spring sun drives out the year at last.
Brooding long, I lie awake in sorrow —
Pine and moon, through the empty window, cast.
poems.n: Legend says that Meng Haoran was hiding in Wang Wei's office when the emperor walked in, and was made to recite a poem; he chose this one — and when the emperor heard "lacking talent, I'm cast off by our wise ruler", he said, "You never sought office; I never cast you off. Why slander me?" and sent him home. Whether true or not, it is a perfect story of a poet undone by a line.

poems.s: day cottage grass two person
z: 寂寂竟何待，朝朝空自归。
欲寻芳草去，惜与故人违。
当路谁相假，知音世所稀。
只应守寂寞，还掩故园扉。
e: In silence, what is it I'm waiting for?
Each day, I come home empty-handed, as before.
I want to go and seek the fragrant grass,
But hate to part from my old friend once more.
Those in power — who will lend me a hand?
True friends who understand are rare in the land.
I should keep to my solitude,
And close my old garden gate, as I'd planned.
poems.n: 737, after failing to win office in the capital. "Fragrant grass" is the hermit's life; Meng's only regret is leaving Wang Wei, the one man in Chang'an who truly understood him. The two were later painted together and are always named together as the masters of landscape verse.

poems.t: 宿业师山房期丁大不至
poems.te: Waiting in Vain for Ding the Elder at Master Ye's Mountain Lodge
poems.s: dusk moon pine mountains temple birds person
z: 夕阳度西岭，群壑倏已暝。
松月生夜凉，风泉满清听。
樵人归欲尽，烟鸟栖初定。
之子期宿来，孤琴候萝径。
e: The setting sun crosses the western ridge;
The valleys all have suddenly gone dark.
The moon through the pines brings the cool of night;
Wind and springs fill my ears, clear to hark.
The woodcutters have nearly all gone home;
In the mist, the birds have just settled to rest.
You promised to come and stay the night —
With my lone zither, I wait on the vine-hung path, your guest.
poems.n: A mountain evening described with exquisite precision, ending with the poet still waiting, zither in hand, for a friend who never comes. The disappointment is never stated.

poems.te: Climbing Orchid Mountain in Autumn: To Zhang the Fifth
poems.s: autumn dusk mountains geese river person clouds
z: 北山白云里，隐者自怡悦。
相望试登高，心随雁飞灭。
愁因薄暮起，兴是清秋发。
时见归村人，沙行渡头歇。
天边树若荠，江畔洲如月。
何当载酒来，共醉重阳节。
e: Among the white clouds of the northern hill,
A hermit finds his quiet joy.
To look for you I climb up high;
My heart flies with the geese, and fades away.
Sorrow rises with the gathering dusk;
Delight is born of the clear autumn day.
Now and then I see villagers going home,
Walking the sand, resting at the ferry's quay.
At the sky's edge, trees look small as shepherd's purse;
By the river, the islet curves like a moon.
When will you bring wine, so we can both
Get drunk on the Double Ninth, and soon?
poems.n: A climb to look toward a friend's home. The distant trees "like shepherd's-purse" (a tiny wild herb) and the sandbar "like the moon" give a precise sense of height and distance. The poem ends, as so often with Meng Haoran, with wine and the Double Ninth festival.

poems.te: Song of Returning to Deer Gate at Night
poems.s: night moon mountains pine temple river boat
z: 山寺钟鸣昼已昏，渔梁渡头争渡喧。
人随沙岸向江村，余亦乘舟归鹿门。
鹿门月照开烟树，忽到庞公栖隐处。
岩扉松径长寂寥，惟有幽人自来去。
e: The mountain temple's bell has rung; day has turned to dusk;
At Fish Weir ferry, people jostle, noisy, to cross.
The crowd goes off along the sandy bank toward the river villages;
I, too, take a boat back home to Deer Gate.
At Deer Gate, moonlight parts the misty trees;
Suddenly I'm at the place where Lord Pang lived hidden.
The rock door and the pine path are always silent —
Only the recluse comes and goes alone.
poems.n: Deer Gate Mountain near Xiangyang, where the Han-dynasty hermit Pang Degong refused all invitations to office and vanished into the hills gathering herbs. Meng Haoran retreated there too. The noisy crowd turns toward the villages; the poet alone turns toward silence.

poems.te: Early Cold on the River: Thoughts of Home
poems.s: autumn geese river sail leaves wind
z: 木落雁南度，北风江上寒。
我家襄水曲，遥隔楚云端。
乡泪客中尽，孤帆天际看。
迷津欲有问，平海夕漫漫。
e: Leaves fall; the wild geese cross toward the south;
The north wind blows; the river's growing cold.
My home is at a bend of the Xiang River,
Far off, beyond the clouds of Chu, I'm told.
My homesick tears are all used up in travel;
I watch a lonely sail at heaven's edge.
Lost, I'd ask the way to the ford —
But the sea-wide river spreads in the dusk past every ledge.
poems.n: Homesick on the lower Yangtze. "Asking the way to the ford" (问津) alludes to Confucius sending a disciple to ask two hermits for the ford — and being told, in effect, that the world was lost. Meng's way home, and his way in life, are both unclear.

poems.te: Seeing Zhu the Elder Off to Qin
poems.s: day rider two mountains wall
z: 游人五陵去，宝剑值千金。
分手脱相赠，平生一片心。
e: You're off to the Five Tombs, traveller;
My precious sword is worth a thousand gold.
At parting I take it off and give it to you —
With it, a whole life's loyal heart to hold.
poems.n: The Five Tombs (五陵) near Chang'an were where wealthy young knights lived. A sword was a gentleman's most treasured possession; giving it away meant giving one's heart. Twenty characters of gallant friendship.

poems.s: dusk desert snow fort horse geese
z: 白日登山望烽火，黄昏饮马傍交河。
行人刁斗风沙暗，公主琵琶幽怨多。
野云万里无城郭，雨雪纷纷连大漠。
胡雁哀鸣夜夜飞，胡儿眼泪双双落。
闻道玉门犹被遮，应将性命逐轻车。
年年战骨埋荒外，空见蒲桃入汉家。
e: By day we climb the hills to watch for beacon fires;
At dusk we water horses by the Jiao's cold tide.
The watch-gongs clang through the dark of wind and sand;
The princess's pipa sings of grief she cannot hide.
Wild clouds for ten thousand li, and not a town or wall;
Rain and snow come swirling down across the desert wide.
The northern geese cry mournfully, night after night they fly;
The Hu boys' tears fall down in pairs, and none can dry.
They say the Jade Gate's still shut against our coming home —
We must follow the light chariots, and stake our lives, and die.
Year after year, the bones of war are buried in the waste —
And all we get is grapes, brought into the Han to taste.
poems.n: An "old" frontier song, set in the Han but aimed at Xuanzong's wars. The princess's pipa recalls the Han princess married off to a Central Asian king, who played her grief on the pipa. When Emperor Wu of Han's army failed against Ferghana, he shut the Jade Gate and forbade the soldiers to return; the only gain from all the dead was the grapevine, brought back to China. The last line is one of the bitterest in Tang poetry.

poems.s: dawn sun sea river sail hills geese
z: 客路青山外，行舟绿水前。
潮平两岸阔，风正一帆悬。
海日生残夜，江春入旧年。
乡书何处达？归雁洛阳边。
e: My road runs on beyond the blue-green hills;
My boat sails on across the jade-green stream.
The tide is high; the banks spread far and wide;
The wind is fair; one sail hangs straight, it seems.
The sea-sun rises while the night still lingers;
The river's spring arrives before the old year's through.
Where can my letter home be sent? —
By the wild geese flying north to Luoyang, carried through.
poems.n: Written near Zhenjiang on the lower Yangtze. The third couplet — the sun born out of the sea while night is not yet over, spring arriving on the river before the old year has ended — so impressed the chief minister Zhang Yue that he hung it in his hall as a model of poetry. It captures time itself moving forward.

poems.s: night moon fort mountains flag
z: 秦时明月汉时关，万里长征人未还。
但使龙城飞将在，不教胡马度阴山。
e: The moon of Qin, the passes of the Han —
Ten thousand li they marched; not one man has come back.
If only the Flying General of Dragon City were alive,
No Hu horse would cross the Yin Hills to attack.
poems.n: "Qin moon, Han passes": the same moon and the same forts have watched a thousand years of frontier war — the whole of history in one line. The Flying General was Li Guang of the Han, whom the Xiongnu feared above all others. Often called the finest quatrain of the Tang.

poems.s: snow mountains clouds fort desert flag
z: 青海长云暗雪山，孤城遥望玉门关。
黄沙百战穿金甲，不破楼兰终不还。
e: Long clouds over Qinghai darken the snowy peaks;
From the lone fort I gaze toward Jade Gate, far away.
A hundred battles in the yellow sand have worn our armour through —
Until we've crushed Loulan, we'll never go home; we'll stay.
poems.n: Qinghai Lake, the snow-capped Qilian range and the Jade Gate Pass trace the whole north-western frontier of the Tang. The soldiers' oath in the last line — 不破楼兰终不还 — is still quoted as a vow of total resolve.

poems.s: dusk desert wind flag rider fort
z: 大漠风尘日色昏，红旗半卷出辕门。
前军夜战洮河北，已报生擒吐谷浑。
e: Across the great desert, wind and dust have dimmed the sun;
Red banners half-furled, they ride out through the camp's gate.
The vanguard fought by night north of the Tao — and won:
The Tuyuhun chief's been taken alive — the news can't wait!
poems.n: A burst of victory: the reinforcements are still marching into the dust storm when word arrives that the vanguard has already won. The Tuyuhun were a nomadic kingdom around Qinghai.

poems.te: Seeing Xin Jian Off at Lotus Tower
poems.s: dawn rain river tower mountains boat
z: 寒雨连江夜入吴，平明送客楚山孤。
洛阳亲友如相问，一片冰心在玉壶。
e: Cold rain spread over the river as night came into Wu;
At dawn I see you off; the hills of Chu stand lone.
If kin and friends in Luoyang ask about me, tell them true:
"A heart of ice in a pot of jade" — that's all I own.
poems.n: Wang Changling, slandered and demoted, sees a friend off to Luoyang from the Lotus Tower at Zhenjiang. 一片冰心在玉壶 — a heart pure as ice in a jade vessel, unchanged by slander — became an idiom for integrity.

poems.s: spring willow tower person
z: 闺中少妇不知愁，春日凝妆上翠楼。
忽见陌头杨柳色，悔教夫婿觅封侯。
e: The young wife in her chamber doesn't know what sorrow is;
One spring day, all made up, she climbs the jade-green tower.
She suddenly sees the green of the willows along the road —
And rues the day she sent her man to seek a lordship's power.
poems.n: A masterpiece of the sudden turn. The willows by the road — the trees of parting — make her realise in an instant what she gave up when she encouraged her husband to win a title (封侯) at the frontier.

poems.s: summer lotus lake boat person
z: 荷叶罗裙一色裁，芙蓉向脸两边开。
乱入池中看不见，闻歌始觉有人来。
e: Lotus leaves and silken skirt are cut from the same green;
Lotus blooms beside her face unfold on either side.
Lost amid the pond, she cannot now be seen —
Until a song rings out, and you know where she hides.
poems.n: The girl is so like the lotus — green skirt, pink cheeks — that she vanishes among the flowers; only her song gives her away.

poems.s: dawn autumn palace crows person
z: 奉帚平明金殿开，暂将团扇共徘徊。
玉颜不及寒鸦色，犹带昭阳日影来。
e: At dawn, with broom in hand, she waits for the golden hall to open,
And lingers for a while beside her round silk fan.
Her jade-white face is worth less than a crow's black feathers —
For the crows still bring the sunlight of Zhaoyang, as only they can.
poems.n: Lady Ban, a virtuous Han consort, was displaced by the dancer Zhao Feiyan and withdrew to the Changxin Palace to serve the Empress Dowager. She once compared herself to a fan, discarded when autumn comes. Here her beauty is worth less than the black crows — who at least fly from Zhaoyang Palace, where the emperor is, with its sunshine (his favour) on their wings.

poems.s: dusk autumn tower fort sun wind
z: 烽火城西百尺楼，黄昏独上海风秋。
更吹羌笛关山月，无那金闺万里愁。
e: West of the beacon-fire city stands a hundred-foot tower;
At dusk I climb it alone; autumn wind blows off the sea.
Then a Qiang flute plays "Moon over the Mountain Pass" — what power
Can ease her grief ten thousand li away, in her golden room, for me?
poems.n: A soldier on the tower at dusk hears a flute playing a frontier song of homesickness — and thinks not of his own grief but of his wife's, far away, which he can do nothing to relieve. The "sea" is Qinghai Lake.

poems.s: night moon mountains river boat two
z: 沅水通波接武冈，送君不觉有离伤。
青山一道同云雨，明月何曾是两乡。
e: The Yuan's waves flow straight on to Wugang;
Seeing you off, I hardly feel the parting's pain.
One range of green hills shares the same clouds and rain —
And when was the bright moon in two lands? It shines on both the same.
poems.n: A rare cheerful farewell, written in exile at Longbiao: the same river, the same hills, the same weather and the same moon join the friends, so they are never really apart.

poems.te: Gazing at the Lingering Snow on Zhongnan
poems.s: dusk winter snow peaks clouds wall
z: 终南阴岭秀，积雪浮云端。
林表明霁色，城中增暮寒。
e: Zhongnan's northern ridges rise in beauty proud;
The lingering snow floats high above the clouds.
The treetops glow with light as skies clear late;
And in the city, evening's cold grows great.
poems.n: An examination poem: required to write twelve lines, Zu Yong stopped at four, saying "the meaning is complete". From Chang'an, the snow on the shaded northern slopes of the Zhongnan mountains catches the clearing sunset — and makes the city below feel colder.

poems.s: night moon window frost
z: 床前明月光，疑是地上霜。
举头望明月，低头思故乡。
e: Before my bed there gleams a silver light —
Could it be frost that settles on the ground?
I raise my head: the moon is shining bright;
I bow my head: my thoughts are homeward bound.
poems.n: The best-known poem in the Chinese language; nearly every child can recite it. Far from home, the traveller wakes to moonlight so pale he takes it for frost. The same moon shines over his distant hometown, and the simple movement of raising and lowering his head carries him there. (床 may be a bed, or — some scholars argue — the railing of a well in the courtyard.)

poems.te: Viewing the Waterfall at Mount Lu
poems.s: day sun peaks waterfall mist
z: 日照香炉生紫烟，遥看瀑布挂前川。
飞流直下三千尺，疑是银河落九天。
e: Sunlight on Censer Peak sets violet mist aglow;
Far off, a waterfall hangs on the stream below.
It flies three thousand feet straight down through air —
The Milky Way, it seems, poured from the Ninth Heaven there.
poems.n: Censer Peak (香炉峰) on Mount Lu in Jiangxi is named for its shape and the incense-like mists that rise from it. "Three thousand feet" is Li Bai's typical grand exaggeration. The Chinese call the Milky Way the "Silver River" (银河), and the Ninth Heaven is the highest of the heavens — so the waterfall becomes the river of stars tumbling to earth.

poems.s: dawn clouds peaks river boat
z: 朝辞白帝彩云间，千里江陵一日还。
两岸猿声啼不住，轻舟已过万重山。
e: At dawn I leave White Emperor town, high in the rosy cloud;
A thousand li to Jiangling — and home within a day.
From both the banks the gibbons cry, unceasing and aloud;
My little boat has slipped ten thousand peaks away.
poems.n: Written in 759. Li Bai, exiled to the far southwest for his part in a prince's rebellion, received a pardon at Baidi, high above the Yangtze. The headlong rush down the Three Gorges mirrors his joy: the boat is "light" (轻舟) in more ways than one, and the gibbons' cries — usually the saddest sound in Chinese poetry — are left behind.

poems.t: 黄鹤楼送孟浩然之广陵
poems.te: Seeing Meng Haoran Off to Guangling at Yellow Crane Tower
poems.s: spring tower river sail willow
z: 故人西辞黄鹤楼，烟花三月下扬州。
孤帆远影碧空尽，唯见长江天际流。
e: My old friend bids the Yellow Crane Tower in the west goodbye;
In the third month's mist of blossom, down to Yangzhou he goes.
His lonely sail, a fading shade, is lost in the blue sky;
Now only the Long River to the edge of heaven flows.
poems.n: Meng Haoran, twelve years older, was a poet Li Bai idolised. The poem names no feeling at all — Li Bai simply stands watching until the sail vanishes, and that long gaze is the friendship. Yangzhou (Guangling) in spring was the most glamorous city of the empire; 烟花 "mist and flowers" became a set phrase for its springtime.

poems.s: spring river boat peach two
z: 李白乘舟将欲行，忽闻岸上踏歌声。
桃花潭水深千尺，不及汪伦送我情。
e: I, Li Bai, am aboard my boat, about to sail away,
When suddenly from shore I hear a stamping, singing throng.
Though Peach Blossom Pool is a thousand feet deep, they say,
It's not so deep as Wang Lun's love that sees me off with song.
poems.n: Wang Lun was a local gentleman of Jingxian (Anhui) who had invited the famous poet to stay. As Li Bai was leaving, Wang came down to the shore with villagers, singing and stamping out the rhythm (踏歌, "stepping song"). Naming himself in the first line is a cheerful informality almost unique in Tang poetry.

poems.s: night moon flowers person jar cup
z: 花间一壶酒，独酌无相亲。
举杯邀明月，对影成三人。
月既不解饮，影徒随我身。
暂伴月将影，行乐须及春。
我歌月徘徊，我舞影零乱。
醒时同交欢，醉后各分散。
永结无情游，相期邈云汉。
e: Among the flowers, a jug of wine;
I pour alone, with no one nigh.
I lift my cup to invite the moon —
With my shadow, we make three: moon, shade and I.
But the moon has never learned to drink,
And my shadow only does what I do;
Yet for a while, with moon and shadow,
Let's revel while the spring is new.
I sing — the moon lingers and sways;
I dance — my shadow reels and sprawls.
Sober, we share our joy together;
Drunk, we each go where slumber calls.
Let us pledge a friendship free of worldly ties,
To meet again beyond the Milky Way's far skies.
poems.n: The first of Li Bai's four poems "Drinking Alone by Moonlight". Loneliness becomes a party of three, then dissolves back into solitude. The closing pledge of a 无情游 — a companionship beyond human feeling, with moon and shadow who have none — to be renewed in the Milky Way (云汉), makes his two silent friends his companions for eternity.

poems.s: night moon river mountains cup jar two
z: 君不见黄河之水天上来，奔流到海不复回。
君不见高堂明镜悲白发，朝如青丝暮成雪。
人生得意须尽欢，莫使金樽空对月。
天生我材必有用，千金散尽还复来。
烹羊宰牛且为乐，会须一饮三百杯。
岑夫子，丹丘生，将进酒，杯莫停。
与君歌一曲，请君为我倾耳听。
钟鼓馔玉不足贵，但愿长醉不复醒。
古来圣贤皆寂寞，惟有饮者留其名。
陈王昔时宴平乐，斗酒十千恣欢谑。
主人何为言少钱，径须沽取对君酌。
五花马，千金裘，呼儿将出换美酒，与尔同销万古愁。
e: Have you not seen the Yellow River's waters, sent from heaven's height,
Rush to the sea and never more return?
Have you not seen, in lofty halls, the mirror mourn hair turned to white —
Black silk at dawn, by dusk like snow? Then learn:
When life goes well, enjoy it to the full;
Don't let your golden goblet face the moon in vain.
Heaven made my talents — they will find their use;
Spend a thousand gold — the gold will come again.
Roast the lamb and kill the ox, and let us make merry —
Three hundred cups at a single sitting we must drain!
Master Cen, and Danqiu, my friend,
Bring in the wine — don't let your cups stand still!
Let me sing a song for you —
Lend me your ears, if you will:
Bells and drums and jade-fine feasts — what are they worth?
I only wish to stay drunk, and never wake again.
The sages and the worthies all lie lonely in the earth;
Only the great drinkers' names remain.
The Prince of Chen once feasted in the Pingle Hall,
Ten thousand cash a cask, carousing without end.
Why does our host say he is short of money? Go and buy it all,
And fill our cups, so we can drink, my friend!
My dappled horse,
My fur worth a thousand gold —
Call the boy, take them out, and trade them for fine wine,
And with you I'll drown the sorrows of ten thousand years untold!
poems.n: "Bring in the Wine" (an old Han ballad title) was written around 752 as Li Bai drank with his friends Cen Xun and Yuan Danqiu. It opens with two images of time's unstoppable flow — the Yellow River pouring from heaven to the sea, hair turning white in a single day — and answers them with defiant joy and boundless self-belief. The Prince of Chen is the poet Cao Zhi, famous for his lavish banquets at Pingle Lodge.

poems.te: The Road to Shu Is Hard
poems.s: day peaks clouds pine waterfall mist birds
z: 噫吁嚱，危乎高哉！
蜀道之难，难于上青天！
蚕丛及鱼凫，开国何茫然！
尔来四万八千岁，不与秦塞通人烟。
西当太白有鸟道，可以横绝峨眉巅。
地崩山摧壮士死，然后天梯石栈相钩连。
上有六龙回日之高标，下有冲波逆折之回川。
黄鹤之飞尚不得过，猿猱欲度愁攀援。
青泥何盘盘，百步九折萦岩峦。
扪参历井仰胁息，以手抚膺坐长叹。
问君西游何时还？畏途巉岩不可攀。
但见悲鸟号古木，雄飞雌从绕林间。
又闻子规啼夜月，愁空山。
蜀道之难，难于上青天，使人听此凋朱颜！
连峰去天不盈尺，枯松倒挂倚绝壁。
飞湍瀑流争喧豗，砯崖转石万壑雷。
其险也如此，嗟尔远道之人胡为乎来哉！
剑阁峥嵘而崔嵬，一夫当关，万夫莫开。
所守或匪亲，化为狼与豺。
朝避猛虎，夕避长蛇；磨牙吮血，杀人如麻。
锦城虽云乐，不如早还家。
蜀道之难，难于上青天，侧身西望长咨嗟！
e: Ah! Oh! How steep! How high!
The road to Shu is hard — harder than climbing the blue sky!
Cancong and Yufu, who founded the land —
How dim and distant, those days, to understand!
For forty-eight thousand years since then,
No smoke of hearths crossed to the Qin frontier's men.
West, by Mount Taibai, runs a track only birds can trace,
That cuts across to Emei's summit face.
Then the earth split, the mountain fell, the strong men died,
And ladders to heaven, stone plank-roads, were linked along the side.
Above, a peak so high the sun's six dragons turn their car;
Below, the rapids dash and twist where the whirling eddies are.
The yellow crane in flight can never cross that height;
The gibbons long to pass, and dread the climb outright.
How Green Mud Ridge goes coiling, coiling round —
Nine turns in a hundred steps, through crags it's wound!
You touch Orion, pass the Well Star, gasp and look on high;
You sit and clutch your chest, and heave a long, long sigh.
I ask you, traveller to the west, when will you come back home?
The road is fearful, sheer the cliffs — no foot can overcome.
You see only mournful birds that cry in ancient trees,
The male in front, the female after, circling through the leaves;
You hear the cuckoo weep beneath the moon at night,
Grieving the empty hills.
The road to Shu is hard — harder than climbing the blue sky!
Just hearing of it, rosy cheeks would fade and youth would fly.
Peak after peak, not a foot from heaven's floor,
Dead pines hang upside down from cliffs they cling to more and more.
The flying torrents, roaring falls, compete in their uproar;
They pound the cliffs and roll the rocks — ten thousand gorges' thunder-roar.
Such is its peril!
Alas, you traveller from afar, why ever come this way?
Sword Gate Pass looms, jagged and steep:
One man can hold it — ten thousand cannot break in to sweep.
And if its guards are not men you can trust,
They'll turn to wolves and jackals, as such men must.
By day beware the tiger, by night beware the snake —
They grind their teeth and suck men's blood, and kill like reapers' rake.
Though Brocade City may be fair, they say,
Better go home without delay.
The road to Shu is hard — harder than climbing the blue sky!
I turn and gaze toward the west, and heave a long, long sigh.
poems.n: Shu is today's Sichuan, cut off from the central plain by mountain ranges crossed only on plank roads pinned to cliff faces. Li Bai, a son of Shu, mixes legend (the ancient kings Cancong and Yufu; five strongmen killed when a mountain collapsed as they dragged a snake from its cave; the six dragons pulling the sun's chariot) with real geography, in wildly irregular lines that lurch like the road itself. When He Zhizhang read it, he called Li Bai "an immortal banished from heaven".

poems.s: winter snow mountains river sail person
z: 金樽清酒斗十千，玉盘珍羞直万钱。
停杯投箸不能食，拔剑四顾心茫然。
欲渡黄河冰塞川，将登太行雪满山。
闲来垂钓碧溪上，忽复乘舟梦日边。
行路难，行路难，多歧路，今安在？
长风破浪会有时，直挂云帆济沧海。
e: Clear wine in cups of gold, ten thousand cash a measure;
Rare dishes on a plate of jade, worth ten thousand more —
I set my cup aside, cast down my chopsticks — no pleasure;
I draw my sword and look around, heart lost, unsure.
I'd cross the Yellow River — ice has choked its flow;
I'd climb the Taihang Mountains — snow lies deep on every height.
Then let me fish, as the old sage did, where green brooks go,
Or dream, like Yi Yin, of sailing toward the sun's own light.
Hard is the road! Hard is the road!
So many forks — and where am I now?
A day will come to ride the wind and break the waves:
I'll hoist my cloud-high sail and cross the boundless sea somehow.
poems.n: Written in 744 when Li Bai left the court at Chang'an, his hopes of a political career in ruins. Ice and snow block every way forward. The fisherman is Lü Shang, who fished in obscurity until King Wen of Zhou discovered him; Yi Yin dreamed of sailing past the sun just before King Tang employed him — both sages who waited for their moment. The famous last couplet turns despair into confidence.

poems.s: day sun mountains river sail
z: 天门中断楚江开，碧水东流至此回。
两岸青山相对出，孤帆一片日边来。
e: The Gate of Heaven splits in two; the Chu River bursts through;
Its blue-green waters, flowing east, here swirl and turn around.
From either bank the green hills stride out, facing, into view —
And from beside the sun there comes a single sail, without a sound.
poems.n: Tianmen ("Heaven's Gate") is a pair of hills facing each other across the Yangtze in Anhui. Sailing downstream, Li Bai sees the hills seem to step forward to meet him as his boat approaches — a moving-camera view, a thousand years before cinema.

poems.s: day mountains clouds birds person pine
z: 众鸟高飞尽，孤云独去闲。
相看两不厌，只有敬亭山。
e: The flocks of birds fly high and disappear;
A lonely cloud drifts off without a care.
We gaze and gaze, and never tire of it —
Just Jingting Mountain, and I, sitting there.
poems.n: Written in 753 near Xuancheng, when Li Bai was past fifty and long out of favour. Birds and clouds — like friends and fortune — all leave him; only the mountain stays, and the two regard each other like old friends who need no words.

poems.te: Staying the Night at a Mountain Temple
poems.s: night stars temple mountains crescent
z: 危楼高百尺，手可摘星辰。
不敢高声语，恐惊天上人。
e: The towering pagoda soars a hundred feet in height;
From here my hand could pluck the stars of night.
I dare not raise my voice above a sigh,
For fear of waking those who dwell on high.
poems.n: A temple tower on a mountaintop, so high that the stars are within reach and heaven's residents might overhear. Built entirely from playful exaggeration, it is one of the first poems Chinese children learn.

poems.te: Song of the Moon over Mount Emei
poems.s: night autumn crescent mountains river boat
z: 峨眉山月半轮秋，影入平羌江水流。
夜发清溪向三峡，思君不见下渝州。
e: Over Mount Emei hangs the autumn half-moon's light;
Its image floats along the Pingqiang's flowing stream.
I leave Clear Creek for the Three Gorges in the night;
I miss you — you are lost to sight — and drift to Yuzhou in a dream.
poems.n: Written around 725 when the young Li Bai first left his home province of Shu. In four lines he names five places — Emei, the Pingqiang River, Clear Creek, the Three Gorges, Yuzhou — yet the poem reads as one smooth glide downstream. The "you" he misses may be the moon itself, hidden now behind the gorge cliffs, or a friend left behind.

poems.te: Hearing a Flute on a Spring Night in Luoyang
poems.s: night spring moon willow tower
z: 谁家玉笛暗飞声，散入春风满洛城。
此夜曲中闻折柳，何人不起故园情。
e: Whose jade flute sends its notes in secret flight,
Scattered by spring winds through Luoyang's every street?
Hearing "Breaking Willows" in the tune tonight,
Whose heart would not for home and garden beat?
poems.n: "Breaking Willows" (折杨柳) was a farewell tune: friends parting gave each other a willow twig, because 柳 (willow) sounds like 留 (stay). Hearing it played by an unseen flautist in the spring night, the poet realises the whole city must be thinking of home.

poems.s: dusk sun hills river wall rider two
z: 青山横北郭，白水绕东城。
此地一为别，孤蓬万里征。
浮云游子意，落日故人情。
挥手自兹去，萧萧班马鸣。
e: Green hills lie stretched beyond the northern wall;
White water winds around the eastern town.
Once we have parted here, you'll be a lonely weed
Ten thousand li along the road, wind-blown.
The drifting clouds — a wanderer's mind;
The setting sun — an old friend's heart.
We wave our hands, and from this place you go;
Your horse, leaving the herd, neighs as we part.
poems.n: A model regulated poem, its middle couplets perfectly parallel. The drifting cloud is the departing friend, the reluctant setting sun the friend left behind. The last line borrows from the *Book of Songs*: 班马 is a horse separated from its companions, crying out — the animals feel the parting too.

poems.s: night moon clouds river boat hills
z: 渡远荆门外，来从楚国游。
山随平野尽，江入大荒流。
月下飞天镜，云生结海楼。
仍怜故乡水，万里送行舟。
e: I've crossed afar, beyond the Jingmen Gate,
To roam among the lands of ancient Chu.
The hills give way as the broad plains begin;
The River pours into the wilds — a boundless view.
The moon drops down, a mirror flying through the sky;
Clouds rise and build sea-towers out of the blue.
Still I love my native river, that has come
Ten thousand li to see my boat off, as friends do.
poems.n: Li Bai at about twenty-four, leaving Sichuan for the first time. Past the Jingmen gorge the mountains suddenly end and the Yangtze spreads into the plains of Hubei. The moon in the water is a "flying mirror", the clouds a mirage of "sea towers". The "farewell" of the title is the river from home seeing him off.

poems.t: 闻王昌龄左迁龙标遥有此寄
poems.te: On Hearing That Wang Changling Was Demoted to Longbiao
poems.s: night moon willow mountains river
z: 杨花落尽子规啼，闻道龙标过五溪。
我寄愁心与明月，随君直到夜郎西。
e: The willow-down has fallen, and the cuckoos weep;
I hear you pass Five Streams, to Longbiao sent away.
I give my grieving heart into the bright moon's keep,
To follow you to the west of Yelang all the way.
poems.n: Wang Changling, a fellow poet and friend, was banished to remote Longbiao (in today's Hunan) around 748. The cuckoo's cry was heard as 不如归去, "better go home". Unable to follow, Li Bai entrusts his heart to the moon, which shines on both of them — one of the best-loved images of friendship in Chinese.

poems.s: night spring moon palace flowers clouds
z: 云想衣裳花想容，春风拂槛露华浓。
若非群玉山头见，会向瑶台月下逢。
e: Clouds bring her robes to mind, and flowers, her face;
The spring wind strokes the rail, the dew lies thick and bright.
If she is not a goddess seen on Jade Mountain's height,
She must be one you'd meet on Jasper Terrace by moonlight.
poems.n: Written to order around 743, when Emperor Xuanzong and his beloved Consort Yang were admiring peonies at the Aloeswood Pavilion. Li Bai, reportedly still drunk, dashed off three songs. In this one the consort and the peony blur into each other, and both into a goddess of the Queen Mother of the West's paradise (Jade Mountain, Jasper Terrace).

poems.s: night autumn moon wall wind
z: 长安一片月，万户捣衣声。
秋风吹不尽，总是玉关情。
何日平胡虏，良人罢远征。
e: One sheet of moonlight over Chang'an lies;
From ten thousand homes the fulling-mallets pound.
The autumn wind blows on and never dies —
All of it heartache, for the Jade Gate bound.
When will we crush the raiders and have peace,
So my good man's long campaigns may cease?
poems.n: Women beat cloth on stones to soften it before sewing winter clothes for husbands at the frontier, so the sound of "pounding clothes" (捣衣) was the sound of autumn longing. The Jade Gate Pass (玉门关) was the gateway to the western frontier. Li Bai turns an old southern love-song form into the voice of a whole city's grief.

poems.te: The Moon over the Mountain Pass
poems.s: night moon clouds mountains fort wind
z: 明月出天山，苍茫云海间。
长风几万里，吹度玉门关。
