汉下白登道，胡窥青海湾。
由来征战地，不见有人还。
戍客望边色，思归多苦颜。
高楼当此夜，叹息未应闲。
e: The bright moon rises over Tianshan's height,
Amid a boundless sea of clouds and haze.
A long wind sweeps ten thousand li of night,
And blows through Jade Gate Pass along its ways.
Han armies marched down Baideng's road;
The Hu still eye the bays of Qinghai's shore.
From these old battlefields, as all men know,
Not one has ever come back home from war.
The soldiers gaze upon the frontier scene,
Their faces bitter, longing to return;
In high towers on this night, their wives, unseen,
Must sigh and sigh, and cannot rest, but yearn.
poems.n: An old ballad title, reworked on an immense scale: the moon over the Tianshan range, a wind blowing ten thousand li to the Jade Gate. Baideng is where the Han founder was besieged by the Xiongnu; Qinghai Lake was a Tang–Tibetan battleground. The last couplet cuts from the frontier to the wives in their towers far away, watching the same moon.

poems.s: night autumn moon palace window
z: 玉阶生白露，夜久侵罗袜。
却下水晶帘，玲珑望秋月。
e: White dew is forming on the jade stair;
The night grows long; it soaks her silken hose.
She lowers the crystal curtain — there,
Through its glinting beads, the autumn moon still glows.
poems.n: A palace lament in which nothing is said of feeling. A woman has waited on the steps so long that the dew soaks her stockings; she goes in and lowers the blind — and still cannot stop gazing at the moon through it. Ezra Pound admired the poem for saying everything by implication.

poems.s: day window palace flowers
z: 美人卷珠帘，深坐颦蛾眉。
但见泪痕湿，不知心恨谁。
e: The beauty rolls the pearly curtain high,
Sits deep within, her moth-brows knit in pain.
You only see the tear-stains, not yet dry —
But whom her heart resents, she won't explain.
poems.n: Another portrait of a woman's sorrow told only through gesture: rolling up the blind (to watch for someone), sitting long, frowning, weeping. "Moth-brows" — long, curved, delicate eyebrows — were the classic mark of beauty. The cause is left a mystery.

poems.t: 宣州谢朓楼饯别校书叔云
poems.te: Farewell to Secretary Shuyun at Xie Tiao's Tower in Xuanzhou
poems.s: autumn day geese tower river mountains wind
z: 弃我去者，昨日之日不可留；
乱我心者，今日之日多烦忧。
长风万里送秋雁，对此可以酣高楼。
蓬莱文章建安骨，中间小谢又清发。
俱怀逸兴壮思飞，欲上青天揽明月。
抽刀断水水更流，举杯销愁愁更愁。
人生在世不称意，明朝散发弄扁舟。
e: What has abandoned me —
Yesterday — I cannot keep;
What troubles my heart —
Today — its cares are deep.
The long wind speeds the autumn geese ten thousand li away;
Facing this, in the high tower, let us drink our fill today.
Your prose has Penglai's grace, my verse the bones of Jian'an's age,
With Little Xie's clear freshness in between, upon the page.
We both are full of soaring moods and thoughts in lofty flight —
We'd climb the azure sky to pluck the moon so bright.
I draw my sword to cut the stream — the stream flows on the more;
I raise my cup to drown my grief — my grief grows all the more.
If life in this world will not go the way we planned,
Tomorrow, hair unpinned, I'll take a skiff and leave the land.
poems.n: Xie Tiao (464–499), a poet Li Bai revered, built this tower in Xuanzhou. "Penglai writing" alludes to the Han imperial library, "Jian'an bones" to the vigour of Cao Cao's era — praise for his kinsman's prose and his own verse. "Cutting water with a sword" became a proverb for sorrow that cannot be stopped; unpinning the hair meant leaving official life for a free one.

poems.te: A Dream Journey to Mount Tianmu: A Farewell
poems.s: night moon peaks clouds waterfall lake mist crane
z: 海客谈瀛洲，烟涛微茫信难求；
越人语天姥，云霞明灭或可睹。
天姥连天向天横，势拔五岳掩赤城。
天台四万八千丈，对此欲倒东南倾。
我欲因之梦吴越，一夜飞度镜湖月。
湖月照我影，送我至剡溪。
谢公宿处今尚在，渌水荡漾清猿啼。
脚著谢公屐，身登青云梯。
半壁见海日，空中闻天鸡。
千岩万转路不定，迷花倚石忽已暝。
熊咆龙吟殷岩泉，栗深林兮惊层巅。
云青青兮欲雨，水澹澹兮生烟。
列缺霹雳，丘峦崩摧。
洞天石扉，訇然中开。
青冥浩荡不见底，日月照耀金银台。
霓为衣兮风为马，云之君兮纷纷而来下。
虎鼓瑟兮鸾回车，仙之人兮列如麻。
忽魂悸以魄动，恍惊起而长嗟。
惟觉时之枕席，失向来之烟霞。
世间行乐亦如此，古来万事东流水。
别君去兮何时还？且放白鹿青崖间，须行即骑访名山。
安能摧眉折腰事权贵，使我不得开心颜！
e: Seafarers tell of Yingzhou, isle of the immortals' rest —
Through misty waves so dim and far, it's truly hard to find;
But men of Yue speak of Mount Tianmu, whose crest
In flickering cloud and rosy light may sometimes be divined.
Tianmu joins the sky and lies across the sky's expanse;
It overtops the Five Great Peaks and hides the Red Wall Hill;
Tiantai, forty-eight thousand feet, at a single glance
Seems to topple southeast before it, bowing lower still.
So, longing for Wu and Yue, I dreamed — and in one night
Flew over Mirror Lake beneath the moon.
The lake-moon lit my shadow, and it led me with its light
To Shan Creek, where Lord Xie once lodged; it stands there still,
With clear green waters rippling, and the gibbons' crying shrill.
I put on Lord Xie's climbing clogs
And mounted the ladder of blue cloud.
Halfway up the cliff I saw the sun rise from the sea,
And heard the Heavenly Rooster crow aloud.
A thousand crags, ten thousand turns — the path would twist and stray;
Lost among flowers, leaning on rocks, I found the light had gone away.
Bears roared and dragons chanted, booming through the rocks and springs;
The deep woods shook, the topmost peaks were startled at such things.
The clouds were dark and heavy, close to rain;
The waters rippled, breathing mist again.
Then lightning split the sky, and thunder roared;
The hills and ridges crumbled and collapsed.
The stone gates of the grotto-heaven
With a crash flew open wide.
A blue void, vast and fathomless, lay beyond;
Sun and moon shone on terraces of gold and silver inside.
With rainbows for their robes and winds for horses,
The Lords of the Clouds came streaming down in throngs;
Tigers struck the zithers, phoenixes drew the carriages round;
Immortals stood in ranks, as thick as hemp upon the ground.
Then suddenly my soul was shaken, my spirit stirred —
I started up awake with a long sigh;
There was only the pillow and the mat I woke upon;
The mist and rosy clouds of before were gone.
The pleasures of this world are just the same:
Since ancient times, all things flow east like water, and are gone.
I leave you now — when shall I return?
For now I'll set my white deer free among the green cliffs to roam,
And ride it, when I must, to visit the famous mountains, my true home.
How could I bow my brows and bend my back to serve the great,
And never let my heart be glad, and never let my face be bright?
poems.n: Written in 745 as Li Bai left eastern Shandong for the south, a year after leaving the court. The dream climbs Mount Tianmu in Zhejiang in the footsteps of Xie Lingyun (Lord Xie), the 5th-century landscape poet who invented special clogs for mountain climbing, and bursts into a vision of an immortals' paradise — which vanishes on waking. The moral explodes in the last line: no worldly glory is worth bending the back to the powerful. It became a creed for independent spirits.

poems.s: day clouds tower river hills sail
z: 凤凰台上凤凰游，凤去台空江自流。
吴宫花草埋幽径，晋代衣冠成古丘。
三山半落青天外，二水中分白鹭洲。
总为浮云能蔽日，长安不见使人愁。
e: On Phoenix Terrace phoenixes once used to play;
The phoenixes are gone, the terrace bare; the river flows its way.
The flowers and grasses of the Wu palace bury hidden lanes;
The robes and caps of Jin are ancient mounds today.
The Three Peaks, half-dissolving, lean beyond the blue;
Two waters split around White Egret Isle midway.
It's all because the drifting clouds can hide the sun —
Chang'an is lost to sight, and grief has come to stay.
poems.n: Jinling (Nanjing) had been the capital of six dynasties, all long vanished. Li Bai's poem deliberately echoes Cui Hao's *Yellow Crane Tower*, which he had admired. The ending turns from history to politics: the "drifting clouds" hiding the sun are the slanderers who cut Li Bai off from the emperor in Chang'an.

poems.s: autumn river person mountains window
z: 白发三千丈，缘愁似个长。
不知明镜里，何处得秋霜。
e: My white hair hangs three thousand yards —
So long, because my grief is long as well.
Into the bright mirror I stare:
Where did this autumn frost come from? I cannot tell.
poems.n: From a series of seventeen songs on the Qiupu River in Anhui, written in Li Bai's fifties. "White hair three thousand *zhang*" (about 10 km!) is the most famous exaggeration in Chinese poetry, and it is somehow perfectly true to the feeling of seeing oneself suddenly old.

poems.s: dusk sun cup jar person cottage
z: 兰陵美酒郁金香，玉碗盛来琥珀光。
但使主人能醉客，不知何处是他乡。
e: The fine wine of Lanling breathes of turmeric's scent;
Poured in a bowl of jade, it gleams with amber light.
If only my host can get his guest well drunk tonight,
I'll never know which land is foreign, or where I went.
poems.n: Lanling (in Shandong) was famous for its wine, scented with 郁金 (turmeric or curcuma). Most travel poems are homesick; this one, from Li Bai's carefree younger days, cheerfully proposes that good enough wine makes anywhere home.

poems.s: dusk palace birds flowers person
z: 越王勾践破吴归，义士还家尽锦衣。
宫女如花满春殿，只今惟有鹧鸪飞。
e: King Goujian of Yue came home, the land of Wu destroyed;
His loyal warriors returned, all dressed in brocade.
Palace girls, like flowers, filled the spring halls he enjoyed —
And now, there's only partridges flying where they played.
poems.n: Goujian, king of Yue, was crushed by Wu, slept on brushwood and tasted gall for years to keep his vengeance alive, and finally destroyed Wu in 473 BC. Three lines of triumph and splendour; then one line of desolation sweeps it all away.

poems.te: Question and Answer in the Mountains
poems.s: spring peaks river petals peach person
z: 问余何意栖碧山，笑而不答心自闲。
桃花流水窅然去，别有天地非人间。
e: You ask me why I dwell among the green hills here;
I smile and don't reply — my heart is calm and free.
Peach blossoms on the water drift away, and disappear:
There is another world, not of men, for me.
poems.n: Peach blossoms floating on a stream recall Tao Yuanming's *Peach Blossom Spring*, a hidden paradise found by following petals upstream. The best answer to "why live in the mountains?" is a smile.

poems.te: Drinking with a Recluse in the Mountains
poems.s: spring mountains flowers two cup jar
z: 两人对酌山花开，一杯一杯复一杯。
我醉欲眠卿且去，明朝有意抱琴来。
e: We two sit drinking where the mountain flowers bloom —
One cup, another cup, and then another cup.
I'm drunk and want to sleep — be off now, leave the room!
Tomorrow, if you like, bring your zither, and come up.
poems.n: Spontaneity itself: the second line simply repeats "one cup" three times. The third line borrows from Tao Yuanming, who used to tell his guests "I'm drunk and want to sleep — you may go" — the frankness of true friends.

poems.s: night moon clouds pine tower
z: 小时不识月，呼作白玉盘。
又疑瑶台镜，飞在青云端。
e: When I was small, I didn't know the moon —
I called it a white jade plate up in the sky,
Or thought it was the Jasper Terrace mirror,
Flying above the blue clouds, way up high.
poems.n: The opening of a longer poem, recited by every Chinese child: a little boy's guesses at what the moon must be. The Jasper Terrace (瑶台) is the dwelling of immortals, so the moon is their mirror.

poems.s: autumn river butterfly cottage maple person
z: 妾发初覆额，折花门前剧。
郎骑竹马来，绕床弄青梅。
同居长干里，两小无嫌猜。
十四为君妇，羞颜未尝开。
低头向暗壁，千唤不一回。
十五始展眉，愿同尘与灰。
常存抱柱信，岂上望夫台。
十六君远行，瞿塘滟滪堆。
五月不可触，猿声天上哀。
门前迟行迹，一一生绿苔。
苔深不能扫，落叶秋风早。
八月蝴蝶黄，双飞西园草。
感此伤妾心，坐愁红颜老。
早晚下三巴，预将书报家。
相迎不道远，直至长风沙。
e: When my hair was cut in bangs above my brow,
I played by the gate, picking flowers in the sun;
You came riding on your bamboo horse, and how
We circled the well-rail, tossing green plums, just for fun.
We lived together in the lane of Changgan,
Two little ones, without suspicion or care.
At fourteen I became your wife, my man —
So shy I never smiled, I'd hardly dare;
I hung my head and faced the shadowed wall;
A thousand times you called — I never turned at all.
At fifteen my brows unknit; I wished to be
With you as dust and ashes, endlessly.
I kept the faith of the man who held the pillar fast —
Why would I climb the Watching-for-Husband Tower at last?
At sixteen you went far away from me,
Past Qutang Gorge, where Yanyu's rocks rear high —
In the fifth month, no boat can touch them safely,
And the gibbons wail up in the sky.
Before the gate, the footprints that you left behind
Have each grown over, one by one, with moss of green;
The moss is deep, too deep to sweep, I find;
Leaves fall early in the autumn wind, I've seen.
In the eighth month, yellow butterflies,
In pairs, fly over the west garden's grass;
It wounds my heart to see them; my youth flies,
And I sit grieving as my looks fade and pass.
Sooner or later, when you come down from the Three Ba,
Send me a letter home ahead — I'll go and wait;
I won't say it's far: I'll come to meet you,
All the way to Long Wind Sands, beyond the gate.
poems.n: A young merchant's wife writes to her husband trading far up the Yangtze. Her childhood with him gave Chinese two idioms for childhood sweethearts — 青梅竹马 "green plums and bamboo horse" and 两小无猜 "two little ones without suspicion". The "man who held the pillar" waited for his love under a bridge until the flood drowned him; the Watching-for-Husband Tower is where wives waited in vain. Ezra Pound's free version, *The River-Merchant's Wife: A Letter*, is one of the most famous translations in English.

poems.s: spring palace flowers clouds mist
z: 一枝红艳露凝香，云雨巫山枉断肠。
借问汉宫谁得似，可怜飞燕倚新妆。
e: A spray of crimson glory, fragrance gathered in the dew —
The goddess of Wu's cloud and rain broke hearts, but all in vain.
Who in the Han palace could have matched her? Tell me, who?
Sweet Flying Swallow, maybe — after making up again.
poems.n: The second of the three peony songs for Consort Yang. The goddess of Mount Wu, who visited a king "as cloud at dawn and rain at dusk", is no match for her; only Zhao Feiyan ("Flying Swallow"), the Han emperor's slender favourite, comes close — and only after doing her make-up. Later enemies claimed the comparison was a veiled insult, since Feiyan was notorious; it may have helped get Li Bai sent away from court.

poems.s: spring palace flowers pavilion
z: 名花倾国两相欢，长得君王带笑看。
解释春风无限恨，沉香亭北倚阑干。
e: The famous flower and the beauty who could topple states delight each other so,
And win the sovereign's smiling gaze forever, as they stand.
They melt away the endless sorrows that the spring winds blow —
North of the Aloeswood Pavilion, leaning on the rail, hand in hand.
poems.n: The last of the peony songs: flower and woman are now one pair, both 倾国 — beauty that "topples a kingdom", a phrase from a Han song. Leaning on the balustrade of the Aloeswood Pavilion, they dispel all of spring's melancholy. Within a dozen years the An Lushan rebellion would topple the kingdom in earnest, and Consort Yang would be put to death.

poems.s: night autumn moon leaves crows
z: 秋风清，秋月明，
落叶聚还散，寒鸦栖复惊。
相思相见知何日？此时此夜难为情！
入我相思门，知我相思苦，
长相思兮长相忆，短相思兮无穷极。
早知如此绊人心，何如当初莫相识。
e: Autumn wind clear,
Autumn moon bright;
Fallen leaves gather, then scatter in flight;
Cold crows settle, then start up in fright.
When shall we, who long for each other, meet? Who knows?
This hour, this night, how hard to bear these woes!
Once you have entered love's gate,
You know how bitter longing can be:
Long longing — long remembering;
Short longing — no end that I see.
Had I known how it would bind my heart so,
Better we'd never met, long ago.
poems.n: Called the "three-five-seven-character poem" for its lines that grow from three to five to seven characters, like a rising breath. The leaves that gather and scatter, the crows that settle and are startled, mirror the restless heart. The famous last couplet — "had I known it would bind my heart like this, better we had never met" — is still quoted by lovers today.

poems.s: spring pavilion willow wind two
z: 天下伤心处，劳劳送客亭。
春风知别苦，不遣柳条青。
e: Of all the places under heaven where hearts break,
None like Laolao Pavilion, where travellers are sent.
The spring wind knows how bitter partings make —
It will not let the willows green, for that's what partings meant.
poems.n: Laolao Pavilion, south of Nanjing, was the traditional place to see travellers off. Because parting friends broke off willow twigs as keepsakes, the poet imagines the spring wind kindly holding back the willows' green — no twigs, no partings.

poems.te: Climbing Xie Tiao's North Tower at Xuancheng in Autumn
poems.s: autumn dusk tower river bridge hills mist
z: 江城如画里，山晚望晴空。
两水夹明镜，双桥落彩虹。
人烟寒橘柚，秋色老梧桐。
谁念北楼上，临风怀谢公。
e: The river town lies as if painted in a scroll;
At evening, from the hills, I watch the cloudless sky.
Two streams enclose a mirror, bright and whole;
Twin bridges fall like rainbows from on high.
Chimney smoke chills the oranges and pomelos;
Autumn's colour ages the wutong trees.
Who'd think that here, upon the North Tower, someone knows
And thinks of Lord Xie, facing the breeze?
poems.n: Xuancheng (Anhui), between two rivers, was governed in the 5th century by the poet Xie Tiao, whom Li Bai revered. The middle couplets are among the most painterly in Tang verse — the bridges reflected as rainbows, the cold blue smoke among the fruit trees, autumn "aging" the wutongs. Li Bai, alone at the top, feels a kinship across three centuries.

poems.te: Listening to the Monk Jun of Shu Play the Qin
poems.s: autumn dusk pine mountains temple person clouds
z: 蜀僧抱绿绮，西下峨眉峰。
为我一挥手，如听万壑松。
客心洗流水，余响入霜钟。
不觉碧山暮，秋云暗几重。
e: A monk from Shu, his Green Silk qin in hand,
Came west from the peaks of Emei's height.
He swept his hand across the strings for me —
I heard ten thousand valleys' pines take flight.
My traveller's heart was washed as by a stream;
The echoes merged with frosty temple bells.
I did not notice the green hills grow dark,
Till autumn clouds had dimmed them, swells on swells.
poems.n: The qin (seven-stringed zither) was the scholar's instrument. Green Silk (绿绮) was the name of a famous ancient qin. "Flowing water" recalls the legendary friendship of Boya, who played, and Ziqi, who alone understood him — so the music both cleanses the poet and makes the two men soul-friends. The bell rung in frost was said to resonate of itself.

poems.s: day pine clouds mountains person cottage
z: 吾爱孟夫子，风流天下闻。
红颜弃轩冕，白首卧松云。
醉月频中圣，迷花不事君。
高山安可仰，徒此揖清芬。
e: I love you, Master Meng, my friend —
Your grace and style the whole world knows.
In youth you spurned the carriage and the crown;
Now white-haired, you lie where pine and cloud repose.
Drunk by the moon, you often "hit the sage";
Lost in the flowers, you will serve no king.
A mountain so high — how can I look up to it?
I can only bow to your pure fragrance as I sing.
poems.n: Li Bai's tribute to Meng Haoran, the older poet who never held office. "Hitting the sage" (中圣) was Wei-dynasty slang for getting drunk — "sage" meant clear wine. The last couplet quotes the *Book of Songs*: "the high mountain I look up to" — a phrase for supreme admiration.

poems.te: Mooring at Niuzhu at Night, Thinking of the Past
poems.s: night autumn moon river boat maple leaves
z: 牛渚西江夜，青天无片云。
登舟望秋月，空忆谢将军。
余亦能高咏，斯人不可闻。
明朝挂帆席，枫叶落纷纷。
e: At Niuzhu, on the Western River, night;
Not one cloud flecks the blue sky's face.
I climb the deck to watch the autumn moon,
And think in vain of General Xie's grace.
I, too, can chant my poems loud and high —
But such a man will never hear my song.
Tomorrow I will hoist my mat-sail and go,
While maple leaves fall, scattering along.
poems.n: In the 4th century General Xie Shang, mooring here on a moonlit night, overheard a poor boatman named Yuan Hong chanting his own poems, and was so impressed he made him his protégé. Li Bai moors in the same spot — and no patron comes. The falling maple leaves carry the disappointment.

poems.te: Farewell at a Wine Shop in Jinling
poems.s: spring willow cottage river jar cup two
z: 风吹柳花满店香，吴姬压酒劝客尝。
金陵子弟来相送，欲行不行各尽觞。
请君试问东流水，别意与之谁短长？
e: The wind blows willow-down; the whole shop smells of spring;
A girl of Wu presses the wine and bids the guests to taste.
The young men of Jinling have come to see me off — we cling:
I go, yet don't; and each drains cup on cup in haste.
I ask you, friends, go ask the river flowing east —
Which is longer: its flow, or this parting's feast?
poems.n: Li Bai, about 25, leaving Nanjing for Yangzhou. "Pressing the wine" means straining fresh rice wine from the mash. The image of the endless eastward-flowing river as a measure of feeling became a favourite device of later poets.

poems.te: Holding My Cup, I Ask the Moon
poems.s: night moon clouds sea person cup
z: 青天有月来几时？我今停杯一问之。
人攀明月不可得，月行却与人相随。
皎如飞镜临丹阙，绿烟灭尽清辉发。
但见宵从海上来，宁知晓向云间没。
白兔捣药秋复春，嫦娥孤栖与谁邻？
今人不见古时月，今月曾经照古人。
古人今人若流水，共看明月皆如此。
唯愿当歌对酒时，月光长照金樽里。
e: How long has the moon been in the blue sky? Here,
I put my cup down for a while to ask it so.
Men try to climb up to the moon — it's never near;
Yet as they walk, the moon walks with them where they go.
Bright as a flying mirror over the crimson gate,
When the green mists all have melted, it pours out its clear light.
We see it rising from the sea each night, but late,
Who knows where it sinks among the clouds at dawn's first light?
The white hare pounds its herbs from autumn into spring;
Chang'e lives alone — who is her neighbour there?
People today never saw the ancient moon a-shining,
Yet this moon once shone on the ancients, just as fair.
The ancients and the moderns flow on like a stream,
And all have watched the bright moon, just as we.
I only hope, when I sing over wine, its beam
Will shine into my golden cup eternally.
poems.n: Written at a friend's request. Li Bai muses on the moon's eternity against human transience: the moon follows us yet cannot be reached; it watched the ancients as it watches us. The white hare and the goddess Chang'e are the moon's legendary inhabitants. Su Shi's famous "When will the bright moon appear?" owes much to this poem.

poems.te: Leaving My Children at Nanling for the Capital
poems.s: autumn dusk sun cottage fields person rider
z: 白酒新熟山中归，黄鸡啄黍秋正肥。
呼童烹鸡酌白酒，儿女嬉笑牵人衣。
高歌取醉欲自慰，起舞落日争光辉。
游说万乘苦不早，著鞭跨马涉远道。
会稽愚妇轻买臣，余亦辞家西入秦。
仰天大笑出门去，我辈岂是蓬蒿人。
e: The white wine has just ripened as I come back to the hills;
The yellow hens peck millet, in the autumn fat and fine.
I call the boy to cook a chicken and to pour the wine;
My children laugh and tug my clothes with giggles and with trills.
I sing aloud and drink my fill to soothe my soul;
I rise to dance, and vie in brilliance with the setting sun.
Too late, I've come to counsel the Lord of Ten Thousand Chariots — the goal!
I whip my horse and ride the long road till it's done.
The foolish wife of Kuaiji scorned Zhu Maichen once, they say;
I, too, now leave my home and go west, to Qin, away.
I throw back my head and laugh aloud, and out the gate I stride —
Are men like me to live and die in brambles, cast aside?
poems.n: In 742, aged 41, Li Bai was summoned to court by Emperor Xuanzong. Zhu Maichen was a Han woodcutter whose wife left him for his poverty — and who later rose to high office. The last couplet, a shout of vindication, is one of the most quoted lines Li Bai wrote. (The court career lasted less than two years.)

poems.s: day clouds sea wind birds
z: 大鹏一日同风起，扶摇直上九万里。
假令风歇时下来，犹能簸却沧溟水。
世人见我恒殊调，闻余大言皆冷笑。
宣父犹能畏后生，丈夫未可轻年少。
e: The great Peng bird, one day, will rise up with the wind,
And spiral straight ninety thousand li into the sky;
And even if the wind should drop, and it come down,
It still could toss the waters of the vast sea high.
The people of the world find all my tunes odd,
And when they hear my boasts they sneer and scoff;
But Confucius said the young deserve respect —
A real man shouldn't brush a young man off.
poems.n: Written by the young Li Bai to Li Yong, a famous senior official who had treated him dismissively. The Peng is the colossal bird in *Zhuangzi* that rises ninety thousand li on a whirlwind. Confucius had said "the young are to be held in awe" — so Li Bai turns the sage's words against his elder.

poems.t: 下终南山过斛斯山人宿置酒
poems.te: Coming Down Zhongnan Mountain, I Stay with the Recluse Husi, Who Sets Out Wine
poems.s: dusk moon mountains bamboo cottage two pine
z: 暮从碧山下，山月随人归。
却顾所来径，苍苍横翠微。
相携及田家，童稚开荆扉。
绿竹入幽径，青萝拂行衣。
欢言得所憩，美酒聊共挥。
长歌吟松风，曲尽河星稀。
我醉君复乐，陶然共忘机。
e: At dusk I came down from the jade-green hill;
The mountain moon came home with me.
Looking back on the path I'd come along,
I saw blue haze across the green slopes lie, so free.
Hand in hand, we came to his farmhouse;
The children opened up the thorn-wood gate.
Green bamboo lined the hidden path,
Green vines brushed my clothes as I walked straight.
We talked and laughed, so glad to rest,
And shared the fine wine, cup by cup.
We sang long songs to the wind in the pines,
Till the songs were done, and few stars still were up.
I was drunk, and you were merry too —
Content, we both forgot the world's deceit and its ado.
poems.n: A pastoral evening in the manner of Tao Yuanming. Zhongnan Mountain, south of Chang'an, was home to many hermits. 忘机 — "forgetting scheming" — is the Daoist ideal of a mind free of calculation: a man who has forgotten scheming, the story goes, can play among the seagulls without frightening them.

poems.s: night moon sea clouds sail
z: 日本晁卿辞帝都，征帆一片绕蓬壶。
明月不归沉碧海，白云愁色满苍梧。
e: Lord Chao of Japan has left the imperial capital;
His single sail went circling round the Isles of Penglai.
The bright moon has not returned — it sank beneath the blue sea;
White clouds of sorrow fill the Cangwu sky.
poems.n: Chao Heng was Abe no Nakamaro, a Japanese scholar who passed the Tang examinations and served at court for decades, a friend of Li Bai and Wang Wei. In 753 he set sail for Japan and was reported drowned. In fact he was shipwrecked on the coast of Vietnam and made his way back to Chang'an — but the poem, written in grief, stayed. He is the "bright moon" lost at sea.

poems.s: spring window grass willow wind
z: 燕草如碧丝，秦桑低绿枝。
当君怀归日，是妾断肠时。
春风不相识，何事入罗帏？
e: In Yan, the grass is like fine jade-green thread;
In Qin, the mulberry bows its green boughs low.
The day you long for home at last, I dread,
Will be the day my heart breaks — long ago.
Spring wind, you are a stranger here to me —
Why do you slip into my silken bed-curtains so?
poems.n: A wife in Qin (around Chang'an) thinks of her husband in Yan (the far north-east). Spring comes late in Yan: when his grass is only just sprouting, her mulberries are already heavy — her heart has been breaking for a long time. The last couplet's prim rebuke to the spring wind is a declaration of fidelity.

poems.s: snow mountains fort flag rider
z: 五月天山雪，无花只有寒。
笛中闻折柳，春色未曾看。
晓战随金鼓，宵眠抱玉鞍。
愿将腰下剑，直为斩楼兰。
e: In the fifth month there's still snow on the Tianshan peaks:
No flowers bloom; there's nothing here but cold.
Only in the flute's "Breaking Willows" spring still speaks;
The spring itself, no eye here can behold.
At dawn we fight, to the gongs' and war-drums' beat;
At night we sleep with jade saddles in our arms.
I only wish the sword here at my waist
Could cut down Loulan's king and end these harms.
poems.n: The Tianshan range in Central Asia, where even midsummer is winter. The soldiers know spring only from the tune "Breaking Willows" played on a flute. In 77 BC the Han envoy Fu Jiezi assassinated the treacherous king of Loulan, a desert oasis kingdom; "beheading Loulan" became the soldier's dream of decisive victory.

poems.te: Viewing the Past at Gusu Terrace
poems.s: night moon willow palace lake
z: 旧苑荒台杨柳新，菱歌清唱不胜春。
只今惟有西江月，曾照吴王宫里人。
e: Old parks, a ruined terrace — yet the willows are new;
The water-chestnut songs ring clear, too full of spring to bear.
Now only the moon above the Western River, true,
Once shone on the ladies of the King of Wu's palace there.
poems.n: Gusu Terrace in Suzhou was built by Fuchai, King of Wu, for the legendary beauty Xi Shi, before his kingdom fell to Yue. The new willows and the girls' songs make the ruin unbearable; the moon is the only witness left from those days. Companion piece to *Viewing the Past at Yue*.

poems.s: night autumn moon window clouds candle
z: 长相思，在长安。
络纬秋啼金井阑，微霜凄凄簟色寒。
孤灯不明思欲绝，卷帷望月空长叹。
美人如花隔云端！
上有青冥之高天，下有渌水之波澜。
天长路远魂飞苦，梦魂不到关山难。
长相思，摧心肝！
e: Endless longing —
In Chang'an town.
The crickets cry in autumn by the golden well-rail's crown;
A light frost, chill and bleak; my bamboo mat is cold.
My lonely lamp burns dim; my longing's near to death;
I roll the curtain, watch the moon, and sigh with empty breath.
My love, like a flower, is far beyond the clouds!
Above, the blue and boundless height of heaven;
Below, the clear and rippling waves.
The sky is wide, the road is long; my soul's flight is hard;
Even in dreams my spirit can't cross the mountain passes barred.
Endless longing —
It breaks my heart!
poems.n: An old ballad title. The beloved "like a flower beyond the clouds" may be a woman — or, in a long tradition of Chinese allegory, the emperor whom the exiled poet longs to serve. Either reading makes the soul that cannot even reach its goal in dreams heartbreaking.

poems.te: Seeing a Friend Off to Shu
poems.s: spring peaks clouds rider river wall
z: 见说蚕丛路，崎岖不易行。
山从人面起，云傍马头生。
芳树笼秦栈，春流绕蜀城。
升沉应已定，不必问君平。
e: They say the road to Cancong's land of Shu
Is steep and rough, and hard to travel through:
Mountains rise right up before your face;
Clouds are born beside your horse's head.
Yet fragrant trees will shade the plank roads of Qin,
And spring streams circle Shu's walled town, instead.
Your rise or fall in life is fixed already —
No need to ask Junping to have it read.
poems.n: Gentler than *The Road to Shu Is Hard*: the dizzying middle lines — mountains rising from in front of your face, clouds born beside the horse's head — give way to spring trees and streams. Yan Junping was a famous Han fortune-teller of Chengdu. Li Bai, recently out of favour himself, offers a friend philosophical calm.

poems.te: Staying with Old Mother Xun Below Five Pines Mountain
poems.s: night autumn moon cottage pine fields
z: 我宿五松下，寂寥无所欢。
田家秋作苦，邻女夜舂寒。
跪进雕胡饭，月光明素盘。
令人惭漂母，三谢不能餐。
e: I stayed the night beneath Five Pines,
So lonely, with no pleasure there to find.
Farm folk toil bitterly in autumn;
Next door, girls pound grain in the cold at night.
She knelt to offer me wild-rice dinner —
The moonlight lit the plain white plate.
I felt ashamed, as before the washer-woman,
And thanked her thrice, but could not eat.
poems.n: A rare glimpse of Li Bai humbled. A poor old farm woman serves him precious wild rice (雕胡, the grain of *Zizania*). The washer-woman (漂母) fed the starving young Han Xin, later a great general, who rewarded her with a thousand gold; Li Bai knows he can never repay such kindness.

poems.s: night moon petals river person birds
z: 对酒不觉暝，落花盈我衣。
醉起步溪月，鸟还人亦稀。
e: Drinking, I didn't notice dusk come on;
Fallen blossoms filled the folds of my gown.
Drunk, I rise and walk along the moonlit stream;
The birds are home; few people are around.
poems.n: Twenty characters of pure contentment. Time slips by unnoticed, petals pile up on his clothes, and he wanders tipsily by a stream full of moonlight as the world goes quiet.

poems.s: spring sun flowers hills
z: 红豆生南国，春来发几枝。
愿君多采撷，此物最相思。
e: Red beans grow in the southern land;
When spring comes, how many sprigs appear?
I hope you'll gather many in your hand —
They hold the deepest longing, dear.
poems.n: The red bean (红豆), a bright scarlet seed of the south, is called the "love-longing seed" (相思子) after a legend of a woman who wept beneath a tree for her husband killed at the frontier until her tears turned into red beans. Wang Wei wrote the poem for his friend, the singer Li Guinian, who sang it at banquets; it became one of the most-sung lyrics of the Tang.

poems.s: dusk mountains pine sun mist
z: 空山不见人，但闻人语响。
返景入深林，复照青苔上。
e: On the empty mountain, no one can be seen —
Yet voices echo, somewhere, faintly heard.
The sunset's light comes back into the deep woods,
And shines again upon the moss of green.
poems.n: One of the twenty quatrains of the *Wangchuan Collection*, written at Wang Wei's country estate. Nothing happens — voices without people, a slant of evening light on moss — yet the poem has been called the purest expression of Chan (Zen) stillness in Chinese verse. Translators love it: Eliot Weinberger wrote a whole book, *Nineteen Ways of Looking at Wang Wei*, comparing versions of these twenty characters.

poems.s: night moon bamboo person
z: 独坐幽篁里，弹琴复长啸。
深林人不知，明月来相照。
e: Alone I sit among the dark bamboo,
I pluck my zither, then I whistle long.
Deep in the woods, where no one knows I'm here,
The bright moon comes to shine upon my song.
poems.n: Another Wangchuan poem. "Long whistling" (长啸) was a Daoist breathing art and a free spirit's way of expressing feeling. No one hears the music — except the moon, which comes as a friend.

poems.s: night spring moon mountains petals birds
z: 人闲桂花落，夜静春山空。
月出惊山鸟，时鸣春涧中。
e: At ease, I hear the cassia blossoms fall;
The night is still; the spring hills empty lie.
The rising moon startles the mountain birds —
From time to time, they in the spring ravine cry.
poems.n: So quiet that one can hear tiny flowers dropping; so still that moonrise startles the birds. Sound is used to deepen silence — a classic technique of Chinese verse. (桂花 here is probably a spring-flowering cassia or osmanthus.)

poems.s: dusk autumn moon pine mountains river bamboo lotus boat
z: 空山新雨后，天气晚来秋。
明月松间照，清泉石上流。
竹喧归浣女，莲动下渔舟。
随意春芳歇，王孙自可留。
e: In the empty hills, after fresh rain,
The evening air brings autumn on.
The bright moon shines among the pines;
Clear spring water over stones runs on.
Bamboos rustle — washing girls come home;
Lotus leaves stir — down go fishing boats.
Let spring's fragrance fade as it will:
Here a prince may stay, content to remain.
poems.n: Wang Wei's best-loved regulated poem. The famous second couplet — moon among pines, water over stones — is a perfect ink painting. An old song called on "princes" (gentlemen) to leave the wild mountains, since "spring grasses grow, and you cannot stay"; Wang Wei turns it around: the hills, even in autumn, are where one belongs.

poems.te: Seeing Off Yuan the Second on His Mission to Anxi
poems.s: dawn spring rain willow cottage cup two
z: 渭城朝雨浥轻尘，客舍青青柳色新。
劝君更尽一杯酒，西出阳关无故人。
e: The morning rain in Weicheng lays the light dust low;
Around the inn, the willows' fresh green glows.
Come, drink one more cup of wine before you go —
West of Yang Pass, there's no old friend who knows.
poems.n: Anxi was the Tang protectorate in Central Asia; Yang Pass, near Dunhuang, was the last gate of China. This quatrain was set to music as the *Three Refrains at Yang Pass* (阳关三叠), the most famous farewell song in Chinese history, sung at partings for a thousand years. The willows, as always, are a parting gift.

poems.te: Thinking of My Brothers in Shandong on the Double Ninth
poems.s: autumn mountains chrysanthemum person
z: 独在异乡为异客，每逢佳节倍思亲。
遥知兄弟登高处，遍插茱萸少一人。
e: Alone, a stranger in a stranger's land,
At every festival I miss my family twice as much.
Far off, I know my brothers climb the heights,
Each wearing dogwood — all but one, out of touch.
poems.n: Written when Wang Wei was only seventeen, living in the capital. On the Double Ninth (the 9th day of the 9th month), families climbed hills and wore sprigs of cornel (茱萸) to ward off evil. Instead of saying "I miss them", he imagines them missing him. Line two is the proverb every Chinese person far from home quotes at festival time.

poems.s: dusk sun desert smoke river geese rider
z: 单车欲问边，属国过居延。
征蓬出汉塞，归雁入胡天。
大漠孤烟直，长河落日圆。
萧关逢候骑，都护在燕然。
e: With a single carriage I go to visit the frontier,
Past Juyan and the vassal lands beyond.
Like tumbleweed blown out of the Han passes,
Like a wild goose winging home into the Hu sky.
Across the vast desert, a lone smoke rising straight;
Above the long river, the setting sun hangs round.
At Xiao Pass I meet a mounted scout:
"The Protector-General is at Mount Yanran."
poems.n: 737: Wang Wei was sent as an envoy to congratulate a general on a victory in the north-west. The third couplet — a single plume of beacon smoke dead straight in the windless desert, the sun perfectly round over the Yellow River — was praised in *Dream of the Red Chamber* as the ideal of a line that is "unreasonable, yet more true than reason". Mount Yanran was where a Han general carved a record of his victory over the Xiongnu.

poems.s: winter plum window snow
z: 君自故乡来，应知故乡事。
来日绮窗前，寒梅著花未？
e: You've just come from our old hometown —
You must know how things there are going.
The day you left, before my latticed window,
Had the winter plum begun its blossoming?
poems.n: Of all the things he could ask about home — family, friends, the harvest — the poet asks only about one plum tree outside his window. The smallest detail carries the whole of homesickness.

poems.s: dusk spring mountains cottage grass
z: 山中相送罢，日暮掩柴扉。
春草明年绿，王孙归不归？
e: In the hills, I've seen my friend off on his way;
At dusk I close my rough brushwood gate.
When spring grass turns green again next year,
Will you come back, my prince, or will I wait?
poems.n: The farewell is already over in the first line; the poem lives in the moment after — the gate closed in the dusk, and a question thrown forward to next spring. "Spring grass and the wandering prince" echoes the *Songs of Chu*: "The prince wanders and does not return; spring grass grows thick."

poems.s: day mountains clouds rider two cup
z: 下马饮君酒，问君何所之？
君言不得意，归卧南山陲。
但去莫复问，白云无尽时。
e: Dismount and drink this wine with me —
Where are you going, may I ask?
You say the world has not gone well for you;
You'll lie down by the Southern Mountains, leave your task.
Then go — I'll ask no more:
White clouds are endless, as before.
poems.n: A friend gives up his career to become a recluse. Wang Wei does not argue or console; the white clouds — symbol of the free, unworldly life — are "without end", unlike fame and office. The restraint is the comfort.

poems.s: day mountains clouds river person pine
z: 中岁颇好道，晚家南山陲。
兴来每独往，胜事空自知。
行到水穷处，坐看云起时。
偶然值林叟，谈笑无还期。
e: In middle age I came to love the Way;
In later years I made my home where the South Hills end.
When the mood comes, I often go alone;
Its joys are mine to know, and no one else's, friend.
I walk to where the stream runs out,
And sit to watch the clouds begin to rise.
By chance I meet an old man of the woods;
We talk and laugh, and lose track of the time that flies.
poems.n: "Walk to where the water ends, sit and watch the clouds rise" (行到水穷处，坐看云起时) is one of the most quoted couplets in Chinese — a Zen image of following life wherever it goes: where one path ends, another begins in the sky.

poems.s: day river mountains boat mist wall
z: 楚塞三湘接，荆门九派通。
江流天地外，山色有无中。
郡邑浮前浦，波澜动远空。
襄阳好风日，留醉与山翁。
e: Here Chu's frontier joins the three Xiang rivers;
At Jingmen, nine branches of the River meet.
The river flows beyond heaven and earth;
The hills' hues hover between being and not being.
Towns and cities float on the shore ahead;
The waves set the far sky trembling, shaking free.
Xiangyang has such fine wind and sun —
Let me stay drunk here, like the Old Mountain Man, with glee.
poems.n: Wang Wei was a painter as much as a poet, and line four — mountains "between existence and non-existence" — is a description of ink-wash painting itself, where distant hills dissolve into blank silk. The Old Mountain Man was Shan Jian, a Jin-dynasty governor of Xiangyang famous for getting drunk at its scenic pools.

poems.s: winter wind rider horse fields clouds birds
z: 风劲角弓鸣，将军猎渭城。
草枯鹰眼疾，雪尽马蹄轻。
忽过新丰市，还归细柳营。
回看射雕处，千里暮云平。
e: The wind is strong; the horn-bows twang —
The general hunts by Weicheng town.
The grass is withered; sharp are the falcons' eyes;
The snow is gone; the horses' hooves fly light.
Suddenly they're past the Xinfeng market,
And back again at Willow Camp tonight.
He turns to look where he shot down the eagle:
A thousand li of evening clouds lie flat and bright.
poems.n: Admired for its opening — the sound of the bows comes before we even see the general — and its sweeping close. Willow Camp (细柳营) was the camp of the famously disciplined Han general Zhou Yafu; "shooting the eagle" (射雕) was the mark of a supreme archer.

poems.s: spring mountains flowers petals river
z: 木末芙蓉花，山中发红萼。
涧户寂无人，纷纷开且落。
e: On the tips of the branches, lotus-like blooms
Put out their red buds in the hills.
By the stream-side huts, silent, no one —
They open, and then fall, in flurries, still.
poems.n: From the *Wangchuan Collection*. The magnolia (辛夷) blooms high on bare branches like lotus flowers. No one sees them; they open and fall, entirely for themselves. A Buddhist image of things arising and passing away, without purpose or witness.

poems.s: dusk sun fields cottage person birds
z: 斜光照墟落，穷巷牛羊归。
野老念牧童，倚杖候荆扉。
雉雊麦苗秀，蚕眠桑叶稀。
田夫荷锄至，相见语依依。
即此羡闲逸，怅然吟式微。
e: The slanting light falls on the village;
Down the lanes the cattle and sheep come home.
An old man, thinking of the herd-boy,
Leans on his staff and waits by the thorn-wood gate.
Pheasants call; the wheat is in the ear;
Silkworms sleep; the mulberry leaves grow thin.
Farmers come back with hoes on their shoulders;
They meet and chat, reluctant to part.
It's this I envy — such leisure and ease;
Wistfully I chant, "Why not go home?"
poems.n: A gentle evening of farm life, envied by an official tired of the court. "Why not go home" (式微) is the refrain of a *Book of Songs* poem urging a return home — here, to a simple life.

poems.te: Written at Wangchuan Villa after Long Rain
poems.s: summer rain fields crane oriole cottage smoke pine
z: 积雨空林烟火迟，蒸藜炊黍饷东菑。
漠漠水田飞白鹭，阴阴夏木啭黄鹂。
山中习静观朝槿，松下清斋折露葵。
野老与人争席罢，海鸥何事更相疑。
e: After long rain, in the empty woods, the cooking smoke climbs slow;
Steamed greens and millet go out to the eastern fields below.
Across the misty paddies, white egrets glide;
In the shady summer trees, golden orioles sing.
In the hills I practise stillness, watching morning glories close;
Under the pines, I keep a pure fast, picking dewy mallows' green.
This old rustic no longer jostles others for a seat —
Why should the seagulls still suspect what I mean?
poems.n: Wang Wei, a devout Buddhist, at his country villa. The middle couplets are famous for their painterly colours. The ending alludes to two Daoist stories: a man who gave up his airs found strangers no longer deferred to him at inns; and a man without guile could play with seagulls — until the day he meant to catch one, and they flew away.

poems.s: winter mountains river maple mist
z: 荆溪白石出，天寒红叶稀。
山路元无雨，空翠湿人衣。
e: White stones jut out in the Jing Creek;
The weather's cold; red leaves are few.
Along the mountain path there was no rain —
Yet the empty green dampens my clothes through.
poems.n: The last two lines are a famous paradox: no rain fell, but the mountain greenery is so dense and moist that it seems to soak the walker. Su Shi said of Wang Wei, "in his poems there are paintings" — with this poem as an example.

poems.s: night moon pine person river fisher
z: 晚年惟好静，万事不关心。
自顾无长策，空知返旧林。
松风吹解带，山月照弹琴。
君问穷通理，渔歌入浦深。
e: In my late years I care for stillness only;
The world's ten thousand things are not my care.
I look at myself: I have no grand designs,
Just the knowledge to go back to my old forest there.
The pine wind blows my loosened belt;
The mountain moon lights me as I play.
You ask me the truth of failure and success? —
A fisherman's song drifts deep into the bay.
poems.n: A friend asked Wang Wei about the principles of worldly success and failure. His answer is no answer: a fisherman's song fading into the reeds. In the *Songs of Chu*, a fisherman sang to Qu Yuan of adapting to the times — but Wang Wei just lets the song drift away.

poems.te: Visiting the Temple of Gathered Fragrance
poems.s: dusk mountains pine temple clouds lake
z: 不知香积寺，数里入云峰。
古木无人径，深山何处钟。
泉声咽危石，日色冷青松。
薄暮空潭曲，安禅制毒龙。
e: I did not know the Temple of Gathered Fragrance;
For miles I climbed into the cloudy peaks.
Ancient trees, no path for human feet;
Deep in the hills, a bell — from where it speaks?
The spring's voice chokes among the jagged rocks;
The sunlight chills upon the green pines' crown.
At dusk, beside the bend of an empty pool,
Calm meditation tames the poison dragon down.
poems.n: The temple is never reached in the poem — only sensed, through a bell and the stillness. The famous fifth and sixth lines turn sound into a sob and light into cold. The "poison dragon" is a Buddhist image of the passions, subdued by meditation.

poems.s: day peaks clouds mist river person
z: 太乙近天都，连山到海隅。
白云回望合，青霭入看无。
分野中峰变，阴晴众壑殊。
欲投人处宿，隔水问樵夫。
e: Taiyi soars close to heaven's capital;
Range on range, it runs to the sea's far end.
White clouds close behind me as I look back;
Blue haze vanishes as I step in.
The central peak divides the starry fields;
Sun and shade are different in each ravine.
Wanting a place where people live, to spend the night,
I call across the stream to a woodcutter, seen.
poems.n: Zhongnan (also called Taiyi), south of Chang'an, is so huge that its central peak was said to divide two astrological zones. The second couplet captures the experience of walking into mist: clouds close up behind, haze dissolves ahead. A single tiny woodcutter at the end gives the scale.

poems.s: spring tower willow horse rider
z: 新丰美酒斗十千，咸阳游侠多少年。
相逢意气为君饮，系马高楼垂柳边。
e: Xinfeng's fine wine costs ten thousand a jug;
Xianyang's gallant knights are mostly young.
When they meet and hearts take fire, they drink to each other,
Their horses tied by the high tower where the willows hung.
poems.n: A dashing glimpse of the young knights-errant of the capital: fine wine, instant friendship, horses tethered beneath the willows of a wine tower. Written when Wang Wei himself was young.

poems.s: spring mountains waterfall flowers birds
z: 远看山有色，近听水无声。
春去花还在，人来鸟不惊。
e: From afar, the mountains have their colours;
Close up, the water makes no sound.
Spring has gone, yet the flowers remain;
People come, yet the birds don't flutter round.
poems.n: A riddle-poem that every Chinese child learns: what landscape has silent water, flowers that never fade, and birds that never fly away? A painting. The attribution to Wang Wei is traditional but uncertain.

poems.te: Seeing Shen Zifu Off to Jiangdong
poems.s: spring willow river boat two
z: 杨柳渡头行客稀，罟师荡桨向临圻。
惟有相思似春色，江南江北送君归。
e: At the willow ferry, few travellers remain;
The boatman rows his oars toward Linqi's shore.
Only my longing, like the colours of spring,
Will follow you home, south and north of the River, evermore.
poems.n: The final image is lovely: spring is everywhere on both banks of the Yangtze, and so is the poet's affection, accompanying his friend all the way home.

poems.s: day rain cottage grass window
z: 轻阴阁小雨，深院昼慵开。
坐看苍苔色，欲上人衣来。
e: Light clouds hold back the drizzle;
The deep courtyard gate, at noon, I'm too lazy to undo.
I sit and gaze at the green of the moss —
It seems about to climb onto my clothes, too.
poems.n: A drowsy moment after rain. The moss is so vividly green that, in the stillness, it seems ready to creep up onto the watcher — the boundary between self and world dissolving.

poems.s: dusk autumn sun mountains river birds wall rider
z: 清川带长薄，车马去闲闲。
流水如有意，暮禽相与还。
荒城临古渡，落日满秋山。
迢递嵩高下，归来且闭关。
e: A clear stream girds the long thickets;
My carriage moves at an easy pace.
The flowing water seems to have a will;
The evening birds fly home with me apace.
A ruined city by an ancient ferry;
The setting sun fills the autumn hills.
Far off, below the heights of Mount Song,
I'll come home and shut my gate, and keep still.
poems.n: A journey home into retirement. The water and the homing birds seem to share his mood; the ruined city and sunset bring a touch of melancholy before the final resolution — to close the gate on the world.

poems.s: dawn spring peach willow mist cottage oriole
z: 桃红复含宿雨，柳绿更带朝烟。
花落家童未扫，莺啼山客犹眠。
e: Pink peach blossoms still hold last night's rain;
Green willows wear the morning's misty veil.
Fallen flowers — the houseboy hasn't swept them;
Orioles sing — the mountain guest still sleeps, all hale.
poems.n: A rare six-character quatrain, every line packed with colour and parallelism. Nothing needs doing: the petals can lie, the guest can sleep.

poems.s: spring palace flowers window
z: 莫以今时宠，能忘旧日恩。
看花满眼泪，不共楚王言。
e: Don't think that the favour she's shown today
Could make her forget the love of before.
She gazes at flowers, her eyes full of tears,
And will not speak to the King of Chu anymore.
poems.n: In 680 BC the King of Chu destroyed the state of Xi and took its queen for himself. She bore him two sons but, the *Zuo Zhuan* records, never spoke to him. Wang Wei wrote this at a banquet where a prince had taken a pancake-seller's wife; shown her old husband, she wept — and the prince let her go home.

poems.s: dusk tower river clouds crane grass mist
z: 昔人已乘黄鹤去，此地空余黄鹤楼。
黄鹤一去不复返，白云千载空悠悠。
晴川历历汉阳树，芳草萋萋鹦鹉洲。
日暮乡关何处是？烟波江上使人愁。
e: The sage of old has ridden off upon the yellow crane;
Here only Yellow Crane Tower is left, standing alone.
The yellow crane, once gone, has never come again;
For a thousand years white clouds drift on, aimless, on their own.
Across the sunlit river, the trees of Hanyang are clear;
On Parrot Isle the fragrant grasses grow so thick and green.
The sun goes down — where is my home? It isn't here;
The mist upon the river's waves brings sorrow to the scene.
poems.n: Legend says an immortal flew away from this spot in Wuhan on a yellow crane. Cui Hao's poem breaks the rules of regulated verse — "yellow crane" appears three times in four lines — yet it was hailed as the greatest seven-character regulated poem of the Tang. Li Bai, visiting the tower, is said to have sighed: "Before my eyes is a scene I cannot describe, for Cui Hao's poem is already above it."

poems.s: day river boat two
z: 君家何处住？妾住在横塘。
停船暂借问，或恐是同乡。
e: "Where is your home, sir? Tell me, do —
I live at Hengtang, down by the shore.
I stopped my boat to ask you this:
Perhaps we're from the same town — I'm not sure."
poems.n: A tiny drama in twenty characters: a girl on one boat calls out to a stranger on another, using the excuse of a shared hometown to start a conversation — shy, bold and charming at once.

poems.s: winter snow geese clouds sun two rider
z: 千里黄云白日曛，北风吹雁雪纷纷。
莫愁前路无知己，天下谁人不识君。
e: A thousand li of yellow cloud; the white sun's dim and low;
The north wind blows the wild geese on through swirling snow.
Don't fear the road ahead will hold no friend who knows your name —
Who in all the world is there who doesn't know your fame?
poems.n: Dong the Elder was Dong Tinglan, the greatest qin player of the age. Gao Shi, then poor and unknown, sees him off in a snowstorm with no gift but this encouragement — one of the most heartening farewell poems ever written.

poems.s: night winter candle cottage person
z: 旅馆寒灯独不眠，客心何事转凄然。
故乡今夜思千里，霜鬓明朝又一年。
e: At the inn, beside a cold lamp, alone and wide awake —
Why does this traveller's heart turn so forlorn and drear?
Tonight, a thousand li away, my family thinks of me;
By morning, my frost-grey temples will have aged another year.
poems.n: New Year's Eve, the great night of family reunion, spent alone at an inn. Again the turn: it is his family who are thinking of him. At midnight everyone in China grows a year older — his grey hair with them.

poems.te: Hearing a Flute on the Frontier
poems.s: night moon fort mountains horse petals snow
z: 雪净胡天牧马还，月明羌笛戍楼间。
借问梅花何处落，风吹一夜满关山。
e: The snow is gone; beneath the Hu sky, the horse herds come back home;
In bright moonlight a Qiang flute plays among the watchtowers there.
And where, I ask, do the plum blossoms fall?
The wind blows them all night, filling the passes everywhere.
poems.n: A beautiful double image. "Plum Blossoms Falling" (梅花落) was a flute tune; the poet imagines its notes, like petals, blown by the wind over all the mountain passes. Flowers, music and homesickness merge.

poems.s: dusk desert fort flag rider mountains
z: 汉家烟尘在东北，汉将辞家破残贼。
男儿本自重横行，天子非常赐颜色。
𪭢金伐鼓下榆关，旌旆逶迤碣石间。
校尉羽书飞瀚海，单于猎火照狼山。
山川萧条极边土，胡骑凭陵杂风雨。
战士军前半死生，美人帐下犹歌舞。
大漠穷秋塞草腓，孤城落日斗兵稀。
身当恩遇恒轻敌，力尽关山未解围。
铁衣远戍辛勤久，玉箸应啼别离后。
少妇城南欲断肠，征人蓟北空回首。
边庭飘飖那可度，绝域苍茫更何有。
杀气三时作阵云，寒声一夜传刁斗。
相看白刃血纷纷，死节从来岂顾勋。
君不见沙场征战苦，至今犹忆李将军。
e: Smoke and dust of war rise in the Han's north-east;
Han generals leave their homes to crush the rebels, to the least.
Men of spirit prize the chance to ride across the land;
The Son of Heaven grants them favour, rare and grand.
With clanging gongs and pounding drums they march down through Elm Pass;
Their banners wind among the crags of Jieshi, mass on mass.
The colonels' feathered war-reports fly over the desert sea;
On Wolf Mountain the khan's hunting fires blaze free.
Mountains and rivers are desolate to the edge of the frontier ground;
Hu horsemen charge with wind and rain, swarming all around.
At the front, the soldiers — half are dead and half alive;
Beneath the general's tent, the beauties sing and dance and thrive.
In the great desert, autumn's end; the frontier grass is sere;
The lone fort at sunset — few soldiers left to fight are here.
So favoured by the emperor, the general scorned the foe;
Now, strength spent at the passes, the siege won't lift or go.
In iron mail on distant guard through long and bitter years —
Since parting, their wives must weep their jade-chopstick tears.
South of the city, young wives' hearts are breaking with despair;
North in Ji, the soldiers turn their heads in vain, to stare.
The frontier's wild and windswept — how can it be crossed?
The far land's vast and empty — nothing there but loss.
All day the killing-air forms battle clouds on high;
All night the watchmen's gongs ring out their freezing cry.
They face each other's naked blades; the blood in spatters flies —
To die for duty, who would think of honours or of prize?
Have you not seen the bitterness of fighting on the sands?
To this day the soldiers long for General Li to lead their bands.
poems.n: Written in 738 after news of a disastrous campaign in the north-east, where a general's arrogance and false victory reports cost many lives. "At the front, half the soldiers dead; in the general's tent, beauties still singing and dancing" is the most damning couplet in frontier poetry. "Jade chopsticks" are a woman's two streams of tears. General Li is Li Guang of the Han, who shared every hardship with his men.

poems.s: spring wall flowers birds person
z: 国破山河在，城春草木深。
感时花溅泪，恨别鸟惊心。
烽火连三月，家书抵万金。
白头搔更短，浑欲不胜簪。
e: The state lies broken; hills and rivers stay;
Spring in the city: grass and trees grow deep.
Grieved by the times, I see the flowers weep;
Hating our parting, birdsong makes my heart leap.
The beacon fires have burned three months on end;
A letter from home is worth ten thousand gold.
I scratch my white head; the hair grows thinner still —
Soon it will be too thin a pin to hold.
poems.n: Spring 757 in Chang'an, occupied by An Lushan's rebels. Du Fu was trapped in the ruined capital while his family was far away. The first line sets the empire's collapse against the indifferent permanence of nature. Lines 3–4 can be read both ways at once — the flowers and birds weep and start with him, or he weeps and starts at them. A scholar wore his hair in a topknot held with a pin; Du Fu's is falling out from grief.

poems.s: autumn peaks river leaves birds person wind
z: 风急天高猿啸哀，渚清沙白鸟飞回。
无边落木萧萧下，不尽长江滚滚来。
万里悲秋常作客，百年多病独登台。
艰难苦恨繁霜鬓，潦倒新停浊酒杯。
e: The wind is swift, the sky is high, the gibbons cry their grief;
The isle is clear, the sand is white, the birds wheel back around.
Endlessly the falling leaves come rustling, leaf on leaf;
Unendingly the Long River comes rolling on with sound.
Ten thousand li from home, in mournful autumn, a stranger everywhere,
Sick all my life, I climb the terrace alone — no friend of mine.
Hardship and bitter grief have frosted all my hair;
Worn out, I've just given up my cup of cloudy wine.
poems.n: Written in autumn 767 at Kuizhou on the Yangtze, on the Double Ninth Festival, when people climbed heights with their families and drank chrysanthemum wine. Du Fu, fifty-five, sick and far from home, climbs alone — and has had to give up wine for his health. Often called the greatest seven-character regulated poem ever written: every line is part of a parallel pair, and the middle couplet's falling leaves and endless river are an image of time itself.

poems.te: Welcome Rain on a Spring Night
poems.s: night spring rain river boat flowers cottage
z: 好雨知时节，当春乃发生。
随风潜入夜，润物细无声。
野径云俱黑，江船火独明。
晓看红湿处，花重锦官城。
e: Good rain knows its proper season:
It comes in spring, when all things start to grow.
It slips in with the wind by night,
And nourishes the world — so fine, so silent, slow.
The country paths are black with cloud;
A lone boat's lantern on the river is aglow.
At dawn, look where it's red and wet:
Brocade City's flowers hang heavy, row on row.
poems.n: Chengdu, 761, during the happiest years of Du Fu's life, at his thatched cottage. The rain is a considerate friend who "knows" when it is needed and arrives quietly in the night. Brocade City (锦官城) is Chengdu, once the seat of the official in charge of the silk-brocade industry — and in the morning it is indeed brocaded with flowers.

poems.s: spring willow oriole crane mountains snow river sail window
z: 两个黄鹂鸣翠柳，一行白鹭上青天。
窗含西岭千秋雪，门泊东吴万里船。
e: Two golden orioles sing in the emerald willow;
A line of white egrets climbs the blue of the sky.
My window frames the West Range's thousand-autumn snow;
At my gate, boats from Eastern Wu, ten thousand li, lie by.
poems.n: Four lines, four perfectly parallel images — yellow and green, white and blue; near and far; sound and stillness — like four panels of a painted screen. Written at his Chengdu cottage in 764 when peace had briefly returned: the boats from Wu, on the lower Yangtze, mean the river route east is open again.

poems.s: dawn peaks clouds birds mist
z: 岱宗夫如何？齐鲁青未了。
造化钟神秀，阴阳割昏晓。
荡胸生曾云，决眦入归鸟。
会当凌绝顶，一览众山小。
e: What is it like, Mount Tai, the lord of peaks?
Over Qi and Lu its green goes on and on.
Creation gathered here its wonder and its grace;
Its shaded and its sunlit sides divide the dusk and dawn.
Layer on layer the clouds rise, and stir my breast;
Home-flying birds dart into my straining eyes.
One day I'll stand upon its highest crest,
And see how small all other mountains lie.
poems.n: Written by the twenty-four-year-old Du Fu after failing the imperial examination. Mount Tai (岱宗, "the ancestor of mountains") in Shandong, the holiest of China's Five Great Peaks, is so vast that its green spans the old states of Qi and Lu. The last couplet, all youthful ambition, echoes Mencius: "Confucius climbed Mount Tai and found the world small."

poems.te: Meeting Li Guinian South of the River
poems.s: spring petals river two pavilion
z: 岐王宅里寻常见，崔九堂前几度闻。
正是江南好风景，落花时节又逢君。
e: In Prince Qi's mansion I saw you often then;
In Cui the Ninth's great hall I heard you sing.
Now in the south, the scenery's fine again —
And I meet you as the blossoms fall from spring.
poems.n: Li Guinian was the most celebrated singer at Emperor Xuanzong's court in the golden years before the An Lushan rebellion. In 770, the last year of Du Fu's life, the two old men met again as refugees in the south. Nothing sad is said; "the season of falling flowers" says everything about the lost golden age — and about the two of them.

poems.te: Hearing That the Imperial Army Has Recovered Henan and Hebei
poems.s: spring river boat peaks person
z: 剑外忽传收蓟北，初闻涕泪满衣裳。
却看妻子愁何在，漫卷诗书喜欲狂。
白日放歌须纵酒，青春作伴好还乡。
即从巴峡穿巫峡，便下襄阳向洛阳。
e: Beyond Sword Pass, the news has come — the North has been restored!
When first I heard, my tears ran down and drenched my clothes right through.
I look at wife and children — where's their sorrow? Out the door!
I roll my books up, mad with joy — what else is there to do?
In broad daylight I'll sing aloud and drink till I am done;
Spring's green will keep us company — how good to journey home!
Straight from the Gorge of Ba, we'll thread the Gorge of Wu, and run
Down to Xiangyang, and on to Luoyang, never more to roam.
poems.n: Spring 763: after eight years, the An Lushan rebellion was crushed when government troops retook the rebels' base in the north-east (Jibei). Du Fu, a refugee in Sichuan beyond the Sword Gate Pass, hears the news. Called "the most joyful poem of his life", it ends by racing through four place-names, as if the journey home were already happening.

poems.te: Song of My Thatched Hut Torn by the Autumn Wind
poems.s: autumn wind rain cottage bamboo river person
z: 八月秋高风怒号，卷我屋上三重茅。
茅飞渡江洒江郊，高者挂罥长林梢，下者飘转沉塘坳。
南村群童欺我老无力，忍能对面为盗贼。
公然抱茅入竹去，唇焦口燥呼不得，归来倚杖自叹息。
俄顷风定云墨色，秋天漠漠向昏黑。
布衾多年冷似铁，娇儿恶卧踏里裂。
床头屋漏无干处，雨脚如麻未断绝。
自经丧乱少睡眠，长夜沾湿何由彻！
安得广厦千万间，大庇天下寒士俱欢颜，风雨不动安如山。
呜呼！何时眼前突兀见此屋，吾庐独破受冻死亦足！
e: In the eighth month, autumn's high; the wind howls in its rage,
And rolls away three layers of the thatch from off my roof.
The thatch flies over the river, strewn across the farther bank;
The high bits catch and tangle in the treetops of the wood,
The low bits whirl and spin, and sink in hollows of the pond.
The boys of South Village bully me — I'm old and have no strength —
And have the heart to rob me to my face!
They carry off the thatch in broad daylight into the bamboo;
My lips are parched, my mouth is dry, I shout to no avail;
I come back, lean on my stick, and sigh alone.
Soon the wind drops; the clouds turn black as ink;
The autumn sky grows dim and dark toward night.
My cotton quilt, years old, is cold as iron;
My darling boy sleeps badly, and has kicked its lining through.
Above the bed the roof leaks — not a single spot is dry;
The rain falls thick as hemp threads, and never stops.
Since the troubles came I've hardly slept —
Soaked through, how can I last this long night till the light?
Oh, for a mansion of ten thousand rooms and more,
To shelter all the poor scholars under heaven and make them smile,
Unshaken by wind and rain, as steady as a mountain!
Ah! If ever I could see such a house rise up before my eyes,
Then let my hut alone be broken, and I freeze to death — I'd be content!
poems.n: Chengdu, autumn 761. The hut that a year earlier had brought Du Fu such peace is wrecked in a storm. The poem moves from comic misery — the village boys making off with his thatch, his exhausted shouting — to a vast compassion: he would gladly freeze if every poor scholar in the world could have a roof. It is among the most loved expressions of selflessness in Chinese literature.

poems.s: night crescent cottage wall person two
z: 暮投石壕村，有吏夜捉人。
老翁逾墙走，老妇出门看。
吏呼一何怒！妇啼一何苦！
听妇前致词：三男邺城戍。
一男附书至，二男新战死。
存者且偷生，死者长已矣！
室中更无人，惟有乳下孙。
有孙母未去，出入无完裙。
老妪力虽衰，请从吏夜归。
急应河阳役，犹得备晨炊。
夜久语声绝，如闻泣幽咽。
天明登前途，独与老翁别。
e: At dusk I lodged at Shihao village late;
By night an officer came, seizing men.
The old man fled across the wall; his wife went to the gate.
How fierce the officer's shouts! How bitter her crying then!
I heard her come before him and explain:
"My three sons went to guard the city of Ye.
From one of them a letter came again:
Two sons have just been killed in the fray.
The living one scrapes by from day to day;
The dead are gone, forever passed away.
There's no one else inside our home,
But a grandson at his mother's breast;
For him his mother's stayed — but she can't roam:
She hasn't one whole skirt in which she could be dressed.
This old woman's strength is weak, I know,
But let me go with you tonight, I pray:
To answer Heyang's muster, quick, I'll go,
And cook the troops their breakfast at break of day."
Deep in the night the voices died away;
I seemed to hear someone sobbing low.
At dawn I set out on my way,
And only the old man saw me go.
poems.n: Spring 759, after the government army's defeat at Ye, when press-gangs were seizing anyone they could find. Du Fu, lodging in a village in Henan, records without a word of comment: at night the old woman gives herself up to save her family; at dawn only the old man is left to say goodbye. One of the "Three Officers" (三吏), his great war ballads.

poems.te: Thinking of My Brothers on a Moonlit Night
poems.s: night autumn moon geese fort frost
z: 戍鼓断人行，边秋一雁声。
露从今夜白，月是故乡明。
有弟皆分散，无家问死生。
寄书长不达，况乃未休兵。
e: The garrison drums have stopped all travellers on their way;
At the autumn frontier, one wild goose cries in the night.
From tonight on, the dew turns white, as the old seasons say;
The moon, I know, at home is shining far more bright.
I have brothers, but they're scattered far apart;
No home is left to ask if they're alive or dead.
The letters that I send never reach their mark —
And still the wars go on, and still no peace ahead.
poems.n: Qinzhou, autumn 759. The night is "White Dew" (白露), one of the twenty-four solar terms, marking the turn into autumn. A single wild goose — geese fly in families, and stand for brothers — cries alone. "The moon is brighter over my hometown" became a proverb: everything is better at home.

poems.s: night moon stars river boat grass birds
z: 细草微风岸，危樯独夜舟。
星垂平野阔，月涌大江流。
名岂文章著，官应老病休。
飘飘何所似，天地一沙鸥。
e: Fine grass, a gentle breeze along the shore;
A tall mast, and my lonely boat by night.
The stars hang low above the boundless plain;
The moon wells up as the great River takes flight.
Fame — has my writing ever won me that?
Old and sick, I let my office pass me by.
Drifting, drifting — what is it I'm like?
A lone gull between the earth and sky.
poems.n: Written in 765 as Du Fu, having lost his patron in Chengdu, sailed down the Yangtze. The vast, luminous middle couplet — stars sagging to the plain, the moon surging in the current — sets up the final image: one small gull in the immensity of the universe.

poems.s: day lake tower boat clouds person
z: 昔闻洞庭水，今上岳阳楼。
吴楚东南坼，乾坤日夜浮。
亲朋无一字，老病有孤舟。
戎马关山北，凭轩涕泗流。
e: Long had I heard of Dongting's waters wide;
Today I climb the Yueyang Tower's height.
Here Wu and Chu split east and south apart;
Heaven and earth float on it day and night.
From kin and friends, not one word comes to me;
Old and sick, I have one lonely boat.
North of the passes, war-horses still ride —
I lean on the rail and let my tears run free.
poems.n: 768, two years before Du Fu's death. Dongting Lake in Hunan is so vast that the ancient lands of Wu and Chu seem split by it, and the whole universe floats upon it. Against this immensity, Du Fu has nothing — no letters, only a boat, and war still raging in the north.

poems.s: spring pine temple oriole grass
z: 丞相祠堂何处寻？锦官城外柏森森。
映阶碧草自春色，隔叶黄鹂空好音。
三顾频烦天下计，两朝开济老臣心。
出师未捷身先死，长使英雄泪满襟。
e: Where shall I seek the shrine of the great Chancellor of Shu?
Outside Brocade City, where the cypress trees grow tall.
The green grass on the steps makes spring's colour for itself;
Behind the leaves the orioles sing, for no one, after all.
Three visits, urgent, sought his plans to set the world aright;
Two reigns he served, the old minister, with all his heart and might.
He led his army out, but died before the victory —
And ever since, heroes have wept their sleeves wet at the sight.
poems.n: Zhuge Liang (181–234), chancellor of the Shu-Han kingdom in the Three Kingdoms era, is China's model of wisdom and loyalty. Liu Bei visited his thatched hut three times to beg for his counsel; Zhuge Liang served him and then his son, and died in camp in 234 on his fifth northern campaign. Du Fu visited the shrine in Chengdu in 760. The last couplet is quoted whenever a great endeavour is cut short.

poems.te: Remembering Li Bai on a Spring Day
poems.s: spring dusk clouds river willow
z: 白也诗无敌，飘然思不群。
清新庾开府，俊逸鲍参军。
渭北春天树，江东日暮云。
何时一樽酒，重与细论文。
e: Li Bai — your poems have no peer;
Your thoughts float free, far from the crowd's ways:
Fresh and clear as Lord Yu Xin's,
Bold and graceful as Bao Zhao's lays.
North of the Wei, I see spring trees;
East of the River, you watch evening clouds.
When shall we share a jug of wine again,
And talk of poetry, line by line, aloud?
poems.n: Du Fu met Li Bai in 744 and travelled with him; after 745 they never met again. Du Fu wrote some fifteen poems about Li Bai. Yu Xin and Bao Zhao were great poets of the Southern Dynasties. "Spring trees north of the Wei, dusk clouds east of the River" — Du Fu in Chang'an, Li Bai in the south — became a set phrase for friends who miss each other.

poems.s: day clouds river wall flowers
z: 锦城丝管日纷纷，半入江风半入云。
此曲只应天上有，人间能得几回闻。
e: In Brocade City, strings and pipes play every day,
Half on the river wind, half to the clouds they float away.
Such music surely only heaven should possess —
How many times can mortals hear it? Few, I'd say.
poems.n: General Hua Jingding had put down a rebellion in Chengdu, then let his troops loot the city — and, many commentators believe, used music reserved for the emperor at his feasts. Du Fu's lavish praise may be a veiled rebuke: "this belongs in heaven" — that is, at the imperial court, not here.

poems.te: Walking Alone by the River in Search of Flowers (VI)
poems.s: spring flowers peach butterfly oriole cottage
z: 黄四娘家花满蹊，千朵万朵压枝低。
留连戏蝶时时舞，自在娇莺恰恰啼。
e: At Fourth Sister Huang's, the path is filled with flowers;
Thousands of blossoms, myriads, bend the branches low.
The playful butterflies keep dancing, lingering for hours;
The carefree orioles sing their sweet songs, just so.
poems.n: One of seven quatrains Du Fu wrote in Chengdu on a solitary walk in search of spring flowers. Fourth Sister Huang was a neighbour. The doubled sounds 留连, 时时, 自在, 恰恰 make the lines dance and sing like the creatures they describe.

poems.s: spring sun river swallows flowers grass
z: 迟日江山丽，春风花草香。
泥融飞燕子，沙暖睡鸳鸯。
e: Long spring days: the rivers and the hills are fair;
The spring breeze brings the scent of flowers and grass.
The mud has thawed — the swallows fly to build;
On warm sand, mandarin ducks doze as the hours pass.
poems.n: Chengdu, 764. A first poem for many Chinese schoolchildren: four lines, four images of spring — light, scent, motion (swallows gathering soft mud for their nests) and stillness (a pair of mandarin ducks, symbols of devoted couples, asleep on the warm sand).

poems.s: night moon window mist cottage
z: 今夜鄜州月，闺中只独看。
遥怜小儿女，未解忆长安。
香雾云鬟湿，清辉玉臂寒。
何时倚虚幌，双照泪痕干。
e: Tonight the moon shines over Fuzhou far away;
In her chamber, she is watching it alone.
I think with pity of our little ones —
Too young to know I'm in Chang'an, not home.
The scented mist must dampen her cloud-soft hair;
The clear light chills her jade-white arms tonight.
When shall we lean by the thin curtain, side by side,
Our tear-stains dried together in the moonlight?
poems.n: Autumn 756. Du Fu had left his wife and children at Fuzhou to join the new emperor, but was captured by rebels and held in Chang'an. Instead of describing his own longing, he imagines his wife gazing at the moon alone — one of the very few Tang poems about a man's love for his wife, and one of the most tender.

poems.s: spring river cottage flowers birds two jar
z: 舍南舍北皆春水，但见群鸥日日来。
花径不曾缘客扫，蓬门今始为君开。
盘飧市远无兼味，樽酒家贫只旧醅。
肯与邻翁相对饮，隔篱呼取尽余杯。
e: North and south of my house, spring waters everywhere,
And only flocks of gulls come visiting each day.
My flowered path was never swept for any guest;
My wicker gate today, for you, first opens its way.
The market's far — my dinner has no second dish;
My house is poor — the wine's last year's old brew, I fear.
If you'd be willing, let us drink with my old neighbour —
I'll call him over the fence to drain the last cups here.
poems.n: Chengdu, 761: a visit from a county magistrate named Cui. Du Fu's apologies for his humble fare are full of warmth, and the closing picture — calling the old neighbour over the hedge to finish the wine — is the essence of simple country friendship.

poems.s: day river mountains clouds
z: 功盖三分国，名成八阵图。
江流石不转，遗恨失吞吴。
e: His deeds outshone the kingdoms of the three;
The Eight-Array Plan won him undying fame.
The river flows; its stones will never shift —
Regret for the war on Wu is all that still remains.
poems.n: The Eight-Array Plan was Zhuge Liang's battle formation; stone mounds said to mark it stood on a sandbar of the Yangtze at Kuizhou, unmoved by floods for centuries — like his loyalty. The last line has two readings: regret that Liu Bei's disastrous attack on Wu broke their alliance, or regret at never conquering Wu at all.

poems.te: Thinking of Li Bai at the Edge of the Sky
poems.s: autumn wind geese river clouds
z: 凉风起天末，君子意如何？
鸿雁几时到，江湖秋水多。
文章憎命达，魑魅喜人过。
应共冤魂语，投诗赠汨罗。
e: A cool wind rises at the edge of the sky —
My friend, what are your thoughts tonight, I wonder?
When will the wild geese bring your letter by?
The lakes and rivers swell with autumn water.
Fine writing hates a man whose fate goes right;
The goblins gloat when travellers pass their way.
You'll talk, I think, with the wronged ghost tonight,
And cast a poem to him in the Miluo's spray.
poems.n: Qinzhou, 759: Du Fu has heard that Li Bai is being sent into exile in Yelang. "Literature hates a fortunate fate" (文章憎命达) — great writers are doomed to suffer — became proverbial. The "wronged ghost" is Qu Yuan, the slandered poet who drowned himself in the Miluo River, near Li Bai's route into exile. Wild geese were said to carry letters.

poems.s: autumn maple peaks river boat chrysanthemum mist
z: 玉露凋伤枫树林，巫山巫峡气萧森。
江间波浪兼天涌，塞上风云接地阴。
丛菊两开他日泪，孤舟一系故园心。
寒衣处处催刀尺，白帝城高急暮砧。
e: Jade dew has withered and wounded the maple woods;
Wu Mountain and Wu Gorge lie bleak and drear.
On the river, waves leap up to touch the sky;
Over the passes, wind-clouds darken the earth near.
Twice now the chrysanthemums bloom — tears of other days;
My lonely boat stays moored — my heart to my old garden tied.
Everywhere, winter clothes speed knife and ruler on;
High Baidi town, at dusk, hears the pounding mallets outside.
poems.n: The first of "Autumn Meditations", eight linked poems written at Kuizhou in 766 and often considered the summit of Du Fu's art. Autumn in the Three Gorges: the chrysanthemums have bloomed twice since he arrived — two years stranded — and the boat that should take him home stays tied, like his heart. The sound of women beating cloth for winter clothes closes the poem in dusk and cold.

poems.s: dusk mountains desert grass sun
z: 群山万壑赴荆门，生长明妃尚有村。
一去紫台连朔漠，独留青冢向黄昏。
画图省识春风面，环佩空归夜月魂。
千载琵琶作胡语，分明怨恨曲中论。
e: The mountains and ten thousand gorges rush toward Jingmen's gate;
Here's the village where the Bright Consort was born and bred.
Once gone from the Purple Palace to the northern deserts' waste,
She left only a green tomb, facing the dusk ahead.
From a painting, the emperor half-knew her spring-wind face;
Her soul comes home in vain, jade pendants chiming, by moonlight.
For a thousand years the pipa has sung in foreign ways,
And in its melodies her bitter grief is told outright.
poems.n: Wang Zhaojun, the "Bright Consort" (明妃), a Han palace lady, was married off to a Xiongnu khan in 33 BC. Legend says the court painter made her portrait ugly because she refused to bribe him, so the emperor never noticed her until the day she left. Her tomb on the steppe was said to stay green when all the grass around it withered. She became the symbol of talent unrecognised — and of Du Fu himself, far from court.

poems.s: spring tower flowers river clouds mountains
z: 花近高楼伤客心，万方多难此登临。
锦江春色来天地，玉垒浮云变古今。
北极朝廷终不改，西山寇盗莫相侵。
可怜后主还祠庙，日暮聊为梁甫吟。
e: Flowers beside the tower wound a traveller's heart;
In times of trouble everywhere, I climb this height.
Spring on Brocade River fills all heaven and earth;
Clouds on Jade Rampart change, as ages take their flight.
Like the Pole Star, our court will never change;
You bandits of the Western Hills — don't dare invade!
Alas, the Last Lord of Shu still has his temple here;
At dusk I'll chant the Liangfu Song as shadows fade.
poems.n: Chengdu, spring 764. Tibetan armies had briefly taken Chang'an the year before and were raiding Sichuan (the "Western Hills"). Du Fu declares that the Tang court, like the Pole Star, will endure. Liu Shan, the feeble Last Lord of Shu-Han, lost his kingdom yet still has a shrine — a pointed reminder to the reigning emperor. The *Liangfu Song* was a favourite of Zhuge Liang.

poems.s: day bridge wall rider horse flag wind
z: 车辚辚，马萧萧，行人弓箭各在腰。
耶娘妻子走相送，尘埃不见咸阳桥。
牵衣顿足拦道哭，哭声直上干云霄。
道旁过者问行人，行人但云点行频。
或从十五北防河，便至四十西营田。
去时里正与裹头，归来头白还戍边。
边庭流血成海水，武皇开边意未已。
君不闻汉家山东二百州，千村万落生荆杞。
纵有健妇把锄犁，禾生陇亩无东西。
况复秦兵耐苦战，被驱不异犬与鸡。
长者虽有问，役夫敢申恨？
且如今年冬，未休关西卒。
县官急索租，租税从何出？
信知生男恶，反是生女好。
生女犹得嫁比邻，生男埋没随百草。
君不见青海头，古来白骨无人收。
新鬼烦冤旧鬼哭，天阴雨湿声啾啾！
e: The chariots rumble, the horses neigh,
Bows and arrows at each marcher's waist on the way.
Fathers, mothers, wives and children run to see them go;
The dust is so thick that Xianyang Bridge no longer shows.
They clutch at clothes, they stamp, they block the road and cry;
The sound of weeping rises straight up to the sky.
A passer-by beside the road asks one of the men;
The man just says, "They call us up again and again.
Some went north at fifteen to guard the Yellow River's shore;
At forty they were sent out west to farm the army's store.
When they left, the village head bound up their hair;
They came home white — and now they're sent back to the frontier.
At the border, blood has flowed until it formed a sea,
But the Martial Emperor still wants more land — he won't let be.
Have you not heard? In Han's two hundred districts east of the hills,
Ten thousand villages lie choked with thorns that no one tills.
Even where strong wives take the hoe and plough in hand,
The crops grow wild and tangled, every which way, on the land.
And since the men of Qin are tough and can endure the fight,
They're driven out like dogs and chickens, day and night.
Though you, sir, ask me this,
How dare a conscript tell you what's amiss?
Take this winter — even now
They haven't sent the western troops back to the plough.
The county officers press hard for tax that we can't pay —
Where is it to come from? Tell me, sir, I pray.
Truly, it's bad luck to have a son, we've learned;
Far better to have a daughter — the tables have turned.
A girl can still be married to the neighbours next door;
A boy lies buried in the grass, and is seen no more.
Have you not seen, beside the Qinghai Lake,
White bones from ancient times that no one comes to take?
New ghosts rage at their wrongs, and the old ghosts wail;
When skies are dark and the rain is wet, you hear them cry in the gale."
poems.n: About 751, a protest against Emperor Xuanzong's endless wars of conquest. Du Fu disguises the present emperor as "the Martial Emperor" — Emperor Wu of Han — and lets a conscript speak. The reversal of the age-old preference for sons ("a son is buried in the grass") was shocking. Xianyang Bridge crossed the Wei River west of Chang'an, where the troops set out; Qinghai Lake was a killing ground in the wars with Tibet.

poems.s: day fort flag rider mountains
z: 挽弓当挽强，用箭当用长。
射人先射马，擒贼先擒王。
杀人亦有限，列国自有疆。
苟能制侵陵，岂在多杀伤。
e: To draw a bow, then draw a strong one;
To use an arrow, use a long one.
To shoot a man, first shoot his mount;
To catch the bandits, catch their king — that counts.
But killing, too, should have its limit,
And every land has borders — stay within it.
If we can halt the invaders' aggression,
What need for slaughter past all discretion?
poems.n: From a series of nine poems in the voice of a soldier on Xuanzong's campaigns. The first four lines sound like military maxims ("to catch bandits, first catch their king" became a proverb); then the soldier turns: war should be for defence, not conquest.

poems.te: For the Recluse Wei the Eighth
poems.s: night rain cottage candle two jar
z: 人生不相见，动如参与商。
今夕复何夕，共此灯烛光。
少壮能几时，鬓发各已苍。
访旧半为鬼，惊呼热中肠。
焉知二十载，重上君子堂。
昔别君未婚，儿女忽成行。
怡然敬父执，问我来何方。
问答乃未已，驱儿罗酒浆。
夜雨剪春韭，新炊间黄粱。
主称会面难，一举累十觞。
十觞亦不醉，感子故意长。
明日隔山岳，世事两茫茫。
e: In this life, old friends so seldom meet —
Like Shen and Shang, two stars that never share the sky.
What night is this night, then, so sweet,
That we two share this candle's light, you and I?
How long can youth and vigour stay?
Already both our temples have turned grey.
I ask for old friends — half are ghosts by now;
I cry out, and my heart burns, I don't know how.
Who'd think that twenty years would go
Before I climbed into your hall again?
When last we parted, you'd no wife, I know;
Now sons and daughters stand in line — and then
They greet their father's friend with smiling grace
And ask me what far place I've journeyed from.
Before our questions and replies have run their race,
You send them off: "Bring wine, and quickly come!"
Spring chives are cut out in the night rain;
New-cooked rice is mixed with yellow grain.
"It's hard for us to meet," my host declares,
And drinks ten cups to me in one long go;
Ten cups — and still I'm sober: unawares,
Your old affection moves me so.
Tomorrow mountains rise between us two,
