And the world's affairs will be lost from view.
poems.n: 759, a time of war: Du Fu spends a night with an old friend, a scholar who never took office. Its power lies in homely detail — the children politely asking where he has come from, spring chives cut in the rain. Shen (Orion) and Shang (Antares) lie on opposite sides of the sky: when one rises, the other has set.

poems.s: day river mountains clouds
z: 王杨卢骆当时体，轻薄为文哂未休。
尔曹身与名俱灭，不废江河万古流。
e: Wang, Yang, Lu, Luo — they wrote in their own day's style;
Glib critics mock their work and never cease to jeer.
But you will perish, body and name, in a little while,
While they, like the great rivers, flow forever here.
poems.n: One of six playful quatrains on literary criticism. The "Four Paragons of the Early Tang" — Wang Bo, Yang Jiong, Lu Zhaolin and Luo Binwang — were sneered at by later critics as old-fashioned. Du Fu's retort is now quoted for any achievement that outlasts its critics.

poems.s: summer river cottage swallows birds two
z: 清江一曲抱村流，长夏江村事事幽。
自去自来梁上燕，相亲相近水中鸥。
老妻画纸为棋局，稚子敲针作钓钩。
但有故人供禄米，微躯此外更何求？
e: A bend of the clear river hugs the village as it flows;
Long summer days in the river village pass in quiet ease.
The swallows on the rafters come and go just as they choose;
The gulls upon the water draw together as they please.
My old wife draws a chessboard on a paper sheet;
My little son is hammering a needle for a hook.
With an old friend to send me rice, my life's complete —
What more could this frail body seek, or where else look?
poems.n: Chengdu, summer 760, at the newly built thatched cottage. After years of war and wandering, Du Fu enjoys a rare peace: swallows and gulls, his wife's homemade chessboard, his son's homemade fish-hook. The rice came from his patron and friend Yan Wu.

poems.te: Song of the Eight Immortals of the Wine Cup
poems.s: day palace cup jar rider
z: 知章骑马似乘船，眼花落井水底眠。
汝阳三斗始朝天，道逢麴车口流涎，恨不移封向酒泉。
左相日兴费万钱，饮如长鲸吸百川，衔杯乐圣称避贤。
宗之潇洒美少年，举觞白眼望青天，皎如玉树临风前。
苏晋长斋绣佛前，醉中往往爱逃禅。
李白一斗诗百篇，长安市上酒家眠。
天子呼来不上船，自称臣是酒中仙。
张旭三杯草圣传，脱帽露顶王公前，挥毫落纸如云烟。
焦遂五斗方卓然，高谈雄辩惊四筵。
e: He Zhizhang sways on horseback as if he's sailing in a boat;
Eyes swimming, he falls down a well, and sleeps on the bottom, content.
The Prince of Ruyang drinks three pecks before he goes to court;
He drools when he meets a brewer's cart along the way he went,
And wishes his fief were moved to the town of Wine Spring.
The Chancellor of the Left spends ten thousand cash a day,
Drinks like a great whale gulping a hundred rivers away;
Cup at his lips, he "loves the sage and shuns the worthy", so they say.
Cui Zongzhi, a handsome youth, so carefree and so free,
Lifts his goblet, rolls his eyes at the blue sky —
Bright as a jade tree standing in the breeze.
Su Jin keeps a long fast before the embroidered Buddha's shrine,
But drunk, he often likes to slip away from Zen to wine.
Li Bai — one peck of wine, a hundred poems!
He sleeps in taverns in Chang'an's market streets.
When the Son of Heaven summons him, he won't board the royal boat:
"Your servant is an immortal of wine," is what he repeats.
Zhang Xu — three cups, and he's the Sage of Cursive Script, it's said;
Before the princes and the lords he takes his cap off, bares his head;
His brush falls on the paper like clouds and mists outspread.
Jiao Sui needs five pecks before he's at his best;
Then his lofty talk and fierce debate astonish every guest.
poems.n: A comic gallery of eight famous drinkers of Chang'an around 740: the poet He Zhizhang, Prince Li Jin of Ruyang, the chancellor Li Shizhi, the dandy Cui Zongzhi, the devout Su Jin, Li Bai, the calligrapher Zhang Xu and the debater Jiao Sui — each sketched in a few lines. The Li Bai lines made his legend. Wine Spring (Jiuquan) is a real town on the Silk Road; "the sage" and "the worthy" were drinkers' slang for clear and cloudy wine; "white eyes" meant looking down on the vulgar.

poems.s: spring river flowers butterfly person
z: 朝回日日典春衣，每日江头尽醉归。
酒债寻常行处有，人生七十古来稀。
穿花蛱蝶深深见，点水蜻蜓款款飞。
传语风光共流转，暂时相赏莫相违。
e: Back from court each day, I pawn my clothes of spring,
And every evening by the river come home drunk as can be.
Wine debts are common — I owe them everywhere I go;
A man who lives to seventy has always been rare to see.
Deep among the flowers the butterflies are glimpsed;
Dipping the water, dragonflies drift slow and free.
I send word to the spring: let us drift on together,
And enjoy each other a while — don't turn away from me.
poems.n: Spring 758, at Qujiang ("Winding River"), the pleasure park of Chang'an. Du Fu, holding a minor post at court, pawns his clothes to drink — less from joy than from disillusion. "Since ancient times, seventy has been rare" gave Chinese the word 古稀 for the age of seventy. (Du Fu himself died at fifty-eight.)

poems.s: autumn cottage two
z: 堂前扑枣任西邻，无食无儿一妇人。
不为困穷宁有此？只缘恐惧转须亲。
即防远客虽多事，便插疏篱却甚真。
已诉征求贫到骨，正思戎马泪盈巾。
e: Let our west neighbour knock the dates down from the tree —
A woman with no food, no children, all alone.
Would she do this if she weren't in poverty?
She's frightened — so be kinder than you've shown.
Her fear of you, a stranger, may be needless, it is true,
But fencing off the tree would make her fears seem right.
She's told me that the levies have bled her to the bone —
I think of war, and tears soak my kerchief through tonight.
poems.n: Du Fu had moved out of his cottage at Kuizhou and lent it to a relative, Mr Wu, who put up a fence to stop a poor widow next door from knocking down dates — as Du Fu had always let her do. This gentle poem-letter asks him to take it down. Few poems anywhere show such quiet, practical compassion.

poems.s: day horse desert wind
z: 胡马大宛名，锋棱瘦骨成。
竹批双耳峻，风入四蹄轻。
所向无空阔，真堪托死生。
骁腾有如此，万里可横行。
e: A western horse, of the famous Ferghana breed,
All sharp edges, built of bone so lean;
Its ears stand pointed like bamboo sliced for speed;
The wind flies in its hooves — so light, so keen.
Wherever it goes, no space is too wide;
You could trust it with your life and with your death.
With such fierce swiftness at your side,
You could ride ten thousand li in a breath.
poems.n: An early poem (c. 740) on a fine horse belonging to an army officer named Fang. Dayuan (Ferghana, in Central Asia) was famous for its "heavenly horses". The horse is also a portrait of the kind of man the young Du Fu hoped to become.

poems.s: night crescent maple river mountains window
z: 死别已吞声，生别常恻恻。
江南瘴疠地，逐客无消息。
故人入我梦，明我长相忆。
恐非平生魂，路远不可测。
魂来枫林青，魂返关塞黑。
君今在罗网，何以有羽翼？
落月满屋梁，犹疑照颜色。
水深波浪阔，无使蛟龙得。
e: A parting by death — one swallows the sobs at last;
A parting in life brings grief that never ends.
South of the River, the fever lands are vast,
And no news comes from the exile, my friend.
Last night you came into my dream,
To show you know I think of you always.
I fear it was no living soul, it would seem —
The road's too long to fathom, all those days.
Your soul came while the maple woods were green;
Your soul went home through mountain passes black.
You're snared in the net — so how, I mean,
Could you have wings to fly here and fly back?
The setting moon floods all the rafters bright;
I half believe it's shining on your face.
The waters are deep, the waves are wide tonight —
Don't let the dragons drag you from your place!
poems.n: 759. Li Bai had been sentenced to exile in Yelang for joining Prince Yong's rebellion, and rumours said he was dead. Du Fu dreams of him and fears the visitor was a ghost. The green maple woods are the south; the black passes, the north where Du Fu lies sleeping. The flood-dragons (蛟龙) are the dangers — and the enemies — on the waters of the south.

poems.te: Song of White Snow: Seeing Judge Wu Off to the Capital
poems.s: winter snow mountains fort flag rider
z: 北风卷地白草折，胡天八月即飞雪。
忽如一夜春风来，千树万树梨花开。
散入珠帘湿罗幕，狐裘不暖锦衾薄。
将军角弓不得控，都护铁衣冷难着。
瀚海阑干百丈冰，愁云惨淡万里凝。
中军置酒饮归客，胡琴琵琶与羌笛。
纷纷暮雪下辕门，风掣红旗冻不翻。
轮台东门送君去，去时雪满天山路。
山回路转不见君，雪上空留马行处。
e: The north wind rolls the land and snaps the white grass low;
In the eighth month, the northern sky is flying thick with snow.
As if, in a single night, the breeze of spring had come,
A thousand trees, ten thousand trees, burst into pear-blossom.
It drifts through pearl curtains, soaks the silken tent within;
Fox furs give no warmth, and brocade quilts seem thin.
The general cannot draw his horn-bow, stiff with cold;
The Protector's iron armour is too chill to hold.
The desert sea is cracked with ice a hundred fathoms high;
Gloomy clouds, ten thousand li, are frozen as they lie.
In the central tent we set out wine to toast the parting guest,
With Hu fiddles, pipas and Qiang flutes playing their best.
At dusk the snow falls thick and fast upon the camp's front gate;
The red flag, frozen stiff, won't flutter in the wind's weight.
By Luntai's eastern gate I see you on your way;
Snow fills the road across the Tianshan as you leave today.
The mountain bends, the road turns, and you're lost from view;
Only hoofprints in the snow remain, where your horse went through.
poems.n: Luntai, in today's Xinjiang, 754: Cen Shen sees off a colleague returning to Chang'an. Snow arriving overnight like pear blossom on a spring wind is the most famous snow image in Chinese poetry. The ending — the friend gone, only hoofprints left in the snow — is pure longing.

poems.te: Meeting an Envoy Bound for the Capital
poems.s: day desert rider horse two
z: 故园东望路漫漫，双袖龙钟泪不干。
马上相逢无纸笔，凭君传语报平安。
e: I gaze east toward my home — the road goes on and on;
Both my sleeves are soaked with tears that never dry.
We meet on horseback — no brush, no paper, none;
Please tell my family I'm safe and well, as you pass by.
poems.n: On his way to the Central Asian frontier in 749, Cen Shen meets an envoy heading back to Chang'an. No time to write — only a spoken message: "I'm safe." The simplest words carry the deepest feeling.

poems.s: dusk desert moon rider horse
z: 走马西来欲到天，辞家见月两回圆。
今夜不知何处宿，平沙万里绝人烟。
e: I ride west till it seems I'll reach the edge of the sky;
Twice since I left my home I've seen the moon grow round.
Tonight I do not know where I shall lie —
Ten thousand li of sand, and not a hearth-smoke to be found.
poems.n: Crossing the Gobi (碛) in 749. Two full moons measure two months away from home; the endless sand without "the smoke of human fires" measures the loneliness.

poems.te: On the March at the Double Ninth, Thinking of My Garden in Chang'an
poems.s: autumn chrysanthemum fort flag hills
z: 强欲登高去，无人送酒来。
遥怜故园菊，应傍战场开。
e: I force myself to climb the heights today,
But no one's here to bring me any wine.
I think with pity of my garden's flowers far away —
They must be blooming by the battle line.
poems.n: The Double Ninth festival of 757, with the army in the field; Chang'an, Cen Shen's home, was in rebel hands. Instead of drinking chrysanthemum wine with friends, he imagines the chrysanthemums of his abandoned garden flowering beside the fighting. Tao Yuanming once sat out this festival with no wine until a friend sent some; here, no one does.

poems.s: night spring window river crescent
z: 洞房昨夜春风起，遥忆美人湘江水。
枕上片时春梦中，行尽江南数千里。
e: Last night the spring wind stirred inside my chamber's door;
I thought of my love, far off by the Xiang River's shore.
Upon my pillow, in a moment's dream of spring,
I travelled thousands of li south of the Yangtze, and more.
poems.n: A lovely paradox of time and distance: a dream lasting a moment covers thousands of li to reach a loved one. "Spring dream" (春梦) is also an image of fleeting happiness.

poems.te: Glad That My Cousin Lu Lun Stays the Night
poems.s: night autumn rain maple leaves cottage candle two
z: 静夜四无邻，荒居旧业贫。
雨中黄叶树，灯下白头人。
以我独沉久，愧君相见频。
平生自有分，况是蔡家亲。
e: A quiet night, and no neighbours near;
In my bare house, my old estate is poor.
In the rain, a tree of yellow leaves;
Beneath the lamp, a white-haired man, and nothing more.
I've long been sunk in solitude, alone —
I'm ashamed you come so often to my door.
Each has his share in life; and more than that,
We're kin, like Cai and Yang, as those before.
poems.n: The poet Lu Lun, Sikong Shu's cousin, comes to stay. 雨中黄叶树，灯下白头人 — "in the rain, a tree of yellow leaves; under the lamp, a white-haired man" — is one of the most admired couplets of the Tang: the old man and the autumn tree mirror each other. The Cai and Yang families of the Jin dynasty were joined by marriage, as the two poets were.

poems.te: The Spirit of the Xiang Plays Her Zither: An Examination Poem
poems.s: day river peaks mist lake
z: 善鼓云和瑟，常闻帝子灵。
冯夷空自舞，楚客不堪听。
苦调凄金石，清音入杳冥。
苍梧来怨慕，白芷动芳馨。
流水传潇浦，悲风过洞庭。
曲终人不见，江上数峰青。
e: On her cloud-wood zither she plays with skill —
Often we've heard of the river goddess's art.
The River Lord dances, but in vain;
The exile from Chu cannot bear it in his heart.
Her bitter notes make metal and stone grieve;
Her clear tones pierce the dark void far away.
From Cangwu comes the sorrow of her longing;
White angelica stirs its fragrance in the spray.
The flowing water bears it down the Xiao;
A mournful wind sweeps over Dongting's sheen.
The music ends — and no one can be seen;
Upon the river, a few peaks rise, green.
poems.n: Written for the imperial examination of 751 on a set theme: the goddess of the Xiang River — a daughter of the sage-king Yao, who drowned herself in grief when her husband Shun died at Cangwu — playing her zither. Most of the poem is an examination exercise, but the last couplet, as the music ends and the goddess vanishes, leaving only green peaks on the river, is pure magic. Legend says Qian Qi heard those lines spoken by a ghost.

poems.te: Lodging with the Master of Lotus Mountain in Snow
poems.s: night winter snow mountains cottage wind person
z: 日暮苍山远，天寒白屋贫。
柴门闻犬吠，风雪夜归人。
e: At sunset, the grey-blue mountains far away;
The sky is cold; the thatched hut, white and poor.
A dog barks at the brushwood gate — someone, late,
Comes home through wind and snow, at night, to the door.
poems.n: Twenty characters, a complete short film: a traveller finds shelter at dusk in a poor mountain hut; in the night a dog barks — the master is coming home through the storm. 风雪夜归人, "a man coming home on a night of wind and snow", is one of the best-loved images in Chinese.

poems.s: dusk sun temple bamboo mountains person
z: 苍苍竹林寺，杳杳钟声晚。
荷笠带斜阳，青山独归远。
e: The bamboo-grove temple, dark and green;
Far off, the evening bell is sounding slow.
His bamboo hat bears the slanting sun;
Alone, into the green hills far, I watch him go.
poems.n: A farewell to the monk-poet Lingche. The poet stays behind; the monk, his rain-hat lit by the setting sun, grows smaller and smaller among the green hills — a painting in twenty characters.

poems.s: night pine person moon
z: 泠泠七弦上，静听松风寒。
古调虽自爱，今人多不弹。
e: Clear and cool, the seven strings sing;
I listen to "Wind in the Pines", cold and lone.
These ancient tunes are what I love the most —
But few play them now; their time has flown.
poems.n: "Wind in the Pines" (风入松) was an old qin tune. On the surface, a lament that the pure music of the qin has given way to flashier new music from Central Asia; underneath, Liu Changqing's own integrity, out of fashion in his age.

poems.te: The Meditation Hall Behind Poshan Temple
poems.s: dawn sun temple pine flowers lake birds
z: 清晨入古寺，初日照高林。
曲径通幽处，禅房花木深。
山光悦鸟性，潭影空人心。
万籁此都寂，但余钟磬音。
e: At early dawn I enter the old temple's gate;
The first rays of the sun light up the forest tall.
A winding path leads to a secret, hidden place,
Where flowers and trees grow deep round the meditation hall.
The mountain light delights the nature of the birds;
The pool's reflections empty out the hearts of men.
Here all the sounds of the world fall silent,
Save for the bell and the stone chime, now and then.
poems.n: Poshan Temple is in Changshu, Jiangsu. 曲径通幽处, "a winding path leads to a secluded place", became a proverb and a principle of Chinese garden design. The poem moves from the outer landscape to inner stillness — the reflections in the pool empty the mind of desire — and ends with nothing but the temple bells.

poems.s: spring rain mountains river peach fisher crane
z: 西塞山前白鹭飞，桃花流水鳜鱼肥。
青箬笠，绿蓑衣，斜风细雨不须归。
e: Before Xisai Mountain, the white egrets wing;
Peach petals on the stream; the perch grow fat in spring.
A hat of green bamboo, a cape of green straw:
In slanting wind and drizzle — why go home at all?
poems.n: An early *ci* lyric by "the Old Fisherman of the Misty Waves". The fisherman, free and content in any weather, is the ideal of the recluse; the emperor himself sent for paintings of the scene. 鳜鱼 is the mandarin fish, at its best in peach-blossom season.

poems.s: dusk spring rain river boat oriole grass
z: 独怜幽草涧边生，上有黄鹂深树鸣。
春潮带雨晚来急，野渡无人舟自横。
e: I love the hidden grasses growing by the stream,
While orioles sing high up in the deep green trees.
The spring tide, swelled with rain, at evening rushes strong;
At the lonely ferry, no one — the boat turns idly in the breeze.
poems.n: Chuzhou (Anhui), where Wei Yingwu was governor. The last line — an empty ferryboat swinging crosswise in the current — became a favourite subject of painters, and has been read as the poet himself: idle, unused, at peace.

poems.te: On an Autumn Night, to Qiu Dan
poems.s: night autumn moon pine mountains person
z: 怀君属秋夜，散步咏凉天。
空山松子落，幽人应未眠。
e: On this autumn night I think of you,
And stroll, and chant beneath the cool sky.
In empty hills, the pine cones drop —
And you, the hermit, lie sleepless, as do I.
poems.n: A letter-poem to Qiu Dan, a friend who had become a Daoist recluse. The sound of a pine cone falling in the silence links the two sleepless friends across the distance.

poems.te: Happy to Meet an Old Friend from Liangchuan on the Huai
poems.s: autumn hills river two cup
z: 江汉曾为客，相逢每醉还。
浮云一别后，流水十年间。
欢笑情如旧，萧疏鬓已斑。
何因不归去？淮上有秋山。
e: Once by the Jiang and Han we roamed as guests;
Whenever we met, we drank, and came home merry.
Then we parted, like the floating clouds;
Ten years have flowed like water, in a hurry.
Our laughter and our love are as of old,
But our thin hair at the temples has turned grey.
You ask me why I don't go home —
The autumn hills along the Huai make me stay.
poems.n: A reunion after ten years. The middle couplet compresses a decade: "a parting like floating clouds, ten years like flowing water". The answer to "why not go home?" — "because there are autumn hills here" — hides behind a love of landscape a reluctance to return home with nothing to show.

poems.te: To Li Dan and Yuan Xi
poems.s: night spring moon tower flowers
z: 去年花里逢君别，今日花开又一年。
世事茫茫难自料，春愁黯黯独成眠。
身多疾病思田里，邑有流亡愧俸钱。
闻道欲来相问讯，西楼望月几回圆。
e: Last year, among the flowers, I met you and we parted;
The flowers bloom today — and one more year has flown.
The world's affairs are vast, and no one can foresee them;
In spring's dark melancholy I fall asleep alone.
My body's full of illness; I long for fields and home;
With refugees in my district, I'm ashamed to draw my pay.
I hear you plan to come and visit me —
From the west tower, how many full moons have I watched, while you delay?
poems.n: Written around 784, while Wei Yingwu governed Chuzhou in the troubled years after the great rebellions. 邑有流亡愧俸钱 — "with refugees in my district, I am ashamed of my salary" — was praised for a thousand years as the conscience of the ideal official.

poems.s: night crescent pine grass wind rider
z: 林暗草惊风，将军夜引弓。
平明寻白羽，没在石棱中。
e: Dark woods; the grass starts up as wind sweeps by;
The general draws his bow at dead of night.
At dawn they seek his white-fletched arrow — why,
It's buried in a rock, sunk out of sight!
poems.n: Based on a story of the Han general Li Guang, who shot at what he took for a tiger in the dark grass — and in the morning found his arrow buried in a rock. The "grass startled by wind" hints at the tiger without naming it.

poems.s: night winter snow geese rider horse
z: 月黑雁飞高，单于夜遁逃。
欲将轻骑逐，大雪满弓刀。
e: No moon; the wild geese fly up high and far;
The khan has fled, escaping in the night.
We'd chase him down with our light horse —
Heavy snow covers bows and blades in white.
poems.n: The night is so dark that the khan's escape is known only from the startled geese. The last line — the cavalry poised, snow piling on their weapons — freezes the moment before the chase.

poems.s: day palace person flowers window
z: 鸣筝金粟柱，素手玉房前。
欲得周郎顾，时时误拂弦。
e: The zither sings on bridges flecked with gold;
White hands play by the jade room, deft and slow.
To win a glance from Master Zhou, so bold,
She strikes a wrong note now and then — just so.
poems.n: In the Three Kingdoms period, the young general Zhou Yu was such a fine musician that "if a note was wrong, Master Zhou would turn and look". So the clever player misplays on purpose — to make the handsome listener look at her.

poems.te: Hearing a Flute at Night on the Wall of Shouxiang
poems.s: night moon desert fort frost
z: 回乐烽前沙似雪，受降城外月如霜。
不知何处吹芦管，一夜征人尽望乡。
e: Before Huile's beacon tower, the sand lies white as snow;
Outside the Surrender City walls, the moon is like the frost.
From somewhere — who knows where? — a reed pipe's playing low;
All night the soldiers gaze toward home, and feel what they have lost.
poems.n: Shouxiang ("Accepting Surrender") was a fortress on the Yellow River in the far north. Sand and moonlight turn the world white; an unseen reed pipe plays; every soldier turns toward home. Set to music, the poem was sung all over the empire.

poems.s: day river boat person
z: 嫁得瞿塘贾，朝朝误妾期。
早知潮有信，嫁与弄潮儿。
e: I married a merchant of Qutang Gorge;
Every day he breaks his word to me.
Had I known the tide keeps faith so true,
I'd have wed a boy who rides the tides at sea.
poems.n: A merchant's wife, in the voice of a southern folk song. The tide comes back on time, every time; her husband never does — so she'd rather have married one of the young men who play in the great tidal bore of the Qiantang River. Funny and sad at once.

poems.s: night candle cottage person window
z: 慈母手中线，游子身上衣。
临行密密缝，意恐迟迟归。
谁言寸草心，报得三春晖。
e: The thread in a loving mother's hand
Becomes the coat her wandering son will wear.
Before he goes, she stitches close and tight,
Afraid he'll long be gone, away from her care.
Who says a blade of grass, an inch in height,
Could ever repay the spring sun's light so fair?
poems.n: The most beloved poem in Chinese about a mother's love. Meng Jiao wrote it at fifty, when he finally received a minor post and could bring his mother to live with him. The child is "an inch of grass"; the mother's love is the sunshine of spring, which no grass can ever repay.

poems.s: spring rider horse flowers wall
z: 昔日龌龊不足夸，今朝放荡思无涯。
春风得意马蹄疾，一日看尽长安花。
e: My meagre days of old aren't worth a word;
Today, set free, my thoughts roam without bound.
Proud in the spring wind, my horse's hooves have whirred —
In one day I've seen every flower in Chang'an town.
poems.n: Meng Jiao passed the *jinshi* examination in 796, aged forty-six, after two failures. New graduates paraded through the capital and toured its gardens. Two idioms come from this poem: 春风得意, "proud in the spring wind" (flushed with success), and 走马观花, "viewing flowers from horseback" (seeing things in a hurry).

poems.s: night autumn crescent frost maple river boat temple crows
z: 月落乌啼霜满天，江枫渔火对愁眠。
姑苏城外寒山寺，夜半钟声到客船。
e: The moon has set; crows caw; frost fills the sky;
By river maples and fishing fires, I lie in grief, half asleep.
Outside Gusu's walls, the Cold Mountain Temple stands nearby;
Its midnight bell rings out to the traveller's boat, slow and deep.
poems.n: Written around 756 near Suzhou (Gusu) by a traveller fleeing the An Lushan rebellion. Sight, sound and feeling blend in the dark: setting moon, cawing crows, frost, red maples and fishing lights — and finally the bell. The poem made Hanshan ("Cold Mountain") Temple famous; crowds still gather there on New Year's Eve to hear its bell.

poems.s: dusk spring palace willow petals smoke
z: 春城无处不飞花，寒食东风御柳斜。
日暮汉宫传蜡烛，轻烟散入五侯家。
e: In the spring city, petals fly in every lane;
At Cold Food, the east wind bends the palace willows down.
At dusk the Han court sends out candles, lit again;
Their light smoke drifts into the Five Lords' mansions in the town.
poems.n: At the Cold Food Festival, just before Qingming, no fires could be lit for three days; at the end, the palace sent new fire to favoured households. Only the "Five Lords" — the emperor's eunuch favourites — receive it first: a delicate satire hidden in a lovely spring picture. Emperor Dezong loved the poem so much that he appointed its author by quoting the first line.

poems.s: night spring moon stars cottage window
z: 更深月色半人家，北斗阑干南斗斜。
今夜偏知春气暖，虫声新透绿窗纱。
e: Late at night, the moon lights half the houses' face;
The Northern Dipper slants; the Southern sinks in place.
Tonight I know at last the air of spring is warm —
The insects' songs come newly through the green window's lace.
poems.n: The first insect song of the year, heard through the window screen, tells the poet that spring has come — a discovery made by ear, in the moonlit night.

poems.s: dusk spring petals palace window
z: 纱窗日落渐黄昏，金屋无人见泪痕。
寂寞空庭春欲晚，梨花满地不开门。
e: Past the gauze window the sun goes down; the dusk falls slow;
In her golden chamber, no one sees her tear-stained face.
The empty courtyard's lonely; spring is nearly gone, I know;
Pear blossoms cover the ground; the gate stays shut in place.
poems.n: A forgotten palace lady — "golden chamber" recalls a Han emperor's promise to house his beloved in a house of gold. The unopened gate among fallen pear petals says that no one comes, and that she no longer expects anyone.

poems.s: autumn wind wall person candle
z: 洛阳城里见秋风，欲作家书意万重。
复恐匆匆说不尽，行人临发又开封。
e: In Luoyang town I feel the autumn wind blow;
I sit to write home — ten thousand thoughts to tell.
Afraid that in my haste I've left things out, I know,
As the courier's leaving, I open it up again as well.
poems.n: A tiny gesture says everything: the letter is sealed, the messenger is ready to go — and the homesick writer tears it open once more. The autumn wind recalls the Jin official Zhang Han, who saw the autumn wind, thought of the perch of his home river, resigned his post and went home.

poems.s: day palace tower window person
z: 君知妾有夫，赠妾双明珠。
感君缠绵意，系在红罗襦。
妾家高楼连苑起，良人执戟明光里。
知君用心如日月，事夫誓拟同生死。
还君明珠双泪垂，恨不相逢未嫁时。
e: You knew I had a husband — still, you sent
A pair of shining pearls to me.
Moved by the love and tenderness they meant,
I tied them to my red silk robe, to see.
My family's tower rises by the royal park;
My husband bears a halberd in the Bright Hall's guard.
I know your heart is clear as sun and moon,
But I've vowed to share my husband's life and death, however hard.
I give you back your pearls; two tears fall down —
If only we had met before I wore the bridal crown!
poems.n: On the surface, a faithful wife gently refusing a suitor's pearls. In fact it is a political allegory: Zhang Ji was declining an invitation to serve the powerful warlord Li Shidao, who was defying the Tang court — the "husband" is the emperor. 恨不相逢未嫁时, "if only we had met before I married", became the classic line for love that came too late.

poems.te: Gazing at the Moon on the Fifteenth Night
poems.s: night autumn moon crows cottage
z: 中庭地白树栖鸦，冷露无声湿桂花。
今夜月明人尽望，不知秋思落谁家。
e: The courtyard ground is white; crows roost upon the trees;
Cold dew, in silence, wets the cassia's blooms.
Tonight the moon is bright, and all look up to see —
I wonder in whose house the autumn longing looms?
poems.n: The Mid-Autumn Festival, when families gather under the full moon. The ground white with moonlight, crows silent in the trees, dew falling on the cassia (the tree that grows in the moon) — and a gentle question: everyone is looking at the moon, but whose heart is missing someone most?

poems.s: day cottage smoke person two
z: 三日入厨下，洗手作羹汤。
未谙姑食性，先遣小姑尝。
e: On the third day, I went into the kitchen,
Washed my hands, and made a pot of soup.
Not knowing yet how Mother likes her food,
I let her daughter taste it first — to see if it would suit.
poems.n: On the third day after the wedding a bride had to cook for her new mother-in-law. Clever and tactful, she asks her husband's little sister — who knows her mother's tastes — to try it first. A smiling glimpse of domestic life.

poems.te: Passing a Mountain Village in the Rain
poems.s: summer rain bamboo bridge cottage flowers fields
z: 雨里鸡鸣一两家，竹溪村路板桥斜。
妇姑相唤浴蚕去，闲着中庭栀子花。
e: In the rain, from one or two homes, the cocks are crowing;
By the bamboo creek, the village path, a plank bridge leaning.
Mother and daughter-in-law call each other off to wash the silkworm eggs,
Leaving the gardenias in the yard alone and gleaming.
poems.n: A mountain village in the rain at silkworm season. Everyone is busy, so only the gardenias in the courtyard are "idle" — a lovely detail of farm life.

poems.t: 早春呈水部张十八员外（其一）
poems.te: Early Spring: To Zhang the Eighteenth of the Ministry of Waters
poems.s: spring rain grass willow wall
z: 天街小雨润如酥，草色遥看近却无。
最是一年春好处，绝胜烟柳满皇都。
e: The fine rain on the royal streets is soft as cream;
The grass, from far away, looks green — up close, there's none.
Of all the year, spring's best is now, I deem —
Better than misty willows veiling the capital later on.
poems.n: Han Yu, aged fifty-six, to his friend Zhang Ji. Line two is a famous observation: new grass so faint that you see it as a green haze from afar, but not when you look at your feet. Early spring, barely begun, is more precious than full spring.

poems.te: Demoted, at Lan Pass: To My Grand-Nephew Xiang
poems.s: winter snow mountains clouds rider horse
z: 一封朝奏九重天，夕贬潮州路八千。
欲为圣明除弊事，肯将衰朽惜残年！
云横秦岭家何在？雪拥蓝关马不前。
知汝远来应有意，好收吾骨瘴江边。
e: At dawn I sent one memorial to the Ninefold Gate;
By dusk I was banished to Chaozhou, eight thousand li.
I sought to rid our wise lord of a harmful state —
Would I, old and worn, begrudge what years are left to me?
Clouds lie across the Qinling — where now is my home?
Snow chokes the Lan Pass, and my horse won't take a step.
I know you've followed me so far with purpose:
To gather up my bones beside the fever-river's edge.
poems.n: In 819 Emperor Xianzong had a finger-bone of the Buddha paraded into the palace. Han Yu, a stern Confucian, sent a memorial condemning it, was nearly executed, and was banished to Chaozhou on the far southern coast. At the snowbound Lan Pass his grand-nephew Han Xiang caught up with him. Expecting to die in the malarial south, he asks the young man to collect his bones. (He survived, and was recalled within a year.)

poems.s: spring flowers petals willow wind
z: 草树知春不久归，百般红紫斗芳菲。
杨花榆荚无才思，惟解漫天作雪飞。
e: The grass and trees know spring will not stay long,
And vie in every red and purple, blooming bright.
The willow-down and elm-seeds lack the talent of that throng —
They only know to fill the sky like snowflakes in their flight.
poems.n: Flowers compete in beauty before spring leaves, while plain willow catkins and elm seeds, with no colour to show, simply fill the sky like snow. Mockery — or quiet admiration for those who give what they can? Readers have argued both ways.

poems.s: dusk sun swallows bridge cottage grass
z: 朱雀桥边野草花，乌衣巷口夕阳斜。
旧时王谢堂前燕，飞入寻常百姓家。
e: By Vermilion Bridge the wild grass is in flower;
At Black Robe Lane, the sunset slants its light.
The swallows that once nested in the Wang and Xie halls of power
Now fly into the homes of common folk tonight.
poems.n: Black Robe Lane in Nanjing was home to the Wang and Xie clans, the greatest aristocratic families of the 4th and 5th centuries. Four hundred years later the mansions have vanished — but the swallows still return to the same spot, now full of ordinary houses. The rise and fall of the great, seen in a swallow's flight.

poems.s: night moon wall river mountains
z: 山围故国周遭在，潮打空城寂寞回。
淮水东边旧时月，夜深还过女墙来。
e: The hills still ring the fallen capital around;
The tide beats on the empty city, and lonely, ebbs away.
East of the Qinhuai, the moon that once shone here
Still climbs the parapets at midnight, as in the olden day.
poems.n: Stone City was the fortress of Nanjing, capital of six fallen dynasties. Only the hills, the tide and the moon — which shone on all those vanished courts — remain. Bai Juyi said that after this poem, later poets would have nothing left to say about Nanjing.

poems.s: spring willow river rain sun boat
z: 杨柳青青江水平，闻郎江上唱歌声。
东边日出西边雨，道是无晴却有晴。
e: Green, green the willows; the river's calm and wide;
I hear my lover singing on the river, drifting by.
Sun in the east, and rain upon the western side —
You'd say there's no sunshine, yet there's sunshine in the sky.
poems.n: Liu Yuxi adapted the "Bamboo Branch" folk songs he heard in exile in the south-west. 晴 (clear weather) and 情 (love) are both pronounced *qíng*, so the last line means both "you'd say it isn't sunny, yet it is" and "you'd think he has no feelings for me, yet he does" — a girl's uncertainty in a sun-shower.

poems.s: autumn day crane clouds mountains
z: 自古逢秋悲寂寥，我言秋日胜春朝。
晴空一鹤排云上，便引诗情到碧霄。
e: Since ancient times, men sigh at autumn's lonely gloom;
I say that autumn days surpass the mornings of the spring.
In the clear sky, one crane soars up through the clouds' plume,
And draws my poet's heart into the blue upon its wing.
poems.n: Written in exile in 805. Against a thousand years of poems mourning autumn, Liu Yuxi declares autumn better than spring — the crane breaking through the clouds is his own unbroken spirit. A rare poem of defiant optimism.

poems.t: 酬乐天扬州初逢席上见赠
poems.te: Reply to Bai Juyi at Our First Meeting in Yangzhou
poems.s: spring river sail boat two cup
z: 巴山楚水凄凉地，二十三年弃置身。
怀旧空吟闻笛赋，到乡翻似烂柯人。
沉舟侧畔千帆过，病树前头万木春。
今日听君歌一曲，暂凭杯酒长精神。
e: In Ba's bleak hills and Chu's cold streams I spent
Twenty-three years, discarded and alone.
I mourn lost friends, and chant "The Flute" in lament;
Home now, I'm like the woodsman who came back to a world unknown.
Beside the sunken ship, a thousand sails go by;
Before the withered tree, ten thousand trees break into spring.
Today I've heard you sing a song for me —
Let this cup of wine lift up my spirits on its wing.
poems.n: Liu Yuxi met Bai Juyi in Yangzhou in 826, after twenty-three years of exile. "Hearing the Flute" is a rhapsody mourning executed friends; the woodsman who stopped to watch immortals play chess went home to find his axe-handle rotted and a century gone. Then comes the great couplet — the sunken ship and the withered tree, while life sails and blooms on all around — which Bai Juyi called divine: there is no self-pity, only the knowledge that life goes on.

poems.s: night autumn moon lake hills
z: 湖光秋月两相和，潭面无风镜未磨。
遥望洞庭山水翠，白银盘里一青螺。
e: The lake's sheen and the autumn moon are blended into one;
The calm pool's face — a bronze mirror, not yet polished, dim.
From afar I gaze at Dongting's isle, so green —
A green conch lying on a silver platter's rim.
poems.n: Dongting Lake on a still autumn night: the lake is an old bronze mirror, slightly misted; Junshan Island at its centre is a small green conch shell on a silver plate. A perfect miniature of a vast scene.

poems.te: Thinking of the Past at Xisai Mountain
poems.s: autumn river mountains reeds sail fort
z: 王濬楼船下益州，金陵王气黯然收。
千寻铁锁沉江底，一片降幡出石头。
人世几回伤往事，山形依旧枕寒流。
今逢四海为家日，故垒萧萧芦荻秋。
e: Wang Jun's towered warships sailed down from Yizhou's shore;
The royal aura over Jinling faded and was gone.
The iron chains, a thousand fathoms long, sank to the river floor;
From Stone City a flag of surrender was hoisted on.
How many times have men lamented what has passed?
The hill still lies, as ever, pillowed on the cold stream's flow.
Now the four seas are one family, at last —
The old forts sigh among the autumn reeds below.
poems.n: In 280 the Jin general Wang Jun sailed great towered warships down the Yangtze from Sichuan to conquer the kingdom of Wu; Wu's iron chains across the river at Xisai Mountain were melted with torches, and its last ruler surrendered at Stone City (Nanjing). Kingdoms rise and fall; the mountain stays. The ending is a quiet warning: the empire is united now — but the ruined forts in the reeds show how fragile unity is.

poems.s: day river desert stars clouds
z: 九曲黄河万里沙，浪淘风簸自天涯。
如今直上银河去，同到牵牛织女家。
e: The Yellow River's nine great bends, ten thousand li of sand,
Washed by waves and tossed by winds, come from the edge of sky.
Now let us ride straight up the Silver River, hand in hand,
To the Herdboy's and the Weaver's home, way up high.
poems.n: An old legend held that the Yellow River joins the Milky Way (the "Silver River"), and that a man who sailed up it reached the stars. In a folk-song voice, the poet proposes to follow the river all the way to the two star-lovers.

poems.s: day river person reeds sun
z: 莫道谗言如浪深，莫言迁客似沙沉。
千淘万漉虽辛苦，吹尽狂沙始到金。
e: Don't say that slander runs as deep as waves can go;
Don't say an exile sinks like sand, to stay below.
Though panning, sifting countless times is hard and slow,
When all the sand is blown away, the gold will show.
poems.n: Slandered and exiled for twenty-three years, Liu Yuxi answers with a gold-panner's patience: truth, like gold, survives every sifting. 千淘万漉, "a thousand washings, ten thousand siftings", became an idiom for hard-won results.

poems.s: spring peach temple rider petals
z: 紫陌红尘拂面来，无人不道看花回。
玄都观里桃千树，尽是刘郎去后栽。
e: Along the purple lanes, red dust brushes every face;
No one comes by who hasn't just been out to see the flowers.
A thousand peach trees bloom in Xuandu Temple's grounds —
All planted after Master Liu was driven from the city's towers.
poems.n: Full title: *Written in Jest for the Gentlemen Viewing the Flowers, on Coming to the Capital from Langzhou in 815*. Recalled after ten years of exile, Liu Yuxi found everyone flocking to the peach blossoms of the Xuandu Daoist temple. His joke — all those trees were planted after I left — meant: all these newly powerful officials rose after my party fell. The court took the hint, and sent him away for fourteen more years.

poems.s: spring temple flowers grass person
z: 百亩庭中半是苔，桃花净尽菜花开。
种桃道士归何处？前度刘郎今又来。
e: Half the great courtyard is covered now with moss;
The peaches are all gone; the cabbage flowers grow.
The Daoist who planted the peaches — where has he gone?
The Master Liu of last time is back again — hello!
poems.n: Fourteen years later, in 828, Liu Yuxi was recalled again — and went straight back to Xuandu Temple. The peach trees (the upstarts) are gone, the gardener (the minister who exiled him) is gone, and Master Liu is back: one of the most cheerfully defiant poems in Chinese. 前度刘郎, "the Master Liu of last time", became a phrase for someone returning to an old haunt.

poems.s: spring tower flowers butterfly person
z: 新妆宜面下朱楼，深锁春光一院愁。
行到中庭数花朵，蜻蜓飞上玉搔头。
e: Fresh make-up on her face, she leaves the crimson tower;
Spring's light is locked within a courtyard full of gloom.
She walks into the yard and counts each flower —
A dragonfly lands on her jade pin, mistaking her for a bloom.
poems.n: A lament with a lovely detail: idly counting flowers for lack of anything else to do, she stands so still and looks so fresh that a dragonfly settles on her jade hairpin as if on a flower — but no one else comes to look at her.

poems.s: spring flowers palace lotus
z: 庭前芍药妖无格，池上芙蕖净少情。
唯有牡丹真国色，花开时节动京城。
e: The garden's herbaceous peonies are pretty, but have no grace;
The lotus on the pond is pure, but cool and passionless.
Only the tree peony has a true queen's face —
When it blooms, the whole capital is stirred with happiness.
poems.n: In the Tang the tree peony (牡丹) was queen of flowers, and Chang'an went peony-mad every spring, paying fortunes for rare plants. The peony's epithet 国色天香, "beauty of the nation, fragrance of heaven", owes much to this poem.

poems.te: Written at a Farm South of the Capital
poems.s: spring peach cottage person petals
z: 去年今日此门中，人面桃花相映红。
人面不知何处去，桃花依旧笑春风。
e: Last year, this day, within this very door,
A face and peach blossoms glowed pink, each on each.
Where has the face gone now? I don't know any more —
The peach blossoms still smile in the spring breeze, as before.
poems.n: The legend: Cui Hu, out walking at Qingming, asked for water at a farmhouse south of Chang'an and was served by a lovely girl among the peach trees. A year later he returned, found the gate locked, and wrote this poem on it. (In the story, she read it and pined away — and came back to life when he returned and wept over her; they married.) 人面桃花, "a face among peach blossoms", means a love glimpsed once and lost.

poems.s: autumn fields person sun
z: 春种一粒粟，秋收万颗子。
四海无闲田，农夫犹饿死。
e: In spring they sow a single grain;
In autumn reap ten thousand more.
No field lies idle anywhere —
Yet still the farmers starve, as before.
poems.n: Every Chinese child learns these two poems. The first asks a terrible question: with so much harvested, why do the people who grow it starve? (The answer, left unsaid, is rents and taxes.)

poems.s: summer sun fields person
z: 锄禾日当午，汗滴禾下土。
谁知盘中餐，粒粒皆辛苦。
e: Hoeing the crops beneath the noonday sun,
Their sweat drips on the soil where seedlings grow.
Who thinks, of the rice upon his plate, that every one —
Each single grain — was won with toil and woe?
poems.n: The poem Chinese parents quote to children who leave rice in their bowls: every grain is someone's sweat.

poems.te: Grass on the Ancient Plain: A Farewell
poems.s: spring grass hills wall two rider
z: 离离原上草，一岁一枯荣。
野火烧不尽，春风吹又生。
远芳侵古道，晴翠接荒城。
又送王孙去，萋萋满别情。
e: How lush the grass upon the plain!
Each year it withers, then grows green again.
The wildfires cannot burn it all away;
The spring wind blows, and it springs back to stay.
Its distant fragrance creeps across the ancient road;
Its sunlit green runs to the ruined town's abode.
Once more I see a friend go on his way —
The grass grows thick with all I cannot say.
poems.n: Written at sixteen as an exercise on a set theme ("Composed on the Theme…", 赋得). When the young Bai Juyi brought his poems to the capital, the writer Gu Kuang joked about his name — "Juyi" means "living easily", and "rice is dear in Chang'an; living here is not easy" — until he read the second couplet and exclaimed, "With lines like these, living here will be easy!" "Wildfire cannot burn it out; the spring wind blows and it grows again" became a proverb for indomitable life.

poems.s: dawn spring sun river flowers willow boat
z: 江南好，风景旧曾谙。
日出江花红胜火，春来江水绿如蓝。
能不忆江南？
e: The South is fair —
Its scenery I knew so well:
At sunrise, riverside flowers redder than fire;
In spring, the river's water green as indigo's spell.
How could I not remember the South?
poems.n: Written in old age in Luoyang, remembering his years as governor of Hangzhou and Suzhou. One of the earliest *ci* lyrics by a major poet, set to the tune "Remembering the South". The colours — fire-red and indigo-green — are pure and intense, like memory itself.

poems.te: A Spring Walk by Qiantang Lake
poems.s: spring lake willow swallows oriole flowers horse temple
z: 孤山寺北贾亭西，水面初平云脚低。
几处早莺争暖树，谁家新燕啄春泥。
乱花渐欲迷人眼，浅草才能没马蹄。
最爱湖东行不足，绿杨阴里白沙堤。
e: North of Gushan Temple, west of Lord Jia's pavilion,
The lake has just come level; the clouds hang low and near.
Here and there, early orioles vie for sunny trees;
Whose new swallows peck the spring mud here?
A riot of flowers begins to dazzle the eye;
The tender grass just covers the horses' hooves.
Best I love the lake's east side — I can't walk it enough:
The white-sand causeway in the green willows' shade it moves.
poems.n: Hangzhou's West Lake (then called Qiantang Lake) in early spring, when Bai Juyi was its governor (822–824). Every detail is "just beginning" — early orioles, new swallows, grass just tall enough to hide a hoof. The Bai Causeway, the white-sand dyke he loved, still carries his name.

poems.te: Song of the River at Dusk
poems.s: dusk autumn sun river crescent
z: 一道残阳铺水中，半江瑟瑟半江红。
可怜九月初三夜，露似真珠月似弓。
e: A ray of the setting sun lies spread across the stream:
Half the river emerald-cold, and half aglow with red.
How lovely is this night, the third of the ninth moon:
Dew like real pearls; the moon a bow overhead.
poems.n: Two pictures in one quatrain: sunset with the river half in shadow (瑟瑟, the blue-green of a precious stone) and half aflame; then night, with dewdrops like pearls and a slender crescent moon like a drawn bow.

poems.s: spring peach temple mountains clouds
z: 人间四月芳菲尽，山寺桃花始盛开。
长恨春归无觅处，不知转入此中来。
e: In the world below, the April flowers are gone;
At this mountain temple, peach blossoms just begin.
I always grieved that spring went off and left no trace —
Not knowing it had come up here, and settled in.
poems.n: Mount Lu, 817. High on the mountain the season lags behind the plain, so the poet finds spring still in full bloom. The small scientific observation becomes a happy surprise: spring has not vanished — it simply climbed the mountain.

poems.te: A Question for Liu the Nineteenth
poems.s: dusk winter snow cottage jar cup window
z: 绿蚁新醅酒，红泥小火炉。
晚来天欲雪，能饮一杯无？
e: New-brewed wine with green froth like ants;
A little stove of red clay, burning low.
Evening falls, and the sky threatens snow —
Will you come and drink a cup or no?
poems.n: A tiny invitation that every Chinese reader treasures: the "green ants" are the bubbles floating on fresh unfiltered rice wine; the red stove glows; snow is coming. Who could refuse?

poems.s: winter snow mountains wall rider smoke
z: 卖炭翁，伐薪烧炭南山中。
满面尘灰烟火色，两鬓苍苍十指黑。
卖炭得钱何所营？身上衣裳口中食。
可怜身上衣正单，心忧炭贱愿天寒。
夜来城外一尺雪，晓驾炭车辗冰辙。
牛困人饥日已高，市南门外泥中歇。
翩翩两骑来是谁？黄衣使者白衫儿。
手把文书口称敕，回车叱牛牵向北。
一车炭，千余斤，宫使驱将惜不得。
半匹红绡一丈绫，系向牛头充炭直。
e: The old charcoal seller
Cuts wood and burns charcoal in the Southern Hills.
His face is grimed with dust and ash, the colour of smoke and fire;
His temples are grey, his ten fingers black as the coal he fills.
What does he want with the money he gets for his charcoal?
Clothes on his back and food in his mouth — no more.
Pitiful — his clothes are thin, and yet
He hopes for cold, afraid the price will be poor.
Last night a foot of snow fell outside the town;
At dawn he drives his cart through ruts of ice.
The ox is weary, he is hungry, the sun is high;
He rests in the mud outside the south market gate, to wait a price.
Who are those two riders, prancing on their way?
A eunuch in yellow, and his boy in white.
Document in hand, they shout, "Imperial decree!"
And turn the cart, and drive the ox north, out of sight.
A cartload of charcoal — over a thousand pounds —
The palace envoys drive it off; he can't hold on.
Half a bolt of red gauze and ten feet of silk
They tie to the ox's head as payment — and are gone.
poems.n: One of Bai Juyi's *New Yuefu*, written to expose abuses. Palace eunuchs would "buy" goods in the markets of Chang'an at whatever price they liked. The old man's wish — cold weather, though he is freezing — is one of the most poignant lines in Chinese. A worthless scrap of silk pays for his whole winter's labour.

poems.s: summer lotus lake boat person
z: 小娃撑小艇，偷采白莲回。
不解藏踪迹，浮萍一道开。
e: A little child poles a little boat,
Sneaking home with white lotus she has picked.
She hasn't learned to hide her tracks —
Through the duckweed, a clear path has been flicked.
poems.n: A comic snapshot: the child thinks the theft is secret, but the open lane through the floating duckweed gives her away.

poems.s: night winter snow bamboo window cottage
z: 已讶衾枕冷，复见窗户明。
夜深知雪重，时闻折竹声。
e: I'm surprised my quilt and pillow are so cold,
Then see the window has grown bright.
Deep in the night, I know the snow is heavy:
Now and then, I hear bamboo snap in the night.
poems.n: Snow is never seen directly: it is felt as cold, seen as a glow on the window-paper, and heard as bamboo stems cracking under its weight.

poems.s: night autumn moon fields frost cottage
z: 霜草苍苍虫切切，村南村北行人绝。
独出前门望野田，月明荞麦花如雪。
e: Frosted grass is grey; the insects chirr and chirr;
South of the village, north of it, no traveller can be seen.
Alone I step out of my gate to gaze at the fields:
In the moonlight, buckwheat flowers are white as snow, serene.
poems.n: 811, when Bai Juyi was at his family home in mourning for his mother. Grey, silent, lonely — and then a sudden whiteness of moonlit buckwheat blossoms brightens the whole poem.

poems.te: A Flower That Is Not a Flower
poems.s: night mist clouds flowers moon
z: 花非花，雾非雾。
夜半来，天明去。
来如春梦几多时？去似朝云无觅处。
e: A flower, yet not a flower;
A mist, yet not a mist.
She comes at midnight,
She leaves at dawn's first tryst.
She comes like a spring dream — how long can it last?
She goes like morning cloud, gone without trace, gone past.
poems.n: A riddling love song with no subject named — a lover's secret visits, perhaps, or a dream, or life itself. The "morning cloud" recalls the goddess of Mount Wu, who visited a king in his dream and was "morning cloud and evening rain".

poems.s: night moon river tower hills person
z: 汴水流，泗水流，流到瓜州古渡头。
吴山点点愁。
思悠悠，恨悠悠，恨到归时方始休。
月明人倚楼。
e: The Bian flows on, the Si flows on,
Flowing to Guazhou's ancient ferry stair;
The hills of Wu, dot after dot, are sorrow there.
Longing, so long — regret, so long —
Regret that ends only when he comes home again.
In the bright moon, she leans on the tower stair.
poems.n: An early *ci* lyric with a folk-song lilt. A woman follows in her mind the rivers her man travelled down, all the way to the ferry at Guazhou on the Yangtze; even the distant hills of Wu look like spots of grief. The repetitions (流…流, 悠悠…悠悠) imitate both the rivers and the endlessness of longing.

poems.s: night autumn moon temple pavilion river
z: 江南忆，最忆是杭州。
山寺月中寻桂子，郡亭枕上看潮头。
何日更重游？
e: Of the South, what I remember best
Is Hangzhou, above all the rest:
At the hill temple, seeking cassia seeds beneath the moon;
At the prefect's pavilion, on my pillow, watching the tide's crest.
When shall I go back on that quest?
poems.n: Legend said that cassia seeds fell from the moon (where a cassia tree grows) around Hangzhou's Lingyin Temple each autumn. The tidal bore of the Qiantang River, which could be watched from the governor's pavilion, is one of the great sights of China.

poems.s: night palace candle window
z: 泪湿罗巾梦不成，夜深前殿按歌声。
红颜未老恩先断，斜倚熏笼坐到明。
e: Tears soak her silk handkerchief; she cannot sleep or dream;
Deep in the night, from the front hall, comes music and song.
Her rosy face not yet old, the emperor's favour's gone;
She leans on the incense cage, and sits there all night long.
poems.n: One of three thousand palace women, forgotten while the emperor feasts in the front hall with another. The incense cage (熏笼) was a basket over a brazier used to warm and perfume clothes — the only warmth she has left.

poems.te: Thinking of Home on the Winter Solstice at Handan
poems.s: night winter candle cottage person
z: 邯郸驿里逢冬至，抱膝灯前影伴身。
想得家中夜深坐，还应说着远行人。
e: At the Handan post-station, the Winter Solstice comes;
Hugging my knees by the lamp, my shadow keeps me company.
I picture my family at home, sitting up late tonight —
They must be talking of the one who's far away: of me.
poems.n: The Winter Solstice was one of the great family festivals of the Tang. Like Wang Wei's Double Ninth poem, the homesickness is turned around: he imagines them missing him.

poems.s: summer sun fields person two
z: 田家少闲月，五月人倍忙。
夜来南风起，小麦覆陇黄。
妇姑荷箪食，童稚携壶浆，
相随饷田去，丁壮在南冈。
足蒸暑土气，背灼炎天光，
力尽不知热，但惜夏日长。
复有贫妇人，抱子在其旁，
右手秉遗穗，左臂悬敝筐。
听其相顾言，闻者为悲伤。
家田输税尽，拾此充饥肠。
今我何功德？曾不事农桑。
吏禄三百石，岁晏有余粮。
念此私自愧，尽日不能忘。
e: Farm families have few idle months;
In the fifth month they're twice as busy as before.
Last night the south wind rose, and now
The ripe wheat covers the ridges, yellow to the core.
Wives and mothers carry baskets of food;
The children bring jugs of gruel along;
Together they take the meal to the fields,
Where the men toil on the southern ridge, strong.
Their feet are steamed by the hot earth;
Their backs are scorched by the blazing sun;
Worn out, they don't even feel the heat,
And only wish the long summer day weren't done.
And there's a poor woman, too,
With a baby in her arms, beside the rest;
In her right hand, the ears of grain she's gleaned;
On her left arm, a broken basket pressed.
I hear her talking with the others —
Whoever hears her grieves:
"Our own fields all went to pay the tax;
I glean these to fill our stomachs with the sheaves."
And what merit have I, I ask myself?
I've never farmed or tended silk.
My salary is three hundred bushels;
At year's end, I've grain to spare, and milk.
Thinking of this, I'm secretly ashamed,
And all day long I can't forget the shame I bear.
poems.n: 806, when Bai Juyi was a county magistrate near Chang'an. The farmers want the day to be longer so they can harvest more, though it is killing them; the gleaning widow has lost her land to taxes. The poem's last lines — an official confessing he has done nothing to deserve his salary — are rare and remarkable in any literature.

poems.s: day mountains pine person
z: 赠君一法决狐疑，不用钻龟与祝蓍。
试玉要烧三日满，辨材须待七年期。
周公恐惧流言日，王莽谦恭未篡时。
向使当初身便死，一生真伪复谁知？
e: I'll give you a way to settle every doubt
Without cracking tortoise shells or casting yarrow stalks:
To test true jade, you burn it three whole days;
To judge good timber, wait seven years — then talk.
The Duke of Zhou lived in fear when rumours spread;
Wang Mang seemed humble — till he seized the throne.
Had either died before the truth came out,
Who would have known what each one was? Who'd have known?
poems.n: Written in exile in 815. True jade survives three days in fire; the camphor tree is only distinguishable from a lesser tree after seven years of growth. The Duke of Zhou, the most loyal of regents, was rumoured to be plotting usurpation; Wang Mang, who did usurp the Han throne, was famous for his humility beforehand. Only time reveals the truth of a person.

poems.s: summer lotus lake boat person
z: 菱叶萦波荷飐风，荷花深处小船通。
逢郎欲语低头笑，碧玉搔头落水中。
e: Water-chestnut leaves twine on the waves; lotus sways in the wind;
Deep among the lotus blooms, a little boat glides through.
She meets her young man, wants to speak — lowers her head and smiles,
And her green jade hairpin slips into the water, too.
poems.n: A lotus-gathering girl meets her sweetheart; too shy to speak, she bows her head — and loses her hairpin in the lake. The tiny accident says everything about her flustered heart.

poems.s: autumn river boat willow two wind
z: 南浦凄凄别，西风袅袅秋。
一看肠一断，好去莫回头。
e: At South Shore, a sad farewell;
The west wind sighs — it's autumn now.
Each look back breaks my heart once more —
Go well, and don't look back somehow.
poems.n: South Shore (南浦) was a stock name for a place of parting, from the *Songs of Chu*: "I see you off at the southern shore." The simple, broken plea — "go well, don't turn your head" — is because every glance back is another heartbreak.

poems.te: Reading Yuan the Ninth's Poems in My Boat
poems.s: night river boat candle wind
z: 把君诗卷灯前读，诗尽灯残天未明。
眼痛灭灯犹暗坐，逆风吹浪打船声。
e: I read your book of poems by the lamp;
The poems end, the lamp burns low — still not yet dawn.
My eyes ache; I put the lamp out, sit on in the dark;
Against the wind, the waves strike the boat on and on.
poems.n: 815: Bai Juyi, on his way into exile at Jiangzhou, reads the poems of his dearest friend Yuan Zhen, himself in exile. The wind and waves battering the boat in the dark stand for the storms that have scattered them both.

poems.s: night moon palace clouds mist pavilion
z: 汉皇重色思倾国，御宇多年求不得。
杨家有女初长成，养在深闺人未识。
天生丽质难自弃，一朝选在君王侧。
回眸一笑百媚生，六宫粉黛无颜色。
春寒赐浴华清池，温泉水滑洗凝脂。
侍儿扶起娇无力，始是新承恩泽时。
云鬓花颜金步摇，芙蓉帐暖度春宵。
春宵苦短日高起，从此君王不早朝。
承欢侍宴无闲暇，春从春游夜专夜。
后宫佳丽三千人，三千宠爱在一身。
金屋妆成娇侍夜，玉楼宴罢醉和春。
姊妹弟兄皆列土，可怜光彩生门户。
遂令天下父母心，不重生男重生女。
骊宫高处入青云，仙乐风飘处处闻。
缓歌慢舞凝丝竹，尽日君王看不足。
渔阳鼙鼓动地来，惊破霓裳羽衣曲。
九重城阙烟尘生，千乘万骑西南行。
翠华摇摇行复止，西出都门百余里。
六军不发无奈何，宛转蛾眉马前死。
花钿委地无人收，翠翘金雀玉搔头。
君王掩面救不得，回看血泪相和流。
黄埃散漫风萧索，云栈萦纡登剑阁。
峨嵋山下少人行，旌旗无光日色薄。
蜀江水碧蜀山青，圣主朝朝暮暮情。
行宫见月伤心色，夜雨闻铃肠断声。
天旋地转回龙驭，到此踌躇不能去。
马嵬坡下泥土中，不见玉颜空死处。
君臣相顾尽沾衣，东望都门信马归。
归来池苑皆依旧，太液芙蓉未央柳。
芙蓉如面柳如眉，对此如何不泪垂。
春风桃李花开日，秋雨梧桐叶落时。
西宫南内多秋草，落叶满阶红不扫。
梨园弟子白发新，椒房阿监青娥老。
夕殿萤飞思悄然，孤灯挑尽未成眠。
迟迟钟鼓初长夜，耿耿星河欲曙天。
鸳鸯瓦冷霜华重，翡翠衾寒谁与共。
悠悠生死别经年，魂魄不曾来入梦。
临邛道士鸿都客，能以精诚致魂魄。
为感君王辗转思，遂教方士殷勤觅。
排空驭气奔如电，升天入地求之遍。
上穷碧落下黄泉，两处茫茫皆不见。
忽闻海上有仙山，山在虚无缥渺间。
楼阁玲珑五云起，其中绰约多仙子。
中有一人字太真，雪肤花貌参差是。
金阙西厢叩玉扃，转教小玉报双成。
闻道汉家天子使，九华帐里梦魂惊。
揽衣推枕起徘徊，珠箔银屏迤逦开。
云鬓半偏新睡觉，花冠不整下堂来。
风吹仙袂飘飘举，犹似霓裳羽衣舞。
玉容寂寞泪阑干，梨花一枝春带雨。
含情凝睇谢君王，一别音容两渺茫。
昭阳殿里恩爱绝，蓬莱宫中日月长。
回头下望人寰处，不见长安见尘雾。
惟将旧物表深情，钿合金钗寄将去。
钗留一股合一扇，钗擘黄金合分钿。
但教心似金钿坚，天上人间会相见。
临别殷勤重寄词，词中有誓两心知。
七月七日长生殿，夜半无人私语时。
在天愿作比翼鸟，在地愿为连理枝。
天长地久有时尽，此恨绵绵无绝期。
e: The Han emperor prized beauty, longed for one to topple states;
Through all his years upon the throne, he sought and found no mate.
The Yang clan had a daughter who was just in her first bloom,
Raised deep within the women's rooms, unknown beyond her room.
But beauty given by heaven is hard to hide away:
She was chosen for the sovereign's side one day.
She turned her head and smiled — a hundred charms were born;
The painted ladies of the Six Palaces looked colourless and worn.
In the chill of spring he let her bathe in Huaqing's waters fine;
The silken springs washed over skin like cream, divine.
Her maids helped her up, so delicate, so weak —
That was when the emperor's favour first touched her cheek.
Cloud-like hair, a flowered face, a golden hairpin's swing;
Behind warm lotus curtains they spent the nights of spring.
Spring nights were all too short; he rose when the sun was high;
From then on he held no morning court — he let the dawns go by.
She shared his feasts and pleasures, never with an hour to rest;
In spring she joined his spring rides; night after night she was his guest.
Three thousand beauties filled the inner palace halls;
The love meant for three thousand on one woman falls.
In her Golden House, made up, she charmed him through the night;
At the Jade Tower, the feasting done, she was drunk with spring's delight.
Her sisters and her brothers all were granted lands and fame —
How dazzling was the glory shining on her family's name!
So parents everywhere beneath the sky now changed their mind:
Not sons, but daughters, were the children they most hoped to find.
High on Mount Li, the palace rose into the blue clouds' height;
Immortal music on the wind was heard there, day and night.
Slow songs, unhurried dances held the strings and flutes in thrall;
All day the sovereign watched, and never had enough at all.
Then the war-drums of Yuyang came, shaking the ground,
And shattered "Rainbow Skirt and Feathered Coat" with their sound.
Smoke and dust rose from the nine-walled city's towers;
A thousand chariots, ten thousand riders fled southwest in those hours.
The kingfisher banners swayed; they marched and stopped once more,
A hundred li out west, beyond the capital's door.
The Six Armies would not march — what could be done?
Before the horses, the moth-browed beauty died, her struggle done.
Her flowered ornaments lay where they fell, and no one gathered them:
Kingfisher plumes, gold sparrows, and a jade pin's broken stem.
The sovereign hid his face — he could not save her, try as he might;
Looking back, his tears and blood flowed mingled at the sight.
Yellow dust blew all around; the wind was bleak and sere;
By cloud-high plank roads winding, they climbed to Sword Pavilion here.
Below Mount Emei, few travellers came by;
The banners lost their lustre, and the sun grew pale in the sky.
The rivers of Shu are green, the mountains of Shu are blue;
Morning and evening, the sovereign's longing grew.
In his travelling palace, the moon was heartbreak to see;
In night rain, the harness bells rang out in agony.
The world turned round; the dragon carriage was coming home at last;
Reaching here, he hesitated, and could not go past.
Beneath the slope of Mawei, in the mud and clay,
No jade face could be seen — just the empty place she lay.
Lord and ministers looked at each other, tears soaking every gown;
Eastward, they let the horses find their own way back to town.
Returning, the pools and gardens were all as they had been —
The lotus of Taiye Lake, the willows of Weiyang green.
The lotus was like her face, the willow like her brow —
Facing them, how could his tears not fall now?
In spring winds, when the peach and plum trees bloom;
In autumn rains, when wutong leaves fall through the gloom;
The Western Palace and the Southern Court were deep in autumn grass;
Red leaves lay thick upon the steps, unswept, as seasons pass.
The players of the Pear Garden had hair turned newly white;
The maids of the Pepper Chamber had lost their youthful light.
In the evening hall fireflies flitted; he sat in silent thought;
He trimmed his lonely lamp till it burned out — but sleep came not.
Slow, slow the bells and drums began the long night's span;
Bright, bright the Milky Way, before the dawn began.
The mandarin-duck roof tiles were cold, the frost lay thick and fair;
The kingfisher quilt was chill — and who was there to share?
Distant, distant, life and death apart through all the years —
Her soul had never come into his dreams to dry his tears.
A Daoist priest from Linqiong, a guest at the capital gate,
Could summon spirits of the dead by his devotion's weight.
Moved by the sovereign's tossing, turning longing and his pain,
They sent this master out to search with all his might and main.
He split the sky and rode the wind, as swift as lightning flies;
He searched the depths beneath the earth, and searched the highest skies —
Up to the blue void, down to the Yellow Springs below:
Both were vast and empty; she was nowhere, high or low.
Then he heard of an immortal mountain in the sea,
A mountain set amid the void, in misty mystery.
Its exquisite towers rose where five-coloured clouds unfurled;
Within lived many graceful fairies, far beyond the world.
And one among them bore the name of Taizhen, so they said,
With snowy skin and flower face — much like the one now dead.
At the golden palace's west wing, he knocked on the door of jade,
And asked Little Jade to tell Shuangcheng, who would tell the lady's maid.
Hearing that an envoy of the Han emperor had come,
Within her nine-flowered curtains, her dreaming soul was struck dumb.
She pushed her pillow, caught her robe, rose up and paced the floor;
The pearl blinds and the silver screens unfolded, door by door.
Her cloud of hair hung half aside — she had only just awoken;
Her flower crown askew, she came down the hall, her calm all broken.
The wind blew her immortal sleeves; they fluttered as she swayed,
As though "Rainbow Skirt and Feathered Coat" were being played.
Her jade-white face was lonely, tears streaming without end —
A spray of pear blossom in spring rain, beneath the drops to bend.
Gazing with deep feeling, she thanked her sovereign lord:
"Since we parted, voice and face are lost — no word, no sight restored.
In Zhaoyang Hall, our love and favour have been cut;
In Penglai Palace, days and months are long, the door is shut.
I turn my head and look down toward the world of men —
I cannot see Chang'an, only dust and mist again.
Let these old keepsakes show you that my love is true:
This inlaid box and golden hairpin — take them back with you.
One prong of the hairpin I keep, one half of the box I hold:
I break the hairpin's gold in two, and split the inlaid gold.
If only our hearts stay as firm as gold and inlay are,
In heaven or on earth we'll meet again, however far."
At parting she sent words again, with care, for him to bear;
In them was a vow known only to the two who'd shared it there:
"On the seventh of the seventh month, in the Hall of Long Life,
At midnight, when no one was near, we whispered, man and wife:
'In heaven, may we be two birds that fly wing to wing;
On earth, two trees whose branches intertwine and cling.'"
Heaven is long and earth endures, yet both will one day end —
But this sorrow will go on forever, and never mend.
poems.n: Written in 806, when Bai Juyi was thirty-four: the love of Emperor Xuanzong (thinly disguised as "the Han emperor") and Consort Yang Guifei — her rise, the An Lushan rebellion (the "war-drums of Yuyang"), the flight to Sichuan, the mutinous troops at Mawei who demanded her death, the emperor's endless grief, and a Daoist magician who finds her soul on an island of immortals. Her vow — to be "birds flying wing to wing, branches intertwined" (比翼鸟, 连理枝) — is the most famous pledge of love in Chinese, and the closing couplet gave the poem its title.

poems.s: night autumn moon river boat maple reeds two
z: 浔阳江头夜送客，枫叶荻花秋瑟瑟。
主人下马客在船，举酒欲饮无管弦。
醉不成欢惨将别，别时茫茫江浸月。
忽闻水上琵琶声，主人忘归客不发。
寻声暗问弹者谁？
琵琶声停欲语迟。
移船相近邀相见，添酒回灯重开宴。
千呼万唤始出来，犹抱琵琶半遮面。
转轴拨弦三两声，未成曲调先有情。
弦弦掩抑声声思，似诉平生不得志。
低眉信手续续弹，说尽心中无限事。
轻拢慢捻抹复挑，初为《霓裳》后《六幺》。
大弦嘈嘈如急雨，小弦切切如私语。
嘈嘈切切错杂弹，大珠小珠落玉盘。
间关莺语花底滑，幽咽泉流冰下难。
冰泉冷涩弦凝绝，凝绝不通声暂歇。
别有幽愁暗恨生，此时无声胜有声。
银瓶乍破水浆迸，铁骑突出刀枪鸣。
曲终收拨当心画，四弦一声如裂帛。
东船西舫悄无言，唯见江心秋月白。
沉吟放拨插弦中，整顿衣裳起敛容。
自言本是京城女，家在虾蟆陵下住。
十三学得琵琶成，名属教坊第一部。
曲罢曾教善才服，妆成每被秋娘妒。
五陵年少争缠头，一曲红绡不知数。
钿头银篦击节碎，血色罗裙翻酒污。
今年欢笑复明年，秋月春风等闲度。
弟走从军阿姨死，暮去朝来颜色故。
门前冷落鞍马稀，老大嫁作商人妇。
商人重利轻别离，前月浮梁买茶去。
去来江口守空船，绕船月明江水寒。
夜深忽梦少年事，梦啼妆泪红阑干。
我闻琵琶已叹息，又闻此语重唧唧。
同是天涯沦落人，相逢何必曾相识！
我从去年辞帝京，谪居卧病浔阳城。
浔阳地僻无音乐，终岁不闻丝竹声。
住近湓江地低湿，黄芦苦竹绕宅生。
其间旦暮闻何物？
杜鹃啼血猿哀鸣。
春江花朝秋月夜，往往取酒还独倾。
岂无山歌与村笛？
呕哑嘲哳难为听。
今夜闻君琵琶语，如听仙乐耳暂明。
莫辞更坐弹一曲，为君翻作《琵琶行》。
感我此言良久立，却坐促弦弦转急。
凄凄不似向前声，满座重闻皆掩泣。
座中泣下谁最多？
江州司马青衫湿。
e: By the Xunyang River, at night, I saw a guest away;
Maple leaves and reed flowers rustled in the autumn grey.
I, the host, dismounted; my guest was in his boat;
We raised our cups to drink — but there was no music, not one note.
Drunk, yet joyless, sadly we were about to part;
At parting, the moon lay steeped in the boundless river's heart.
Then suddenly, across the water, came a pipa's sound;
The host forgot to leave; the guest stayed, outward-bound.
We followed the sound and softly asked who it was that played;
The pipa stopped; she was slow to answer, and delayed.
We moved our boat beside hers and asked her to appear;
We poured more wine, relit the lamps, and spread the feast with cheer.
At last, after a thousand pleas, she came out with slow grace,
Still holding up her pipa so it half-concealed her face.
She turned the pegs and plucked the strings — a note or two, or three;
Before a tune had even formed, there was feeling, plain to see.
Each string was muffled, every note was heavy with thought,
As if she told a lifetime's grief, of hopes that came to naught.
Head bowed, she let her hand play on, continuing on and on,
And told the countless sorrows of her heart, one by one.
Lightly she pressed and slowly twisted, swept, and plucked the strings:
First "Rainbow Skirt", then "Green Waist" — the tunes of courts and kings.
The heavy strings roared like a sudden squall of rain;
The fine strings murmured like lovers' whispers, low and plain.
Roaring and murmuring, interwoven as she played —
Like pearls, both large and small, that fall upon a plate of jade.
Now orioles chattered, liquid, gliding under flowers;
Now a choked spring sobbed, struggling under ice for hours.
The icy spring grew cold and halting; the strings congealed and died;
Congealed, cut off, the sound fell still — the music paused, held still inside.
A different, deeper sorrow, a hidden grief, was born:
Now silence spoke more eloquently than sound — and more forlorn.
Then suddenly a silver vase burst, and water splashed about;
Armoured horsemen charged, and swords and spears rang out.
The tune ended: she swept her plectrum across the strings' heart;
The four strings cried as one, like silk being torn apart.
On boats to east and west, a hush; no one spoke at all —
Only the autumn moon, white in mid-river, over all.
Thoughtfully she laid the plectrum down between the strings,
Straightened her clothes, rose, composed her face, and spoke of things:
"I was a girl of the capital once," she said. "My home
Was down by Toad Mound — that's where I used to roam.
At thirteen I had learned to play the pipa with full skill;
My name stood in the first rank of the Music Academy's bill.
My playing made the master musicians bow in admiration;
My beauty, when made up, roused even Qiuniang's indignation.
The young lords of the Five Tombs vied to shower me with gifts;
For one song, rolls of red silk past counting, piled in drifts.
Silver combs with jewelled heads broke as they beat the time;
Blood-red silk skirts were stained with spilt wine — I was in my prime.
This year was laughter, and the next year laughter too;
Autumn moons and spring breezes passed, and idly through.
My brother joined the army, and the madam passed away;
Evenings went and mornings came; my looks faded day by day.
Before my door it grew deserted; fewer horses came;
Grown old, I married a merchant, and took a merchant's name.
A merchant cares for profit, and thinks little of goodbye;
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea, and left me by.
Since then, at the river's mouth, I guard the empty boat;
Around it, bright moonlight; the river cold, remote.
Late at night I suddenly dreamed of my young days;
I wept in my dream, and red tears through my rouge ran in a glaze."
Hearing the pipa, I had sighed already, deep;
Hearing her story, I sighed again, and began to weep.
We both are outcasts, drifting at the far ends of the earth;
Meeting like this, what need to have known each other since our birth?
"Since last year I left the capital, I've lived in banishment;
I lie here sick in Xunyang town, where I was demoted and sent.
Xunyang is remote, and there's no music to be found;
All year I've never heard the strings or flutes resound.
I live beside the Pen, where the ground is low and damp;
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo surround my house like a camp.
What do I hear here, morning and evening long?
The cuckoo crying blood, the gibbons' mournful song.
On spring river mornings full of flowers, on autumn nights of moon,
I often take my wine and drink alone, and end too soon.
Of course there are hill songs and village flutes — but they
Are shrill and harsh and croaking, painful when they play.
Tonight I heard your pipa speak, and it seemed
Like heavenly music — my ears for a while were redeemed.
Don't refuse; sit down again and play us one more song,
And I will write for you 'The Ballad of the Pipa' before long."
Moved by what I said, she stood a long while there,
Then sat, and tightened the strings; the notes grew quick and spare.
So mournful, so unlike the music played before,
That all who heard it hid their faces, weeping once more.
And of them all, whose tears were falling most? I'd say
The Marshal of Jiangzhou's — his blue robe soaked that day.
poems.n: Written in 816 at Jiangzhou (Jiujiang), where Bai Juyi had been demoted to the empty post of marshal (司马). Seeing a friend off on the river at night, he hears a former star musician of the capital, now a merchant's neglected wife. The description of her playing — "large pearls and small pearls falling on a plate of jade", "now silence was more eloquent than sound", "a silver vase bursting" — is the most famous evocation of music in Chinese. "We are both outcasts at the ends of the earth; why must we have known each other before?" became the motto of every exile. Blue-green robes were worn by the lowest-ranking officials.

poems.s: winter snow mountains river fisher
z: 千山鸟飞绝，万径人踪灭。
孤舟蓑笠翁，独钓寒江雪。
e: A thousand hills — no bird in flight;
Ten thousand paths — no human trace.
One boat; one old man, straw-caped, alone,
Fishing the snow on the cold river's face.
poems.n: Written in exile at Yongzhou (Hunan) after 805. The first characters of the four lines spell 千万孤独, "utterly alone". In a world emptied of life and buried in snow, one old fisherman sits unmoved — Liu Zongyuan's image of his own lonely integrity, and one of the most painted poems in Chinese art.

poems.s: dawn mist river fisher mountains clouds
z: 渔翁夜傍西岩宿，晓汲清湘燃楚竹。
烟销日出不见人，欸乃一声山水绿。
回看天际下中流，岩上无心云相逐。
e: The fisherman beneath the western cliff spends the night;
At dawn he draws the clear Xiang and burns Chu bamboo.
The mist melts, the sun climbs — not a soul in sight;
"Ai-nai!" — one oar-song, and the hills and streams turn green and new.
Looking back to the sky's edge, he drifts down midstream;
Above the cliffs, the carefree clouds chase each other through.
poems.n: "Ai-nai" (欸乃) is the creak of an oar or a boatman's call; at that sound the landscape seems to spring into colour as the mist clears — one of the most magical lines in Chinese. The aimless, "heartless" clouds (无心) are the fisherman's — and the exiled poet's — freedom from desire.

poems.t: 登柳州城楼寄漳汀封连四州
poems.te: From the City Tower of Liuzhou, to Four Friends in Exile
poems.s: day rain wind tower wall lotus mountains river
z: 城上高楼接大荒，海天愁思正茫茫。
惊风乱飐芙蓉水，密雨斜侵薜荔墙。
岭树重遮千里目，江流曲似九回肠。
共来百越文身地，犹自音书滞一乡。
e: From the tall tower on the wall I face the wilderness;
Sea and sky stretch boundless as my grief and care.
A sudden wind tears at the lotus on the water;
Dense rain lashes slantwise at the ivy-covered wall there.
The ridge-top trees block my thousand-li gaze;
The river twists, as my insides twist in ninefold pain.
We came together to this tattooed land of Yue —
Yet our letters lie stranded, each in his own domain.
poems.n: In 815 Liu Zongyuan and four friends of the failed reform party, briefly recalled, were exiled again — each to a remote southern prefecture. From his tower at Liuzhou (Guangxi) he writes to the other four. The storm battering the fragrant lotus and the creepers is the political storm that broke the good men.

poems.s: day river fields cottage boat person
z: 久为簪组累，幸此南夷谪。
闲依农圃邻，偶似山林客。
晓耕翻露草，夜榜响溪石。
来往不逢人，长歌楚天碧。
e: So long weighed down by hatpin and by seal,
I'm lucky to be banished to the southern wild.
At leisure, I live next to farmers' plots;
By chance I'm like a hermit of the hills, beguiled.
At dawn I plough and turn the dewy grass;
At night my oar knocks on the creek stones as I row.
I come and go and never meet a soul,
And sing long songs beneath Chu's blue sky, alone.
poems.n: Exiled to Yongzhou, Liu Zongyuan calls his banishment "lucky" — free of the hatpin and seal-ribbon of office, living like a farmer. The cheerfulness is real, but also bitterly ironic: no one comes; no one sees him.

poems.t: 与浩初上人同看山寄京华亲故
poems.te: Viewing the Mountains with the Monk Haochu: To My Family in the Capital
poems.s: autumn peaks sea person
z: 海畔尖山似剑铓，秋来处处割愁肠。
若为化得身千亿，散上峰头望故乡。
e: The sharp peaks by the sea are like sword blades;
In autumn, everywhere, they cut my sorrowing heart.
If I could split into a thousand million selves,
I'd climb each peak to gaze toward home, each self apart.
poems.n: The jagged karst peaks around Liuzhou become blades slicing his homesick heart. The wish to multiply his body like a Buddha's manifestations, so that a self might stand on every peak looking north, suits a poem written with a monk.

poems.s: day sea clouds mountains flowers
z: 曾经沧海难为水，除却巫山不是云。
取次花丛懒回顾，半缘修道半缘君。
e: Once you have seen the sea, no other water is the same;
Beside Wu Mountain's clouds, no other clouds are true.
I pass through clumps of flowers, and never turn my head —
Half for the Way I follow; half because of you.
poems.n: One of five poems mourning Yuan Zhen's wife Wei Cong, who died in 809 at twenty-seven. Mount Wu's clouds are the goddess who visited a king in dreams "as morning cloud and evening rain". 曾经沧海难为水 — "once you have seen the ocean, no other water will do" — is quoted for any incomparable experience, especially a first love. (Yuan Zhen remarried within two years; readers have long noted the irony.)

poems.s: day palace flowers person two
z: 寥落古行宫，宫花寂寞红。
白头宫女在，闲坐说玄宗。
e: The old travelling palace, lonely and decayed;
Its flowers bloom red, with no one there to see.
White-haired palace maids are all that stayed —
They sit and talk of Xuanzong's days, idly.
poems.n: Twenty characters holding half a century. The women were chosen as girls to serve Emperor Xuanzong, who never came back after the rebellion; now white-haired, they reminisce about him among the red flowers. Critics have called it the most concise poem of the Tang.

poems.s: night candle cottage window person
z: 昔日戏言身后意，今朝都到眼前来。
衣裳已施行看尽，针线犹存未忍开。
尚想旧情怜婢仆，也曾因梦送钱财。
诚知此恨人人有，贫贱夫妻百事哀。
e: We used to joke of what would come when one of us was dead;
Today it's all come true, before my eyes, as if we'd known.
Your clothes I've given away — they're almost gone, as you said;
Your sewing box I keep, but can't bear to open it alone.
Remembering your love, I'm kind to the maids you knew;
Once, after a dream, I burned paper money for you.
I know this sorrow is a thing that everyone must share —
But for a couple who were poor, each memory brings despair.
poems.n: The second of three elegies for Yuan Zhen's wife, who had shared his years of poverty before he rose in office. The details — her clothes given away, her sewing unopened, money burned for her after a dream — made these some of the most moving elegies in Chinese. 贫贱夫妻百事哀 does not mean poverty spoils marriage; it means that for a couple who suffered together, every memory now hurts.

poems.s: dusk autumn chrysanthemum cottage person sun
z: 秋丛绕舍似陶家，遍绕篱边日渐斜。
不是花中偏爱菊，此花开尽更无花。
e: Autumn clusters ring my house, as at Tao Qian's home;
Around the hedge I wander, till the sun is low.
It isn't that, of all the flowers, I prefer the chrysanthemum —
But when this one has faded, there are no more flowers to show.
poems.n: Chrysanthemums have been linked with Tao Yuanming ever since he wrote of "picking chrysanthemums by the eastern hedge". Yuan Zhen gives a simple, touching reason for loving them: they are the last flowers of the year.

poems.te: On Hearing That Bai Juyi Has Been Made Marshal of Jiangzhou
poems.s: night rain wind window candle
z: 残灯无焰影幢幢，此夕闻君谪九江。
垂死病中惊坐起，暗风吹雨入寒窗。
e: The dying lamp burns low, its shadows flickering;
Tonight I hear you're banished to Jiujiang, far away.
Though sick to death, I start up in my bed;
Dark wind blows rain through the cold window's grey.
poems.n: 815: Yuan Zhen, himself exiled and gravely ill in Tongzhou, hears that his best friend Bai Juyi has been demoted to Jiangzhou (Jiujiang). Bai Juyi wrote that he could never read the poem without pain. The dark wind blowing rain through the window is the whole bleak world they shared.

poems.te: Seeking the Hermit, Not Finding Him
poems.s: day pine mountains clouds person two
z: 松下问童子，言师采药去。
只在此山中，云深不知处。
e: I asked the boy beneath the pine;
"My master's gone for herbs," he said.
"He's on this mountain, somewhere there —
The clouds are deep; I can't say where."
poems.n: Visiting a hermit and not finding him is a whole genre in Chinese poetry. Three questions are implied, three answers given; the hermit himself, lost somewhere in the clouds, becomes part of the mountain.

poems.te: Written at Li Ning's Secluded Dwelling
poems.s: night moon cottage bridge birds lake person
z: 闲居少邻并，草径入荒园。
鸟宿池边树，僧敲月下门。
过桥分野色，移石动云根。
暂去还来此，幽期不负言。
e: His quiet home has hardly any neighbour;
A grassy path leads to the wild garden's gloom.
Birds are roosting in the trees beside the pond;
A monk knocks at the gate beneath the moon.
Across the bridge, the wild hues change and part;
Moving the stones stirs up the roots of cloud.
I leave for now, but will come back again —
I won't break faith with this quiet place, as vowed.
poems.n: The source of the story of 推敲 (*tuīqiāo*, "push–knock"): riding his donkey, Jia Dao could not decide whether the monk should "push" (推) or "knock at" (敲) the gate, and, lost in thought, rode into the procession of the governor Han Yu — who, instead of punishing him, said "knock" was better. Ever since, 推敲 means to weigh one's words with care.

poems.s: day person mountains
z: 十年磨一剑，霜刃未曾试。
今日把示君，谁有不平事？
e: Ten years I've spent in grinding this one sword;
Its frost-bright blade has never yet been tried.
Today I hold it up for you to see —
Who suffers wrong that wants to be set right?
poems.n: 十年磨一剑, "ten years to grind one sword", is now the proverb for long, patient preparation. The sword is Jia Dao's talent, honed through years of study and ready for use — if only someone would give him the chance.

poems.s: night palace candle person
z: 故国三千里，深宫二十年。
一声何满子，双泪落君前。
e: Three thousand li from home she came;
Twenty years locked deep within the palace walls.
She sings "He Manzi" once — the very name —
And before her lord, a pair of tears falls.
poems.n: "He Manzi" was a heartbreaking song named after a singer condemned to death, who sang it hoping for a pardon. A palace singer, far from home for twenty years, sings it before the emperor and weeps. Legend says a consort of Emperor Wuzong sang it at his deathbed and died of grief.

poems.s: night crescent river tower boat
z: 金陵津渡小山楼，一宿行人自可愁。
潮落夜江斜月里，两三星火是瓜洲。
