e: By Jinling Ferry, a little inn upon the hill;
A traveller who spends the night here can't help but grieve.
The tide ebbs; the night river lies under the slanting moon, still;
Two or three twinkling lights across — that's Guazhou, I believe.
poems.n: This Jinling Ferry is at Zhenjiang on the Yangtze, opposite Guazhou. A sleepless traveller looks across the dark river: a few distant lights are all there is of the far shore — and of the world.

poems.s: summer river grass person reeds
z: 蓬头稚子学垂纶，侧坐莓苔草映身。
路人借问遥招手，怕得鱼惊不应人。
e: A tousle-headed little boy is learning how to fish;
He sits on mossy stones, half hidden by the grass.
When someone asks the way, he waves from far away —
Afraid to scare the fish, he won't reply as people pass.
poems.n: A perfect little genre painting. The child, absorbed in his first fishing, treats a stranger's question with the seriousness of a professional — a wave, not a word.

poems.te: Song of the Governor of Yanmen
poems.s: dusk autumn clouds wall fort flag rider frost
z: 黑云压城城欲摧，甲光向日金鳞开。
角声满天秋色里，塞上燕脂凝夜紫。
半卷红旗临易水，霜重鼓寒声不起。
报君黄金台上意，提携玉龙为君死。
e: Black clouds press on the walls — the city's close to breaking;
Our armour flashes in the sun like golden scales unfolding.
The bugles fill the sky amid the colours of the fall;
On the frontier, rouge-red earth congeals to purple as night is falling.
Half-furled, the red flags reach the river Yi;
The frost is thick; the drums are cold; their beat won't rise at all.
To repay my lord, who raised me to his Golden Terrace high,
I'll grasp my jade-dragon sword, and for him I'll die.
poems.n: Li He, about eighteen, brought this poem to Han Yu, who — so the story goes — was so struck by the first line that he refastened his belt and invited the young man in. A battle painted in colours: black clouds, golden armour, rouge-red earth turning purple with blood, red flags, white frost. The Golden Terrace was where King Zhao of Yan welcomed men of talent; the "jade dragon" is a sword.

poems.s: night autumn crescent desert horse mountains
z: 大漠沙如雪，燕山月似钩。
何当金络脑，快走踏清秋。
e: The desert's sand is white as snow;
Over Mount Yan, the moon hangs like a hook.
When will I wear a golden bridle, and go
Galloping through clear autumn? — Now I can only look.
poems.n: One of twenty-three "Horse Poems", in which a fine horse waiting for a worthy master is the talented young Li He waiting for recognition — which never came. The golden bridle is an honoured place in the emperor's service.

poems.s: day palace tower flag rider
z: 男儿何不带吴钩，收取关山五十州。
请君暂上凌烟阁，若个书生万户侯？
e: Why shouldn't a man wear a hooked sword of Wu,
And win back fifty prefectures beyond the passes' gate?
Just climb the Lingyan Pavilion for a moment, and view —
Which bookish scholar there was made a lord of high estate?
poems.n: The Lingyan Pavilion displayed portraits of the twenty-four heroes who helped found the Tang — nearly all of them generals. Li He, a sickly scholar barred from the examinations on a technicality, chafes: the fifty prefectures held by rebellious warlords will be won back by the sword, not the pen.

poems.s: night autumn moon clouds mountains palace
z: 吴丝蜀桐张高秋，空白凝云颓不流。
江娥啼竹素女愁，李凭中国弹箜篌。
昆山玉碎凤皇呌，芙蓉泣露香兰笑。
十二门前融冷光，二十三丝动紫皇。
女娲炼石补天处，石破天惊逗秋雨。
梦入坤山教神妪，老鱼跳波瘦蛟舞。
吴质不眠倚桂树，露脚斜飞湿寒兔。
e: Wu silk on Shu wood, strung in high autumn's air;
In empty hills the clouds congeal and halt, as if to hear.
The river goddess weeps on bamboo; the White Maiden's in despair —
In the capital, Li Ping plays the konghou harp, so clear.
Like Kunlun jade that shatters, like the phoenix crying high;
Like lotus weeping dew, and fragrant orchids laughing bright.
Before the twelve gates of the city, it melts the cold light;
Its twenty-three strings move the Purple Emperor in the sky.
Where Nüwa smelted stones to mend the heavens long ago,
The stones break — heaven shudders — autumn rain comes pouring through.
In dreams it climbs the holy mountain, teaching the goddess who would know;
Old fishes leap the waves, and lean dragons dance anew.
Wu Gang, sleepless, leans against the cassia tree;
The slanting dew falls down and wets the cold moon-hare, I see.
poems.n: Li Ping was the most famous player of the konghou, a vertical harp, at court. Li He describes the music not by its sound but by its effects across the universe: clouds stop, goddesses weep, the Purple Emperor of heaven is moved, the stone that the goddess Nüwa used to patch the sky cracks and lets the rain through, and in the moon Wu Gang and the jade hare are drenched with dew. With Bai Juyi's *Pipa Player*, one of the great Tang poems on music.

poems.te: The Bronze Immortal Takes Leave of Han
poems.s: night autumn moon palace wall wind
z: 茂陵刘郎秋风客，夜闻马嘶晓无迹。
画栏桂树悬秋香，三十六宫土花碧。
魏官牵车指千里，东关酸风射眸子。
空将汉月出宫门，忆君清泪如铅水。
衰兰送客咸阳道，天若有情天亦老。
携盘独出月荒凉，渭城已远波声小。
e: Lord Liu of Maoling, guest of the autumn wind's lament —
At night his horses neighed; by dawn they'd left no trace.
By painted rails the cassia trees still hang their autumn scent;
In the thirty-six palaces, green moss covers every place.
The officers of Wei drag off the cart a thousand li;
At the eastern gate, a bitter wind stings the eyes.
Only the Han moon goes with him through the palace gate, to see;
Remembering his lord, his tears fall like molten lead, in sighs.
Withered orchids see the traveller off along the Xianyang road —
If heaven had feelings, heaven, too, would age and grow old.
Holding his plate, he goes out alone in the bleak moon's glow;
Weicheng is far behind; the river's murmur fades to low.
poems.n: In 233 the Wei emperor had the great bronze statue of an immortal — holding a plate to catch heavenly dew for Emperor Wu of Han's elixirs — carted from Chang'an to Luoyang; legend said the statue wept as it left. Li He, a distant descendant of the Tang royal house, mourns the passing of dynasties through the bronze man's tears. 天若有情天亦老, "if heaven had feelings, heaven too would grow old", is one of the most famous lines in Chinese.

poems.s: dusk autumn wind tower wall river reeds willow clouds
z: 一上高城万里愁，蒹葭杨柳似汀洲。
溪云初起日沉阁，山雨欲来风满楼。
鸟下绿芜秦苑夕，蝉鸣黄叶汉宫秋。
行人莫问当年事，故国东来渭水流。
e: I climb the city wall, and grief spreads ten thousand li;
The reeds and willows look like islets on a southern shore.
Clouds rise from the stream; the sun sinks behind the hall's high eaves;
The mountain rain is coming — wind fills the tower's every door.
Birds land in the green weeds of the Qin park as evening falls;
Cicadas cry in yellow leaves where Han palaces stood before.
Traveller, don't ask about the things of long ago —
Past the old capital, from the east, the Wei flows as of yore.
poems.n: Xianyang, capital of the Qin, lies across the Wei River from Chang'an. 山雨欲来风满楼, "the mountain rain is coming; the wind fills the tower", became the proverb for the tense moment before a storm breaks — political or otherwise. The ruined Qin and Han palaces foreshadow the fall of the Tang itself.

poems.s: spring rain peach cottage person
z: 清明时节雨纷纷，路上行人欲断魂。
借问酒家何处有？牧童遥指杏花村。
e: The Qingming rain comes drizzling down without an end;
The travellers on the road are lost in grief, heart-sore.
"Where can I find a tavern?" I ask — and round the bend,
A herd-boy points far off to Apricot Village's door.
poems.n: Qingming ("Clear and Bright", early April) is the festival for sweeping ancestors' graves — a day of mourning, traditionally wet. The tavern and the apricot blossoms promise a little warmth. "Apricot Blossom Village" (杏花村) became the name of a famous liquor, and several towns still claim to be the place.

poems.s: dusk autumn mountains maple clouds cottage rider
z: 远上寒山石径斜，白云生处有人家。
停车坐爱枫林晚，霜叶红于二月花。
e: Far up the cold mountain, a stone path slants and climbs;
Where the white clouds rise, there are homes of people too.
I stop my carriage: I love the maple woods at evening time —
The frosted leaves are redder than spring flowers ever grew.
poems.n: The great autumn poem: Du Mu stops simply to look. The last line overturns the usual melancholy of autumn — frost-touched maples outshine even the flowers of the second month of spring. (坐 here means "because".)

poems.s: spring rain temple flag oriole river mist
z: 千里莺啼绿映红，水村山郭酒旗风。
南朝四百八十寺，多少楼台烟雨中。
e: A thousand li of orioles; the green sets off the red;
Wine pennants flutter in the wind by river towns and hills.
Four hundred eighty temples the Southern Dynasties spread —
How many towers stand in the misty rain there still?
poems.n: The whole of the south in spring, in fourteen characters — then history. The Southern Dynasties (420–589) built hundreds of temples around Nanjing; their emperors' piety did not save them. The temples stand silent in the rain, beautiful and a little ironic.

poems.s: night moon river boat mist lantern
z: 烟笼寒水月笼沙，夜泊秦淮近酒家。
商女不知亡国恨，隔江犹唱后庭花。
e: Mist veils the cold water, moonlight veils the sand;
I moor on the Qinhuai at night, near taverns by the shore.
The singing girls don't know the grief of a fallen land —
Across the river they still sing "Rear Court Flowers", as before.
poems.n: The Qinhuai River in Nanjing was lined with pleasure houses. "Flowers of the Rear Courtyard" was composed by the Last Lord of Chen as his dynasty collapsed in 589 — the very sound of decadence and ruin. The real target is not the singers but the officials who request the song while the Tang itself declines.

poems.s: night autumn stars palace candle
z: 银烛秋光冷画屏，轻罗小扇扑流萤。
天阶夜色凉如水，卧看牵牛织女星。
e: A silver candle's autumn glow chills the painted screen;
With a little silk fan she chases fireflies as they fly.
On the palace steps the night is cool as water's sheen;
She lies and gazes at the Herdboy and the Weaver in the sky.
poems.n: A lonely palace lady on an autumn night. The silk fan was a symbol of a discarded woman, put away when summer ends; fireflies were said to breed in neglected grass. She watches the two star-lovers who meet once a year — more than she can hope for.

poems.s: day river wind sail fort
z: 折戟沉沙铁未销，自将磨洗认前朝。
东风不与周郎便，铜雀春深锁二乔。
e: A broken halberd in the sand — its iron's not yet gone;
I wash and polish it, and know it from that bygone age.
Had the east wind not blown to help young Zhou Yu on,
The two Qiao sisters, deep in spring, would be locked in Bronze Sparrow's cage.
poems.n: At the Battle of Red Cliff (208), Zhou Yu of Wu, helped by a timely east wind, burned Cao Cao's fleet. Du Mu's mischievous what-if: without that wind, Cao Cao would have won — and carried off Zhou Yu's wife and her sister, the famous beauties Da Qiao and Xiao Qiao, to his Bronze Sparrow Terrace. History turned on a gust of wind.

poems.s: dusk river pavilion boat
z: 胜败兵家事不期，包羞忍耻是男儿。
江东子弟多才俊，卷土重来未可知。
e: In war, no one can know beforehand who will win or lose;
To bear the shame and swallow pride — that is what makes a man.
East of the River there were many youths of talent —
Who knows? He might have rolled the dust back up, and come again.
poems.n: At Wujiang the defeated Xiang Yu refused a ferryman's offer to carry him back east of the Yangtze to raise a new army — he could not face the elders whose sons had died for him — and cut his own throat. Du Mu argues he should have endured the shame and tried again. 卷土重来, "rolling the dust back up", became the idiom for a comeback.

poems.s: day palace mountains rider horse
z: 长安回望绣成堆，山顶千门次第开。
一骑红尘妃子笑，无人知是荔枝来。
e: Looking back from Chang'an: hills like heaps of embroidery;
On the summit, a thousand palace gates swing open, one by one.
A horseman in red dust — the Consort smiles with glee;
No one knows it's lychees he has brought, at a run.
poems.n: Huaqing Palace on Mount Li was the winter retreat of Emperor Xuanzong and Consort Yang. She loved fresh lychees, so relays of horsemen galloped them a thousand miles from the far south, killing horses on the way, so they would arrive fresh. A whole empire's waste, in one smile.

poems.te: To Judge Han Chuo in Yangzhou
poems.s: night autumn moon bridge river hills
z: 青山隐隐水迢迢，秋尽江南草未凋。
二十四桥明月夜，玉人何处教吹箫？
e: Green hills grow dim; the waters stretch away;
Autumn ends, yet the southern grass is green.
On a moonlit night at the Twenty-four Bridges, say,
Where are you teaching a jade beauty the flute, unseen?
poems.n: Written to an old friend in Yangzhou, where Du Mu had spent happy, dissolute years. The Twenty-four Bridges of Yangzhou became a byword for romantic nights. "Jade person" can mean a lovely courtesan — or the handsome friend himself, teased about his pleasures.

poems.s: night tower lantern river boat
z: 落魄江湖载酒行，楚腰纤细掌中轻。
十年一觉扬州梦，赢得青楼薄幸名。
e: Down on my luck, I roamed the lakes and rivers, wine in hand,
With slender Chu-waisted girls light enough to dance on a palm.
Ten years — then I woke from my Yangzhou dream, to understand
All I'd won was a heartless rake's name in the houses of charm.
poems.n: Du Mu looks back on his years as a young secretary in Yangzhou, notorious for his nights in the pleasure quarters. King Ling of Chu loved slender waists; the Han beauty Zhao Feiyan was said to be light enough to dance on a palm. The self-mockery is tinged with regret.

poems.s: spring willow tower flowers
z: 娉娉袅袅十三余，豆蔻梢头二月初。
春风十里扬州路，卷上珠帘总不如。
e: So graceful, slender, just past thirteen years —
A cardamom bud on the bough as early spring appears.
Along ten li of Yangzhou's road in spring's warm air,
Roll up every pearl curtain — no beauty there compares.
poems.n: Written for a young singing girl as Du Mu left Yangzhou in 835. 豆蔻年华, "cardamom years" — a phrase from this poem — still means a girl of thirteen or fourteen. Behind every pearl blind on Yangzhou's famous avenue there were beauties; none matched her.

poems.s: night candle window two cup
z: 多情却似总无情，唯觉樽前笑不成。
蜡烛有心还惜别，替人垂泪到天明。
e: So full of love, I seem to have no love at all;
Over our cups I only find I cannot smile.
The candle has a heart, and grieves to see us part —
It sheds its tears for us till dawn, all the while.
poems.n: Too much feeling makes the lovers seem cold and silent. The candle's "heart" is its wick (心 means both), and its "tears" the dripping wax — so the candle weeps for the lovers who cannot.

poems.s: dusk spring petals tower river birds
z: 繁华事散逐香尘，流水无情草自春。
日暮东风怨啼鸟，落花犹似坠楼人。
e: The glory is scattered, gone with the scented dust;
The heartless water flows; the grass grows green, as spring has its way.
At dusk, in the east wind, the crying birds complain;
The falling flowers look like her who fell from the tower that day.
poems.n: The Golden Valley Garden in Luoyang belonged to Shi Chong (249–300), the richest man of the Jin, famous for his extravagance. When a powerful rival demanded his beloved concubine Green Pearl, she threw herself from a tower rather than be taken. Five centuries later, Du Mu finds only grass, water and falling petals.

poems.te: Climbing Leyou Plain Before Leaving for Wuxing
poems.s: day hills clouds rider wall
z: 清时有味是无能，闲爱孤云静爱僧。
欲把一麾江海去，乐游原上望昭陵。
e: To savour life in peaceful times, you must be no use at all;
At leisure I love the lone cloud; in stillness, the monk's way.
Now, with a governor's banner, I'll go where the rivers call —
From Leyou Plain, toward the Zhao Tomb, I gaze today.
poems.n: 850: about to leave the capital to govern Wuxing (Huzhou), Du Mu climbs Leyou Plain and gazes toward the Zhao Tomb of Emperor Taizong, the great founder of the Tang golden age. The first line is ironic: in such "peaceful times", only the useless can enjoy themselves — and he is not wanted. The look toward Taizong's tomb is a silent longing for a ruler who valued talent.

poems.te: Quatrain on the Rear Pond at Qi'an
poems.s: summer rain lake lotus oriole flowers
z: 菱透浮萍绿锦池，夏莺千啭弄蔷薇。
尽日无人看微雨，鸳鸯相对浴红衣。
e: Water-chestnuts push through duckweed — the pond's green brocade;
Summer orioles trill a thousand songs and play among the rose.
All day, no one watches the fine rain drifting through the glade;
Mandarin ducks, face to face, bathe in their red-feathered clothes.
poems.n: Du Mu as governor of Huangzhou (Qi'an). A rainy summer garden with no one in it — except a pair of mandarin ducks, symbols of happy love, whose red feathers are their "red robes". The poet's loneliness is felt only by contrast.

poems.s: autumn day tower mountains maple
z: 楼倚霜树外，镜天无一毫。
南山与秋色，气势两相高。
e: The tower leans out beyond the frosted trees;
The mirror sky has not one speck of grey.
The Southern Hills and autumn's clear expanse
Both soar, and vie in grandeur, high as they may.
poems.n: A crystal-clear autumn day in Chang'an. From a tower, the sky is a spotless mirror, and the Zhongnan mountains and the autumn air itself seem to compete to be loftier.

poems.s: summer wind petals peach
z: 自是寻春去校迟，不须惆怅怨芳时。
狂风落尽深红色，绿叶成阴子满枝。
e: It's I who came too late in search of spring;
I shouldn't grieve, or blame the flowering days.
The wild wind's blown away the crimson blossoming;
Green leaves make shade; the boughs bear fruit in sprays.
poems.n: Legend says the young Du Mu, in Huzhou, saw a lovely girl of about ten and promised her mother he would return to marry her within ten years. He came back fourteen years later to find her married, with children. Without the story, it is simply a gentle poem about missed chances — and about a different fulfilment: the fruit that follows the flowers.

poems.s: night moon river tower person
z: 独上江楼思渺然，月光如水水如天。
同来望月人何处？风景依稀似去年。
e: Alone I climb the river tower; my thoughts drift far and free;
The moonlight's like the water, and the water like the sky.
The one who came to watch the moon with me — where can she be?
The scenery seems just as it was last year, as days go by.
poems.n: A return to a place of happy memory. 月光如水水如天 — moonlight like water, water like sky — dissolves the world into one shimmering emptiness, matching the empty place beside him.

poems.te: Setting Out Early on Mount Shang
poems.s: dawn autumn crescent frost cottage bridge leaves rider
z: 晨起动征铎，客行悲故乡。
鸡声茅店月，人迹板桥霜。
槲叶落山路，枳花明驿墙。
因思杜陵梦，凫雁满回塘。
e: At dawn I rise to the jingle of the carriage bell;
The traveller grieves for home, so far away.
Cockcrow — thatched inn — moon;
Footprints — plank bridge — frost.
Oak leaves fall along the mountain road;
Orange blossoms brighten the post-house wall.
I think of last night's dream of Duling, where
Wild ducks and geese filled the winding pond, all.
poems.n: The second couplet, 鸡声茅店月，人迹板桥霜, is made entirely of nouns — six images, no verbs — yet tells a whole story: an early start, the moon still up, a cock crowing, someone already gone ahead over the frosty bridge. Poets imitated it for centuries, and it anticipates the Imagism of Ezra Pound. Duling, near Chang'an, was the poet's home.

poems.te: Gazing South of the River (Done with Her Toilette)
poems.s: dusk sun river tower sail person
z: 梳洗罢，独倚望江楼。
过尽千帆皆不是，斜晖脉脉水悠悠。
肠断白蘋洲。
e: Done washing, combing her hair,
Alone she leans in the tower by the river.
A thousand sails go by — and none is his;
The slanting sun lingers, loving; the waters flow forever.
Her heart breaks at White Duckweed Isle.
poems.n: A whole day of waiting in five lines: she dresses up in the morning and watches the river until sunset. The slanting light seems tender (脉脉), the water indifferent (悠悠). White Duckweed Isle may be where they parted.

poems.t: 菩萨蛮（小山重叠金明灭）
poems.te: Buddhist Barbarian (Little Hills, Layer on Layer)
poems.s: dawn window palace flowers person
z: 小山重叠金明灭，鬓云欲度香腮雪。
懒起画蛾眉，弄妆梳洗迟。
照花前后镜，花面交相映。
新帖绣罗襦，双双金鹧鸪。
e: Little hills of gold on her screen glimmer, fade and gleam;
Her cloud of hair drifts over cheeks as white as snow.
Lazily she rises to paint her moth-wing brows, as in a dream;
She dawdles over make-up, washing, combing, slow.
With mirrors front and back she checks the flower in her hair:
The flower and her face reflect each other, both so fair.
And on her new silk jacket, freshly sewn, you see
Golden partridges embroidered, two by two.
poems.n: The model of the Huajian ("Among the Flowers") style: a lady's morning toilette in gold, snow-white and silk — and, in the last line, embroidered partridges in pairs, quietly pointing to her solitude. The "little hills" may be the hills painted on her folding screen, glinting gold in the morning light, or her eyebrows, or golden combs in her hair. *Pusa Man* ("Buddhist Barbarian") is the name of the tune.

poems.s: night candle window person
z: 井底点灯深烛伊，共郎长行莫围棋。
玲珑骰子安红豆，入骨相思知不知。
e: Like a lamp lit deep within a well, I deeply bid you, dear:
Go on your long journey, but don't "play Go" and miss our date.
The dainty dice of bone are inlaid with love-beans, red and clear —
This longing's sunk into the bone: do you know it, soon or late?
poems.n: A love song built entirely of puns. A lamp at the bottom of a well is a "deep candle" (深烛), which sounds like 深嘱, "earnestly urge". "Long Journey" (长行) was a dice game; weiqi (围棋, Go) sounds like 违期, "break the appointed day". Dice were made of bone, and their red pips are "red beans" — the seeds of love-longing — so the longing is literally inlaid "into the bone" (入骨). 玲珑骰子安红豆，入骨相思知不知 is one of the most quoted love lines in Chinese.

poems.s: dusk desert river grass fort
z: 誓扫匈奴不顾身，五千貂锦丧胡尘。
可怜无定河边骨，犹是春闺梦里人。
e: They swore to sweep the Xiongnu out, with no thought for their life;
Five thousand men in sable and brocade fell in the northern dust.
Alas — the bones along the Wuding River, white and bare,
Are still the living men in the spring dreams of each wife.
poems.n: The most heartbreaking war poem in Chinese: the wives at home, not yet knowing, still dream of their husbands — who are already bones by the Wuding River ("River of No Fixed Course") on the northern frontier. "Sable and brocade" was the uniform of elite Han troops.

poems.s: night moon sea butterfly mist
z: 锦瑟无端五十弦，一弦一柱思华年。
庄生晓梦迷蝴蝶，望帝春心托杜鹃。
沧海月明珠有泪，蓝田日暖玉生烟。
此情可待成追忆？只是当时已惘然。
e: The patterned zither, for no reason, has fifty strings;
Each string, each bridge, brings back the years of bloom.
Zhuangzi at dawn dreamed he was a butterfly, lost in its wings;
Emperor Wang left his spring heart to the cuckoo's gloom.
On the blue sea, under the moon, the pearls are tears;
At Lantian, in the warm sun, the jade gives off a haze.
Must such a feeling wait for memory, across the years?
Even then, as it was happening, I was lost in a daze.
poems.n: Perhaps the most debated poem in Chinese — a love poem, an elegy for his wife, a lament for his career, or a poem about poetry itself. The legendary fifty-stringed zither was so sad that the god Fuxi split it into twenty-five. Zhuangzi dreamed he was a butterfly and woke unsure which was the dreamer; Emperor Wang of Shu became a cuckoo that cried till it bled; mermaids wept pearls; the jade buried at Lantian gave off a glow like smoke in the sun. Every image is lovely and out of reach — like the past.

poems.s: night spring candle window petals crescent
z: 相见时难别亦难，东风无力百花残。
春蚕到死丝方尽，蜡炬成灰泪始干。
晓镜但愁云鬓改，夜吟应觉月光寒。
蓬山此去无多路，青鸟殷勤为探看。
e: It's hard for us to meet, and just as hard to part;
The east wind has no strength; a hundred flowers fall.
The spring silkworm spins its silk until it dies;
The candle weeps till it is ash, its tears dried after all.
At dawn, before her mirror, she grieves her hair turning grey;
Chanting at night, she must feel the moonlight's cold.
From here to Penglai Mountain is not so far a way —
Bluebird, go faithfully, and see her for me, as of old.
poems.n: The most famous of Li Shangyin's "Untitled" poems. The silkworm and the candle are the supreme images of devotion until death — and 丝 "silk" puns on 思 "longing". The bluebird was the messenger of the Queen Mother of the West, and Penglai is the island of immortals: the beloved is as unreachable as a goddess. Teachers today quote the couplet to honour selfless dedication.

poems.s: night stars tower candle cup
z: 昨夜星辰昨夜风，画楼西畔桂堂东。
身无彩凤双飞翼，心有灵犀一点通。
隔座送钩春酒暖，分曹射覆蜡灯红。
嗟余听鼓应官去，走马兰台类转蓬。
e: Last night's stars, and last night's breeze,
West of the painted tower, east of the cassia hall.
Though I lack the bright phoenix's wings to fly to you with ease,
Our hearts, like the magic horn, are linked through all.
Across the tables we passed the hook; the spring wine glowed warm;
In teams we guessed at hidden things, by candles burning red.
Alas — the drums call me to my desk; I must away from you,
And ride to the Orchid Terrace, a tumbleweed blown ahead.
poems.n: A night of party games — passing a hidden hook, guessing concealed objects — where the poet exchanged glances with someone he could not openly approach. 心有灵犀一点通: the rhinoceros horn was believed to have a white thread running from end to end, so the phrase means two hearts that understand each other instantly. The Orchid Terrace was the imperial library, where Li Shangyin worked as a minor clerk.

poems.te: Written on a Rainy Night, to the North
poems.s: night autumn rain mountains window candle
z: 君问归期未有期，巴山夜雨涨秋池。
何当共剪西窗烛，却话巴山夜雨时。
e: You ask me when I'm coming home — I cannot say just when;
Tonight in the hills of Ba, the rain is filling autumn's pool.
When shall we trim the candle by the west window again,
And talk of tonight, when the rain fell on Ba, so cool?
poems.n: Written in Sichuan (Ba) around 851 to his wife — or a friend — in the north. The present lonely, rainy night is imagined as a future memory shared by candlelight, so the poem folds time back on itself; "Ba hills, night rain" appears twice, once in sorrow and once in comfort. "Trimming the candle at the west window" (西窗剪烛) now means a heart-to-heart talk with someone dear.

poems.s: dusk sun hills wall rider
z: 向晚意不适，驱车登古原。
夕阳无限好，只是近黄昏。
e: Toward evening, my heart was ill at ease;
I drove my carriage up the ancient height.
The setting sun is boundlessly lovely —
It's just that it's so close to night.
poems.n: Leyou Plain was the highest spot in Chang'an, with a view over the whole city. 夕阳无限好，只是近黄昏 — beauty at its height is already ending — is quoted of old age, of the late Tang dynasty itself, and of every last golden moment.

poems.s: night moon stars window candle palace
z: 云母屏风烛影深，长河渐落晓星沉。
嫦娥应悔偷灵药，碧海青天夜夜心。
e: Behind the mica screen, the candle's shadows grow;
The Milky Way sinks slowly, and the morning stars sink low.
Chang'e must regret she stole the elixir away:
Blue sea, blue sky — her lonely heart, night after night, till day.
poems.n: Chang'e stole the elixir of immortality from her husband, the archer Hou Yi, floated up to the moon, and lives there forever, alone. The sleepless speaker — a lonely woman, a Daoist nun, or the poet himself — understands her: immortality without companionship is an endless night.

poems.s: night palace candle two
z: 宣室求贤访逐臣，贾生才调更无伦。
可怜夜半虚前席，不问苍生问鬼神。
e: Seeking worthies, the emperor summoned back the banished man;
Master Jia's brilliance was beyond compare.
At midnight, sadly, the emperor drew his mat close — in vain:
He asked not of the people, but of ghosts and gods up there.
poems.n: Jia Yi, the brilliant young statesman of the Han, had been exiled; Emperor Wen recalled him and talked with him late into the night in the Xuanshi Hall, leaning closer and closer on his mat — about ghosts and spirits. Li Shangyin uses the story to mock rulers who chased Daoist mysticism (several Tang emperors died of "immortality" elixirs) while neglecting their people.

poems.te: Untitled (Your Coming Was an Empty Word)
poems.s: night crescent tower candle window
z: 来是空言去绝踪，月斜楼上五更钟。
梦为远别啼难唤，书被催成墨未浓。
蜡照半笼金翡翠，麝熏微度绣芙蓉。
刘郎已恨蓬山远，更隔蓬山一万重。
e: Your coming was an empty word; you've gone without a trace;
The moon slants on the tower; the fifth-watch bell is tolled.
In dreams we parted far; I wept, and could not call or hold;
I rushed this letter — the ink's too pale, not thick nor bold.
The candlelight half-veils the gold kingfisher quilt;
The musk scent faintly drifts through the embroidered lotus' fold.
Young Liu already grieved that Penglai Mountain was so far —
And you're ten thousand mountains beyond Penglai, I'm told.
poems.n: In a Han legend, Liu Chen met two fairies in the Tiantai Mountains, stayed half a year, and returned to find seven generations had passed — he could never find them again. The lover is now even further than that fairyland. The candle half-lighting the kingfisher-embroidered quilt and the drifting musk are the traces of a night together.

poems.s: dusk palace willow crows river sail
z: 紫泉宫殿锁烟霞，欲取芜城作帝家。
玉玺不缘归日角，锦帆应是到天涯。
于今腐草无萤火，终古垂杨有暮鸦。
地下若逢陈后主，岂宜重问后庭花。
e: The halls of Purple Spring lay locked in mist and rosy haze;
He wanted to make Wucheng his imperial home.
Had the jade seal not gone to the man with the sun-horned brow,
His brocade sails would have reached the world's end, to roam.
Today, in the rotting grass, there are no fireflies;
Forever, on the drooping willows, evening crows remain.
If underground he meets the Last Lord of Chen,
How could he ask for "Flowers of the Rear Court" again?
poems.n: Emperor Yang of Sui (r. 604–618) left his capital for pleasure cruises to Yangzhou (Wucheng) in dragon boats with brocade sails, bankrupting the state; he was murdered, and the empire passed to Li Yuan, founder of the Tang, whose "sun-horned" forehead was a sign of a destined emperor. Yang had fireflies gathered by the bushel to light his night outings, and planted the willows along the Grand Canal. The Last Lord of Chen lost his kingdom — to the Sui — while composing the song "Flowers of the Rear Courtyard". The two decadent rulers would have much to discuss in the underworld.

poems.s: summer dusk willow cottage
z: 本以高难饱，徒劳恨费声。
五更疏欲断，一树碧无情。
薄宦梗犹泛，故园芜已平。
烦君最相警，我亦举家清。
e: Living up high, you can hardly eat your fill;
In vain you cry, resenting the voice you spend.
By the fifth watch your cries grow faint, near still;
The whole green tree is heartless to the end.
A petty official, I drift like a broken spray;
My home garden's overgrown with weeds by now.
I thank you for your stern warning, cicada — I'd say
My whole household is as pure and poor as you, I vow.
poems.n: The cicada, believed to live on dew alone, was a symbol of the incorruptible scholar. Li Shangyin, trapped in minor posts by court factions, sees himself in the insect that sings itself hoarse on a tree that does not care.

poems.s: dusk spring petals pavilion sun
z: 高阁客竟去，小园花乱飞。
参差连曲陌，迢递送斜晖。
肠断未忍扫，眼穿仍欲归。
芳心向春尽，所得是沾衣。
e: The guests have left the high pavilion at last;
In the little garden, petals whirl and fly.
In tangled drifts they line the winding paths;
Far off, they see the slanting sun go by.
Heartbroken, I can't bring myself to sweep;
I gaze till my eyes ache, and long for their return.
Their fragrant hearts have spent themselves on spring —
And all they get is tears that wet my clothes in turn.
poems.n: Written around 846, when Li Shangyin was idle at home after his mother's death, his career stalled. The petals that give their "fragrant heart" to spring and receive only tears in return are his own devotion, unrewarded.

poems.s: day tower wall willow river
z: 迢递高城百尺楼，绿杨枝外尽汀洲。
贾生年少虚垂涕，王粲春来更远游。
永忆江湖归白发，欲回天地入扁舟。
不知腐鼠成滋味，猜意鹓雏竟未休。
e: The high wall winds afar; the tower stands a hundred feet;
Beyond the green willow boughs, there's nothing but isles and shore.
Young Jia Yi shed tears for the state, in vain;
Wang Can in spring went wandering farther than before.
I've always dreamed of going home to rivers and lakes, white-haired —
But first to turn the world around, then sail off in a skiff, set free.
I never dreamed a rotting rat could be such a delicacy,
That they'd suspect the phoenix chick, and never let it be.
poems.n: 838: the young Li Shangyin, having failed a placement exam because of factional politics, climbs a tower at Anding. Jia Yi wept over the empire's troubles as a young man; Wang Can, an exile, wrote a famous poem from a tower. In *Zhuangzi*, an owl clutching a rotten rat screeched at a passing phoenix — which eats only bamboo seed — fearing it wanted the rat. His rivals are the owls; office is the rat.

poems.s: night autumn moon frost tower geese river
z: 初闻征雁已无蝉，百尺楼高水接天。
青女素娥俱耐冷，月中霜里斗婵娟。
e: When first I hear the migrating geese, the cicadas are gone;
From the hundred-foot tower, the water joins the sky.
The Frost Maid and the Moon Goddess both can bear the cold —
In moonlight and in frost they vie, to see whose grace is high.
poems.n: Qingnü (青女) was the goddess of frost; Sue (素娥) is Chang'e, the moon goddess. On a cold, clear autumn night, the white frost and the white moonlight become two goddesses competing in pure, cold beauty.

poems.t: 宿骆氏亭寄怀崔雍崔衮
poems.te: Staying at the Luo Pavilion, Thinking of Cui Yong and Cui Gun
poems.s: autumn rain lotus lake pavilion bamboo
z: 竹坞无尘水槛清，相思迢递隔重城。
秋阴不散霜飞晚，留得枯荷听雨声。
e: The bamboo dock is free of dust, the railings by the water clear;
My longing reaches far to you, past city walls on walls.
The autumn clouds won't lift, and frost is late this year —
The withered lotus leaves are left to hear the rain that falls.
poems.n: Staying at a friend's pavilion, Li Shangyin thinks of two cousins far away. The last line — keep the withered lotus to listen to the rain — is among the most loved lines in Chinese: even dead lotus leaves have their beauty, as an instrument for the sound of rain. In *Dream of the Red Chamber*, Lin Daiyu says it is the one line of Li Shangyin's she likes.

poems.s: dawn spring palace window
z: 为有云屏无限娇，凤城寒尽怕春宵。
无端嫁得金龟婿，辜负香衾事早朝。
e: Behind the mica screen, with all her endless charm,
In Phoenix City, now the cold has gone, she fears the nights of spring:
For no good reason she married a man with a golden tortoise —
He leaves their fragrant quilt for the dawn court of the king.
poems.n: A young wife complains that her husband, a high official — the golden tortoise pouch was a badge of the third rank — leaves her bed before dawn for the morning audience. Light and witty, with a hint that ambition costs love.

poems.s: day palace lake horse clouds
z: 瑶池阿母绮窗开，黄竹歌声动地哀。
八骏日行三万里，穆王何事不重来？
e: At Jasper Pool the Queen Mother opens her latticed window wide;
The "Yellow Bamboo" song rings out, so sad it shakes the ground.
His eight steeds ran thirty thousand li a day, with pride —
So why has King Mu never come back round?
poems.n: King Mu of Zhou, in legend, drove his eight divine horses to the Jasper Pool in the far west to feast with the Queen Mother of the West, who offered immortality and asked him to return. He never did — he died. The poem mocks Tang emperors who sought elixirs of eternal life: even the fastest horses cannot outrun death.

poems.s: night stars palace horse flag
z: 海外徒闻更九州，他生未卜此生休。
空闻虎旅传宵柝，无复鸡人报晓筹。
此日六军同驻马，当时七夕笑牵牛。
如何四纪为天子，不及卢家有莫愁。
e: In vain they told of nine more continents across the sea —
The next life is uncertain; this one's done.
He hears the tiger guards beat out the watches, emptily;
No cockman calls the palace dawn — not one.
That day the Six Armies all reined in their horses there;
That Seventh Night, they'd laughed at the Herdboy's plight.
How could he, four decades the Son of Heaven, fare
Worse than the Lu clan, who kept Mochou home each night?
poems.n: Li Shangyin's sharp reply to the romance of *The Song of Everlasting Sorrow*. The tale that Consort Yang lives on in an immortals' island beyond the sea is empty talk. On the Seventh Night, when the Herdboy and the Weaver Girl meet just once a year, the imperial lovers pitied the stars — yet after nearly fifty years on the throne, Xuanzong could not protect his beloved as well as a commoner of the folk song, whose wife Mochou lived happily at home.

poems.s: night spring rain tower lantern geese
z: 怅卧新春白袷衣，白门寥落意多违。
红楼隔雨相望冷，珠箔飘灯独自归。
远路应悲春晼晚，残宵犹得梦依稀。
玉珰缄札何由达，万里云罗一雁飞。
e: Downcast, I lie in my white robe, the spring just new;
At the White Gate, all is bleak — nothing has come true.
Through the rain, the red tower looks cold, far off;
Past bead curtains and drifting lamps, I walk home alone, too.
On your long road, you must grieve as spring grows late;
In the night's last hours I still dream — faint, but of you.
How can the jade earring and sealed letter reach you? —
Ten thousand li of cloud-net, and one wild goose flying through.
poems.n: The poet returns to the red tower where he once met his love and finds her gone, far away. The "White Gate" is Nanjing, a stock place for lovers' meetings. A jade earring was a love-token; the lone goose, a letter-carrier, is lost in a net of clouds.

poems.s: dusk summer sun tower window birds grass
z: 深居俯夹城，春去夏犹清。
天意怜幽草，人间重晚晴。
并添高阁迥，微注小窗明。
越鸟巢干后，归飞体更轻。
e: Living secluded, I look down on the walled lane's way;
Spring has gone, but summer still is clear and bright.
Heaven pities the shy grass in the shade;
The world treasures the clearing at evening light.
It lengthens the view from the high pavilion;
It gently pours brightness through my small window's frame.
The southern birds' nests are dry at last —
Flying home, they're lighter than when they came.
poems.n: Guilin, 847, as a long rain clears at evening. 天意怜幽草，人间重晚晴 — "Heaven pities the hidden grass; the world treasures the late clearing" — is quoted for kindness to the overlooked and for the beauty of a good old age. Li Shangyin had just found a post after years of frustration; the light, dry birds are his relief.

poems.s: night spring flowers candle person
z: 寻芳不觉醉流霞，倚树沉眠日已斜。
客散酒醒深夜后，更持红烛赏残花。
e: Seeking flowers, I got drunk on rosy wine before I knew;
I leaned against a tree and slept; the sun had slanted low.
The guests gone, I woke sober, deep into the night —
And took a red candle out to see the last blooms glow.
poems.n: "Flowing Rosy Cloud" (流霞) was the wine of the immortals. Sober at midnight, the poet cannot bear to waste the flowers' last hours. Su Shi later borrowed the idea: "afraid the flowers will fall asleep in the night, I light a tall candle to shine on their red faces."

poems.s: dusk autumn mountains temple leaves clouds person
z: 残阳西入崦，茅屋访孤僧。
落叶人何在，寒云路几层。
独敲初夜磬，闲倚一枝藤。
世界微尘里，吾宁爱与憎。
e: The setting sun sinks behind the western peak;
I come to a thatched hut, a lone monk to seek.
Among the falling leaves — where can he be?
Through cold clouds, how many tiers of path to see?
Alone, he strikes the stone chime as night begins;
At ease, he leans upon a single staff of vine.
The whole wide world lies in a mote of dust —
Why should I love or hate? Why should I pine?
poems.n: A visit to a hermit monk on a mountain called Green Vine. The ending is pure Buddhism: if the whole universe can lie within a speck of dust, the poet's own loves and hatreds are as nothing.

poems.s: spring rain lotus lake palace wind
z: 飒飒东风细雨来，芙蓉塘外有轻雷。
金蟾啮锁烧香入，玉虎牵丝汲井回。
贾氏窥帘韩掾少，宓妃留枕魏王才。
春心莫共花争发，一寸相思一寸灰。
e: Soughing, the east wind comes with fine rain;
Beyond the lotus pond, a soft thunder rolls.
The gold-toad lock is fast — yet incense smoke slips in;
The jade-tiger winch draws silk rope, and water climbs the well.
Lady Jia peeked through the curtain, for young Han was fair;
Princess Fu gave her pillow to the Prince of Wei, for his flair.
O spring heart, don't race the flowers to burst into bloom:
For every inch of longing, an inch of ash lies there.
poems.n: Thunder, rain, lotus, a locked door, a well: hints of a secret love. Even a locked door lets in incense, and even a deep well yields its water — 丝 "silk" again punning on 思 "longing". Lady Jia glimpsed the handsome Han Shou through a screen and secretly married him; the goddess of the Luo River (Princess Fu) was said to have left a pillow for the poet Cao Zhi. The last line, "an inch of longing, an inch of ash", is the bitterest image of love's cost in Chinese — like incense that burns itself away.

poems.te: On Chrysanthemums, After Failing the Examination
poems.s: autumn chrysanthemum wall flag wind
z: 待到秋来九月八，我花开后百花杀。
冲天香阵透长安，满城尽带黄金甲。
e: Wait till the autumn comes — the ninth month, the eighth day:
When my flowers open, all the hundred flowers die.
Their fragrance, storming heaven, will sweep through Chang'an's every way,
And the whole city will wear gold armour, gleaming high.
poems.n: Written by Huang Chao after failing the imperial examination. The chrysanthemum, which blooms at the Double Ninth, becomes an army: its golden petals are armour, its fragrance an assault on the capital. In 880 Huang Chao's rebels really did take Chang'an — the poem reads as a prophecy.

poems.s: autumn chrysanthemum wind cottage
z: 飒飒西风满院栽，蕊寒香冷蝶难来。
他年我若为青帝，报与桃花一处开。
e: In the rustling west wind, they fill the courtyard all around;
Their hearts are cold, their scent is chill — no butterflies come near.
If one day I should be the Green Emperor of Spring,
I'd have them bloom beside the peach blossoms, when the spring is here.
poems.n: The Green Emperor (青帝) was the god of spring. Chrysanthemums bloom in the cold of autumn, when no butterflies come; the young rebel vows to give them their place in the warmth of spring — to overturn the order that keeps the poor out in the cold.

poems.te: Summer Day at the Mountain Pavilion
poems.s: summer pavilion lake flowers wind pine
z: 绿树阴浓夏日长，楼台倒影入池塘。
水晶帘动微风起，满架蔷薇一院香。
e: Green trees cast heavy shade; the summer days are long;
The tower's reflection falls upon the pond.
The crystal curtain stirs: a breeze begins to blow;
A trellis full of roses scents the courtyard all around.
poems.n: A cool summer afternoon at a mountain pavilion: shade, reflection, a stirring curtain — and then the scent of roses fills the courtyard. The breeze is never seen, only inferred from the curtain and the perfume.

poems.te: Before the Examination: To Zhang of the Ministry of Waters
poems.s: dawn candle window person two
z: 洞房昨夜停红烛，待晓堂前拜舅姑。
妆罢低声问夫婿，画眉深浅入时无？
e: Last night, the red candles burned in the bridal room;
At dawn I'll go to bow before his parents in the hall.
My make-up done, I whisper to my groom:
"Are my brows painted right — the latest style of all?"
poems.n: A coded letter. Before the examination of 826, Zhu Qingyu sent this poem to the influential official Zhang Ji: the new bride is the candidate, the parents-in-law are the examiners, the eyebrows his essays — "will they pass?" Zhang Ji replied with a poem assuring him she was the loveliest girl of all. He passed.

poems.s: dusk river hills fort grass
z: 泽国江山入战图，生民何计乐樵苏。
凭君莫话封侯事，一将功成万骨枯。
e: The rivers and the hills down south are drawn on maps of war;
How can the people live in peace, cutting firewood and grass?
I beg you, don't speak to me of lordships won in war —
One general's fame is built upon ten thousand bones, alas.
poems.n: Written in 879, as the Tang fought Huang Chao's rebels across the south. 一将功成万骨枯, "one general's success, ten thousand withered bones", became the most quoted line against war in Chinese.

poems.s: spring flowers butterfly mountains
z: 不论平地与山尖，无限风光尽被占。
采得百花成蜜后，为谁辛苦为谁甜？
e: On level plain or mountain peak, wherever blossoms show,
They claim each lovely scene as theirs to roam.
They gather from a hundred flowers, and make their honey — though
For whom the toil? For whom the sweetness, in the comb?
poems.n: The bees work all their lives, and others eat the honey — Luo Yin's sharp parable of the common people who labour for the rich. 为谁辛苦为谁甜 is still said of anyone who works hard for others' benefit.

poems.s: night cup jar person moon
z: 得即高歌失即休，多愁多恨亦悠悠。
今朝有酒今朝醉，明日愁来明日愁。
e: When I win, I sing; when I lose, I let it be;
My many sorrows and regrets — let them drift away.
If I have wine today, I'll drink today, carefree;
Tomorrow's worries can wait until tomorrow's day.
poems.n: Luo Yin failed the imperial examination ten times. His answer — 今朝有酒今朝醉, "if there's wine today, get drunk today" — became the motto of carefree living, quoted sometimes with approval and sometimes not.

poems.s: winter snow wall cottage
z: 尽道丰年瑞，丰年事若何？
长安有贫者，为瑞不宜多。
e: "A good omen for the harvest!" everyone says of the snow.
But what will a good harvest mean, I'd like to know?
In Chang'an there are people who are poor —
For them, let this lucky snow not fall much more.
poems.n: A proverb says "timely snow foretells a good harvest" (瑞雪兆丰年). Luo Yin's dry reply: the well-fed may welcome the omen, but the poor of the capital are freezing in it now.

poems.s: spring rain willow wall river mist birds
z: 江雨霏霏江草齐，六朝如梦鸟空啼。
无情最是台城柳，依旧烟笼十里堤。
e: Fine rain falls on the river; the river grass is green;
Six dynasties have passed like dreams; the birds cry all in vain.
Most heartless are the willows by the Palace Wall —
Still veiling ten li of embankment in their mist, the same.
poems.n: Taicheng, the palace city of Nanjing, was the seat of six short-lived southern dynasties. In the late Tang, as his own dynasty collapsed, Wei Zhuang finds only rain, grass and birds. The willows are "heartless" because they go on being beautiful, untouched by the fall of kingdoms.

poems.t: 菩萨蛮（人人尽说江南好）
poems.te: Buddhist Barbarian (Everyone Says the South Is Fine)
poems.s: spring rain river boat lantern person
z: 人人尽说江南好，游人只合江南老。
春水碧于天，画船听雨眠。
垆边人似月，皓腕凝霜雪。
未老莫还乡，还乡须断肠。
e: Everyone says how fine the South can be;
A traveller should simply grow old here.
The spring water's bluer than the sky I see;
In a painted boat I sleep, the rain sounds near.
The girl who serves the wine is like the moon,
Her pale wrists white as frost and snow.
Don't go home till you are old — too soon,
Going home would break your heart, you know.
poems.n: Written in the south after the sack of Chang'an. The South's beauty — water bluer than the sky, rain on a painted boat, a moon-pale girl by the wine stove — is real; but the last couplet reveals why he stays: home is in ruins, and to go back would break his heart.

poems.te: Longing for the Imperial Capital (A Spring Outing)
poems.s: spring peach petals rider person
z: 春日游，杏花吹满头。
陌上谁家年少，足风流。
妾拟将身嫁与，一生休。
纵被无情弃，不能羞。
e: A spring-day stroll —
Apricot blossoms blowing all over my hair.
Who's that young man on the path,
So dashing, so debonair?
I'll give myself to him to wed,
And give my whole life there.
Even if he heartlessly casts me off,
I won't feel shame — I won't care!
poems.n: One of the boldest love songs of the Tang, in the voice of a girl who falls for a handsome stranger at first sight and decides, on the spot, to marry him whatever happens. Wei Zhuang captures the fearless directness of folk song.

poems.s: day fields cottage person candle
z: 二月卖新丝，五月粜新谷。
医得眼前疮，剜却心头肉。
我愿君王心，化作光明烛。
不照绮罗筵，只照逃亡屋。
e: In the second month he sells his silk, not yet spun;
In the fifth month he sells his grain, not yet grown.
To heal the sore before his eyes, it's done
By cutting out the flesh from his heart's own.
I wish our sovereign's heart would turn
Into a candle, shining clear and bright —
Not lighting silk-robed banquets as they burn,
But the empty homes of those who fled in flight.
poems.n: Desperate farmers borrowed against crops not yet harvested — selling silk in the second month, before the silkworms have even hatched, and grain in the fifth, before the harvest, at ruinous prices. "Healing the sore before your eyes by cutting the flesh from your heart" became the proverb for a desperate short-term fix. The second half begs the emperor to look at the deserted homes of peasants driven off by debt.

poems.s: spring rain flowers butterfly cottage
z: 雨前初见花间蕊，雨后兼无叶里花。
蛱蝶飞来过墙去，却疑春色在邻家。
e: Before the rain, the buds had just appeared among the flowers;
After the rain, there's not a blossom left among the leaves.
The butterflies fly over, then across the wall —
As if spring's colour's moved next door, they seem to believe.
poems.n: The rain has stripped the garden, and the disappointed butterflies flutter over the wall — as if spring had simply moved next door. A light, witty touch on the passing of spring.

poems.s: day cottage window person candle
z: 蓬门未识绮罗香，拟托良媒益自伤。
谁爱风流高格调，共怜时世俭梳妆。
敢将十指夸针巧，不把双眉斗画长。
苦恨年年压金线，为他人作嫁衣裳。
e: Born behind a wicker gate, I've never known the scent of silk;
I'd seek a matchmaker — but that would only hurt me more.
Who loves a noble manner and a lofty, gentle style?
They all prefer the cheap and showy fashions everyone adores.
I dare to boast my fingers have a needle's matchless art;
I won't compete in painting eyebrows long, to steal a heart.
Year after year I bitterly press gold thread — and it's to make
The wedding dresses other girls will wear, for others' sake.
poems.n: A poor, skilled, virtuous girl whom no one marries, while she sews bridal gowns for others — an allegory of the talented scholar without connections, whose work serves other men's advancement. 为他人作嫁衣裳, "making wedding clothes for others", is now a common idiom.

poems.te: Visiting the Golden Gate (The Wind Springs Up)
poems.s: spring wind lake flowers birds person
z: 风乍起，吹皱一池春水。
闲引鸳鸯香径里，手挼红杏蕊。
斗鸭阑干独倚，碧玉搔头斜坠。
终日望君君不至，举头闻鹊喜。
e: The wind springs up —
And ruffles a whole pond of spring.
Idly she lures the mandarin ducks along the fragrant way,
Crushing red apricot buds between her fingers as they cling.
Alone she leans on the rail where ducks once fought;
Her jade hairpin slips aslant.
All day she waits for him, and he does not come —
She looks up, and hears the magpies' joyful chant.
poems.n: The opening — the wind suddenly rising and ruffling a pond of spring water — is a famous image of a heart stirred by nothing in particular. The ruler Li Jing teased Feng Yansi: "A wind ruffling a pond — what has that to do with you?" Magpies were believed to announce good news or an arriving guest, so the poem ends on a flicker of hope.

poems.t: 鹊踏枝（谁道闲情抛掷久）
poems.te: The Magpie Treads the Branch (Who Says I Cast It Off)
poems.s: dusk spring crescent willow bridge person wind
z: 谁道闲情抛掷久？每到春来，惆怅还依旧。
日日花前常病酒，不辞镜里朱颜瘦。
河畔青芜堤上柳，为问新愁，何事年年有？
独立小桥风满袖，平林新月人归后。
e: Who says I'd long since thrown these idle feelings away?
Each time the spring returns,
The old melancholy burns.
Every day, among the flowers, I drink until I'm ill,
And never mind how in my mirror my young face grows thin.
The green weeds by the river, the willows on the dyke —
I ask: why does this new sorrow
Come back each year again?
Alone upon the little bridge, the wind fills up my sleeves;
Over the level woods, the new moon — when everyone's gone in.
poems.n: Melancholy without a cause, renewed every spring like the grass — the essence of the early *ci*. The closing picture — a lone figure on a small bridge, sleeves full of wind, a new moon over the woods after everyone has gone home — is one of the most beautiful endings in the genre.

poems.t: 摊破浣溪沙（菡萏香销翠叶残）
poems.te: Washing Silk in the Stream, Extended (The Lotus Scent Is Gone)
poems.s: autumn lotus lake tower rain wind
z: 菡萏香销翠叶残，西风愁起绿波间。
还与韶光共憔悴，不堪看。
细雨梦回鸡塞远，小楼吹彻玉笙寒。
多少泪珠何限恨，倚阑干。
e: The lotus' scent is gone; its green leaves fade;
The west wind stirs up sorrow on the green waves' face.
She withers with the season's lovely light —
Too sad a sight to face.
In fine rain, waking from a dream — the frontier's far away;
In the small tower, she has played the jade pipes through, so cold.
How many tears, how endless her regret —
Leaning on the rail, alone, as of old.
poems.n: By Li Jing, Li Yu's father and the second ruler of the Southern Tang. Wang Guowei admired the first two lines above all: the withered lotus in the west wind evokes "the sorrow of all beautiful things fading". In the second stanza a dream of the far frontier (Jisai), where her husband is, is broken by the rain, and she plays the reed-organ through the night until its tones — and she — grow cold.

poems.t: 虞美人（春花秋月何时了）
poems.te: The Beautiful Lady Yu (Spring Flowers, Autumn Moons)
poems.s: night spring moon tower palace river
z: 春花秋月何时了？往事知多少。
小楼昨夜又东风，故国不堪回首月明中。
雕栏玉砌应犹在，只是朱颜改。
问君能有几多愁？恰似一江春水向东流。
e: Spring flowers, autumn moons — when will they ever end?
How many past things haunt my memory!
Last night the east wind blew again around my little tower;
In the bright moon, my lost land — I can't bear to turn and see.
The carved rails and the marble steps must still be there,
But the rosy faces have all grown old.
You ask how much sorrow one man can bear? —
As much as a river in spring flood, flowing east, untold.
poems.n: Li Yu's last poem. A prisoner of the Song in Kaifeng, he had this lyric sung on his birthday, the Seventh Night of 978; when the Song emperor heard of its longing for the lost kingdom, he had him poisoned that same night. Sorrow as a river in spring flood, flowing endlessly east, is one of the most famous images in Chinese. *Yu Meiren* ("Beautiful Lady Yu") is the name of the tune.

poems.te: Joy at Meeting (Wordless, I Climb the West Tower)
poems.s: night autumn crescent tower palace
z: 无言独上西楼，月如钩。
寂寞梧桐深院锁清秋。
剪不断，理还乱，是离愁。
别是一般滋味在心头。
e: Without a word, alone, I climb the western tower;
The moon is like a hook.
Lonely wutong trees — the deep courtyard locks in autumn's hour.
Cut it — it won't break;
Untangle it — it's tangled more:
This is the grief of parting —
A taste the heart has never known before.
poems.n: Written in captivity. Grief as a thread that cannot be cut or unravelled — 剪不断，理还乱 — is quoted for every hopelessly tangled feeling. The last line, refusing even to name the taste, is the most famous of all.

poems.te: Joy at Meeting (The Woods Have Lost Their Red)
poems.s: spring rain wind petals palace
z: 林花谢了春红，太匆匆。
无奈朝来寒雨晚来风。
胭脂泪，相留醉，几时重？
自是人生长恨水长东。
e: The flowers in the woods have lost their red of spring —
All too soon!
What can they do, with cold rain every dawn and wind each night?
Rouge-stained tears
Bid me stay and drink —
When again?
Life is forever sorrow, as water forever flows east, out of sight.
poems.n: Fallen blossoms battered by rain and wind are Li Yu's lost kingdom and his own life. The "rouge tears" are rain-wet petals — and the tears of a woman at parting. The last line joins two "forevers": endless regret (长恨) and water forever flowing east (长东).

poems.te: Waves Washing Sand (Beyond the Blind, the Rain)
poems.s: night spring rain window palace petals
z: 帘外雨潺潺，春意阑珊。
罗衾不耐五更寒。
梦里不知身是客，一晌贪欢。
独自莫凭栏，无限江山。
别时容易见时难。
流水落花春去也，天上人间。
e: Beyond the blind, the rain is pattering;
Spring is fading fast.
My silken quilt can't keep out the cold before the dawn.
Dreaming, I forgot I was a captive guest,
And snatched a moment's joy — now past.
Alone, I must not lean upon the rail
And see the boundless land that once was mine.
Parting was easy; meeting again is hard.
The water flows, the flowers fall, the spring is gone:
Heaven above, and the world of men below.
poems.n: Written shortly before Li Yu's death. The cruellest line is the fourth: in his dream he forgot he was a prisoner and enjoyed a moment of his old life — then woke to the cold. He must not lean on the railing alone, because the view of rivers and mountains reminds him of everything he lost.

poems.te: Breaking Through the Ranks (Forty Years of House and State)
poems.s: dusk palace tower clouds mist flag
z: 四十年来家国，三千里地山河。
凤阁龙楼连霄汉，玉树琼枝作烟萝。几曾识干戈？
一旦归为臣虏，沈腰潘鬓消磨。
最是仓皇辞庙日，教坊犹奏别离歌。垂泪对宫娥。
e: Forty years my house and kingdom stood;
Three thousand li of mountains, rivers, lands.
Phoenix halls and dragon towers rose to touch the sky;
Jade trees and gem-like boughs were twined like misty vines.
When did I ever know of shields and spears?
One day I was a captive, bowing to the throne —
My waist grew thin, my temples grey, worn down with the years.
Worst of all, the day I left the ancestral shrine in haste,
The court musicians still were playing songs of parting —
In tears I faced my palace maids, alone.
poems.n: Li Yu looks back on the Southern Tang's forty years and its rich lands, lost when he surrendered to the Song in 975. Shen Yue grew thin and Pan Yue grey with grief — classic images of suffering. Later moralists complained that at the moment of losing his kingdom he wept to his palace maids rather than to his ancestors or people; the poem's honesty is part of its power.

poems.s: spring petals plum geese palace person
z: 别来春半，触目柔肠断。
砌下落梅如雪乱，拂了一身还满。
雁来音信无凭，路遥归梦难成。
离恨恰如春草，更行更远还生。
e: Since we parted, half of spring is gone;
All I see breaks my heart in two.
Fallen plum blossoms swirl like snow below the steps;
I brush them off — again I'm covered through.
The geese come back, but bring no word from you;
The road's too long for dreams to bring me home.
The sorrow of parting is just like spring grass:
The farther you go, the thicker it has grown.
poems.n: Probably written when Li Yu's brother was held as a hostage at the Song court. The last couplet — parting's grief like spring grass, growing thicker the farther one travels — is one of the most admired images in the *ci*.

poems.te: Gazing South of the River (How Much Regret)
poems.s: night spring moon palace flowers horse
z: 多少恨，昨夜梦魂中。
还似旧时游上苑，车如流水马如龙。
花月正春风。
e: How much regret —
In last night's dream I was back again,
Roaming the royal park as in the days of old:
Carriages like flowing water, horses like dragons' train,
Flowers and moonlight in the breeze of spring, as then.
poems.n: A dream of the old splendour of his capital: a stream of carriages, dragon-like horses, flowers and moonlight in the spring breeze. 车如流水马如龙 became the idiom for bustling traffic. The "regret" is that he woke.

poems.s: autumn maple mountains geese chrysanthemum window
z: 一重山，两重山。
山远天高烟水寒，相思枫叶丹。
菊花开，菊花残。
塞雁高飞人未还，一帘风月闲。
e: One range of hills, then two;
Far hills, high sky, cold misty water too;
My longing burns as red as maple leaves.
Chrysanthemums bloom, chrysanthemums die;
The wild geese fly back high, but he has not come by;
The wind and moon stay idle at the blind as she grieves.
poems.n: A woman's longing through the seasons: the maples redden, the chrysanthemums bloom and fade, the geese return — but her man does not. The attribution to Li Yu is traditional.

poems.s: spring rain willow bridge boat person
z: 古木阴中系短篷，杖藜扶我过桥东。
沾衣欲湿杏花雨，吹面不寒杨柳风。
e: I tie my little boat up in the old trees' shade,
And with my goosefoot staff I cross the bridge to the east.
The apricot-blossom rain would almost wet my clothes;
The willow breeze blows on my face, not cold in the least.
poems.n: By a Buddhist monk of the Southern Song. The last couplet — "apricot-blossom rain" that almost but not quite wets you, a "willow wind" that touches your face without chill — is the most delicate description of early spring in Chinese; Zhu Xi praised it highly.

poems.s: winter snow plum person
z: 梅雪争春未肯降，骚人阁笔费评章。
梅须逊雪三分白，雪却输梅一段香。
e: The plum and snow contend for spring, and neither will give way;
The poet sets his brush aside — he can't decide who's won.
The plum must yield the snow some measure of its white;
The snow must yield the plum its scent — and so the contest's done.
poems.n: A playful debate between two winter beauties. The verdict — snow is whiter, plum is sweeter — became a saying about everyone having their own strengths.

poems.s: dusk winter snow plum cottage
z: 有梅无雪不精神，有雪无诗俗了人。
日暮诗成天又雪，与梅并作十分春。
e: Plum blossom without snow has no true spirit;
Snow without a poem makes a person crude and dull.
At dusk the poem's finished — and it's snowing once again:
With plum and snow together, spring is full.
poems.n: The companion poem: plum, snow and poetry together make a perfect spring — the three "pure" things of a scholar's winter.

poems.te: Visiting a Garden, Finding No One Home
poems.s: spring peach cottage flowers
z: 应怜屐齿印苍苔，小扣柴扉久不开。
春色满园关不住，一枝红杏出墙来。
e: Perhaps he fears my wooden clogs would mark his mossy ground;
I tap upon his wicker gate — no answer, none at all.
But a garden full of spring cannot be locked inside:
A spray of red apricot blossom reaches out over the wall.
poems.n: Visiting a friend's garden and finding no one home. The gate stays shut — but spring cannot be locked in. 春色满园关不住，一枝红杏出墙来 is quoted for anything vital and beautiful that cannot be suppressed (and, mischievously, of wandering wives).

poems.te: Written at Night, on What I Saw
poems.s: night autumn wind leaves cottage lantern river
z: 萧萧梧叶送寒声，江上秋风动客情。
知有儿童挑促织，夜深篱落一灯明。
e: The rustling wutong leaves send out a chilly sound;
The autumn wind upon the river stirs a traveller's heart.
I know there must be children out there hunting crickets —
Late at night, a single lantern glows beside the hedge, apart.
poems.n: A homesick traveller on an autumn night sees a lamp by a hedge and knows at once that children are out catching crickets for cricket fights — as he once did at home. The lamp is a window into his own childhood.

poems.s: dusk summer sun lake hills grass person
z: 草满池塘水满陂，山衔落日浸寒漪。
牧童归去横牛背，短笛无腔信口吹。
e: Grass fills the pond, and water fills the dyke to the brim;
The hills hold the setting sun in their teeth, soaked in cold ripples, dim.
The herd-boy rides home, sitting crosswise on the ox's back,
Blowing his short flute — no tune at all, just a whim.
poems.n: A village evening: the hills "bite" (衔) the setting sun, its reflection steeping in the pond, and a herd-boy rides home on his ox, tootling a tuneless flute. A favourite scene of Chinese painting — and of childhood.

poems.te: Little Plum Tree in the Mountain Garden (I)
poems.s: dusk winter moon plum lake crane
z: 众芳摇落独暄妍，占尽风情向小园。
疏影横斜水清浅，暗香浮动月黄昏。
霜禽欲下先偷眼，粉蝶如知合断魂。
幸有微吟可相狎，不须檀板共金尊。
e: When all the flowers have fallen, it alone is fresh and fair,
And claims the charm of my small garden as its own.
Its sparse shadows lie aslant on water clear and shallow;
Its hidden fragrance drifts in the dusk where the moon has shone.
The frost-white birds, about to land, first steal a glance;
The powdered butterflies, if they knew, would faint, every one.
Thank heaven for quiet chanting, to keep it company —
No need for singers' clappers or gold wine cups, none.
poems.n: Lin Bu, the hermit of West Lake, "took plum blossom for his wife and cranes for his children". 疏影横斜水清浅，暗香浮动月黄昏 — "sparse shadows slanting over clear, shallow water; a hidden fragrance floating in the moonlit dusk" — became the definitive description of plum blossom; Jiang Kui named two of his finest lyrics "Hidden Fragrance" and "Sparse Shadows".

poems.s: dusk autumn rain willow river boat pavilion two crescent
z: 寒蝉凄切，对长亭晚，骤雨初歇。
都门帐饮无绪，留恋处、兰舟催发。
执手相看泪眼，竟无语凝噎。
念去去、千里烟波，暮霭沉沉楚天阔。
多情自古伤离别，更那堪、冷落清秋节！
今宵酒醒何处？杨柳岸、晓风残月。
此去经年，应是良辰、好景虚设。
便纵有、千种风情，更与何人说？
e: The autumn cicadas shrill their sad refrain;
Facing the long pavilion at evening,
The sudden rain has just let up again.
Outside the gate we drink in the tent, with no heart;
Just as we linger, loath to leave,
The orchid boat calls me to depart.
Hand in hand, we gaze at each other's tear-filled eyes,
And choke, with not a word to say.
I think of the long road ahead —
A thousand li of misty waves,
The evening haze hangs heavy on the wide Chu sky, so grey.
Since ancient times the tender-hearted grieve at parting —
And how much worse in autumn's chill, so desolate and clear!
Tonight, when I wake from the wine, where will I be?
A willow-lined bank,
The dawn wind, and a waning moon, I fear.
Once gone, for years to come,
The fairest times and loveliest views will be for nothing here.
Even if I had a thousand kinds of tender feelings,
Who would there be to hear?
poems.n: The most famous lyric of parting in the Song, by Liu Yong, the poet of the pleasure quarters, leaving the capital Kaifeng and a beloved courtesan. 今宵酒醒何处？杨柳岸，晓风残月 — "where will I wake tonight? A willow bank, the dawn wind, a waning moon" — became the very image of the gentle "graceful" (婉约) school. When Su Shi asked how his own lyrics compared, he was told Liu Yong's should be sung by a girl of seventeen with ivory clappers, and his by a big man from the west with an iron one.

poems.t: 蝶恋花（伫倚危楼风细细）
poems.te: Butterflies Love Flowers (Leaning Long on the High Tower)
poems.s: dusk spring tower grass mist sun person
z: 伫倚危楼风细细，望极春愁，黯黯生天际。
草色烟光残照里，无言谁会凭阑意。
拟把疏狂图一醉，对酒当歌，强乐还无味。
衣带渐宽终不悔，为伊消得人憔悴。
e: I stand and lean on the high tower in a gentle breeze;
I gaze afar — and spring's grief
Darkly rises where the earth and heaven convene.
The grass, the misty light, in the last of the sun —
Who knows why I lean here, silent, at the rail, unseen?
I thought I'd let myself go wild, and drown it all in wine;
With wine in hand I sing,
But forced joy has no taste of its own.
My belt grows looser, yet I'll never regret —
For her, I'll waste away, worn to skin and bone.
poems.n: 衣带渐宽终不悔，为伊消得人憔悴 — "my belt grows ever looser, but I'll never regret it; for her I waste away" — Wang Guowei made this the second of his "three stages" of every great achievement: wholehearted, sleepless devotion.

poems.te: Gazing at the Tide (The Finest Place in the South-East)
poems.s: day lake river bridge willow lotus boat mountains
z: 东南形胜，三吴都会，钱塘自古繁华。
烟柳画桥，风帘翠幕，参差十万人家。
云树绕堤沙。
怒涛卷霜雪，天堑无涯。
市列珠玑，户盈罗绮，竞豪奢。
重湖叠巘清嘉。
有三秋桂子，十里荷花。
羌管弄晴，菱歌泛夜，嬉嬉钓叟莲娃。
千骑拥高牙。
乘醉听箫鼓，吟赏烟霞。
异日图将好景，归去凤池夸。
e: The finest place in all the south-east,
The great city of the three Wu lands,
Qiantang has flourished since of old.
Misty willows, painted bridges,
Blinds in the breeze and kingfisher screens,
A hundred thousand homes, in rows untold.
Cloud-high trees line the sandy dyke;
The raging tide rolls up its frost and snow —
A moat of heaven, without end.
Its markets glitter with pearls and jade;
Its houses overflow with silks,
As they vie to outspend.
Lakes upon lakes and peaks on peaks, so clear and fine;
There are cassia blossoms in the autumn,
And lotus for ten li.
Qiang flutes play in the sunshine;
Water-chestnut songs float through the night;
Old fishermen and lotus girls laugh with glee.
A thousand horsemen escort the governor's flag;
Tipsy, he listens to flutes and drums,
And sings of the mist and rosy clouds he sees.
Some day he'll paint this lovely scene,
And take it back to court, to boast of these.
poems.n: Hangzhou (Qiantang) in its glory, written by Liu Yong for the city's governor. A legend says that when the Jin ruler Wanyan Liang read of Hangzhou's "cassia in autumn and ten li of lotus", he resolved to conquer the south — a poem so beautiful it started a war. (He failed.)

poems.t: 八声甘州（对潇潇暮雨洒江天）
poems.te: Eight Beats of Ganzhou (Facing the Evening Rain)
poems.s: dusk autumn rain river tower boat sun
z: 对潇潇、暮雨洒江天，一番洗清秋。
渐霜风凄紧，关河冷落，残照当楼。
是处红衰翠减，苒苒物华休。
惟有长江水，无语东流。
不忍登高临远，望故乡渺邈，归思难收。
叹年来踪迹，何事苦淹留？
想佳人、妆楼颙望，误几回、天际识归舟。
争知我、倚阑干处，正恁凝愁！
e: Facing the soughing evening rain that sweeps the river and the sky,
Washing autumn clean once more —
Little by little the frosty wind grows harsh and cold,
The passes and the rivers bleak,
The sunset's last glow on the tower's floor.
Everywhere the reds are fading and the greens grow thin;
Slowly, all the splendour of the world is done.
Only the water of the Long River
Flows silently east, on and on.
I cannot bear to climb up high and gaze afar,
Toward my home, so far beyond my sight;
My longing to go home is hard to hold.
I sigh at all my wandering these years —
Why do I linger here, in such a plight?
I picture my love, gazing from her dressing tower,
How many times mistaking, at the sky's edge, some boat for mine;
How could she know that I, here leaning on the rail,
Am frozen in such sorrow, too, tonight?
poems.n: Su Shi, no admirer of Liu Yong's sentimental songs, said of the lines 渐霜风凄紧，关河冷落，残照当楼 that they were "no less than the heights of the Tang". The second stanza imagines his beloved mistaking every boat on the horizon for his — an echo of Wen Tingyun's "a thousand sails go by, and none is his".

poems.s: dusk autumn sun peaks fort geese smoke frost
z: 塞下秋来风景异，衡阳雁去无留意。
四面边声连角起，千嶂里，长烟落日孤城闭。
浊酒一杯家万里，燕然未勒归无计。
羌管悠悠霜满地，人不寐，将军白发征夫泪。
e: When autumn comes to the frontier, the land looks strange;
The geese fly off to Hengyang, with no wish to remain.
On every side the frontier's sounds rise with the bugles' call;
Among a thousand peaks,
Long smoke, the setting sun, a lonely fort's gates shut again.
A cup of cloudy wine, and home ten thousand li away;
No victory carved on Mount Yanran — so no way home.
The Qiang flutes wail and wail; frost covers all the ground;
No one sleeps:
The general's hair is white; the soldiers weep alone.
poems.n: Fan Zhongyan commanded the north-western frontier against the Western Xia from 1040. Unlike most frontier poems, written by poets who imagined war, this is a general's own lyric — bleak and honest. Geese fly south as far as Hengyang, where they were said to turn back; on Mount Yanran a Han general carved a record of victory, which the Song has not achieved. The last line gives tears to general and soldier alike.

poems.s: dusk autumn sun leaves river hills mist tower
z: 碧云天，黄叶地，秋色连波，波上寒烟翠。
山映斜阳天接水，芳草无情，更在斜阳外。
黯乡魂，追旅思，夜夜除非，好梦留人睡。
明月楼高休独倚，酒入愁肠，化作相思泪。
e: Blue clouds above, yellow leaves below;
The autumn colours meet the waves,
And on the waves, cold mist of jade-green glow.
Hills catch the setting sun; the sky meets the water;
The heartless fragrant grass
Stretches on beyond the sunset's glow.
My homesick soul is dark;
My traveller's thoughts pursue —
Night after night, unless
Sweet dreams can keep me sleeping through.
In bright moonlight, don't lean on the high tower alone:
The wine goes down into a grieving heart,
And turns to tears of longing, too.
poems.n: A rare tender lyric by a stern statesman. 碧云天，黄叶地 — "blue clouds in the sky, yellow leaves on the ground" — was borrowed by Wang Shifu for *The Romance of the Western Chamber*. The fragrant grass stretching beyond the sunset is the road home, endlessly far; and the famous last line: wine poured into a sad heart turns to tears of longing.

poems.s: day river wind fisher boat person
z: 江上往来人，但爱鲈鱼美。
君看一叶舟，出没风波里。
e: The people strolling by the river, to and fro,
Love only the taste of perch — how sweet!
But look at that leaf of a boat out there,
Tossed in and out of sight where the wind and waves meet.
poems.n: The diners on the bank enjoy the perch; few think of the fisherman risking his life in the storm to catch it. A tiny poem of social conscience by a statesman famous for putting the people first.

poems.t: 天仙子（水调数声持酒听）
poems.te: The Celestial Immortal (Wine in Hand, I Hear the Water Song)
poems.s: night spring moon clouds flowers lake birds window
z: 水调数声持酒听，午醉醒来愁未醒。
送春春去几时回？临晚镜，伤流景，往事后期空记省。
沙上并禽池上暝，云破月来花弄影。
重重帘幕密遮灯，风不定，人初静，明日落红应满径。
e: Wine in hand, I listen to a few notes of the "Water Song";
I wake at noon from drink, but my sadness lingers on.
I see the spring off — when will spring come back again?
Facing the evening mirror,
Grieving the years that flow,
I recall the past, and future vows, in vain.
Birds pair on the sand; dusk settles on the pond;
The clouds part, the moon comes out, the flowers play with their shades.
Layer on layer of curtains screen the lamp;
The wind won't settle;
The house is quiet now;
Tomorrow, fallen petals will strew every path, I'm afraid.
poems.n: 云破月来花弄影 — "the clouds part, the moon comes out, and the flowers play with their shadows" — made Zhang Xian famous; with two other lines about shadows it earned him the nickname "Zhang of the Three Shadows". The verb 弄, "play with", brings the whole moonlit garden to life.

poems.t: 浣溪沙（一曲新词酒一杯）
poems.te: Washing Silk in the Stream (A New Song, a Cup of Wine)
poems.s: dusk spring sun swallows petals pavilion person
z: 一曲新词酒一杯，去年天气旧亭台。夕阳西下几时回？
无可奈何花落去，似曾相识燕归来。小园香径独徘徊。
e: A new song, and a cup of wine;
The weather's just like last year's, the same old pavilion, too.
The sun sets in the west — when will it come back in time?
Nothing can be done: the flowers fall away;
As if we'd met before, the swallows come back home.
Along the fragrant garden path, alone I pace and roam.
poems.n: The most famous couplet of the Northern Song: 无可奈何花落去，似曾相识燕归来 — "nothing can be done, the flowers fall; as if old friends, the swallows return." Loss and return, the same and not the same: time's cycle in two lines. Yan Shu is said to have had the second line for years before he found the first.

poems.t: 蝶恋花（槛菊愁烟兰泣露）
poems.te: Butterflies Love Flowers (Chrysanthemums Grieve in Mist)
poems.s: night autumn moon chrysanthemum tower window swallows
z: 槛菊愁烟兰泣露，罗幕轻寒，燕子双飞去。
明月不谙离恨苦，斜光到晓穿朱户。
昨夜西风凋碧树，独上高楼，望尽天涯路。
欲寄彩笺兼尺素，山长水阔知何处？
e: By the railing, chrysanthemums grieve in mist; the orchids weep with dew;
The silk curtains feel a gentle chill;
The swallows fly off, two by two.
The bright moon doesn't know the pain of being apart —
Till dawn its slanting light shines through the red door, through and through.
Last night the west wind stripped the green trees bare;
Alone I climbed the high tower,
And gazed along the road to the world's end — no one there.
I'd send a coloured note, a letter on fine silk —
But mountains are long, the waters wide: who knows where?
poems.n: 昨夜西风凋碧树，独上高楼，望尽天涯路 — Wang Guowei made this the first of his "three stages" of every great achievement: climbing alone, seeing far, setting the goal. In the poem itself, it is a woman gazing down an endless road for someone who does not come.

poems.te: Breaking Through the Ranks (When the Swallows Come)
poems.s: spring willow oriole swallows lake person two
z: 燕子来时新社，梨花落后清明。
池上碧苔三四点，叶底黄鹂一两声，日长飞絮轻。
巧笑东邻女伴，采桑径里逢迎。
疑怪昨宵春梦好，元是今朝斗草赢，笑从双脸生。
e: The swallows come at the spring festival;
The pear blossoms fall at Qingming.
On the pond, three or four flecks of green moss;
Under the leaves, an oriole's one or two notes ring;
The days are long, and willow-down floats light.
The giggling girl next door, my friend,
Meets me on the path to pick mulberry leaves.
"I wondered why I had such a lovely dream last night —
It's because today I won at fighting grass!"
And smiles light up both her cheeks.
poems.n: A sunny spring scene in the voice of young girls, unusual for the stately Yan Shu. "Fighting grass" (斗草) was a game in which girls competed to gather the most kinds of plants, or hooked grass stems together and pulled. The good dream must have been an omen.

poems.t: 玉楼春（东城渐觉风光好）
poems.te: Spring in the Jade Tower (East of the City)
poems.s: dawn spring lake boat willow flowers sun
z: 东城渐觉风光好，縠皱波纹迎客棹。
绿杨烟外晓寒轻，红杏枝头春意闹。
浮生长恨欢娱少，肯爱千金轻一笑？
为君持酒劝斜阳，且向花间留晚照。
e: East of the city, I feel the scenery grow fair;
The rippling waves, like crepe, welcome the boats along.
Beyond the misty willows, the morning chill is light;
On the red apricot boughs, spring breaks into noisy song.
In this brief life, I always grieve that joys are few —
Would I prize a thousand gold above one smile?
For you, I'll raise my cup and toast the setting sun,
And ask it to linger in the flowers a while.
poems.n: 红杏枝头春意闹 — "on the red apricot boughs, spring is in uproar" — one verb, 闹 ("noisy, boisterous"), makes spring audible; Wang Guowei said "with the word 闹, the whole scene comes alive". It earned Song Qi the nickname "the Red Apricot Minister".

poems.s: night moon willow lantern person
z: 去年元夜时，花市灯如昼。
月上柳梢头，人约黄昏后。
今年元夜时，月与灯依旧。
不见去年人，泪湿春衫袖。
e: Last year, on Lantern Night,
The flower market's lamps shone bright as day.
The moon climbed to the willow tips;
We met when dusk was turning grey.
This year, on Lantern Night,
The moon and lanterns shine as then.
But I can't find last year's love —
Tears wet my spring sleeves once again.
poems.n: The Lantern Festival was the one night when young people could meet freely in the crowds. 月上柳梢头，人约黄昏后 — "the moon over the willow tips; a tryst after dusk" — is the most romantic couplet in Chinese. The lyric is traditionally given to Ouyang Xiu, though some editions credit the woman poet Zhu Shuzhen.

poems.t: 蝶恋花（庭院深深深几许）
poems.te: Butterflies Love Flowers (Deep, Deep the Courtyard)
poems.s: dusk spring rain wind willow petals tower
z: 庭院深深深几许？杨柳堆烟，帘幕无重数。
玉勒雕鞍游冶处，楼高不见章台路。
雨横风狂三月暮，门掩黄昏，无计留春住。
泪眼问花花不语，乱红飞过秋千去。
e: Deep, deep the courtyard — how deep can it be?
Willows heaped with mist,
And curtains past all counting, endlessly.
With jade bridle and carved saddle, he roams the pleasure lanes;
The tower's high — the road to Zhangtai is lost to me.
Rain lashing, wind raging, the third month's end;
I close the gate at dusk —
There's no way I can make the spring stay.
With tearful eyes I ask the flowers — the flowers do not speak;
The scattered red flies past the swing, and away.
poems.n: A wife shut deep in a great house while her husband rides off to the pleasure quarters (Zhangtai Lane). Li Qingzhao loved the opening line so much that she began several lyrics with it. The last couplet — the flowers, asked, say nothing, and fly away past the swing where she once played — is one of the most admired in the *ci*.

poems.te: Waves Washing Sand (I Raise My Cup to the East Wind)
poems.s: spring flowers willow wall two cup
z: 把酒祝东风，且共从容。
垂杨紫陌洛城东。总是当时携手处，游遍芳丛。
聚散苦匆匆，此恨无穷。
今年花胜去年红。可惜明年花更好，知与谁同？
e: I raise my cup and pray the east wind:
Linger with us, take your ease.
The willows hang along Luoyang's purple lanes —
Where we walked hand in hand in days like these,
Through all the flowers, under the trees.
Meetings and partings come too fast;
This sorrow has no end.
This year the flowers are redder than last year's;
Next year they'll be lovelier still, my friend —
But who will see them with me then?
poems.n: Luoyang, 1032, at a reunion with his friend Mei Yaochen. The flowers get better every year — but the friends who share them scatter. The last line makes the beauty of next spring a cause of sorrow.

poems.s: spring mountains flowers birds pine
z: 百啭千声随意移，山花红紫树高低。
始知锁向金笼听，不及林间自在啼。
e: A hundred trills, a thousand notes, it flits where it may please,
Among the red and purple mountain blossoms, high and low.
Now I know a bird in a golden cage, for all its ease,
Can never sing as sweetly as one free in the woods below.
poems.n: Written while Ouyang Xiu was demoted to Chuzhou. A thrush in a golden cage — like an official at court — sings less sweetly than one free in the forest: a gentle hymn to freedom, and to his exile.

poems.te: Treading the Grass (At the Inn, the Plum Is Fading)
poems.s: spring willow plum bridge rider hills tower
z: 候馆梅残，溪桥柳细，草薰风暖摇征辔。
离愁渐远渐无穷，迢迢不断如春水。
寸寸柔肠，盈盈粉泪，楼高莫近危阑倚。
平芜尽处是春山，行人更在春山外。
e: At the inn, the plum is fading;
By the stream bridge, the willows slight;
Sweet grass, warm wind — I shake the reins and ride.
The sorrow of parting grows endless as I go,
On and on, unbroken, like a spring river's tide.
Inch by inch, her tender heart;
Brimming, her rouged tears flow.
The tower is high — don't lean against the rail.
Where the level meadows end, there are the spring hills —
And the traveller is further still, beyond them, far away.
poems.n: The first stanza is the traveller riding away, his sorrow growing with every step like a spring river; the second is the woman left behind in her tower. In the famous last couplet she gazes to the edge of the plain, to the spring hills — and he is beyond even them.

poems.t: 采桑子（群芳过后西湖好）
poems.te: Picking Mulberries (When the Flowers Have Passed, West Lake Is Fair)
poems.s: spring rain lake willow swallows petals pavilion
z: 群芳过后西湖好，狼籍残红。飞絮濛濛，垂柳阑干尽日风。
笙歌散尽游人去，始觉春空。垂下帘栊，双燕归来细雨中。
e: When all the flowers have passed, West Lake is lovely still:
The fallen red lies strewn,
The willow-down drifts free,
The willows by the railings sway all day in the breeze.
The songs and pipes are done; the crowds have gone away;
And now I feel how empty spring can be.
I let the curtain down —
And through the fine rain, two swallows come home to me.
poems.n: Ouyang Xiu retired in 1071 to the West Lake of Yingzhou (Fuyang, Anhui — not the lake at Hangzhou) and wrote ten lyrics about it to this tune. Here he finds beauty after the crowds and flowers have gone: quiet, emptiness, and a pair of swallows in the rain.

poems.t: 玉楼春（尊前拟把归期说）
poems.te: Spring in the Jade Tower (Over the Wine, I Meant to Say)
poems.s: spring flowers wall two cup
z: 尊前拟把归期说，未语春容先惨咽。
人生自是有情痴，此恨不关风与月。
离歌且莫翻新阕，一曲能教肠寸结。
直须看尽洛城花，始共春风容易别。
e: Over the wine I meant to tell her when I would return;
Before I'd said a word, her spring-fair face dissolved in tears.
We humans are born fools for love, I've come to learn —
This grief is none of the wind's or moon's affairs.
Don't play the parting song again in a new key —
One tune's enough to tie the heart in knots, inch by inch.
First let us see all Luoyang's flowers, every tree —
Then from the spring wind we can part without a flinch.
poems.n: Leaving Luoyang in 1034. 人生自是有情痴，此恨不关风与月 — "people are simply born fools for love; this grief has nothing to do with wind or moon" — is often quoted: our sorrows come from our own hearts, not the scenery. The last couplet is typical Ouyang Xiu bravado: let us enjoy everything first, and parting will be easy.

poems.s: spring willow wind sun
z: 乱条犹未变初黄，倚得东风势便狂。
解把飞花蒙日月，不知天地有清霜。
e: Its tangled shoots are still the yellow of first spring,
But leaning on the east wind, they grow wild with pride.
They know how to blot out sun and moon with flying down —
