Not knowing heaven and earth have frost on every side.
poems.n: A satire disguised as a nature poem: the newly sprouted willow swaggers in the spring wind and blots out the sky with its catkins — like an upstart official relying on a powerful patron. But autumn frost will come.

poems.s: night spring moon river boat hills
z: 京口瓜洲一水间，钟山只隔数重山。
春风又绿江南岸，明月何时照我还？
e: Jingkou and Guazhou — only a river runs between;
Bell Mountain lies beyond just a few hills more.
Once again the spring wind turns the south bank green —
Bright moon, when will you light me home to my own door?
poems.n: Wang Anshi, mooring at Guazhou on the Yangtze in 1075 on his way back to office as chief minister, looks toward his retirement home at Bell Mountain (Zhongshan) in Nanjing. The verb 绿, "to green", is the most famous word choice in Chinese poetry: his draft is said to have tried "arrives", "passes", "enters", "fills" and a dozen others before he settled on "greens".

poems.s: dawn winter sun cottage smoke wall
z: 爆竹声中一岁除，春风送暖入屠苏。
千门万户曈曈日，总把新桃换旧符。
e: Amid the firecrackers, the old year's chased away;
The spring wind brings its warmth into the New Year wine.
On a thousand gates, ten thousand homes, the sun shines on the day
They take the old peach charms down, and put up new ones, fine.
poems.n: Firecrackers drove away evil spirits; *tusu* wine was drunk for health; peach-wood charms bearing door gods were hung on gates — the ancestors of today's red New Year couplets. Written in 1069 as Wang Anshi launched his great reforms, replacing old charms with new became a symbol of renewal.

poems.s: winter plum snow cottage
z: 墙角数枝梅，凌寒独自开。
遥知不是雪，为有暗香来。
e: In the corner by the wall, a few plum sprays
Have bloomed alone, defying the bitter cold.
From far away I know it isn't snow —
A hidden fragrance on the air has told.
poems.n: Written in retirement after his reforms had failed. White plum blossom looks like snow — but snow has no scent. Like the plum, the person of integrity stands alone in hard times, and is known by a "hidden fragrance".

poems.s: dawn sun peaks temple clouds
z: 飞来山上千寻塔，闻说鸡鸣见日升。
不畏浮云遮望眼，自缘身在最高层。
e: On Flying Peak there stands a pagoda, a thousand fathoms high;
They say at cockcrow you can see the sun come up from there.
I do not fear the floating clouds that block the eye,
Because I'm standing on the highest stair.
poems.n: Written in 1050 by the young Wang Anshi, full of confidence. "Floating clouds" were the standard image for slanderers who obscure the truth; stand high enough, and you will not be deceived. A favourite poem of vision and ambition.

poems.te: Fragrance of the Cassia Branch: Remembering the Past at Jinling
poems.s: dusk autumn sun river peaks sail flag crane
z: 登临送目，正故国晚秋，天气初肃。
千里澄江似练，翠峰如簇。
归帆去棹残阳里，背西风、酒旗斜矗。
彩舟云淡，星河鹭起，画图难足。
念往昔、繁华竞逐，叹门外楼头，悲恨相续。
千古凭高，对此漫嗟荣辱。
六朝旧事随流水，但寒烟衰草凝绿。
至今商女，时时犹唱，后庭遗曲。
e: I climb up high and send my gaze afar:
It's late autumn in the ancient capital,
The air just turning crisp and clear.
A thousand li of river, bright as a sash of silk;
Green peaks clustered like arrows, far and near.
Homeward sails and parting oars in the setting sun;
Their backs to the west wind, wine flags stand askew.
Painted boats in pale clouds,
Egrets rising from the river of stars —
No painting could capture the view.
I think of times long past, when men vied for splendour, and
"Outside the gate, upon the tower" —
Grief followed grief, without an end.
Through the ages men have climbed to face this view,
And sighed in vain at glory and disgrace again.
The Six Dynasties are gone with the flowing water;
Only cold mist and withered grass still hold their green.
And to this day the singing girls,
Now and then, still sing
The song of the Rear Court, as it's been.
poems.n: Nanjing (Jinling), capital of six fallen southern dynasties. "Outside the gate, upon the tower" recalls the fall of Chen in 589, when a Sui general was already at the gate while the last emperor was upstairs with his favourite; that ruler's song "Flowers of the Rear Courtyard" became the emblem of decadence. Of more than thirty lyrics written on this theme in Wang Anshi's day, his was judged the best.

poems.te: Written on the Wall of Master Huyin (I)
poems.s: summer cottage river fields hills flowers
z: 茅檐长扫净无苔，花木成畦手自栽。
一水护田将绿绕，两山排闼送青来。
e: His thatched eaves are swept so often there's no moss at all;
The flowers and trees are set in beds he planted by hand.
A stream protects his fields, wrapping them round in green;
Two hills push open his door and send in their blue-green band.
poems.n: Written on the wall of his neighbour Yang Dezheng ("Master Huyin") near Bell Mountain. The last couplet personifies the landscape — the stream "guards" the fields like a soldier, the hills "push open the door" (排闼) like eager visitors — with phrases borrowed from the *History of the Han*, yet perfectly natural.

poems.s: night spring petals swallows cottage
z: 三月残花落更开，小檐日日燕飞来。
子规夜半犹啼血，不信东风唤不回。
e: In the third month the last flowers fall, then bloom anew;
Beneath the low eaves, swallows come flying day by day.
At midnight still the cuckoo cries until it bleeds —
It won't believe its calls can't bring the east wind back to stay.
poems.n: The end of spring. The cuckoo's cry, said to be so passionate that it coughed blood, is an image of stubborn devotion — refusing to accept that spring cannot be called back. Wang Ling, who died at twenty-seven, wrote with this fierce idealism.

poems.te: Written by Chance on a Spring Day
poems.s: day spring willow flowers river person clouds
z: 云淡风轻近午天，傍花随柳过前川。
时人不识余心乐，将谓偷闲学少年。
e: Pale clouds, a gentle breeze, and nearly noon;
By flowers, past willows, I stroll across the stream.
People don't know the joy within my heart —
They think I'm idling like a boy, it seems.
poems.n: By Cheng Hao, the great Neo-Confucian philosopher. A spring stroll, and an inner joy that others mistake for frivolity: the scholar's delight in the natural order of things. The first line is one of the most popular descriptions of a perfect spring day.

poems.t: 卜算子·送鲍浩然之浙东
poems.te: Song of Divination: Seeing Bao Haoran Off to Eastern Zhejiang
poems.s: spring river hills boat two
z: 水是眼波横，山是眉峰聚。
欲问行人去那边？眉眼盈盈处。
才始送春归，又送君归去。
若到江南赶上春，千万和春住。
e: The rivers are her eyes, their glances flowing;
The mountains are her eyebrows, knitted fair.
You ask me where the traveller is going? —
To where the eyes and brows are lovely, there.
I've only just seen spring off on its way,
And now I'm seeing you off too.
If you catch up with spring in the south,
Then stay with spring — be sure you do!
poems.n: A witty farewell to a friend going home to eastern Zhejiang. The southern landscape becomes a beautiful woman — rivers her glances, hills her eyebrows — and the friend, going home to his wife, goes "where the brows and eyes are lovely". Spring has just left; if he catches it up in the south, he should stay with it.

poems.te: Prelude to the Water Melody (When Did the Bright Moon Appear)
poems.s: night moon clouds palace pavilion cup person
z: 明月几时有？把酒问青天。
不知天上宫阙，今夕是何年。
我欲乘风归去，又恐琼楼玉宇，高处不胜寒。
起舞弄清影，何似在人间。
转朱阁，低绮户，照无眠。
不应有恨，何事长向别时圆？
人有悲欢离合，月有阴晴圆缺，此事古难全。
但愿人长久，千里共婵娟。
e: How long has the bright moon been there?
Wine cup in hand, I ask the azure sky.
I wonder, in the palaces of heaven,
What year it is tonight, on high.
I'd like to ride the wind and fly back home,
But fear those crystal towers and halls of jade
Would be too cold for me, so high.
I rise and dance with my clear shadow here —
Who'd trade the human world for heaven? Not I!
It rounds the red pavilion,
Stoops through the silken window low,
And shines upon the sleepless.
It should bear us no ill will —
Why is it always full when we're apart? I'd like to know.
Men have their griefs and joys, their partings and reunions;
The moon has dark and bright, it waxes and it wanes —
Nothing's been perfect since long ago.
I only wish that we may both live long,
And, a thousand li apart, share the moon's lovely glow.
poems.n: Written at the Mid-Autumn Festival of 1076 in Mizhou, "drunk all night until dawn, thinking of Ziyou" — his brother Su Zhe, whom he had not seen for seven years. Su Shi dreams of flying up to the palaces of the moon but chooses the human world; then he forgives the moon for being full while families are apart, because nothing in life is ever whole. The closing wish — 但愿人长久，千里共婵娟 — is the Mid-Autumn blessing of every Chinese family, and the lyric, set to music in 1983, is known to everyone.

poems.te: The Charms of Niannu: Remembering the Past at Red Cliff
poems.s: day river mountains peaks clouds boat
z: 大江东去，浪淘尽，千古风流人物。
故垒西边，人道是，三国周郎赤壁。
乱石穿空，惊涛拍岸，卷起千堆雪。
江山如画，一时多少豪杰。
遥想公瑾当年，小乔初嫁了，雄姿英发。
羽扇纶巾，谈笑间，樯橹灰飞烟灭。
故国神游，多情应笑我，早生华发。
人生如梦，一尊还酹江月。
e: The Great River flows east;
Its waves have washed away
The gallant heroes of a thousand years.
West of the old fort, there, they say,
Is Red Cliff, where young Zhou fought in the Three Kingdoms' day.
Jagged rocks pierce the clouds,
Wild breakers pound the shore,
Rolling up a thousand drifts of snow.
River and mountains, like a painting —
How many heroes were here, long ago!
I think of Gongjin in those years,
With Little Qiao just newly wed,
Heroic in his bearing, brilliant in his prime;
A feather fan, a silken cap — and, laughing, chatting,
He burned their masts and oars to flying ash and vanished smoke.
My spirit wanders in that ancient land —
How the tender-hearted would laugh at me,
For greying, as I have, before my time!
Life is but a dream:
Let me pour this cup to the river and the moon.
poems.n: Written in 1082 during Su Shi's exile at Huangzhou, at a cliff on the Yangtze that he took — perhaps wrongly — for the site of the Battle of Red Cliff (208), where the young Wu general Zhou Yu (Gongjin), newly married to the beauty Xiao Qiao, burned Cao Cao's fleet. This lyric founded the "heroic and unrestrained" (豪放) school of *ci*: it should be sung, a contemporary said, by a big man from the west beating an iron clapper, not by a girl with castanets. The ending turns from heroism to the dream of life, and a libation to the eternal moon.

poems.t: 江城子·乙卯正月二十日夜记梦
poems.te: River Town: A Dream on the Night of the 20th Day of the First Month, 1075
poems.s: night moon window pine hills person
z: 十年生死两茫茫，不思量，自难忘。
千里孤坟，无处话凄凉。
纵使相逢应不识，尘满面，鬓如霜。
夜来幽梦忽还乡，小轩窗，正梳妆。
相顾无言，惟有泪千行。
料得年年肠断处，明月夜，短松冈。
e: Ten years — the living and the dead, apart, both lost from sight.
I do not try to think of you,
Yet can't forget you, day or night.
Your lonely grave lies a thousand li away;
I have no place to tell my grief, my plight.
Even if we met, you would not know me now —
My face all dust,
My temples frost-white.
Last night in a dream I suddenly came home:
By the little window there,
You sat, combing your hair.
We looked at each other and could not speak —
Only a thousand lines of tears.
I know the place that breaks my heart, year after year:
The moonlit night,
The hill of short pines, there.
poems.n: Written in 1075 on the tenth anniversary of the death of Su Shi's first wife, Wang Fu, who died at twenty-six. The first great elegy in the *ci* form, and perhaps the most moving in Chinese. In the dream she is simply doing her hair by the window, as she did every morning; neither of them can speak. Su Shi had planted pine saplings on her grave.

poems.s: day hills rider horse birds flag
z: 老夫聊发少年狂，左牵黄，右擎苍，锦帽貂裘，千骑卷平冈。
为报倾城随太守，亲射虎，看孙郎。
酒酣胸胆尚开张，鬓微霜，又何妨！
持节云中，何日遣冯唐？
会挽雕弓如满月，西北望，射天狼。
e: This old man, for once, lets loose a young man's wild delight:
A yellow hound upon my left,
A grey hawk on my right.
In brocade caps and sable furs,
A thousand horsemen sweep the hills in flight.
To thank the townsfolk who have followed their governor in force,
I'll shoot the tiger myself, as Sun Quan did, from horse.
Warm with wine, my heart grows bold, my courage swells;
So what if frost has touched my hair?
What harm is there?
When will the court send Feng Tang with its tally to the frontier,
To call me back, and send me there?
I'll draw my carved bow round as the full moon,
Gaze to the north-west,
And shoot down the Wolf Star in the air.
poems.n: Mizhou, 1075. Su Shi, aged thirty-nine, leads a hunt and imagines himself a frontier general. Sun Quan, ruler of Wu, once shot a tiger from horseback. Feng Tang was sent by a Han emperor with a tally to pardon a disgraced general at Yunzhong — Su Shi hopes for such a recall. The Wolf Star (Sirius) stood for invaders from the north-west, the Western Xia and the Liao.

poems.t: 定风波（莫听穿林打叶声）
poems.te: Calming the Waves (Don't Heed the Rain)
poems.s: spring rain bamboo hills person sun
z: 莫听穿林打叶声，何妨吟啸且徐行。
竹杖芒鞋轻胜马，谁怕？一蓑烟雨任平生。
料峭春风吹酒醒，微冷，山头斜照却相迎。
回首向来萧瑟处，归去，也无风雨也无晴。
e: Don't heed the rain that pierces the woods and beats upon the leaves;
Why not chant and whistle as I slowly stroll ahead?
Bamboo staff and straw sandals — lighter than a horse, I know.
Who's afraid?
A straw cape in the misty rain — I'll live my life just so.
The chilly spring wind blows me sober —
A little cold;
On the hilltop, the slanting sun comes out to greet me, bright.
I turn and look back at the place where the storm roared —
Going home,
There's neither wind nor rain, nor sunlight.
poems.n: Huangzhou, 1082. Caught in a sudden shower on a walk, his companions ran for cover; Su Shi kept strolling. The rain is the political storm that had nearly cost him his life; the last line — "neither wind and rain, nor clear skies" — is a Zen-like serenity beyond good and bad fortune. A favourite of people going through hard times.

poems.t: 卜算子·黄州定慧院寓居作
poems.te: Song of Divination: Written While Lodging at Dinghui Temple, Huangzhou
poems.s: night crescent geese river reeds pine
z: 缺月挂疏桐，漏断人初静。
谁见幽人独往来，缥缈孤鸿影。
惊起却回头，有恨无人省。
拣尽寒枝不肯栖，寂寞沙洲冷。
e: A waning moon hangs in the sparse wutong tree;
The water-clock runs dry; the world's begun to rest.
Who sees the hermit coming and going, lonely, free? —
A lone wild goose's shadow, faint, now east, now west.
Startled, it turns its head and looks around,
With grief that no one in the world can see.
It tries each frozen branch, and will not settle down —
The sandbar, lonely, cold as cold can be.
poems.n: Written in 1080, soon after Su Shi reached Huangzhou after months in prison and a near death sentence; he lodged at Dinghui Temple. The lone goose that refuses every cold branch and settles on a freezing sandbar is Su Shi himself — wounded and startled, yet unwilling to compromise.

poems.te: Immortal by the River: Returning to Lingao at Night
poems.s: night crescent river cottage person boat
z: 夜饮东坡醒复醉，归来仿佛三更。
家童鼻息已雷鸣。敲门都不应，倚杖听江声。
长恨此身非我有，何时忘却营营？
夜阑风静縠纹平。小舟从此逝，江海寄余生。
e: Drinking at Dongpo, sober and drunk again,
I come home near the third watch, I'd say.
The houseboy's snores are thundering by then;
I knock, but no one answers —
So, leaning on my stick, I hear the river on its way.
I've long resented that this body's not my own —
When can I forget this endless strife?
The night is late, the wind is still, the ripples smooth as crepe:
In a little boat I'll vanish from here, alone,
And give the rivers and the seas the rest of my life.
poems.n: Huangzhou, 1082. Locked out by his snoring servant, Su Shi stands listening to the Yangtze and longs to be free of office and its "striving" (营营, a word from *Zhuangzi*). Dongpo, "East Slope", was the plot he farmed in exile — and the name he took for himself. Legend says a rumour spread the next day that he had sung this song, hung up his official hat and sailed away; the alarmed governor rushed over and found him snoring in bed.

poems.s: spring willow cottage swallows river flowers
z: 花褪残红青杏小。燕子飞时，绿水人家绕。
枝上柳绵吹又少，天涯何处无芳草！
墙里秋千墙外道。墙外行人，墙里佳人笑。
笑渐不闻声渐悄，多情却被无情恼。
e: The flowers shed their last faded red; the green apricots are small.
When the swallows fly,
Green water circles the homes of all.
The willow-down is blown from the boughs, and less and less remains —
Yet where under heaven is there no sweet grass at all?
Inside the wall, a swing; outside, a road goes by.
Outside, a passer-by;
Inside, a pretty girl laughs high.
The laughter fades; the voice grows faint and dies —
And the one who feels is vexed by one who doesn't, with a sigh.
poems.n: Late spring, willow down blowing away — yet "where under heaven is there no fragrant grass?" (天涯何处无芳草), now said to comfort the broken-hearted. The second stanza is a tiny comedy: a passer-by is charmed by an unseen girl's laughter over a garden wall; she swings on, unaware, and he is left vexed. Su Shi's companion Wang Zhaoyun is said to have wept singing the fourth line, and could never sing it again.

poems.te: Washing Silk in the Stream (Visiting Clear Spring Temple)
poems.s: dusk spring rain pine river temple flowers
z: 山下兰芽短浸溪，松间沙路净无泥，萧萧暮雨子规啼。
谁道人生无再少？门前流水尚能西！休将白发唱黄鸡。
e: Below the hill, short orchid shoots dip in the brook;
Between the pines, the sandy path is clean, without a stain;
The cuckoo cries in the soft evening rain.
Who says a man can never be young again?
The stream before this temple flows back west!
Don't let white hair sing the yellow-cock refrain.
poems.n: Visiting Clear Spring Temple at Qishui in 1082, Su Shi noticed that its stream flowed west — unusual in China, where "all rivers flow east" stands for time's one-way current. So, he says, youth can come back too! "The yellow cock" refers to a sad old song — "the yellow cock calls the dawn, the white sun hurries toward evening" — which the white-haired should not sing.

poems.t: 浣溪沙（细雨斜风作晓寒）
poems.te: Washing Silk in the Stream (Fine Rain, Slanting Wind)
poems.s: dawn winter rain willow river mist cup
z: 细雨斜风作晓寒，淡烟疏柳媚晴滩。入淮清洛渐漫漫。
雪沫乳花浮午盏，蓼茸蒿笋试春盘。人间有味是清欢。
e: Fine rain and slanting wind make the morning cold;
Faint mist and sparse willows grace the sunny shoal;
The clear Luo widens, wide and slow, as into the Huai it's rolled.
Snow-white froth and milky foam float in my noonday tea;
Smartweed shoots and wormwood sprouts — the spring dish, fresh and whole.
Of all life's flavours, the best is plain delight, I'm told.
poems.n: A winter outing near Sizhou in 1084, with frothy whisked tea and a "spring platter" of fresh greens. The last line — 人间有味是清欢, "the true taste of life is simple joy" — has become one of Su Shi's most loved sayings.

poems.t: 水龙吟·次韵章质夫杨花词
poems.te: Water Dragon Chant: Willow Catkins, Matching Zhang Zhifu's Rhymes
poems.s: spring willow wind lake oriole petals
z: 似花还似非花，也无人惜从教坠。
抛家傍路，思量却是，无情有思。
萦损柔肠，困酣娇眼，欲开还闭。
梦随风万里，寻郎去处，又还被、莺呼起。
不恨此花飞尽，恨西园、落红难缀。
晓来雨过，遗踪何在，一池萍碎。
春色三分，二分尘土，一分流水。
细看来，不是杨花点点，是离人泪。
e: Like a flower, and yet not a flower at all,
No one feels pity as it's left to fall.
It leaves its home to drift beside the road;
You'd think it heartless — yet it longs, it yearns.
Twisting its tender heart,
With drowsy, lovely eyes
That want to open, then close again in turns.
In dreams it follows the wind ten thousand li,
To seek the place her love has gone,
Only to be woken by the orioles' calls once more.
I don't regret that all these flowers have flown;
I regret the west garden's fallen red can't be restored.
At dawn the rain has passed — where are their traces now?
A pond of broken duckweed.
Of all spring's colour, three parts:
Two parts are dust,
And one part flowing water.
Look closely: these are not willow catkins at all —
Each dot is a parted lover's tear.
poems.n: A lyric "matching the rhymes" of a friend's poem on willow catkins — the white fluff that drifts from willows and poplars in late spring. Su Shi turns the drifting fluff into a lonely woman dreaming of following her love, and ends with one of the great closing lines of the *ci*: look closely — they are not catkins, but the tears of parted lovers. (Fallen catkins were believed to turn into duckweed.)

poems.te: Gazing South of the River: Written on the Terrace of Transcendence
poems.s: spring rain willow tower wall flowers mist
z: 春未老，风细柳斜斜。
试上超然台上看，半壕春水一城花。烟雨暗千家。
寒食后，酒醒却咨嗟。
休对故人思故国，且将新火试新茶。诗酒趁年华。
e: Spring's not yet old;
The breeze is soft, the willows lean.
I climb the Terrace of Transcendence to behold:
Half a moat of spring water, a whole city's flowers seen,
And a thousand homes in misty rain, dim and green.
After Cold Food,
Sobered up from wine, I sigh.
Don't talk to old friends of the home we left behind;
Let's try new tea on the new fire — you and I.
Poetry and wine, while we're still young, before the years go by!
poems.n: Mizhou, 1076, on the "Terrace of Transcendence" (超然台) that Su Shi had rebuilt. After the Cold Food Festival, when fires were lit again, came the season of new tea. 诗酒趁年华, "poetry and wine, while we are young", is his cheerful remedy for homesickness.

poems.te: Written on the Wall of Xilin Temple
poems.s: day peaks mountains clouds temple pine
z: 横看成岭侧成峰，远近高低各不同。
不识庐山真面目，只缘身在此山中。
e: Seen from the front, a range; from the side, a single peak;
From near, from far, from high, from low — no two views are the same.
I cannot know the real face of Mount Lu I seek,
Because I stand inside the mountain — that's to blame.
poems.n: Written on a wall of Xilin Temple on Mount Lu in 1084. It became a proverb about perspective: 不识庐山真面目，只缘身在此山中 — those inside a situation cannot see it clearly.

poems.te: Drinking on the Lake, First Sun Then Rain (II)
poems.s: day rain lake hills mist boat
z: 水光潋滟晴方好，山色空蒙雨亦奇。
欲把西湖比西子，淡妆浓抹总相宜。
e: The shimmering water's lovely when the sky is clear;
The hills in misty rain hold a magic spell.
If I compare the Western Lake to Xi Shi, it would appear
Light make-up or heavy suits her equally well.
poems.n: Hangzhou, 1073. Drinking on West Lake as a sunny day turns to rain, Su Shi compares the lake to Xi Shi (Xizi), the legendary beauty of the ancient state of Yue — gorgeous in any weather, as she was in any make-up. The comparison stuck: West Lake is still called "Xizi Lake".

poems.s: spring river bamboo peach birds reeds
z: 竹外桃花三两枝，春江水暖鸭先知。
蒌蒿满地芦芽短，正是河豚欲上时。
e: Beyond the bamboo, two or three peach sprays blossom bright;
The ducks are first to know the spring river's warming flow.
Wormwood covers all the ground; reed shoots are short and slight —
Just when the pufferfish swim upriver, as we know.
poems.n: Written on a painting by the monk Huichong. Su Shi adds what a painting cannot show — the warmth of the water, felt first by the ducks, and the pufferfish (a spring delicacy, cooked with wormwood and reed shoots) about to swim upstream. 春江水暖鸭先知 is now said of anyone who senses change first.

poems.s: autumn lotus lake chrysanthemum frost
z: 荷尽已无擎雨盖，菊残犹有傲霜枝。
一年好景君须记，最是橙黄橘绿时。
e: The lotus is done — no leaves left to shelter from the rain;
The fading chrysanthemums still hold up branches frost can't bend.
The finest season of the year — remember it again:
When oranges turn gold and tangerines are green, my friend.
poems.n: Hangzhou, 1090, for Liu Jingwen, a fifty-eight-year-old officer of integrity whom Su Shi admired. Late autumn, when lotus and chrysanthemums fade, is not an ending but the best season of all — the time of ripe fruit: a compliment and an encouragement for a man in later life. The chrysanthemum that "defies the frost" is Liu himself.

poems.t: 六月二十七日望湖楼醉书（其一）
poems.te: Written Drunk at Lake-View Tower on the 27th Day of the Sixth Month (I)
poems.s: summer rain lake clouds boat tower wind
z: 黑云翻墨未遮山，白雨跳珠乱入船。
卷地风来忽吹散，望湖楼下水如天。
e: Black clouds spill ink, but have not hidden all the hills;
White rain leaps up like pearls and bounces in the boat.
A wind rolls in across the ground — the squall is gone, all's still;
Below the Lake-View Tower, the water's like the sky afloat.
poems.n: Hangzhou, summer 1072. A sudden squall sweeps West Lake, from black clouds to shining calm, in four swift lines that move as fast as the storm.

poems.s: winter snow temple geese rider
z: 人生到处知何似，应似飞鸿踏雪泥。
泥上偶然留指爪，鸿飞那复计东西。
老僧已死成新塔，坏壁无由见旧题。
往日崎岖还记否，路长人困蹇驴嘶。
e: What is our life like, everywhere we go?
Like a wild goose stepping on the mud and snow.
By chance it leaves its claw-prints in the mud;
Once flown, who knows if it went east or west, to and fro?
The old monk's dead; a new stupa holds him now;
The ruined wall no longer shows the poems we wrote.
Do you remember still the hard road of those days —
The long way, our weariness, the lame donkey's braying note?
poems.n: A reply to his brother Su Zhe in 1061. Years before, the brothers had stayed at a temple in Mianchi and written poems on its wall; now the monk is dead and the wall has crumbled. 雪泥鸿爪, "a goose's claw-prints in snowy mud", became the idiom for the faint traces of the past — and for life itself: we leave a mark by chance, then fly on.

poems.s: night spring moon flowers candle pavilion
z: 东风袅袅泛崇光，香雾空蒙月转廊。
只恐夜深花睡去，故烧高烛照红妆。
e: The east wind softly breathes, and lustre floats on air;
Through fragrant mist the moon moves round the corridor.
I fear the flowers will fall asleep, so late the hour —
So I light tall candles to see their rouge once more.
poems.n: Huangzhou, 1080: a single crabapple tree, a rare southern beauty growing in exile like the poet himself. As the moon moves away, Su Shi lights candles so the flowers won't "fall asleep" — in fact, so he can keep looking at them.

poems.s: night spring moon tower flowers lantern
z: 春宵一刻值千金，花有清香月有阴。
歌管楼台声细细，秋千院落夜沉沉。
e: A moment of a spring night is worth a thousand gold;
The flowers breathe pure fragrance; the moon lays down its shade.
From towers and terraces, faint songs and pipes float soft;
The courtyard with its swing lies deep in night's dark glade.
poems.n: 春宵一刻值千金, "a moment of a spring night is worth a thousand gold", is one of the most quoted lines in Chinese — a reminder not to waste precious time. The last two lines contrast revellers still singing in their towers with the quiet courtyards already asleep.

poems.te: Pear Blossoms by the East Railing
poems.s: spring willow flowers petals pavilion
z: 梨花淡白柳深青，柳絮飞时花满城。
惆怅东栏一株雪，人生看得几清明。
e: Pear blossoms pale and white, the willows deep and green;
When willow-down is flying, the whole city fills with flowers.
I grieve for the tree of snow by the east railing seen —
In all one life, how many Qingming springtimes are ours?
poems.n: Xuzhou, 1077. The pear tree by the east railing is "a tree of snow" — beautiful, and a reminder of white hair. 清明 is both the Qingming festival and its literal meaning, "clear and bright": how many such clear springs does anyone get?

poems.te: Inscribed on My Portrait at Jinshan
poems.s: day river boat temple person
z: 心似已灰之木，身如不系之舟。
问汝平生功业，黄州惠州儋州。
e: My heart is like wood already burned to ash;
My body, like a boat that's cast adrift and free.
You ask what I achieved in all my life? At last:
Huangzhou, Huizhou, Danzhou — places of exile, three.
poems.n: Written in 1101, two months before his death, on a portrait of himself at Jinshan Temple. "Dead wood" and "an untied boat" come from *Zhuangzi* — images of a mind beyond desire. His life's "achievements"? The three places he was exiled to — Huangzhou, Huizhou, and Danzhou on Hainan Island — where he wrote his greatest work. Self-mockery and pride in one breath.

poems.s: night person pine moon
z: 若言琴上有琴声，放在匣中何不鸣？
若言声在指头上，何不于君指上听？
e: If you say the music lies within the qin,
Why is it silent, put away in its case?
If you say the music's in the fingers, then
Why not just listen to your fingers in its place?
poems.n: A Buddhist riddle in verse, echoing the *Surangama Sutra*: music arises only when instrument and player meet — as all things arise from conditions coming together, with no fixed "self" in any one part.

poems.s: day mountains rain mist river sea
z: 庐山烟雨浙江潮，未到千般恨不消。
到得还来别无事，庐山烟雨浙江潮。
e: Mount Lu in misty rain; the Zhejiang tide;
Till you have seen them, a thousand longings won't subside.
You go, come back — and there is nothing more to say:
Mount Lu in misty rain; the Zhejiang tide.
poems.n: Said to be one of Su Shi's last poems, written for his son. The first and last lines are identical, but mean different things: before, the famous sights are objects of longing; after, they are simply what they are. A Zen saying runs: "Before enlightenment, mountains are mountains; during it, mountains are not mountains; after it, mountains are mountains again."

poems.s: summer mountains sun person cottage
z: 罗浮山下四时春，卢橘杨梅次第新。
日啖荔枝三百颗，不辞长作岭南人。
e: Below Mount Luofu it is spring all the year;
Loquats and bayberries ripen fresh, each in its turn.
With three hundred lychees to eat each day, right here,
I'd gladly live in the south forever — and never return.
poems.n: Exiled at sixty to Huizhou in Guangdong — then a malarial frontier — Su Shi wrote not a lament but a love song to lychees. His cheerful refusal to be miserable is why he is the best-loved figure in Chinese literature.

poems.te: Immortal by the River (After the Dream, the Tower Is Locked)
poems.s: spring rain petals swallows tower moon person
z: 梦后楼台高锁，酒醒帘幕低垂。
去年春恨却来时。落花人独立，微雨燕双飞。
记得小蘋初见，两重心字罗衣。
琵琶弦上说相思。当时明月在，曾照彩云归。
e: After the dream, the tower's locked up high;
I wake from wine; the curtains hang down low.
Last spring's sorrow comes back again, as then:
Amid the falling petals, someone stands alone;
In the fine rain, the swallows fly in pairs.
I remember when I first saw Xiaopin,
In her silk dress embroidered with "heart" twice over.
On the pipa strings she told of love's longing.
The same bright moon was shining then
That lit her, a coloured cloud, as she went home.
poems.n: Yan Jidao remembers Xiaopin, a singing girl in a friend's household. 落花人独立，微雨燕双飞 — "among falling petals, someone stands alone; in fine rain, swallows fly in pairs" — was borrowed from an obscure earlier poem, but made immortal here. The "coloured cloud" is Xiaopin herself, lit home by a moon that still shines though she is gone.

poems.t: 鹧鸪天（彩袖殷勤捧玉钟）
poems.te: Partridge Sky (Your Coloured Sleeves Offered the Jade Cup)
poems.s: night moon tower willow candle two cup
z: 彩袖殷勤捧玉钟，当年拚却醉颜红。
舞低杨柳楼心月，歌尽桃花扇底风。
从别后，忆相逢，几回魂梦与君同。
今宵剩把银釭照，犹恐相逢是梦中。
e: Your coloured sleeves so kindly offered me the cup of jade;
That year I drank without a care, my face aflame with wine.
We danced until the moon sank low above the willowed tower;
We sang until the breeze was spent from your peach-blossom fan, so fine.
Since we parted,
I've remembered how we met;
How many times my dreaming soul has been with you!
Tonight I keep on lifting up the silver lamp to see —
Afraid our meeting's just a dream, and won't come true.
poems.n: A reunion with a singing girl after years apart. The second couplet — dancing till the moon sank over the willows, singing till the breeze of the peach-blossom fan was spent — is one of the most glittering in the *ci*. Holding up the lamp again and again to make sure it is not a dream echoes Du Fu's reunion with his family: "we face each other as if in a dream."

poems.te: Pure Serene Music (Where Has Spring Gone?)
poems.s: spring oriole flowers wind cottage
z: 春归何处？寂寞无行路。
若有人知春去处，唤取归来同住。
春无踪迹谁知？除非问取黄鹂。
百啭无人能解，因风飞过蔷薇。
e: Where has spring gone home?
It's lonely here — no tracks to trace.
If anyone knows where spring has gone,
Call it back to stay with us in this place.
Spring leaves no trace — who knows?
Unless you ask the oriole.
But no one understands its hundred songs —
It rides the wind across the roses, and goes.
poems.n: A playful chase after the departing spring. The only witness, the oriole, sings a hundred songs no one understands, and flies off over the roses — the flowers of early summer. Spring is gone.

poems.s: dusk autumn moon river tower hills leaves
z: 痴儿了却公家事，快阁东西倚晚晴。
落木千山天远大，澄江一道月分明。
朱弦已为佳人绝，青眼聊因美酒横。
万里归船弄长笛，此心吾与白鸥盟。
e: This foolish fellow has finished all his official chores;
I lean on Kuaige's rails, east and west, in the evening's clear light.
With leaves fallen from a thousand hills, the sky is vast;
One clear river, and on it, the moon shining bright.
The red strings are broken — the one who understood is gone;
My "green eyes" turn, for now, to good wine alone.
Ten thousand li home in a boat, playing a long flute —
I've sworn a pact with the white gulls: their freedom will be my own.
poems.n: 1082, when Huang Tingjian was a county magistrate in Jiangxi. "A foolish fellow finishing official business" is a self-mocking quotation from the Jin dynasty. Boya broke his zither strings when the one friend who understood his music died; Ruan Ji showed the "green" of his eyes to people he liked and the "whites" to those he despised. A pact with the gulls — living free and without scheming — is the old recluse's ideal.

poems.s: night rain river candle person
z: 我居北海君南海，寄雁传书谢不能。
桃李春风一杯酒，江湖夜雨十年灯。
持家但有四立壁，治病不蕲三折肱。
想见读书头已白，隔溪猿哭瘴溪藤。
e: I live by the northern sea, and you by the southern sea;
I'd send a letter by wild goose — it says it can't fly so far.
Peach and plum in the spring breeze: one cup of wine;
Night rain on rivers and lakes: ten years of lamplight, where you are.
To keep your house, you have nothing but four bare walls;
To heal the sick, you needn't break your arm three times to learn.
I picture you at your books, your hair already white,
While across the fever stream the gibbons wail in the vines in turn.
poems.n: To an old friend serving as a poor magistrate in remote Guangdong, "the southern sea". Wild geese were said never to fly south of Hengyang, so they "decline" to carry letters. The famous middle couplet sets one cup of wine in the spring breeze, when they last met, against ten years of separate lamps on rainy nights. "Break your arm three times and you become a good doctor" was an old saying: his friend is already a skilled official — yet unrecognised.

poems.te: Song of Divination (I Live Where the River Starts)
poems.s: day river boat hills person
z: 我住长江头，君住长江尾。
日日思君不见君，共饮长江水。
此水几时休？此恨何时已？
只愿君心似我心，定不负相思意。
e: I live where the Long River starts;
You live where the Long River ends.
Day after day I long for you, but you're not here —
Yet we both drink the water the same river sends.
When will this river cease to run?
When will this longing ever end?
I only hope your heart is like my own —
Then I'll keep faith with all this love, my friend.
poems.n: A lyric in the plain voice of a folk song. The great Yangtze both separates the lovers — head and tail, a thousand miles apart — and joins them, for they drink the same water. Its simplicity has made it one of the best-loved love poems in Chinese.

poems.te: Immortals at the Magpie Bridge (Fine Clouds Weave Their Patterns)
poems.s: night stars clouds bridge birds
z: 纤云弄巧，飞星传恨，银汉迢迢暗度。
金风玉露一相逢，便胜却人间无数。
柔情似水，佳期如梦，忍顾鹊桥归路！
两情若是久长时，又岂在朝朝暮暮。
e: Fine clouds weave their clever patterns;
Shooting stars bear sorrow's message far;
Across the Silver River's distance, in secret, she goes.
One meeting in the golden wind and jade-white dew
Is worth more than all the meetings the human world knows.
Their tender love is soft as water;
Their tryst is fleeting as a dream —
How can they bear to look back at the magpie bridge as home they go?
If love between two hearts will last forever,
Why must they be together every dawn and every dusk?
poems.n: On the Seventh Night of the seventh month, the Weaver Girl (Vega) crosses the Silver River (the Milky Way) on a bridge of magpies to meet the Herdboy (Altair) — their one night together each year. Qin Guan turns the usual lament on its head: one meeting of true lovers is worth more than all the ordinary days of humankind, and lasting love does not need to be together "every morning and every evening". Long-distance lovers still quote it.

poems.te: Treading the Grass: At the Inn in Chenzhou
poems.s: dusk spring mist moon tower river mountains cottage
z: 雾失楼台，月迷津渡，桃源望断无寻处。
可堪孤馆闭春寒，杜鹃声里斜阳暮。
驿寄梅花，鱼传尺素，砌成此恨无重数。
郴江幸自绕郴山，为谁流下潇湘去？
e: The mist has hidden the towers,
The moon has blurred the ford;
I gaze for Peach Blossom Spring — it's nowhere to be found.
How can I bear this lonely inn, shut in the spring cold,
At sunset, with the cuckoo's cries all around?
Plum blossoms sent by post,
And letters in a fish —
They pile up into sorrows, more than can be told.
The Chen River ought to circle its own Chen Hill —
For whom, then, does it flow away to the Xiang, so cold?
poems.n: Written in 1097 in exile at Chenzhou (Hunan) — one of the darkest of all *ci*. Peach Blossom Spring, the hidden paradise, cannot be found; the kind letters and gifts of friends only build his sorrow higher. The last two lines — why does the river leave its own mountains to flow away north? — so moved Su Shi that he wrote them on his fan, saying "even ten thousand men could not redeem Qin Guan".

poems.t: 浣溪沙（漠漠轻寒上小楼）
poems.te: Washing Silk in the Stream (A Faint Chill Climbs the Tower)
poems.s: dawn spring rain petals tower window mist
z: 漠漠轻寒上小楼，晓阴无赖似穷秋，淡烟流水画屏幽。
自在飞花轻似梦，无边丝雨细如愁，宝帘闲挂小银钩。
e: A faint, soft chill drifts up the little tower;
The sullen dawn's as gloomy as late fall;
Pale mist and flowing water on the painted screen, a pall.
The drifting petals float as light as dreams;
The endless threads of rain are fine as sorrow;
The jewelled blind hangs idly on its little silver hook — that's all.
poems.n: A lyric made of almost nothing — a cold spring morning, a painted screen, a blind — whose famous couplet makes the intangible concrete: petals "light as dreams", rain "fine as sorrow". One of the most delicate pieces of the "graceful" school.

poems.t: 青玉案（凌波不过横塘路）
poems.s: dusk spring rain river grass willow bridge
z: 凌波不过横塘路，但目送、芳尘去。
锦瑟华年谁与度？月桥花院，琐窗朱户，只有春知处。
飞云冉冉蘅皋暮，彩笔新题断肠句。
若问闲情都几许？一川烟草，满城风絮，梅子黄时雨。
e: Her lightly gliding steps don't come along Hengtang road;
I only watch her fragrant dust drift off.
With whom will she spend the zither-years of youth?
A moonlit bridge, a garden of flowers,
A latticed window, a crimson door —
Only spring knows where.
Slow-drifting clouds; dusk falls on the fragrant shore;
With a coloured brush I write new heartbreaking lines.
You ask how much idle sorrow I have to bear? —
A whole river of misty grass,
A whole city of willow-down in the wind,
And the rain when plums turn yellow everywhere.
poems.n: He Zhu glimpses a beautiful woman — "treading the waves", like the goddess of the Luo River — and never sees her again. His answer to "how much sorrow?" is three images of drifting multitude: misty grass along a whole river, willow-down filling a whole city, and the endless drizzle of the "plum rains" of early summer. It earned him the nickname "He of the Plum Rain".

poems.s: night autumn rain window candle frost
z: 重过阊门万事非，同来何事不同归？
梧桐半死清霜后，头白鸳鸯失伴飞。
原上草，露初晞，旧栖新垄两依依。
空床卧听南窗雨，谁复挑灯夜补衣！
e: Passing through Changmen again, all's changed, all wrong;
We came here together — why can't we go home as two?
The wutong tree is half-dead after the frost,
A white-haired drake that flies alone, his mate gone from view.
The grass upon the plain,
The dew just dried at dawn —
The old home and the new grave: I can't leave either one.
On an empty bed I lie and hear the rain at the south window —
Who'll trim the lamp at night now, and mend my clothes when they're worn?
poems.n: He Zhu's elegy for his wife, written on returning to Suzhou (Changmen is one of its gates), where they had lived together. The half-dead wutong and the lone white-headed mandarin duck are classic images of a widower. Its last line — no one to mend his clothes by lamplight — is often paired with Su Shi's dream of his wife combing her hair, as the two great elegies of the Northern Song.

poems.s: dawn summer lotus lake birds sun cottage
z: 燎沉香，消溽暑。鸟雀呼晴，侵晓窥檐语。
叶上初阳干宿雨，水面清圆，一一风荷举。
故乡遥，何日去？家住吴门，久作长安旅。
五月渔郎相忆否？小楫轻舟，梦入芙蓉浦。
e: I burn the aloeswood incense
To drive away the muggy heat.
The sparrows call for sunny skies;
At dawn they chatter, peeping from the eaves, so sweet.
On the leaves, the morning sun dries last night's rain;
Across the water, clear and round,
The lotus leaves rise in the wind, one by one, complete.
My home is far away —
When shall I go?
My home is by the gates of Wu;
In the capital so long I've been a guest.
Do the fishermen of the fifth month remember me?
A little oar, a little boat —
In dreams I drift into the lotus pool to rest.
poems.n: Zhou Bangyan, a native of Hangzhou serving in the capital Kaifeng, wakes to a summer morning. 叶上初阳干宿雨，水面清圆，一一风荷举 — "on the leaves the first sun dries the night's rain; on the water, fresh and round, the lotus leaves rise one by one in the wind" — Wang Guowei called the line that "truly captures the spirit of the lotus". From the lotus he drifts into homesickness.

poems.te: As in a Dream (Last Night, Scattered Rain)
poems.s: dawn spring wind rain flowers window
z: 昨夜雨疏风骤，浓睡不消残酒。
试问卷帘人，却道海棠依旧。
知否，知否？应是绿肥红瘦。
e: Last night, scattered rain and a gusty wind;
Deep sleep has not dispelled the last of the wine.
I ask the maid who's rolling up the blind —
"The crabapple's just as it was," she says, "it's fine."
"Don't you know? Don't you know?
The green must be fuller now, and the red grown thin."
poems.n: Written by Li Qingzhao as a young woman. A dialogue in miniature: the careless maid says the flowers are fine; the poet, who lay awake listening to the storm, knows better. 绿肥红瘦, "the green grows plump, the red grows thin" — leaves flourishing, blossoms stripped — was admired as a daring and perfect phrase.

poems.te: As in a Dream (I Often Recall the Stream Pavilion)
poems.s: dusk summer lotus lake boat birds crane pavilion
z: 常记溪亭日暮，沉醉不知归路。
兴尽晚回舟，误入藕花深处。
争渡，争渡，惊起一滩鸥鹭。
e: I often recall the stream pavilion at close of day:
So drunk, we never knew the way back home.
Our fun all spent, we turned the boat back late,
And drifted deep among the lotus, lost to roam.
"Row hard! Row hard!" —
And up flew a whole shoal of gulls and egrets, white as foam.
poems.n: A happy memory of girlhood in Jinan: tipsy after a day out, the girls row home in the dusk, lose their way among the lotus, and splash their way out, sending up a flock of startled birds. 争渡 can mean "row hard!" or "how do we get through?" — both fit the giggling panic.

poems.s: dusk autumn rain chrysanthemum window geese wind
z: 寻寻觅觅，冷冷清清，凄凄惨惨戚戚。
乍暖还寒时候，最难将息。
三杯两盏淡酒，怎敌他、晚来风急！
雁过也，正伤心，却是旧时相识。
满地黄花堆积，憔悴损，如今有谁堪摘？
守着窗儿，独自怎生得黑！
梧桐更兼细雨，到黄昏、点点滴滴。
这次第，怎一个愁字了得！
e: Searching, searching, seeking, seeking,
Cold, so cold, so clear, so lonely,
Dreary, dreary, wretched, wretched, grieving, grieving.
In this season of sudden warmth that turns to chill again,
It's hardest to find rest.
Three cups, two bowls of thin wine — how can they stand
Against the wind that rises fierce at evening's end?
The wild geese pass —
Just as my heart is breaking —
Old friends I knew back then.
The ground is heaped with yellow chrysanthemums,
Withered and wasted —
Who would pick them now?
Keeping watch by the window,
Alone — how shall I last until it's dark?
The wutong trees, and now fine rain as well,
Till dusk, dripping, dropping, drop by drop.
This plight —
How can one word, "sorrow", tell it all?
poems.n: The most famous lyric by a woman in Chinese, written after the fall of the north in 1127, the loss of her home and library, and the death of her husband, Zhao Mingcheng. It opens with fourteen doubled characters (寻寻觅觅…) that sound like sobs. The geese that once carried her husband's letters now carry nothing; the chrysanthemums she once picked lie wasted; rain drips on the wutong leaves. And then the famous ending: how could one word, "sorrow", hold all this?

poems.t: 一剪梅（红藕香残玉簟秋）
poems.te: A Sprig of Plum (The Red Lotus' Scent Has Faded)
poems.s: night autumn moon lotus lake boat tower geese
z: 红藕香残玉簟秋。轻解罗裳，独上兰舟。
云中谁寄锦书来？雁字回时，月满西楼。
花自飘零水自流。一种相思，两处闲愁。
此情无计可消除，才下眉头，却上心头。
e: The red lotus' scent has faded; my jade mat feels the fall.
I loosen my silk skirt, alone,
And step into the orchid boat.
Who sends a brocade letter from among the clouds at all?
When the geese return in lines,
The moon fills the west tower, remote.
The petals drift, the water flows, each its own way;
One single longing,
Two places of quiet sorrow.
There's no way I can drive this feeling away:
No sooner has it left my brow
Than it climbs into my heart.
poems.n: Written while her husband Zhao Mingcheng was away. Geese flying in formation spell the characters 人 or 一 across the sky — "goose letters" (雁字) — and were said to carry messages. "One longing, two places": the love is mutual, so the sadness is doubled. The last couplet is a famous image of a feeling that cannot be put down.

poems.t: 醉花阴（薄雾浓云愁永昼）
poems.te: Tipsy in the Flowers' Shade (Thin Mist, Thick Clouds)
poems.s: dusk autumn chrysanthemum window wind mist
z: 薄雾浓云愁永昼，瑞脑销金兽。
佳节又重阳，玉枕纱厨，半夜凉初透。
东篱把酒黄昏后，有暗香盈袖。
莫道不销魂，帘卷西风，人比黄花瘦。
e: Thin mist, thick clouds — I grieve the endless day;
In the golden beast, the camphor incense burns away.
The festival comes round again — the Double Ninth;
On my jade pillow, behind the gauze bed-screen,
At midnight the first chill steals in to stay.
By the eastern hedge, I drink till after dusk;
A secret fragrance fills my sleeves.
Don't say this doesn't break the heart —
When the west wind lifts the blind,
I'm thinner than the yellow flowers.
poems.n: Sent to her husband at the Double Ninth, when families drank chrysanthemum wine together. The story goes that Zhao Mingcheng, determined to outdo her, wrote fifty lyrics in three days and slipped hers among them for a friend to judge; the friend said only three lines were truly fine — the last three of this poem.

poems.t: 武陵春（风住尘香花已尽）
poems.te: Spring at Wuling (The Wind Has Stopped)
poems.s: dusk spring petals river boat person
z: 风住尘香花已尽，日晚倦梳头。
物是人非事事休，欲语泪先流。
闻说双溪春尚好，也拟泛轻舟。
只恐双溪舴艋舟，载不动许多愁。
e: The wind has stopped; the dust is fragrant; all the flowers have gone;
The day is late — I'm too weary to comb my hair.
Things remain, but he does not; all is ended, everyone;
I try to speak — but first the tears are there.
They say at Twin Streams spring is lovely still;
I thought I'd take a little boat out, too.
But I fear the grasshopper skiffs at Twin Streams
Could never carry all the grief I'm going through.
poems.n: Jinhua, 1135. Li Qingzhao, in her fifties, widowed and a refugee, cannot even bring herself to go boating at the famous Twin Streams. 物是人非, "things remain, but people are gone", is now a common phrase; grief too heavy for a little boat to carry is one of her most famous images.

poems.s: dusk river sun person
z: 生当作人杰，死亦为鬼雄。
至今思项羽，不肯过江东。
e: In life, be the hero of all men;
In death, among the ghosts, be a hero still.
To this day I think of Xiang Yu, who then
Would not cross back east of the River — by his own will.
poems.n: Written after the Jurchen invasion of 1127, when the Song court fled south across the Yangtze instead of fighting. Li Qingzhao sets against it Xiang Yu, who chose death rather than retreat east across the river in disgrace. Pointed and fierce — quite unlike her love lyrics.

poems.t: 渔家傲（天接云涛连晓雾）
poems.te: The Fisherman's Pride (The Sky Meets the Waves of Cloud)
poems.s: dawn sea clouds stars sail mist
z: 天接云涛连晓雾，星河欲转千帆舞。
仿佛梦魂归帝所。闻天语，殷勤问我归何处。
我报路长嗟日暮，学诗谩有惊人句。
九万里风鹏正举。风休住，蓬舟吹取三山去！
e: The sky meets the waves of cloud, and joins the morning mist;
The Milky Way begins to turn; a thousand sails dance high.
As if my dreaming soul had gone back to the Emperor's hall,
I hear a voice from heaven
Asking, kindly, where I'm going, and why.
I answer: "The road is long; alas, the sun is low;
I learned to write, but my startling lines are all in vain."
On ninety thousand li of wind, the great Peng bird soars high —
Wind, don't stop!
Blow my little boat to the Isles of the Immortals, far from pain!
poems.n: Li Qingzhao's one great "heroic" lyric, written in her refugee years: a dream voyage among the stars, where the Emperor of Heaven asks where she is bound. The Peng is the colossal bird of *Zhuangzi* that rides the wind ninety thousand li; the Three Mountains are the islands of the immortals. Critics said it could pass for Su Shi.

poems.s: spring flowers cottage person
z: 蹴罢秋千，起来慵整纤纤手。
露浓花瘦，薄汗轻衣透。
见客入来，袜刬金钗溜。
和羞走，倚门回首，却把青梅嗅。
e: She's done with the swing;
She rises, and lazily flexes her slender hands.
Heavy dew; the flowers are slight;
A light sweat soaks her thin dress through.
She sees a guest come in —
In stocking feet, her gold hairpin slipping loose,
She runs off, shy;
Then, leaning on the door, she looks back —
And sniffs a green plum, as if that were what she'd come to do.
poems.n: A girl caught off guard by a visitor — perhaps the young man she will marry — runs off in her socks, then cannot resist peeking back, pretending to smell the green plums. One of the most charming portraits of a girl in Chinese. (Its attribution to Li Qingzhao is traditional, though sometimes questioned.)

poems.te: Joy of Eternal Union (The Setting Sun Melts into Gold)
poems.s: dusk spring sun clouds willow lantern window
z: 落日熔金，暮云合璧，人在何处。
染柳烟浓，吹梅笛怨，春意知几许。
元宵佳节，融和天气，次第岂无风雨。
来相召、香车宝马，谢他酒朋诗侣。
中州盛日，闺门多暇，记得偏重三五。
铺翠冠儿，拈金雪柳，簇带争济楚。
如今憔悴，风鬟霜鬓，怕见夜间出去。
不如向、帘儿底下，听人笑语。
e: The setting sun melts into gold;
The evening clouds join like a ring of jade —
Where is the one I love?
Mist dyes the willows thick;
A flute plays "Plum Blossoms", sad and slow —
How much of spring is here?
The Lantern Festival again,
The weather mild and fair —
Yet who knows if wind and rain may follow?
They come to call, with scented carriages and fine horses;
I thank my drinking friends and poet-friends — and stay.
In the glory days of the Central Plain,
We girls had leisure time to spare,
And how we loved the Lantern Fifteenth!
In caps of kingfisher feathers,
With gold-twisted willow sprays of silk,
We vied to look our finest there.
Now, worn and wasted,
With wind-tossed hair and frosted temples,
I'm afraid to go out at night.
Better to stay behind the blind,
And listen to the laughter of others passing by.
poems.n: The Lantern Festival (the fifteenth of the first month) in Hangzhou, around 1150. The aged, widowed Li Qingzhao sets the festival of her youth in the lost northern capital, Kaifeng, against her present loneliness. 人在何处 can mean "where am I?" or "where is he?" The patriotic poet Liu Chenweng said he wept every time he read it.

poems.t: 凤凰台上忆吹箫（香冷金猊）
poems.te: On Phoenix Terrace, Remembering the Flute (The Gold Lion's Incense Is Cold)
poems.s: dawn tower window river mist person
z: 香冷金猊，被翻红浪，起来慵自梳头。
任宝奁尘满，日上帘钩。
生怕离怀别苦，多少事、欲说还休。
新来瘦，非干病酒，不是悲秋。
休休，这回去也，千万遍阳关，也则难留。
念武陵人远，烟锁秦楼。
惟有楼前流水，应念我、终日凝眸。
凝眸处，从今又添，一段新愁。
e: The gold lion's incense has gone cold;
The quilt is tossed in crimson waves;
I rise, too listless to comb my hair.
Let dust fill up my jewel box,
And the sun climb the curtain hook — who'd care?
I dread the bitter pain of parting so —
How many things I'd say, then leave them there!
I've grown so thin of late —
And not from too much wine,
Nor from autumn's melancholy air.
Enough, enough!
This time he's going —
Though I sang "Yang Pass" ten thousand times,
I still could not make him stay.
I think of him, far off in Wuling;
Mist locks the tower of Qin in grey.
Only the water flowing by the tower
Must pity me, gazing all the day.
Where my gaze rests, from now on,
There will be added
Another new sorrow, come today.
poems.n: Written when her husband Zhao Mingcheng left to take up a post, around 1121. She cannot say what she feels for fear of making the parting harder. "Yang Pass" is Wang Wei's farewell song; the "man of Wuling" — the fisherman who found Peach Blossom Spring and could never find it again — is the absent husband; the tower of Qin belonged to the princess Nongyu, who played the flute with her husband until the two flew away on phoenixes, giving the tune its name.

poems.s: autumn flowers pavilion moon
z: 暗淡轻黄体性柔，情疏迹远只香留。
何须浅碧深红色，自是花中第一流。
梅定妒，菊应羞，画阑开处冠中秋。
骚人可煞无情思，何事当年不见收。
e: Dim and pale yellow, gentle in its grace;
Aloof and far-off, it leaves only scent behind.
What need has it of pale blue or deep red's face? —
It is, by nature, the first flower of its kind.
The plum is surely jealous, the chrysanthemum ashamed;
By the painted railing, it's the crown of autumn's prime.
The old poet of the *Songs of Chu* — how heartless he must have been,
Not to name it among his flowers, in his time!
poems.n: The sweet osmanthus (桂花) has tiny, plain yellow flowers but an overwhelming scent. Li Qingzhao — no conventional beauty, but a supreme talent — calls it "by nature the first among flowers", and scolds Qu Yuan, who named many fragrant plants in his *Encountering Sorrow* but not this one.

poems.t: 添字丑奴儿（窗前谁种芭蕉树）
poems.te: Ugly Slave, Extended (Who Planted the Plantain)
poems.s: night rain window cottage person
z: 窗前谁种芭蕉树，阴满中庭。
阴满中庭，叶叶心心，舒卷有余情。
伤心枕上三更雨，点滴霖霪。
点滴霖霪，愁损北人，不惯起来听。
e: Who planted the plantain tree before my window here?
Its shade fills all the yard;
Its shade fills all the yard.
Leaf by leaf, and heart by heart,
It furls and unfurls with feelings still to spare.
Heartsick, on my pillow, the midnight rain:
Drip, drip, drip, it never ends;
Drip, drip, drip, it never ends.
It wounds this northerner's heart —
I'm not used to rising up to listen there.
poems.n: Written as a refugee in the south. The broad leaves of the plantain (banana) tree, each furled round its "heart", seem full of feeling; at night the rain drums on them without end. Only a "northerner" — someone who has lost her home in the north — would lie awake listening.

poems.s: summer sun mountains river boat oriole pine
z: 梅子黄时日日晴，小溪泛尽却山行。
绿阴不减来时路，添得黄鹂四五声。
e: In plum-yellow season, day after day is fair;
I've sailed the stream to its end, and now I take the mountain way.
The green shade's just as thick as on the road I came,
And four or five oriole songs are added on today.
poems.n: Early summer, the "plum-yellow" season, which is normally rainy — but every day is sunny. A happy little travel poem near Quzhou in Zhejiang: the same green shade going back as coming, with birdsong added.

poems.t: 临江仙·夜登小阁忆洛中旧游
poems.te: Immortal by the River: Climbing a Small Pavilion at Night, Remembering Old Days in Luoyang
poems.s: night moon river pavilion flowers fisher
z: 忆昔午桥桥上饮，坐中多是豪英。
长沟流月去无声。杏花疏影里，吹笛到天明。
二十余年如一梦，此身虽在堪惊。
闲登小阁看新晴。古今多少事，渔唱起三更。
e: I remember drinking long ago on Wuqiao Bridge,
With many heroes gathered in our company.
The moon flowed down the long canal, and made no sound;
In the sparse shadows of the apricot tree,
We played our flutes till dawn.
Twenty years and more have passed, like a dream;
That I'm still alive amazes me.
At leisure I climb the little pavilion to see the new-cleared sky;
How many things of past and present —
And the fishermen's songs rise at midnight, carelessly.
poems.n: Chen Yuyi remembers carefree nights with friends in Luoyang before the Jurchen invasion of 1126 swept it all away; twenty years later, a refugee in the south, he is amazed to be alive. 长沟流月去无声 — "the moon flowed silently away down the long channel" — is time itself, passing unnoticed. The ending dissolves all history into fishermen's songs at midnight.

poems.s: spring river boat clouds petals willow
z: 飞花两岸照船红，百里榆堤半日风。
卧看满天云不动，不知云与我俱东。
e: On both banks, flying blossoms light the boat with red;
A hundred li of elm-lined dyke in half a day of breeze.
Lying back, I watch the sky — the clouds don't move, I said —
Not knowing they and I are sailing east with equal ease.
poems.n: A boat trip with a fair wind: lying on deck, the poet sees the clouds standing still — until he realises they are moving east exactly as fast as he is. A charming observation of relative motion, and an image of going with the flow.

poems.te: The River All Red (My Hair Bristles with Rage)
poems.s: dusk rain tower clouds moon person flag
z: 怒发冲冠，凭栏处、潇潇雨歇。
抬望眼、仰天长啸，壮怀激烈。
三十功名尘与土，八千里路云和月。
莫等闲、白了少年头，空悲切。
靖康耻，犹未雪。臣子恨，何时灭！
驾长车，踏破贺兰山缺。
壮志饥餐胡虏肉，笑谈渴饮匈奴血。
待从头、收拾旧山河，朝天阙。
e: My hair bristles with rage beneath my cap;
I lean on the railing here,
As the soughing rain has ceased.
I raise my eyes,
Look up to heaven and give a long cry —
My heroic heart is fierce, unappeased.
Thirty years of fame and merit — dust and earth;
Eight thousand li of road, through cloud and moon, I've passed.
Don't waste your days in idleness
Till your young head turns white,
And you grieve in vain at last.
The shame of Jingkang
Is not yet wiped away;
A subject's hatred —
When will it be gone?
We'll drive our long war-chariots
To smash through the passes of Mount Helan.
Our hunger we'll feed with the invaders' flesh;
Laughing, our thirst we'll slake with their blood.
Wait till we've won back
All our old rivers and hills, from the start —
Then we'll go to the palace gates, our duty done.
poems.n: Traditionally attributed to Yue Fei (1103–1142), the general who fought to recover the north from the Jurchen Jin and was executed on false charges. "The shame of Jingkang" is the capture of two Song emperors by the Jin in 1127. Some scholars doubt Yue Fei wrote it — it surfaced only in the 16th century — but no lyric in Chinese is more often sung or more stirring; its savage images of revenge reflect a national trauma.

poems.t: 小重山（昨夜寒蛩不住鸣）
poems.te: Lesser Layered Hills (Last Night the Crickets)
poems.s: night autumn moon cottage person pine bamboo
z: 昨夜寒蛩不住鸣。惊回千里梦，已三更。
起来独自绕阶行。人悄悄，帘外月胧明。
白首为功名，旧山松竹老，阻归程。
欲将心事付瑶琴。知音少，弦断有谁听？
e: Last night the cold crickets chirped and would not cease,
And startled me back from a dream a thousand li away —
It was already the third watch.
I rose and paced alone around the steps.
All was quiet;
Beyond the blind, the moon shone hazy grey.
I've grown white-haired in seeking merit and a name;
On my home hills the pines and bamboos have grown old;
My road home is barred.
I'd tell my heart's concerns to my jade zither —
But those who understand are few:
If the strings should snap, who'd hear?
poems.n: A quieter lyric attributed to Yue Fei, probably written when the court was pressing for peace with the Jin and he was kept from fighting. The dream of the front, the sleepless pacing, and a zither with no one to hear (the story of Boya and Ziqi once more): loyalty with no one to understand it.

poems.te: Remembering the Prince: A Spring Song
poems.s: dusk spring rain willow tower flowers cottage
z: 萋萋芳草忆王孙，柳外楼高空断魂，杜宇声声不忍闻。
欲黄昏，雨打梨花深闭门。
e: The lush sweet grass makes me think of my prince far away;
Beyond the willows, in the high tower, my heart breaks in vain;
The cuckoo cries and cries — I cannot bear to hear.
It's almost dusk —
I shut the gate, while pear blossoms are beaten by the rain.
poems.n: "Remembering the Prince" alludes to the *Songs of Chu*: "the prince wanders and does not return; the spring grass grows thick." The last line — rain beating on pear blossoms behind a gate shut tight — is a perfect image of loneliness, later borrowed in *Dream of the Red Chamber*.

poems.s: night candle person cottage
z: 死去元知万事空，但悲不见九州同。
王师北定中原日，家祭无忘告乃翁。
e: I always knew that death would bring an end to everything;
I only grieve I'll never see the nation whole again.
The day the royal army wins back the north for our king,
At the family offering, don't forget to tell your father then.
poems.n: Lu You's last poem, written on his deathbed in 1210 at eighty-five. His whole life's wish — to see the north recovered from the Jurchen Jin — remains unfulfilled, so he asks his sons to report it to his spirit at the ancestral sacrifice. (Seventy years later, the Song itself fell to the Mongols.)

poems.te: Visiting a Village West of the Hills
poems.s: spring hills river willow flowers cottage moon person
z: 莫笑农家腊酒浑，丰年留客足鸡豚。
山重水复疑无路，柳暗花明又一村。
箫鼓追随春社近，衣冠简朴古风存。
从今若许闲乘月，拄杖无时夜叩门。
e: Don't laugh at the farmer's cloudy wine, brewed at the year's end;
In a good year there's chicken and pork enough to keep a guest.
Hill upon hill, stream upon stream — I thought the road would end;
Then dark willows, bright flowers — another village, blessed.
Flutes and drums go round: the spring festival draws near;
Their dress is plain, and the good old ways still linger here.
From now on, if I may come strolling by moonlight,
I'll knock upon your door with my staff, at any hour of night.
poems.n: 1167, in Lu You's home district near Shaoxing, after he was dismissed for urging war against the Jin. 山重水复疑无路，柳暗花明又一村 — "where hills and streams seem to end the road, past dark willows and bright flowers another village appears" — became the Chinese proverb for unexpected hope when all seems lost.

poems.s: spring willow wall pavilion petals peach
z: 红酥手，黄縢酒，满城春色宫墙柳。
东风恶，欢情薄。一怀愁绪，几年离索。错，错，错！
春如旧，人空瘦，泪痕红浥鲛绡透。
桃花落，闲池阁。山盟虽在，锦书难托。莫，莫，莫！
e: Your soft pink hands,
The wine with its yellow seal,
The whole town full of spring, and willows by the palace wall.
The east wind was cruel;
Our joy was thin and frail.
A heart full of sorrow,
Years of parting, all.
Wrong! Wrong! Wrong!
Spring is as it was;
You, thin for nothing, pale;
Rouged tears soak through your silken kerchief, every fall.
The peach blossoms drop
On the idle pond and hall.
Our mountain-vows still stand,
But no letter can be sent at all.
No! No! No!
poems.n: Lu You's first wife, his cousin Tang Wan, was forced to divorce him by his mother. Years later, around 1155, they met by chance in the Shen family garden in Shaoxing; she, remarried, sent him wine and food. He wrote this lyric on the garden wall. The "east wind" is his mother; the refrains 错 ("wrong!") and 莫 ("no more!") are cries of despair. Tang Wan answered with a lyric of her own — and died soon after.

poems.te: Song of Divination: The Plum Blossom
poems.s: dusk winter plum bridge rain wind
z: 驿外断桥边，寂寞开无主。
已是黄昏独自愁，更著风和雨。
无意苦争春，一任群芳妒。
零落成泥碾作尘，只有香如故。
e: Beyond the post-house, by a broken bridge,
It blooms alone, and no one owns it now.
Already dusk, and sad and on its own,
And wind and rain besides upon the bough.
It does not wish to fight for spring's acclaim;
Let all the other flowers envy, if they must.
Though fallen into mud and ground to dust,
Its fragrance stays — forever just the same.
poems.n: The plum blossom, flowering alone in winter by a broken bridge, battered by wind and rain, wanting nothing from spring — and keeping its fragrance even when trampled into dust — is Lu You's portrait of his own integrity, a patriot sidelined by the peace party. Mao Zedong wrote a famous reply to it.

poems.t: 十一月四日风雨大作（其二）
poems.te: A Great Storm on the Fourth Day of the Eleventh Month (II)
poems.s: night winter rain wind cottage person horse
z: 僵卧孤村不自哀，尚思为国戍轮台。
夜阑卧听风吹雨，铁马冰河入梦来。
e: Stiff in my bed in a lonely village, I don't pity my plight;
I still long to guard Luntai for my country's sake.
Late at night I lie and hear the wind lash the rain —
And armoured horses on frozen rivers gallop through my dreams till I wake.
poems.n: Written in 1192, when Lu You was sixty-seven and living in retirement. The winter storm outside becomes, in his dream, cavalry charging across frozen rivers on the northern frontier — the war he was never allowed to fight. Luntai was a Tang frontier fort in Central Asia.

poems.t: 秋夜将晓出篱门迎凉有感（其二）
poems.te: Going Out at the Hedge Gate Before Dawn on an Autumn Night (II)
poems.s: dawn autumn river mountains peaks
z: 三万里河东入海，五千仞岳上摩天。
遗民泪尽胡尘里，南望王师又一年。
e: Thirty thousand li, the Yellow River rolls east to the sea;
Five thousand fathoms, Mount Hua soars up to scrape the sky.
Under foreign dust, the people left behind have wept their eyes dry,
Looking south for the royal army — another year goes by.
poems.n: Before dawn on an autumn night in 1192, Lu You pictures the Yellow River and Mount Hua — symbols of the north, held by the Jin for sixty-five years — and the Chinese still living there, who have wept themselves dry waiting year after year for an army from the south that never comes.

poems.s: autumn snow river boat fort horse
z: 早岁那知世事艰，中原北望气如山。
楼船夜雪瓜洲渡，铁马秋风大散关。
塞上长城空自许，镜中衰鬓已先斑。
出师一表真名世，千载谁堪伯仲间。
e: When young, how could I know the world's affairs were hard?
I gazed north at the Central Plain, my spirit like a mountain high.
Towered warships, night snow, at the Guazhou crossing;
Armoured horses, autumn wind, at Dasan Pass nearby.
I once called myself the frontier's Great Wall — in vain;
My temples in the mirror are already turning grey.
The Memorial for the Campaign made Zhuge Liang's name eternal —
Who in a thousand years has been his equal, I'd say?
poems.n: 1186: Lu You at sixty-one, out of office. In youth he had served at the front — at Guazhou on the Yangtze, where the Song navy repelled the Jin in 1161, and at Dasan Pass in the north-west. A southern general once called himself "the Great Wall", and Lu You had thought the same of himself. Now he can only admire Zhuge Liang, whose memorial before marching north vowed to give his all until death.

poems.s: night spring rain tower cottage flowers window
z: 世味年来薄似纱，谁令骑马客京华？
小楼一夜听春雨，深巷明朝卖杏花。
矮纸斜行闲作草，晴窗细乳戏分茶。
素衣莫起风尘叹，犹及清明可到家。
e: These years the taste of the world has grown as thin as gauze;
Who made me ride a horse to be a guest in the capital again?
All night in my little tower I listen to the spring rain;
Tomorrow, in the deep lane, they'll be selling apricot blossoms, then.
On short paper, in slanting lines, I idly write in running hand;
By the sunny window I play at whisking tea to a fine, milky foam.
White robe, don't sigh about the dust and wind of the capital —
By Qingming, I'll still be in time to get back home.
poems.n: Hangzhou (Lin'an), 1186, waiting for an audience to receive a minor post. 小楼一夜听春雨，深巷明朝卖杏花 — "all night in my little tower I hear the spring rain; tomorrow, in the deep lane, they'll sell apricot blossoms" — is one of the loveliest couplets in Chinese, though its mood is idle frustration: an old patriot reduced to calligraphy and tea games. A Jin-dynasty line said the capital's dust turns white clothes black.

poems.te: Reading on a Winter Night: To My Son Yu
poems.s: night winter candle window person
z: 古人学问无遗力，少壮工夫老始成。
纸上得来终觉浅，绝知此事要躬行。
e: The ancients spared no effort in their studies, young or old;
What they began in youth was only finished when they aged.
What's learned from books will always seem a shallow hold —
To truly know a thing, in doing it you must engage.
poems.n: Advice to his youngest son on a winter night of reading. 纸上得来终觉浅，绝知此事要躬行 — "knowledge from paper is always shallow; to truly know, you must do it yourself" — is one of the most quoted maxims on learning in Chinese.

poems.t: 诉衷情（当年万里觅封侯）
poems.te: Telling My Heart (Once I Rode Ten Thousand Li)
poems.s: day cottage river person horse
z: 当年万里觅封侯，匹马戍梁州。
关河梦断何处？尘暗旧貂裘。
胡未灭，鬓先秋，泪空流。
此生谁料，心在天山，身老沧洲。
e: Once I rode ten thousand li to win a noble's place,
Alone on my horse, to guard Liangzhou.
Where did that dream of passes and of rivers break?
Dust dims my old sable coat now.
The foe is not destroyed;
My temples are already autumn-grey;
My tears flow on in vain.
Who'd have thought, in this life,
My heart would be in the Tianshan,
And my body grow old by the water, far away?
poems.n: An old man's lament. In 1172 Lu You served on the north-western front near Liangzhou (Hanzhong), planning a campaign that never came. Now his old army coat gathers dust; his heart is still at the Tianshan frontier, but his body grows old by the waters of his retirement (沧洲, the recluse's riverside).

poems.s: dusk spring sun bridge lake willow wall
z: 城上斜阳画角哀，沈园非复旧池台。
伤心桥下春波绿，曾是惊鸿照影来。
e: On the city wall, the sun slants low; the painted horn laments;
Shen Garden's pond and terrace aren't the ones I knew.
Beneath the bridge of heartbreak, the spring ripples are green —
Where once a startled swan's reflection came in view.
poems.n: Written in 1199, forty-four years after the meeting with Tang Wan in Shen Garden, when Lu You was seventy-five. The "startled swan" (惊鸿) is an image of a beautiful woman, from Cao Zhi's *Goddess of the Luo*: her reflection once passed over this very water.

poems.s: spring willow lake pavilion person
z: 梦断香消四十年，沈园柳老不吹绵。
此身行作稽山土，犹吊遗踪一泫然。
e: The dream has broken, the fragrance faded — forty years ago;
Shen Garden's willows are too old to shed their down.
This body will soon be earth on Kuaiji's hills below —
Yet still I mourn these traces, and my tears fall down.
poems.n: The second of the pair. Tang Wan had died some forty years before; the willows are old, and so is the poet, who knows he will soon lie buried in the hills of Kuaiji. Still he comes back to weep.

poems.te: Meeting Light Rain on the Road to Sword Gate
poems.s: spring rain peaks mountains rider
z: 衣上征尘杂酒痕，远游无处不消魂。
此身合是诗人未？细雨骑驴入剑门。
e: My robe is stained with travel dust and drops of wine;
On this long road, each place I pass has moved my heart.
Am I then meant to be a poet — is that line mine? —
In the fine rain, on a donkey, through Sword Gate I depart.
poems.n: 1172: Lu You was moved from the front line to a desk job in Chengdu — the end of his military hopes. Poets rode donkeys (Li Bai, Du Fu, Jia Dao all did); soldiers rode horses. Riding a donkey into Sichuan through the Sword Gate in the rain, he asks bitterly: is a poet all I am meant to be?

poems.s: winter plum mountains snow person
z: 闻道梅花坼晓风，雪堆遍满四山中。
何方可化身千亿，一树梅花一放翁。
e: I hear the plum blossoms have opened in the morning breeze,
Like drifts of snow all through the hills on every side.
If only I could split into a million selves, to please
Each plum tree with an old Fangweng beside!
poems.n: Lu You called himself Fangweng, "the Old Man Unrestrained". He loved plum blossom so much that he wished he could multiply himself, so that every tree could have its own admirer.

poems.t: 四时田园杂兴（昼出耘田夜绩麻）
poems.te: Seasonal Country Poems (By Day They Weed the Fields)
poems.s: summer fields cottage person two
z: 昼出耘田夜绩麻，村庄儿女各当家。
童孙未解供耕织，也傍桑阴学种瓜。
e: By day they weed the fields; by night they spin the hemp;
In the village, boys and girls all do their share.
The little grandkids can't yet plough or weave —
But in the mulberries' shade they learn to plant melons there.
poems.n: One of sixty "Miscellaneous Poems on the Four Seasons of Country Life", written in retirement around 1186. Everyone in the family works — even the smallest children, copying the grown-ups by planting melons in the shade. A warm, accurate picture of farm life.

poems.t: 四时田园杂兴（梅子金黄杏子肥）
poems.te: Seasonal Country Poems (The Plums Are Golden)
poems.s: summer fields cottage butterfly flowers
z: 梅子金黄杏子肥，麦花雪白菜花稀。
日长篱落无人过，惟有蜻蜓蛱蝶飞。
e: The plums are golden yellow, and the apricots are fat;
The wheat flowers snowy white, the rape flowers few.
The days are long; no one passes by the hedge —
Only dragonflies and butterflies flit through.
poems.n: Early summer, the busiest farming season: everyone is out in the fields, so the village is empty — except for dragonflies and butterflies. Colour and stillness in four lines.

poems.s: day bridge wall person two
z: 州桥南北是天街，父老年年等驾回。
忍泪失声询使者：几时真有六军来？
e: North and south of Zhou Bridge runs the old Imperial Way;
Year after year the elders wait for the emperor's return.
Fighting back their tears, they ask the envoy, voices breaking: "Say —
When will the royal army truly come? When will we learn?"
poems.n: In 1170 Fan Chengda travelled as envoy to the Jin court through the old Song capital Kaifeng, lost forty-three years before. At Zhou Bridge, on the old imperial avenue, Chinese living under Jin rule stopped him to ask, in tears, when the Song army would come. It never did.

poems.s: summer lotus lake pine butterfly
z: 泉眼无声惜细流，树阴照水爱晴柔。
小荷才露尖尖角，早有蜻蜓立上头。
e: The spring wells up in silence, loath to lose its slender flow;
The tree shade on the water loves the soft and sunny day.
A tiny lotus bud has only just poked up its tip —
And there's a dragonfly already standing on it, come to stay.
poems.n: Yang Wanli's genius for the tiny and fleeting. Everything in the little pond is treated with affection — the spring "treasures" its trickle, the shade "loves" the sunshine — and the climax is a dragonfly on a lotus bud. One of the first poems Chinese children learn.

poems.te: Seeing Off Lin Zifang from Jingci Temple at Dawn
poems.s: dawn summer sun lake lotus temple
z: 毕竟西湖六月中，风光不与四时同。
接天莲叶无穷碧，映日荷花别样红。
e: West Lake in the middle of the sixth month, after all,
Has scenery unlike the other seasons of the year:
The lotus leaves reach the sky, an endless sea of green;
The lotus flowers in the sun, a red beyond compare.
poems.n: Seeing a friend off at dawn from Jingci Temple on West Lake in midsummer. 接天莲叶无穷碧，映日荷花别样红 — "lotus leaves stretching to the sky in endless green; lotus flowers in the sun, a red like no other" — is the most famous description of West Lake in summer.

poems.te: Staying at Mr Xu's Inn in Xinshi (II)
poems.s: spring fields flowers butterfly cottage person
z: 篱落疏疏一径深，树头新绿未成阴。
儿童急走追黄蝶，飞入菜花无处寻。
e: A sparse hedge, and a little path that winds on deep;
The treetops' new green leaves don't give much shade as yet.
The children run full tilt to catch a yellow butterfly —
It flies into the yellow rape flowers — and that's the end of it!
poems.n: Spring at a village inn. The joke is all in the colour: a yellow butterfly vanishes into a field of yellow rapeseed flowers, and the children cannot find it. Pure delight.

poems.te: Rising from a Nap in Early Summer (I)
poems.s: summer window cottage willow person
z: 梅子留酸软齿牙，芭蕉分绿与窗纱。
日长睡起无情思，闲看儿童捉柳花。
e: The plums have left a sourness, setting my teeth on edge;
The plantain shares its green with the window's gauze.
The days are long; I wake from my nap with nothing on my mind,
And idly watch the children catching willow-down, with no cause.
poems.n: A drowsy early-summer afternoon: the sour taste of green plums, green light through the window, children chasing catkins. Nothing happens — and that is the pleasure.

poems.te: The Phoenix Hairpin (The World's Ways Are Cold)
poems.s: dusk rain petals pavilion wall person
z: 世情薄，人情恶，雨送黄昏花易落。
晓风干，泪痕残。欲笺心事，独语斜阑。难，难，难！
人成各，今非昨，病魂常似秋千索。
角声寒，夜阑珊。怕人寻问，咽泪装欢。瞒，瞒，瞒！
e: The world's ways are cold,
And people cruel;
Rain sends the dusk, and flowers fall with ease.
The morning wind dries
My tears' last trace.
I want to write my heart out —
Instead I lean on the rail and speak to the breeze.
Hard! Hard! Hard!
We've gone our ways;
Today's not yesterday;
My sick soul swings like a swing's rope, never still.
The bugle's cold;
The night's near done.
Afraid that people ask,
I swallow tears and feign a smile, against my will.
Hide! Hide! Hide!
poems.n: Tang Wan's answer to Lu You, written — tradition says — beneath his lyric on the garden wall. Her pain is doubled: she must hide it from her new husband and from everyone around her. She died not long after. (Some scholars believe the lyric was later reconstructed from fragments.)

poems.s: spring flowers river sun person
z: 胜日寻芳泗水滨，无边光景一时新。
等闲识得东风面，万紫千红总是春。
e: On a fine day I seek the flowers by the River Si;
The boundless scenery is all at once made new.
I see the east wind's face, as easily as can be —
Ten thousand purples, a thousand reds: it's spring all through.
poems.n: On the surface a spring outing. But the Si River was where Confucius taught, and in Zhu Xi's day it lay in Jin territory — he never went there. The "spring" is the vitality of Confucius's teaching, whose countless forms all express one principle. 万紫千红 is now an everyday phrase for profusion and splendour.

poems.s: day lake clouds pavilion
z: 半亩方塘一鉴开，天光云影共徘徊。
问渠那得清如许？为有源头活水来。
e: A small square pond lies open like a mirror to the sky,
Where daylight and cloud shadows wander to and fro.
How can it stay so clear? I ask it — and here's why:
From its source, the living water keeps on flowing in below.
poems.n: The mind is a pond, kept clear only by fresh water flowing in — constant study and reflection. 源头活水, "living water from the source", is now a common phrase for fresh ideas and inspiration.

poems.s: spring river boat sail
z: 昨夜江边春水生，艨艟巨舰一毛轻。
向来枉费推移力，此日中流自在行。
e: Last night the spring floods rose along the river,
And the huge warship floats as light as down.
All our efforts once to push it were in vain —
Today in midstream it sails freely on its own.
poems.n: Understanding cannot be forced. Struggle uselessly with a problem, and one day — when enough knowledge has accumulated, like a spring flood — it moves easily of itself.

poems.te: The Charms of Niannu: Crossing Dongting
poems.s: night autumn moon lake boat stars
z: 洞庭青草，近中秋、更无一点风色。
玉鉴琼田三万顷，著我扁舟一叶。
素月分辉，明河共影，表里俱澄澈。
悠然心会，妙处难与君说。
应念岭表经年，孤光自照，肝胆皆冰雪。
短发萧骚襟袖冷，稳泛沧溟空阔。
尽挹西江，细斟北斗，万象为宾客。
扣舷独啸，不知今夕何夕！
e: Dongting and Green Grass Lake,
Near the Mid-Autumn day,
Not one breath of wind at all.
A jade mirror, a crystal field, thirty thousand acres wide,
Bears my one small leaf of a boat.
The white moon spreads its light;
The Milky Way shares its reflection;
Inside and out, all is clear as crystal.
Serenely my heart understands —
But the wonder is too fine to tell to you.
I think of my year beyond the Ridges,
Where the lonely moon shone on me alone,
And my heart and soul were clear as ice and snow.
Now, my thin hair tousled, my sleeves chilled,
I drift on the vast, wide waters, steady and slow.
I'll scoop up all the Western River,
Pour it carefully with the Dipper for a ladle,
And make all things in the world my guests.
I tap the side of my boat and whistle alone —
What night is this? I do not know!
poems.n: 1166: Zhang Xiaoxiang, dismissed from his post at Guilin (beyond the Five Ridges), crosses Dongting Lake on a windless night near Mid-Autumn. The lake becomes a mirror for a soul "clear as ice and snow". Then a cosmic banquet: the West River for wine, the Big Dipper for a ladle, the universe for guests — inspired by Su Shi's *Red Cliff* rhapsodies.

poems.s: night spring lantern stars flowers palace
z: 东风夜放花千树，更吹落、星如雨。
宝马雕车香满路。凤箫声动，玉壶光转，一夜鱼龙舞。
蛾儿雪柳黄金缕，笑语盈盈暗香去。
众里寻他千百度，蓦然回首，那人却在，灯火阑珊处。
e: The east wind blows by night, and a thousand trees burst into flower,
And blows down showers of stars like rain.
Fine horses, carved carriages — the road is filled with scent.
The phoenix flutes are playing,
The jade-pot moon is turning,
All night the fish and dragon lanterns dance again.
In moth-wing ornaments and gold-threaded willow sprays,
The ladies pass, laughing, a faint perfume behind.
A thousand times I searched the crowd for her —
Then suddenly I turned my head,
And there she was,
Where the lantern light was dim, where few would find.
poems.n: The Lantern Festival in Hangzhou: fireworks like flowering trees and falling stars, lanterns shaped like fish and dragons, women in their finery. Amid it all the poet seeks one person — and finds her apart from the crowd, where the lights are fading. Wang Guowei cited the last lines as the third and highest of the "three stages" of any great achievement: after long searching, sudden discovery. Many read "her" as the poet's own lonely integrity.

poems.t: 破阵子·为陈同甫赋壮词以寄之
poems.te: Breaking Through the Ranks: A Heroic Lyric for Chen Tongfu
poems.s: night candle fort flag horse rider
z: 醉里挑灯看剑，梦回吹角连营。
八百里分麾下炙，五十弦翻塞外声。沙场秋点兵。
马作的卢飞快，弓如霹雳弦惊。
了却君王天下事，赢得生前身后名。可怜白发生！
e: Drunk, I trim the lamp to gaze upon my sword;
I wake from dreams to bugles sounding through the camps.
The roast of the great ox is shared among the men;
The fifty-stringed zithers play the frontier's songs —
On autumn fields of battle, the troops are mustered, ranks on ranks.
The horses fly as swift as Dilu;
The bowstrings twang like thunder in the night.
To finish for my king the task of winning back the world,
And win a name in life, and after death —
But alas — my hair's gone white!
poems.n: Written for his friend Chen Liang (Tongfu), another patriot who longed to recover the north. Xin Qiji, in his late forties and long kept from command, dreams of leading an army again — a whole battle in nine lines — and the last line drops him back into reality: an old man who will never get the chance. Dilu was the horse that leapt a river to save Liu Bei.

poems.t: 永遇乐·京口北固亭怀古
poems.te: Joy of Eternal Union: Remembering the Past at Beigu Pavilion, Jingkou
poems.s: dusk sun river tower mountains flag
z: 千古江山，英雄无觅，孙仲谋处。
舞榭歌台，风流总被，雨打风吹去。
斜阳草树，寻常巷陌，人道寄奴曾住。
想当年，金戈铁马，气吞万里如虎。
元嘉草草，封狼居胥，赢得仓皇北顾。
四十三年，望中犹记，烽火扬州路。
可堪回首，佛狸祠下，一片神鸦社鼓。
凭谁问：廉颇老矣，尚能饭否？
e: These rivers and these hills endure a thousand years,
But heroes are no longer found —
No Sun Quan, who once ruled here.
The dancing halls and singing towers, all their style,
Are beaten down by rain, and blown away by wind.
In the slanting sunlight, grass and trees,
An ordinary lane —
Where Jinu lived, they say.
I think of those years:
Gilded spears and armoured steeds,
His spirit swallowing ten thousand li like a tiger in his day.
In Yuanjia's reign, in reckless haste,
They tried to carve their name on far Langjuxu,
And won only a panicked glance back north, in fear.
