Forty-three years —
I gaze, and still recall
The beacon fires along the Yangzhou road, so near.
How can I bear to look back now?
Below the shrine of the Tartar khan,
Sacred crows and village drums are all I hear.
Who will come and ask of me:
"Lian Po is old —
Can he still eat his fill, this year?"
poems.n: 1205: Xin Qiji, sixty-five, is given a post at last at Jingkou (Zhenjiang) on the Yangtze, as the court rashly prepares to attack the Jin. He recalls Sun Quan, who held the south against the north, and Liu Yu ("Jinu"), who marched north to retake the old capitals — and warns, through the disastrous rush north of the Yuanjia era (450), against an ill-prepared war. Forty-three years before, he had fled south through war-torn Yangzhou. Now the locals worship at a shrine to Foli, the northern khan who invaded — they have forgotten. And no one asks whether old Xin, like the aged general Lian Po, who ate a huge meal to prove he could still fight, is fit to serve.

poems.te: West River Moon: Walking at Night on the Yellow Sand Road
poems.s: night summer moon stars fields cottage bridge birds
z: 明月别枝惊鹊，清风半夜鸣蝉。
稻花香里说丰年，听取蛙声一片。
七八个星天外，两三点雨山前。
旧时茅店社林边，路转溪桥忽见。
e: The bright moon on a far branch startles a magpie;
At midnight, in the cool breeze, the cicadas sing.
In the scent of rice flowers, they talk of a good harvest's yield —
Listen: a chorus of frogs from everything.
Seven or eight stars beyond the sky;
Two or three drops of rain before the hill.
The old thatched inn by the shrine's woods —
The road turns at the creek bridge — and there it is still!
poems.n: A night walk through the countryside near Shangrao, where Xin Qiji lived in enforced retirement. Magpie, cicadas, rice flowers and frogs make a summer night's music; a sudden shower sends him looking for shelter — and there, round the bend, is the old inn he had forgotten. Pure joy in small things.

poems.s: summer cottage river grass lotus two person
z: 茅檐低小，溪上青青草。
醉里吴音相媚好，白发谁家翁媪？
大儿锄豆溪东，中儿正织鸡笼。
最喜小儿亡赖，溪头卧剥莲蓬。
e: The thatched eaves are low and small;
Along the creek the grass grows green.
Tipsy, in soft Wu dialect, so sweet to hear —
Whose white-haired couple is this I've seen?
The eldest boy is hoeing beans east of the stream;
The middle one is weaving a coop for the hens.
But best of all, the youngest, the little rascal,
Sprawled by the creek, peeling lotus pods.
poems.n: A happy farm family seen by the retired general: an old couple chatting tipsily in their soft local dialect, and three sons — two hard at work, and the youngest, a lazy scamp, lying by the creek snacking on lotus seeds. Every Chinese child learns it.

poems.te: Ugly Slave: Written on a Wall on the Road to Mount Bo
poems.s: autumn tower mountains person wind
z: 少年不识愁滋味，爱上层楼。爱上层楼，为赋新词强说愁。
而今识尽愁滋味，欲说还休。欲说还休，却道天凉好个秋！
e: When young, I didn't know what sorrow tasted like, back then;
I loved to climb up high towers.
I loved to climb up high towers,
To write new songs, and fake a sorrow with my pen.
Now I have tasted every sorrow on the way,
I want to speak, but stop.
I want to speak, but stop —
And only say: "How cool it is — a fine autumn day!"
poems.n: Written on a wall along the road to Mount Bo during his long retirement. The young poet, knowing nothing of grief, invented it to sound profound; the old man, who knows it all too well, can only talk about the weather. One of the most quoted lyrics in Chinese.

poems.te: Buddhist Barbarian: Written on a Wall at Zaokou, Jiangxi
poems.s: dusk river mountains tower birds
z: 郁孤台下清江水，中间多少行人泪。
西北望长安，可怜无数山。
青山遮不住，毕竟东流去。
江晚正愁余，山深闻鹧鸪。
e: Below Yugu Terrace runs the clear river's flow —
How many refugees' tears are mingled in its stream!
I gaze north-west toward Chang'an — but no:
Alas, the countless mountains block the scene.
The green hills cannot hold it back —
At last, it flows away east.
At evening on the river, my heart is sad;
Deep in the hills, the partridge cries, "You cannot go!"
poems.n: Zaokou in Jiangxi, where in 1129 Jin cavalry pursued the Song empress dowager and refugees fled south. "Chang'an" stands for the lost northern capital. The mountains cannot stop the river — as obstacles cannot stop the patriot's will — but the partridge's cry, heard as "you cannot go on, brother", ends the poem in doubt.

poems.t: 南乡子·登京口北固亭有怀
poems.te: Southern Village: Thoughts on Climbing Beigu Pavilion at Jingkou
poems.s: day tower river mountains flag
z: 何处望神州？满眼风光北固楼。
千古兴亡多少事？悠悠。不尽长江滚滚流。
年少万兜鍪，坐断东南战未休。
天下英雄谁敌手？曹刘。生子当如孙仲谋。
e: Where can I gaze upon the Central Land?
All I see is the view from Beigu's tower.
How many rises and falls through the ages, past understanding? —
On and on,
Like the endless Yangtze, rolling, hour after hour.
Young, he led ten thousand men in helmets,
And held the south-east, fighting on without rest.
Who among the heroes of the world could match him?
Cao and Liu alone.
"If I have a son," said Cao, "let him be like Sun Quan — the best."
poems.n: Jingkou again, 1204. The "Divine Land" (神州) is the lost north. Sun Quan (Zhongmou), as a young man, held the south against Cao Cao and Liu Bei; Cao Cao himself said, "A son should be like Sun Zhongmou." The implied contrast with the feeble Song court is plain.

poems.te: Water Dragon Chant: Climbing the Pavilion of the Joyful Heart at Jiankang
poems.s: dusk autumn sun tower river mountains geese
z: 楚天千里清秋，水随天去秋无际。
遥岑远目，献愁供恨，玉簪螺髻。
落日楼头，断鸿声里，江南游子。
把吴钩看了，栏杆拍遍，无人会，登临意。
休说鲈鱼堪脍，尽西风，季鹰归未？
求田问舍，怕应羞见，刘郎才气。
可惜流年，忧愁风雨，树犹如此！
倩何人唤取，红巾翠袖，揾英雄泪！
e: A thousand li of southern sky in clear autumn's light;
The water runs with the sky; autumn has no end.
I gaze at the distant hills —
They offer only sorrow, bring only regret,
Like jade hairpins, like conch-shell knots of hair.
At sunset on the tower,
Among the cries of a lone wild goose,
A wanderer in the south am I.
I've stared at my Wu sword,
And slapped the railings all along —
But no one understands
Why I have climbed up here.
Don't tell me the perch is fine for slicing —
The west wind blows; yet has Zhang Han gone home?
To seek out fields and houses for myself
Would make me blush to face
Liu Bei and his great heart.
Alas, the years flow by,
In worry, wind and rain —
Even the trees grow old like this!
Whom can I ask to call
A girl in red scarf and green sleeves,
To wipe away a hero's tears?
poems.n: Nanjing, 1174. Xin Qiji, a northerner who came south to fight, climbs the Pavilion of the Joyful Heart. The distant hills, like a woman's hairpins and topknots, offer only sorrow; he slaps every railing in frustration. He will not go home like Zhang Han, who resigned to eat the perch of his native river, nor buy land like the petty men Liu Bei despised. As the general Huan Wen said, seeing willows he had planted grown huge: "If even trees age like this, how can men bear it?" — and there is no one to wipe his tears.

poems.t: 摸鱼儿（更能消几番风雨）
poems.te: Groping for Fish (How Many More Storms)
poems.s: dusk spring sun petals willow tower mist
z: 更能消、几番风雨，匆匆春又归去。
惜春长怕花开早，何况落红无数。
春且住，见说道、天涯芳草无归路。
怨春不语。算只有殷勤，画檐蛛网，尽日惹飞絮。
长门事，准拟佳期又误，蛾眉曾有人妒。
千金纵买相如赋，脉脉此情谁诉？
君莫舞，君不见、玉环飞燕皆尘土！
闲愁最苦。休去倚危栏，斜阳正在，烟柳断肠处。
e: How many more storms can spring withstand?
In haste, the spring is leaving once again.
Loving spring, I always feared the flowers would bloom too soon —
And now, the fallen petals past all count!
Spring, stay a while!
They say the fragrant grass at the world's end has blocked your way back home.
I'm angry that the spring says not a word.
It seems that only, faithfully,
The spiders' webs beneath the painted eaves
Spend all day catching willow-down that drifts.
That business at the Long Gate Palace —
The promised day again was missed;
Her moth-brows once made others burn with spite.
Though she paid a thousand gold for Xiangru's plea,
Who can she tell of this deep, silent love?
You others, do not dance!
Don't you see? Yuhuan and Feiyan are dust!
Idle sorrow is the bitterest.
Don't go and lean upon the high rail —
The setting sun is there,
Where misty willows break the heart.
poems.n: 1179, as Xin Qiji was transferred yet again, far from any chance to fight. On the surface, a lament for the passing of spring and for Empress Chen, who, abandoned in the Long Gate Palace, paid the poet Sima Xiangru a thousand gold for a rhapsody to win back the emperor's love. Underneath, the sorrow of a loyal servant pushed aside by jealous rivals — who, the poem warns, will turn to dust like the favourite consorts Yang Yuhuan and Zhao Feiyan. The emperor is said to have been displeased when he read it.

poems.te: Congratulating the Bridegroom (How Old I've Grown)
poems.s: day mountains clouds window cup person wind
z: 甚矣吾衰矣。
怅平生、交游零落，只今余几！
白发空垂三千丈，一笑人间万事。
问何物、能令公喜。
我见青山多妩媚，料青山、见我应如是。
情与貌，略相似。
一尊搔首东窗里。
想渊明、停云诗就，此时风味。
江左沉酣求名者，岂识浊醪妙理。
回首叫、云飞风起。
不恨古人吾不见，恨古人、不见吾狂耳。
知我者，二三子。
e: How old I've grown, how frail!
I grieve my lifelong friends have scattered far —
How many now remain?
My white hair hangs for nothing, three thousand yards long;
With one laugh I dismiss the world's affairs.
What could still make me glad, you ask?
I find the green mountains so charming —
And I'd guess they find me charming too.
In heart and looks,
We're much alike, we two.
A cup of wine; I scratch my head by the east window;
I think of Tao Yuanming, his "Lingering Clouds" just done —
He must have felt like this.
Those south of the River, drunk on fame —
What do they know of the deep wisdom of cloudy wine?
I turn and shout — the clouds fly, the wind rises!
I don't regret I never saw the ancients;
I regret the ancients never saw my wild delight.
Those who know me
Are just two or three.
poems.n: Written in retirement around 1200, in a pavilion named after Tao Yuanming's poem "Lingering Clouds", which mourns absent friends. 我见青山多妩媚，料青山见我应如是 — "I find the green mountains charming; I expect they find me so too" — is among the most quoted lines Xin Qiji wrote: a lonely man finding his only equal in the mountains. "The clouds fly, the wind rises" echoes Liu Bang's *Song of the Great Wind*.

poems.t: 鹧鸪天（陌上柔桑破嫩芽）
poems.te: Partridge Sky (Tender Mulberries Bud by the Path)
poems.s: dusk spring fields hills crows cottage flag river flowers
z: 陌上柔桑破嫩芽，东邻蚕种已生些。
平冈细草鸣黄犊，斜日寒林点暮鸦。
山远近，路横斜，青旗沽酒有人家。
城中桃李愁风雨，春在溪头荠菜花。
e: Along the paths, the tender mulberries put out their buds;
Next door, a few silkworm eggs have hatched already, small.
On the flat ridge, the yellow calves low in the fine grass;
In the slanting sun, the cold woods are dotted with crows, all.
Hills far and near,
Roads crossing at a slant;
Where a blue flag flies, a cottage sells its wine.
In town, the peach and plum trees fear the wind and rain —
But spring is by the creek, where shepherd's-purse flowers shine.
poems.n: Village spring in Xin Qiji's retirement. The last couplet becomes philosophy: the delicate city flowers, peach and plum, beloved of the fashionable, are battered by every storm, while spring truly lives in the humble shepherd's-purse by the creek — like the hardy common people, or a retired official in the countryside.

poems.t: 太常引·建康中秋夜为吕叔潜赋
poems.te: Taichang Melody: Mid-Autumn Night at Jiankang, for Lü Shuqian
poems.s: night autumn moon clouds person cup
z: 一轮秋影转金波，飞镜又重磨。
把酒问姮娥：被白发、欺人奈何？
乘风好去，长空万里，直下看山河。
斫去桂婆娑，人道是、清光更多。
e: The autumn moon's round shadow turns and spills its golden waves;
The flying mirror's polished bright again.
Wine in hand, I ask the Moon Goddess:
"White hair is cheating me — what can be done, and when?"
I'd ride the wind and soar away,
Ten thousand li across the sky,
And look straight down on all the rivers and the hills below.
I'd chop the swaying cassia down —
For then, they say, the moon's clear light would brighter glow.
poems.n: Mid-Autumn, 1174, in Nanjing. A cassia tree was said to grow in the moon, endlessly chopped at by the immortal Wu Gang. Xin Qiji would cut it down so the moon shines brighter — read as a wish to clear away the corrupt officials who darken the court.

poems.te: West River Moon: Venting My Feelings
poems.s: night pine person moon jar
z: 醉里且贪欢笑，要愁那得工夫。
近来始觉古人书，信着全无是处。
昨夜松边醉倒，问松我醉何如。
只疑松动要来扶，以手推松曰去！
e: When I'm drunk, I'll just enjoy a laugh —
Who has the time to worry?
Lately I've come to feel the books of the ancient wise
Are useless, if you trust them through and through.
Last night, beside a pine, I fell down drunk;
I asked the pine, "How drunk am I?" — I knew
The pine was moving to help me up, it seemed —
I pushed the pine and said, "Away with you!"
poems.n: A comic self-portrait of the frustrated hero in retirement. "Believing everything in books is worse than having no books" was a saying of Mencius; Xin Qiji's books promised that loyalty would be rewarded, and life has proved them wrong. Then the pine-tree scene — pure comedy with an edge: even drunk, he refuses help.

poems.t: 清平乐·独宿博山王氏庵
poems.te: Pure Serene Music: Alone for the Night at the Wang Family Hut on Mount Bo
poems.s: night autumn rain wind pine cottage candle
z: 绕床饥鼠，蝙蝠翻灯舞。
屋上松风吹急雨，破纸窗间自语。
平生塞北江南，归来华发苍颜。
布被秋宵梦觉，眼前万里江山。
e: Hungry rats scurry round the bed;
Bats flit and dance around the lamp.
On the roof, the pine wind drives a sudden rain;
The torn paper window mutters to itself in the damp.
All my life — north of the frontier, south of the River;
I've come home grey-haired, my face grown old.
Under a cotton quilt I wake from a dream on an autumn night —
Before my eyes, ten thousand li of rivers and hills unrolled.
poems.n: A night alone in a ruined hut on Mount Bo: rats, bats, rain, a flapping paper window. Then the last line — waking from a dream, he sees "ten thousand li of rivers and mountains": the lost lands of the north he still dreams of winning back.

poems.s: dusk winter moon bridge wall river fields
z: 淮左名都，竹西佳处，解鞍少驻初程。
过春风十里，尽荠麦青青。
自胡马窥江去后，废池乔木，犹厌言兵。
渐黄昏，清角吹寒，都在空城。
杜郎俊赏，算而今、重到须惊。
纵豆蔻词工，青楼梦好，难赋深情。
二十四桥仍在，波心荡、冷月无声。
念桥边红药，年年知为谁生？
e: The famous city east of the Huai,
The lovely spot of Bamboo West —
I unsaddle, and stop on my journey here a while.
Down Du Mu's "ten li of spring breeze"
There's only shepherd's purse and wheat, green mile on mile.
Since the Tartar horses came to spy on the River and left,
The ruined pools and towering trees
Still hate to hear of war.
As dusk draws on,
The clear bugles blow the cold
Through the empty city, as before.
Du Mu, so fine a judge of beauty,
If he came back now, would be dismayed.
Though his "cardamom" lines were skilled,
His "dream in the blue towers" sweet,
He could not sing this grief, so deeply laid.
The Twenty-four Bridges still remain;
In the waves, the cold moon rocks without a sound.
I think of the red peonies by the bridge —
For whom do they still bloom, year after year?
poems.n: Jiang Kui passed through Yangzhou in the winter of 1176, fifteen years after a Jin invasion devastated it. He sets the city of Du Mu's poems — "ten li of spring breeze", "cardamom" girls, the Twenty-four Bridges in moonlight — against the cold, empty ruin. "The ruined pools and old trees still hate to speak of war" is famous: even the trees are traumatised.

poems.t: 点绛唇·丁未冬过吴松作
poems.te: Rouged Lips: Passing Wusong in the Winter of 1187
poems.s: dusk winter lake geese clouds peaks bridge willow
z: 燕雁无心，太湖西畔随云去。
数峰清苦，商略黄昏雨。
第四桥边，拟共天随住。
今何许？凭阑怀古，残柳参差舞。
e: The wild geese from the north have no cares;
West of Lake Tai, they follow the clouds away.
A few peaks, cold and bleak,
Are planning the rain at the end of the day.
Here by the Fourth Bridge,
I'd live with Tiansui, if I could.
Where is he now?
I lean on the rail and think of the past,
While broken willows dance, as willows would.
poems.n: Written passing Wusong near Suzhou, where the Tang poet Lu Guimeng ("Tiansui"), a recluse Jiang Kui revered, had lived. The mountains "discussing" the evening rain is one of the most celebrated personifications in the *ci*. The wandering geese, free of care, are everything the drifting poet is not.

poems.te: Written at an Inn in Lin'an
poems.s: day lake hills tower boat palace
z: 山外青山楼外楼，西湖歌舞几时休？
暖风熏得游人醉，直把杭州作汴州。
e: Green hills beyond green hills, and towers beyond towers —
When will the songs and dances on West Lake be done?
The warm breeze makes the pleasure-seekers drunk for hours,
Till they take Hangzhou for Bianzhou, the capital that's gone.
poems.n: Written on the wall of an inn in Hangzhou (Lin'an), the Southern Song's "temporary" capital, by an otherwise unknown scholar. Comfortable by West Lake, the court had forgotten the lost northern capital, Bianzhou (Kaifeng); the "warm wind" is the soft air of pleasure. The sharpest political quatrain of the age.

poems.s: night summer rain lake candle window person
z: 黄梅时节家家雨，青草池塘处处蛙。
有约不来过夜半，闲敲棋子落灯花。
e: In the season of yellow plums, there's rain at every door;
The grassy ponds are full of frogs croaking everywhere.
My guest has promised to come, but it's past midnight now —
I idly tap the chessmen, and the lamp's charred wick falls there.
poems.n: A friend was to come for a game of weiqi on a rainy summer night. Midnight passes; the poet sits tapping the stones — and knocks off the charred "lamp-flower" of the wick, a traditional omen that a visitor is coming. Impatience, disappointment and a hint of humour in one gesture.

poems.te: Verse on "The Ordinary Mind Is the Way"
poems.s: day mountains flowers moon
z: 春有百花秋有月，夏有凉风冬有雪。
若无闲事挂心头，便是人间好时节。
e: Spring has its hundred flowers; autumn has its moon;
Summer has its cool breeze, and winter has its snow.
If no idle worries hang upon your heart,
Then every season is the finest one we know.
poems.n: A verse by the Chan (Zen) master Wumen Huikai from *The Gateless Gate*, on the koan "the ordinary mind is the Way". Every season brings its gift; the only obstacle to joy is the clutter in one's own mind.

poems.te: Tang Duo Ling: Sorrow at Parting
poems.s: night autumn moon tower willow river boat
z: 何处合成愁？离人心上秋。纵芭蕉、不雨也飕飕。
都道晚凉天气好，有明月、怕登楼。
年事梦中休，花空烟水流。燕辞归、客尚淹留。
垂柳不萦裙带住，漫长是、系行舟。
e: What makes up sorrow, as it's made?
Autumn upon a parted heart.
The plantains sigh and rustle, though no rain has come.
They all say the evening cool is fine —
But with the moon so bright, I dare not climb the tower, apart.
The year's affairs have ended, like a dream;
The flowers gone, the misty waters flow.
The swallow's gone home; the traveller lingers still.
The willows would not twine her skirt-sash, to keep her here —
Instead they tie my boat forever, and won't let go.
poems.n: The famous opening is a character riddle: 愁 (sorrow) is made of 秋 (autumn) on top of 心 (heart) — "autumn on the heart of one who is parted". Wu Wenying's lover has left; the willows that should have held her back hold only his boat.

poems.s: summer rain fields mountains river person birds
z: 绿遍山原白满川，子规声里雨如烟。
乡村四月闲人少，才了蚕桑又插田。
e: Green covers hills and plains; the streams are full and white;
The cuckoo calls; the rain falls fine as mist.
In the village, the fourth month leaves no one idle in sight —
The silkworms done, the rice is planted, and nothing's missed.
poems.n: Early summer in the Zhejiang countryside: flooded paddies white with sky, green hills, the cuckoo — whose call was heard as "plant the rice!" — and a village where no one has a moment to spare.

poems.s: night winter moon plum window cottage two
z: 寒夜客来茶当酒，竹炉汤沸火初红。
寻常一样窗前月，才有梅花便不同。
e: A guest arrives on a cold night; I serve him tea for wine;
In the bamboo stove the water boils; the fire has just turned red.
The same old moon that always shines outside the window —
But tonight, with plum blossom, it's a different moon instead.
poems.n: The simplest hospitality: tea instead of wine on a winter night. The moon is the same as ever — but the plum blossom, and the friend, make it new. 寻常一样窗前月，才有梅花便不同 is quoted for how a small touch, or a friend, transforms the ordinary.

poems.s: day sea boat clouds rain person
z: 辛苦遭逢起一经，干戈寥落四周星。
山河破碎风飘絮，身世浮沉雨打萍。
惶恐滩头说惶恐，零丁洋里叹零丁。
人生自古谁无死？留取丹心照汗青。
e: My trials all began when I passed the exam on the Classics;
Four years now, amid the dying wars, we've fought on, few.
The land is shattered, like willow-down blown in the wind;
My life sinks and rises, like duckweed the rain beats through.
At Panic Rapids, I spoke of panic;
On the Lonely Sea, I sigh, alone.
Since ancient times, who has ever lived and never died?
Let my loyal heart shine on in history, my own.
poems.n: Written in 1279 as a prisoner on a Mongol warship crossing the Lingdingyang ("Lonely Sea") near today's Hong Kong, on the way to witness the final destruction of the Song fleet. The Mongol commander asked Wen Tianxiang to write urging the Song loyalists to surrender; he handed over this poem instead. Panic Rapids (惶恐滩) was where he had once retreated in defeat. The last couplet — 人生自古谁无死？留取丹心照汗青 — is the most famous declaration of patriotic faith in Chinese. He was executed in 1283.

poems.te: The Beautiful Lady Yu: Listening to the Rain
poems.s: night rain temple candle person
z: 少年听雨歌楼上，红烛昏罗帐。
壮年听雨客舟中，江阔云低、断雁叫西风。
而今听雨僧庐下，鬓已星星也。
悲欢离合总无情，一任阶前、点滴到天明。
e: When young, I heard the rain in towers of song,
Red candles dim behind the silken curtains, all night long.
In my prime, I heard the rain in a traveller's boat,
The river wide, the clouds hung low,
A lone goose crying in the west wind's throat.
Now I hear the rain beneath a temple's eaves;
My hair is flecked with grey like frost.
Grief and joy, parting and meeting — none of them has a heart;
Let the rain drip on the steps before me
Until the dawn.
poems.n: A whole life in three rains. The young man hears rain in the pleasure houses; the grown man, in a boat on the river amid war; the old man, after the fall of the Song, under the eaves of a Buddhist temple, where he lets the rain fall without feeling. One of the most perfectly shaped lyrics in the *ci*.

poems.te: A Sprig of Plum: Passing Wujiang by Boat
poems.s: spring rain wind river boat bridge flag
z: 一片春愁待酒浇。江上舟摇，楼上帘招。
秋娘渡与泰娘桥，风又飘飘，雨又萧萧。
何日归家洗客袍？银字笙调，心字香烧。
流光容易把人抛，红了樱桃，绿了芭蕉。
e: A spell of spring sorrow waits for wine to drown;
The boat rocks on the river;
The tavern banner beckons from the tower down.
Past Qiuniang's Ferry and Tainiang's Bridge —
The wind keeps gusting,
The rain keeps falling down.
When shall I go home and wash my travel-stained gown,
Tune the silver-lettered pipes,
And burn the heart-shaped incense down?
How easily time flies, and leaves us all behind:
It's reddened the cherries,
And greened the plantain leaves.
poems.n: Written as Jiang Jie drifted as a refugee after the Mongol conquest. The last couplet — time "reddens the cherries, greens the plantains" — turns the passing of time into colour, using adjectives as verbs, and is one of the most quoted endings in the *ci*.

poems.te: Groping for Fish: The Goose Mound
poems.s: dusk winter snow geese clouds mountains river
z: 问世间，情是何物，直教生死相许？
天南地北双飞客，老翅几回寒暑。
欢乐趣，离别苦，就中更有痴儿女。
君应有语，渺万里层云，千山暮雪，只影向谁去？
横汾路，寂寞当年箫鼓，荒烟依旧平楚。
招魂楚些何嗟及，山鬼暗啼风雨。
天也妒，未信与，莺儿燕子俱黄土。
千秋万古，为留待骚人，狂歌痛饮，来访雁丘处。
e: I ask the world: what is this thing called love,
That makes two souls vow to live and die as one?
North and south, through all the sky, two wanderers on the wing —
How many winters and summers have their old wings flown?
The joy of being together,
The pain of being apart —
And among them, one more lovesick than us all.
You must have something to say:
Across ten thousand li of clouds,
A thousand peaks of evening snow —
To whom will your lone shadow go, alone?
Along the road by the Fen River,
The flutes and drums of long ago are silent;
The wild mist lies as ever on the plain.
To call your soul with songs of Chu — what good would sighing do?
The mountain spirits weep in secret in the wind and rain.
Heaven itself is jealous —
I don't believe that you,
Like orioles and swallows, will just turn to yellow dust in vain.
For a thousand autumns, ten thousand years,
You'll wait here for the poets,
Who'll sing wild songs and drink deep,
And come to visit the Goose Mound again.
poems.n: In 1205 the sixteen-year-old Yuan Haowen, on his way to the examinations, met a hunter who had caught a wild goose; its mate, which had escaped, circled crying and then dashed itself to death on the ground. Yuan bought both birds, buried them by the Fen River, and called the grave "Goose Mound". 问世间，情是何物，直教生死相许 — "I ask the world: what is love, that it makes two vow to live and die together?" — became the most famous line about love in Chinese, quoted endlessly (not least in Jin Yong's martial-arts novels).

poems.s: dusk autumn sun cottage crows geese hills river leaves chrysanthemum
z: 孤村落日残霞，轻烟老树寒鸦，一点飞鸿影下。
青山绿水，白草红叶黄花。
e: A lonely village, setting sun, the last of the rosy cloud;
Light mist, an old tree, cold crows;
A single wild goose's shadow, flying low.
Green hills, green water;
White grass, red leaves, and yellow flowers aglow.
poems.n: Written to the same tune as Ma Zhiyuan's song, but with the opposite mood: the first half is the usual bleak autumn; the second bursts into five colours — green, green, white, red, yellow — and autumn becomes beautiful.

poems.s: day willow river hills tower person
z: 自送别，心难舍，一点相思几时绝？
凭阑袖拂杨花雪。溪又斜，山又遮，人去也。
e: Since I saw you off,
My heart can't let you go;
This thread of longing — when will it ever end?
I lean on the rail and brush away the willow-down's snow.
The stream curves round,
The hills cut off the view —
And you're gone, out of sight, I know.
poems.n: A woman watches her beloved leave until the winding stream and the hills hide him from view. Plain, colloquial and piercing — the spirit of the Yuan *sanqu*.

poems.s: dusk autumn sun crows bridge river cottage horse rider
z: 枯藤老树昏鸦，小桥流水人家，古道西风瘦马。
夕阳西下，断肠人在天涯。
e: Withered vines, old trees, crows at dusk;
A little bridge, a flowing stream, a home;
An ancient road, the west wind, a bony horse.
The setting sun goes down in the west —
A heartbroken man at the world's end, alone.
poems.n: The most famous *sanqu* song of all: twenty-eight characters, mostly bare nouns — nine images in the first three lines, and hardly a verb in the whole poem. Wang Guowei said it equalled the best Tang quatrains. The cosy home by the little bridge makes the homeless traveller lonelier still.

poems.te: Duanzheng Hao (Blue Clouds Above) — from The Western Chamber
poems.s: dawn autumn maple geese clouds chrysanthemum pavilion two
z: 碧云天，黄花地，西风紧，北雁南飞。
晓来谁染霜林醉？总是离人泪。
e: Blue clouds above, yellow flowers on the ground,
The west wind blowing hard, the wild geese flying south.
Who dyed the frosted woods so drunken-red at dawn?
It's all the tears of those who part, I've found.
poems.n: From *The Romance of the Western Chamber*: Cui Yingying sees off her lover Zhang Junrui as he leaves for the capital examinations. It borrows Fan Zhongyan's "blue clouds in the sky, yellow leaves on the ground", and its conceit — that the red autumn maples were dyed by the lovers' tears — is the most famous line in Chinese drama.

poems.te: Sheep on the Hillside: Thinking of the Past at Tong Pass
poems.s: dusk mountains peaks river fort
z: 峰峦如聚，波涛如怒，山河表里潼关路。
望西都，意踌躇。
伤心秦汉经行处，宫阙万间都做了土。
兴，百姓苦；亡，百姓苦。
e: The peaks and ridges crowd as if they'd gathered here;
The waves and torrents roar as if in rage;
Mountain and river, fold on fold, guard the Tong Pass road.
I gaze toward the western capital,
Lost in thought, I stand and wonder.
It grieves me, where the Qin and Han once passed:
Ten thousand palace halls have turned to dust.
Kingdoms rise — the people suffer;
Kingdoms fall — the people suffer.
poems.n: In 1329 the sixty-year-old Zhang Yanghao came out of retirement to bring famine relief to Shaanxi, and died there of exhaustion within months. Passing Tong Pass, the gateway to the old capitals of Qin and Han, he wrote songs on history. The ending — 兴，百姓苦；亡，百姓苦, "rise: the people suffer; fall: the people suffer" — is the most famous verdict on Chinese history ever written.

poems.s: winter plum lake cottage
z: 吾家洗砚池头树，个个花开淡墨痕。
不要人夸好颜色，只留清气满乾坤。
e: The tree that grows beside my ink-stained pond
Has every blossom tinged with ink's pale trace.
It doesn't need the world to praise its colour —
It only means to fill the earth and sky with purity and grace.
poems.n: Wang Mian, the self-taught master of ink plum painting, inscribed this on one of his paintings. The ink-washing pond recalls the calligrapher Wang Xizhi, whose pond turned black from rinsing brushes. Plum blossom painted in ink has no bright colour to win praise — only the "pure spirit" (清气) of integrity, like the painter who refused every offer of office.

poems.s: night spring moon candle window person
z: 平生不会相思，才会相思，便害相思。
身似浮云，心如飞絮，气若游丝。
空一缕余香在此，盼千金游子何之。
证候来时，正是何时？灯半昏时，月半明时。
e: All my life I never knew what lovesickness could be;
Just learning lovesickness,
I'm sick with lovesickness, you see.
My body's like a floating cloud,
My heart like drifting down,
My breath as thin as gossamer, and free.
A wisp of lingering fragrance still is here;
The one I long for, far away — where can he be?
When does the sickness strike?
When the lamp is half dim,
When the moon's half bright, and shines on me.
poems.n: A girl's first love, in a song that plays on 相思, "lovesickness", three times in a row. Every symptom is described with comic precision — body like a cloud, heart like a catkin, breath like a silk thread — and the attack comes late at night, when lamp and moon are both half-bright.

poems.s: day mountains smoke cottage
z: 千锤万凿出深山，烈火焚烧若等闲。
粉骨碎身浑不怕，要留清白在人间。
e: A thousand hammers, ten thousand chisels dig it from the mountain deep;
It treats the raging fires of the kiln as nothing much at all.
Though its bones are crushed and its body ground to dust, it does not fear,
If only it can leave its spotless whiteness in the world for all.
poems.n: Said to have been written by Yu Qian at seventeen, watching lime being made: quarried, burned in a kiln, slaked to powder — and finally used to whitewash walls. It became his creed. He saved Beijing from the Mongols in 1449, and was executed on false charges in 1457, leaving his "pure whiteness" behind.

poems.s: dusk sun river person
z: 明日复明日，明日何其多。
我生待明日，万事成蹉跎。
世人若被明日累，春去秋来老将至。
朝看水东流，暮看日西坠。
百年明日能几何？请君听我明日歌。
e: Tomorrow and tomorrow — so many tomorrows ahead!
If I keep waiting for tomorrow, nothing will be done.
If the world's people are tied to tomorrow's thread,
Spring goes, autumn comes, and old age has begun.
At dawn I watch the water flowing east;
At dusk I watch the sun sink in the west.
A hundred years — how many tomorrows, at the least?
I beg you, hear my Song of Tomorrow, and do your best.
poems.n: The Ming scholar Qian Fu's warning against putting things off — "tomorrow, and tomorrow, and tomorrow" — is taught to every Chinese schoolchild. Several versions exist; this is the common one.

poems.te: Song of the Peach Blossom Hut
poems.s: spring peach cottage petals person jar
z: 桃花坞里桃花庵，桃花庵里桃花仙。
桃花仙人种桃树，又摘桃花换酒钱。
酒醒只在花前坐，酒醉还来花下眠。
半醒半醉日复日，花落花开年复年。
但愿老死花酒间，不愿鞠躬车马前。
车尘马足富者趣，酒盏花枝贫者缘。
若将富贵比贫贱，一在平地一在天。
若将贫贱比车马，他得驱驰我得闲。
别人笑我太疯癫，我笑他人看不穿。
不见五陵豪杰墓，无花无酒锄作田。
e: In Peach Blossom Dock there stands a Peach Blossom Hut;
In the Peach Blossom Hut lives a Peach Blossom Immortal, no less.
The Peach Blossom Immortal plants peach trees, and then
Picks peach blossoms to sell, to pay for his wine, I confess.
When I'm sober, I sit in front of the flowers;
When I'm drunk, I come back and sleep beneath them, too.
Half sober, half drunk, day after day;
The flowers fall and bloom, year after year, anew.
I'd rather grow old and die among flowers and wine
Than bow before the carriages and horses of the great.
Carriage dust and horses' hooves — that's the rich man's fun;
A wine cup and a flower spray — that's the poor man's fate.
If you compare the rich and noble with the poor,
One's on the ground, the other's in the sky;
But if you compare the poor with those in carriages,
They get the rushing about — the leisure's mine, say I.
Others laugh at me for being far too mad;
I laugh at them for never seeing through.
Don't you see the tombs of the great lords of the Five Tombs? —
No flowers, no wine: they've all been ploughed to fields, too.
poems.n: Tang Yin (Tang Bohu), the legendary Suzhou painter, barred from office for life by an examination scandal, built a "Peach Blossom Hut" in Suzhou and lived on his paintings and his wine. Repeating "peach blossom" like a folk song, he mocks the rich and powerful, whose grand tombs end up ploughed into farmland. "Others laugh at me for being mad; I laugh at them for not seeing through" is still quoted.

poems.te: The Mountain Study Where the Moon Is Hidden
poems.s: night moon mountains cottage
z: 山近月远觉月小，便道此山大于月。
若人有眼大如天，当见山高月更阔。
e: The hill is near, the moon is far — so the moon looks small,
And people say the hill is bigger than the moon.
But one whose eyes were wide as the whole sky
Would see the hill is high — but the moon is wider than them all.
poems.n: Written by Wang Yangming at eleven, in a study where a hill hid the moon. A child's observation of perspective becomes a philosopher's lesson: our judgements depend on where we stand, and a wider view changes everything.

poems.t: 临江仙（滚滚长江东逝水）
poems.te: Immortal by the River (On and On the Long River Flows)
poems.s: dusk sun river mountains fisher boat two
z: 滚滚长江东逝水，浪花淘尽英雄。
是非成败转头空。青山依旧在，几度夕阳红。
白发渔樵江渚上，惯看秋月春风。
一壶浊酒喜相逢。古今多少事，都付笑谈中。
e: On and on, the Long River rolls away to the east;
Its waves have washed away the heroes, every one.
Right and wrong, success and failure — turn your head, all gone;
The green hills still stand as they did;
How many times has the sunset blazed red, and done?
White-haired fishermen and woodsmen on the river isles
Have watched the autumn moons and spring winds come and go.
Over a jug of cloudy wine, they're glad to meet;
Of all the things of past and present, high and low —
They leave them all to laughter and to talk, you know.
poems.n: Written by Yang Shen in exile in Yunnan, as part of a long ballad of Chinese history. Three centuries later it was chosen to open the novel *Romance of the Three Kingdoms*, and as the theme song of the 1994 television series it became known to every Chinese person. All the heroes' rivalries end as stories over wine for old fishermen.

poems.s: night stars sea cottage person
z: 小筑暂高枕，忧时旧有盟。
呼樽来揖客，挥麈坐谈兵。
云护牙签满，星含宝剑横。
封侯非我意，但愿海波平。
e: In my small house I rest a while, my pillow high;
To share the nation's cares is an oath I swore long ago.
I call for wine to greet my guests,
And, waving my whisk, sit discussing war and foe.
The clouds guard shelves of ivory-tagged books;
The starlight gleams on the sword laid crosswise there.
To be made a lord is not my wish —
I only pray the waves of the sea be calm and fair.
poems.n: Qi Jiguang was the Ming general who drove the *wokou* pirates from China's south-east coast in the 1550s and 1560s. 封侯非我意，但愿海波平 — "to be made a lord is not my wish; I only hope the sea's waves are calm" — expresses the soldier's true aim: not glory, but peace.

poems.t: 皂罗袍（原来姹紫嫣红开遍）
poems.te: Black Silk Robe (So All the Gorgeous Flowers Have Bloomed) — from The Peony Pavilion
poems.s: spring flowers palace pavilion rain boat
z: 原来姹紫嫣红开遍，似这般都付与断井颓垣。
良辰美景奈何天，赏心乐事谁家院？
朝飞暮卷，云霞翠轩；雨丝风片，烟波画船——锦屏人忒看的这韶光贱！
e: So all the gorgeous purples and the reds have bloomed —
And all of them abandoned to the broken well and ruined wall!
A lovely day, a lovely scene — but what's heaven's will?
Who has the joy and pleasure of this garden, after all?
Flying at dawn, furled at dusk —
Rosy clouds round the green pavilion;
Silk threads of rain, a wind in flakes,
The misty waves, the painted boat —
The girl behind her brocade screen has held this spring too cheap, and small!
poems.n: The most famous aria of Kun opera, from Tang Xianzu's *The Peony Pavilion* (1598). Sixteen-year-old Du Liniang, kept indoors all her life, steps into her family's neglected garden for the first time and discovers the full glory of spring — wasted on broken walls, and on her. She goes on to dream of a young scholar, die of love, and return to life.

poems.t: 木兰花·拟古决绝词柬友
poems.te: Magnolia: A Farewell in the Old Style, for a Friend
poems.s: night autumn moon palace window
z: 人生若只如初见，何事秋风悲画扇。
等闲变却故人心，却道故人心易变。
骊山语罢清宵半，泪雨霖铃终不怨。
何如薄幸锦衣郎，比翼连枝当日愿。
e: If life could always be as when we first met,
Why would the autumn wind make the painted fan grieve?
You changed your heart so easily, without regret,
And say it's hearts of old friends that are quick to leave.
At midnight on Mount Li their whispered vows were made;
Though tears fell like the rain and bells, she did not blame.
You can't compare with that faithless lord in brocade —
At least he swore "wing to wing, branches joined", all the same.
poems.n: Nalan Xingde's most famous line opens the lyric: 人生若只如初见 — "if only life could always be like our first meeting". The autumn fan recalls Lady Ban, discarded like a fan when summer ends; the second stanza recalls Emperor Xuanzong and Consort Yang, who vowed eternal love on Mount Li, and the "bells in the rain" the emperor heard after her death. Written "in the style of an old poem of final farewell", it may be about a lover — or a friend.

poems.s: night winter snow wind mountains fort lantern
z: 山一程，水一程，身向榆关那畔行，夜深千帐灯。
风一更，雪一更，聒碎乡心梦不成，故园无此声。
e: A stretch of hills, a stretch of streams;
We march toward the far side of Yuguan Pass;
Deep in the night, a thousand tents' lamps gleam.
A watch of wind, a watch of snow;
Their din breaks my homesick heart — I cannot dream;
At home there was no sound like this, I know.
poems.n: 1682: Nalan Xingde, an imperial bodyguard, accompanied the Kangxi Emperor beyond Shanhai Pass to the ancestral tombs in Manchuria. The plain repetitions march like the journey itself; "late at night, the lamps of a thousand tents" is one of the grandest images in the *ci* — and the homesick young man inside one of those tents cannot sleep.

poems.t: 浣溪沙（谁念西风独自凉）
poems.te: Washing Silk in the Stream (Who Cares That I'm Cold in the West Wind?)
poems.s: dusk autumn sun leaves window wind person
z: 谁念西风独自凉，萧萧黄叶闭疏窗，沉思往事立残阳。
被酒莫惊春睡重，赌书消得泼茶香，当时只道是寻常。
e: Who cares that I'm alone and cold in the west wind?
The yellow leaves rustle; I close the lattice tight;
Lost in memories, I stand there in the fading light.
When I was drunk, she let me sleep in spring, and didn't wake me;
We'd bet on books, and laugh, and spill the fragrant tea —
At the time, it all just seemed so ordinary.
poems.n: An elegy for Nalan Xingde's wife, Lu Shi, who died in 1677 after three years of marriage. The memories are tiny: she let him sleep off his wine; they played the game Li Qingzhao and her husband once played — betting on which page of which book a quotation came from — and laughed till they spilled the tea. The last line, 当时只道是寻常, "at the time, we thought it all so ordinary", is one of the most heartbreaking in Chinese.

poems.t: 蝶恋花（辛苦最怜天上月）
poems.te: Butterflies Love Flowers (How I Pity the Toiling Moon)
poems.s: night moon window swallows butterfly flowers
z: 辛苦最怜天上月，一昔如环，昔昔都成玦。
若似月轮终皎洁，不辞冰雪为卿热。
无那尘缘容易绝，燕子依然，软踏帘钩说。
唱罢秋坟愁未歇，春丛认取双栖蝶。
e: How I pity the toiling moon up in the sky:
Full as a ring for just one night,
And every other night a broken jade.
If only you'd stay round like the moon, forever bright,
I'd gladly brave the ice and snow to keep you warm, unafraid.
But earthly bonds are broken all too soon;
The swallows, as they always do,
Tread lightly on the curtain hook and chatter.
I sing the autumn graveside songs, but grief has not passed;
Among spring's flowers I'll find two butterflies — and know they're us at last.
poems.n: Another elegy for his wife. The moon is full only one night a month — like their brief happiness. "I'd warm you through ice and snow" recalls Xun Can, who, when his wife had a fever in winter, stood out in the cold and then lay against her to cool her. The ending recalls the Butterfly Lovers, Liang Shanbo and Zhu Yingtai, who became a pair of butterflies after death.

poems.t: 画堂春（一生一代一双人）
poems.te: Spring in the Painted Hall (One Life, One Pair)
poems.s: spring river bridge moon person
z: 一生一代一双人，争教两处销魂。
相思相望不相亲，天为谁春？
浆向蓝桥易乞，药成碧海难奔。
若容相访饮牛津，相对忘贫。
e: One life, one lifetime, one pair made to be —
Why must we break our hearts, apart, in two places?
We long for each other, we gaze, but can't be close —
For whom does heaven send its springtime graces?
Begging a drink at Blue Bridge would be easy;
But even with the elixir, I can't fly to the moon above.
If I could cross to the Ford of the Drinking Ox,
We'd face each other, poor, and forget it all for love.
poems.n: A love made for a lifetime but kept apart — perhaps Nalan's first love, said to have been taken into the palace. Pei Hang won a fairy bride at Blue Bridge by begging a drink of water; Chang'e flew to the moon with the elixir and could never return; the Herdboy and the Weaver Girl meet only once a year at the Ford of the Drinking Ox. If only he could reach her, poverty would mean nothing.

poems.s: day bamboo mountains wind
z: 咬定青山不放松，立根原在破岩中。
千磨万击还坚劲，任尔东西南北风。
e: It bites into the green hill, and won't let go;
Its roots are planted in a crack of broken stone.
Ground down a thousand times, struck ten thousand, it stays strong —
Blow, winds, from east or west, from south or north — blow on!
poems.n: Inscribed by Zheng Banqiao on a painting of bamboo growing out of rock. The bamboo, rooted in a crevice and unbowed by any wind, is a character no pressure can bend — one of the most quoted poems of integrity in Chinese.

poems.t: 潍县署中画竹呈年伯包大中丞括
poems.te: Painting Bamboo at the Weixian Yamen, for Governor Bao
poems.s: night bamboo window cottage person wind
z: 衙斋卧听萧萧竹，疑是民间疾苦声。
些小吾曹州县吏，一枝一叶总关情。
e: Lying in my study, I hear the bamboo's whispering sound,
And wonder if it's the people's suffering crying out.
We're only small officials of a county or a town —
But every branch and every leaf is what we care about.
poems.n: Written in 1746, when Zheng Banqiao was magistrate of Weixian (Shandong) during a famine. He opened the granaries without waiting for permission, and was later dismissed. He painted bamboo and sent it with this poem to the provincial governor: even a minor official must feel every leaf of the people's suffering.

poems.te: On The Story of the Stone
poems.s: night candle window person
z: 满纸荒唐言，一把辛酸泪。
都云作者痴，谁解其中味？
e: Pages and pages of absurd words,
A handful of bitter tears.
They all say the author is a fool —
But who has tasted what's within, through all these years?
poems.n: The verse Cao Xueqin set at the opening of *Dream of the Red Chamber* (also called *The Story of the Stone*), the greatest Chinese novel, written in poverty over ten years after the ruin of his family. The "absurd words" are the novel's dreamlike fiction; the "bitter tears", its truth.

poems.s: summer pine fields person
z: 牧童骑黄牛，歌声振林樾。
意欲捕鸣蝉，忽然闭口立。
e: A herd-boy rides upon a yellow ox;
His song rings out and shakes the woodland shade.
He wants to catch a singing cicada —
He suddenly shuts his mouth and stands, not a sound made.
poems.n: A child in a split second: loud singing, then frozen silence as he spots a cicada. Yuan Mei championed poetry of "natural spirit" (性灵) — fresh, spontaneous, true to life — and this is a perfect example.

poems.s: spring grass flowers cottage
z: 白日不到处，青春恰自来。
苔花如米小，也学牡丹开。
e: Where the bright sun never reaches, in the shade,
The green of spring arrives all on its own.
Moss flowers, tiny as grains of rice,
Learn to blossom too, like peonies full-grown.
poems.n: Even the humblest life, in places the sun never reaches, has its own spring and its own flowering. Neglected for two centuries, the poem became famous in 2018 when a village teacher and his pupils sang it on Chinese television, moving the whole country.

poems.s: day mountains river person
z: 李杜诗篇万口传，至今已觉不新鲜。
江山代有才人出，各领风骚数百年。
e: Li Bai's and Du Fu's poems are on ten thousand tongues;
By now they've come to feel a little stale.
In every age the land brings forth new talents,
Each to lead poetry a few centuries — that's the tale.
poems.n: A bold claim for originality: even the greatest models grow stale through imitation, and every age must find its own voice. 江山代有才人出，各领风骚数百年 — "every age brings forth its own talents, each to lead for a few hundred years" — is quoted whenever a new generation rises.

poems.s: night candle person cottage
z: 仙佛茫茫两未成，只知独夜不平鸣。
风蓬飘尽悲歌气，泥絮沾来薄幸名。
十有九人堪白眼，百无一用是书生。
莫因诗卷愁成谶，春鸟秋虫自作声。
e: To be an immortal or a Buddha — I've failed at both, it seems;
I only know, alone at night, to cry out at the world's wrong.
Like windblown tumbleweed, my mournful songs have spent their force;
Like catkins in the mud, I've earned a heartless name, so long.
Nine people out of ten deserve the whites of my eyes;
Of all the useless things, a scholar is the worst.
Don't fear my book of poems will prove a sad prophecy —
The spring birds and autumn insects simply sing because they must.
poems.n: Huang Jingren, a gifted, impoverished poet who died at thirty-four. 十有九人堪白眼，百无一用是书生 — "nine in ten deserve the whites of my eyes; of all things, a scholar is the most useless" — is still the classic bitter joke of frustrated intellectuals. The "whites of the eyes" are Ruan Ji's look of contempt.

poems.s: night stars flowers wall person
z: 几回花下坐吹箫，银汉红墙入望遥。
似此星辰非昨夜，为谁风露立中宵。
缠绵思尽抽残茧，宛转心伤剥后蕉。
三五年时三五月，可怜杯酒不曾消。
e: How many times beneath the flowers I sat and played the flute,
Gazing at the Milky Way, the red wall far away.
Like stars tonight that are not last night's stars —
For whom do I stand in wind and dew at midnight, till the day?
My lingering love is drawn out, like the last silk from a cocoon;
My heart is wounded like a plantain stripped, layer by layer, in decay.
At fifteen, in the fifteenth night's full moon —
Alas, no cup of wine has ever washed that pain away.
poems.n: The fifteenth of sixteen poems remembering a first love — a girl he met at fifteen and lost. 似此星辰非昨夜，为谁风露立中宵 — "these stars are not last night's stars; for whom do I stand at midnight in the wind and dew?" — answers Li Shangyin's "last night's stars, last night's wind", and is one of the most quoted lines of longing in Chinese.

poems.t: 赴戍登程口占示家人（其二）
poems.te: Setting Out for Exile: Lines for My Family (II)
poems.s: day rider horse mountains desert
z: 力微任重久神疲，再竭衰庸定不支。
苟利国家生死以，岂因祸福避趋之？
谪居正是君恩厚，养拙刚于戍卒宜。
戏与山妻谈故事，试吟断送老头皮。
e: My strength is small, my task was great; I'm long worn out and spent;
To strain my poor old talents more would surely see me fall.
If it will serve my country, I'll give my life or death to it —
Should I chase luck or flee misfortune? Not at all!
My banishment is surely proof of my lord's great grace;
To nurse my clumsiness, a soldier's post is just my place.
In jest I tell my wife the tale of long ago,
And chant the line, "There goes the old man's head!" — with a smile on my face.
poems.n: In 1842 Lin Zexu, who had destroyed the British opium at Humen, was made the scapegoat for the Opium War and exiled to Xinjiang. Taking leave of his family, he wrote 苟利国家生死以，岂因祸福避趋之 — "if it serves the country, I will give my life or death; how could I seek fortune or flee disaster?" — the most quoted line of public duty in modern China. The ending is a joke: a Song recluse summoned to court was sent off by his wife with a verse, "this time there goes the old man's head".

poems.s: dusk spring sun petals rider flowers
z: 浩荡离愁白日斜，吟鞭东指即天涯。
落红不是无情物，化作春泥更护花。
e: Vast as the sea, my sorrow at parting; the sun is slanting low;
I point my whip east, chanting — and the world's end lies ahead.
But fallen petals are not heartless things, you know:
They turn to mud in spring, to feed the flowers in their bed.
poems.n: 1839: Gong Zizhen resigns from office in Beijing and heads home to the south. He compares himself to a fallen petal — no longer on the branch, but still devoted. 落红不是无情物，化作春泥更护花 is now quoted in praise of teachers and anyone who quietly serves the next generation.

poems.s: day clouds wind horse mountains
z: 九州生气恃风雷，万马齐喑究可哀。
我劝天公重抖擞，不拘一格降人才。
e: The Nine Provinces need wind and thunder to come alive;
Ten thousand horses standing mute — how sad to see!
I urge the Lord of Heaven to rouse himself once more,
And send down talents of every kind, unbound and free.
poems.n: Written as the Qing empire stagnated on the eve of the Opium War. "Ten thousand horses all mute" is a silenced, conformist officialdom; China needs "wind and thunder" — great change — and talents chosen "not in one mould" (不拘一格). The last line is now a slogan for open-minded recruitment.

poems.s: spring willow oriole grass fields person two
z: 草长莺飞二月天，拂堤杨柳醉春烟。
儿童散学归来早，忙趁东风放纸鸢。
e: The grass grows tall, the orioles fly, in the second month of spring;
The willows brush the dyke, and, drunk with spring's soft mist, they sway.
The children have come home from school early today,
To fly their paper kites in the east wind while they may.
poems.n: The happiest poem of the late Qing: early spring in the countryside, willows "drunk" in the misty air, and children running home to fly kites. Every Chinese child learns it — often while flying a kite.

poems.s: day wall person sun clouds
z: 望门投止思张俭，忍死须臾待杜根。
我自横刀向天笑，去留肝胆两昆仑。
e: Like Zhang Jian, may my friends find shelter at any door;
Like Du Gen, may they bear death a while, until the time is right.
As for me, I'll hold my sword and laugh at heaven —
The ones who flee, the one who stays: two Kunlun peaks of might.
poems.n: Written on his prison wall in 1898, after the Empress Dowager Cixi crushed the Hundred Days' Reform. Tan Sitong refused to flee: "No country has ever been reformed without bloodshed; let it begin with me." Zhang Jian and Du Gen were Han loyalists who survived persecution — he wishes his escaping comrades the same luck. Those who flee to carry on the struggle and the one who stays to die are "two Kunlun mountains" of equal courage. He was executed days later, aged thirty-three.

poems.s: day sea person cup
z: 不惜千金买宝刀，貂裘换酒也堪豪。
一腔热血勤珍重，洒去犹能化碧涛。
e: I'll spend a thousand gold without a care to buy a sword;
To trade my sable coat for wine is gallant, too.
This chestful of hot blood — I'll guard it, treasure it;
For spilled, it still can turn to jade-green waves anew.
poems.n: Qiu Jin, revolutionary and feminist, left an arranged marriage to study in Japan and plot against the Qing. Blood "turning to green jade" recalls Chang Hong, a loyal Zhou official whose spilled blood became green jade three years after his unjust death. She was beheaded in 1907, aged thirty-one.

poems.t: 蝶恋花（阅尽天涯离别苦）
poems.te: Butterflies Love Flowers (I've Seen All the Pain of Parting)
poems.s: dusk spring petals window candle two
z: 阅尽天涯离别苦，不道归来，零落花如许。
花底相看无一语，绿窗春与天俱莫。
待把相思灯下诉，一缕新欢，旧恨千千缕。
最是人间留不住，朱颜辞镜花辞树。
e: I've seen all the pain of parting at the ends of the earth —
But never thought, on coming home,
To find the flowers fallen, all this way.
Beneath the flowers we gaze at each other, wordless;
At the green window, spring and the light both fade away.
I'd tell her all my longing by the lamp —
A single thread of new joy,
A thousand threads of old pain, grey.
What this world can least keep, most of all:
Young faces leaving the mirror; flowers leaving the spray.
poems.n: Wang Guowei — whose "three stages" of achievement appear in several notes on this site — comes home after long travels to find his wife aged and the spring gone. 最是人间留不住，朱颜辞镜花辞树 — "what the world can least keep: rosy youth leaving the mirror, blossoms leaving the tree" — is the most quoted line of his own lyrics.
